### Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

Containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with a number of manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; supplied with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, and also with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture and in which places of their works they did so.

An exceedingly accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others when the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time gathers together in our library six hundred fragments, minor works, and booklets previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## The Complete Works of St. Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon

After the recension of the monks of the Order of St. Benedict from the Congregation of St. Maur, and above all that of Jean Martianay of this Order; again corrected against Roman, Ambrosian, Veronese, and many other manuscripts, as well as against all French and foreign editions; augmented by very many monuments previously entirely unpublished, and by other labors of the holy Doctor previously disseminated only in separate publications; elucidated by innumerable notes, observations, and corrections; through the study and labor of Vallarsi and Maffei, presbyters of Verona, with other learned men in that same city contributing their assistance.

The latest Paris edition, based on the second edition, has been so revised by the later efforts of the Veronese editors and so enriched by more recently discovered materials that the present edition, by its extent alone and leaving aside all other corrections, materially surpasses all preceding editions, even the Benedictine ones, by one third, or a third part. Prepared and finally revised by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Jerome

[Column 0009]

## Preface

The works contained in this, the tenth volume of Jerome’s writings, are those which Jerome translated from the Greek text of the sacred codex into Latin, with the exception of one or two short books, after the Hebrew canon had long since been completed. The series of our recension—or, more accurately, the kind of Jerome’s interpretation derived from the second source of Scripture—seemed to demand this place and arrangement for itself. This volume is divided into two parts: one contains the not very numerous remnants of the Old Testament that survived the great shipwreck; the other embraces the whole of the New Testament. Both are derived from the Greek, except that the former reproduces an ἀπόγραφον (*apographon*, a copy), while the latter reproduces the original and archetypal text. In order that you may properly understand this, the matter must, as is customary, be explained in greater detail, and the subject must be reviewed somewhat further back before you begin to read.

Jerome, than whom no one since the human race began ever excelled more greatly in knowledge of the divine Scriptures, and no one devoted more diligence and industry to acquiring it, first tested his talents and learning by bringing the Latin version of his own time—which teemed with defects, whether through the fault of translators or of scribes—into conformity with and correcting it according to the native text of the Septuagint. He opened the way for so great an undertaking with that recension of the Psalms, almost, I would say, improvised, which, as he himself says, while stationed at Rome with Damasus, he prepared hastily and only to a considerable extent.

Perhaps he was not then using any other Greek edition than the one that was at hand and was called the Κοινὴ (*Koinē*, “Common”), because it was in general use. Certainly the work itself makes it clear that the Hexaplar edition of Origen, marked with asterisks, was not even employed in the undertaking. Yet since this first attempt turned out well and was approved especially by the support of the Roman Church—for it is still called the Roman Psalter—he applied his mind to refashioning that entire version from the beginning according to the Greek, and specifically according to the much more carefully corrected Hexaplar text.

Nor does it seem at all doubtful that, having carried out his plan in each individual part, he polished the entire Old Testament canon by that continuous comparison with the archetype. Nevertheless, although only two books now survive complete from that recension, Job and the Psalter, together with two prologues to the books of Solomon and to Chronicles—which make us all the more regret the loss of the work—if that labor had survived through the ages, we would possess a treasure of sacred learning of incalculable value. From it we could often restore the Hexaplar edition itself, and, with the aid of asterisks and obeli, the remains of the Old Latin version; and we could easily distinguish the interpreter’s meaning and intention in the most corrupt passages.

Those who eagerly desire to investigate the sacred Scriptures according to the mind of the ancients and by reference to the original books readily perceive how great these things are. Now, since we have been permitted to enjoy only that small portion, we ought to embrace it with all the greater care and zeal, so that in preparing its edition we may contribute every possible effort.

There have nevertheless been, and formerly were, other learned critics, among them Serarius in his *Prolegomena*, who are so far from regretting this loss that they rather maintain that Jerome revised according to the Greek no books other than those mentioned above. For a long time Martianay, too, regarded this opinion as uncertain. We, however, contend that all their arguments have no force, and that St. Jerome himself bears witness in favor of the position we hold.

They say that Jerome mentions only these books by name against Rufinus, when he was defending this translation of his according to the Septuagint against Rufinus’s accusations; that, moreover, when he speaks of these books, he never mentions others in the prefaces to the same books translated from the Hebrew; and finally, that although prefaces survive to the lost books of Solomon and Chronicles from that recension, no such prefaces survive for any others, nor can a plausible reason be offered why the antiquarians who preserved those prefaces among their collection would have omitted others, if they had existed.

They add that none of the ancient writers ever knew of any others besides those mentioned. But St. Augustine, in Epistle 104 among the Hieronymian letters, which concerns the year 403, when he had seen the translation of Job, was so far from supposing that the holy Doctor was the author of a complete revision of the Latin version that he did not even conjecture that Jerome had restored the whole of it, in the same manner, [Column 0011] with obelis and asterisks, to the ancient truth according to the Greek exemplar.

These arguments are sound in appearance, but they possess only the force of what is called a negative argument, and the history of the facts completely destroys them. Jerome praises only the six books which they say he mentions by name as corrected by his own labor against Rufinus—not because he had not devoted the same labor to others, but because, as he himself says elsewhere, he had allowed only those six to be published for the honor of the edition.

Nor could he defend his reliability on behalf of books that had not appeared publicly. Nor was there any reason for him to mention the others individually in the prefaces to the translations from the Hebrew, since they were kept locked away in a cabinet within his private quarters and could not be consulted by a reader as evidence of the matter.

Moreover, by that time many things had perhaps already been compiled by someone unknown. This is the very complaint made by the holy Interpreter in Letter 134 to Augustine, at the end: “I cannot obey your instructions, especially concerning the edition of the Septuagint, which is marked with asterisks and spits; for most of the earlier labor has been lost through the fraud of someone or other.” Thus it was not in his interest to mention piecemeal those labors of which he himself had already been deprived.

It is highly favorable to our position that, in addition to the portions that were then commonly available and that still survive, he calls the remainder “most” of the work; from this very passage one may understand that he had revised the whole edition.

As for the fact that the prefaces with which he was accustomed to fortify each book are lacking, while those that he composed for the lost books of Solomon and Chronicles survive, this is by no means evidence that other books were not corrected. It rather proves what we said: that he did not publish them. The holy Doctor was accustomed to place prefaces before his labors only when, by making them public, he dedicated them to some friend.

Finally, it is false that the ancient writers knew of no books other than those mentioned. St. Augustine himself, in Letter 116 among the Hieronymian letters, says that after previously admiring only Jerome’s version of Job, he was later informed about the revision of the entire canon. He writes to Jerome: “I beg you to send me your translation of the Septuagint, which I did not know you had published.”

Cassiodorus speaks much more clearly. He indicates that he himself had found those very portions that Jerome had lost and restored them to the body of his edition. “The third division,” he says in *Divine Institutes*, chapter 13, “is contained, among other works, in a larger codex written in clearer letters. It has ninety-five quires, and in it the translation of the Septuagint interpreters of the Old Testament is contained in forty-four books. To these are appended twenty-six books of the New Testament; thus there are seventy books in all, in the number of the palms, and so forth. This text, altered by the translation of many persons, was corrected by the diligent care of Father Jerome and left in an established form.”

The context and heading of his chapter plainly prove that the author is speaking of Jerome’s correction of the translation according to the Septuagint interpreters. The editor’s marginal note itself confirms this by stating: “This is called the text of the Septuagint interpreters corrected by blessed Jerome.”

Yet, to conceal nothing even here, I am somewhat uncertain whether Cassiodorus’s praise of Father Jerome’s labor should be referred to a revision of the New Testament alone. Nevertheless, the testimonies of the holy Interpreter himself are stronger than any possible objection. When he says that he corrected the Septuagint edition *simply* (*ἀπλῶς*) from the Greek into Latin and contrasts it with another translation from the Hebrew, it is clear that he means not a few books but the whole canon.

That notable passage occurs in Letter 112 to Augustine, §19:

“You ask why my earlier translation of the canonical books has asterisks and prefixed strokes, and why I later published another translation without these signs. With your permission, I would say that you seem not to understand what you have asked. For that translation is the translation of the Septuagint interpreters; and wherever strokes—that is, obeli—are marked, they signify …”

And shortly afterward:

“I did not so much attempt to abolish the ancient things as to translate into Latin from the Greek, corrected for the speakers of my language, those things which …”

The matter is still clearer in the prologue to the books of Solomon translated from the Hebrew:

“If anyone prefers the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, he has it corrected by us.”

Likewise, in Book II against Rufinus:

“Have I spoken against the Septuagint interpreters, whom many years ago I most diligently corrected and gave to the students of my language?”

And again in Book III, in almost the same words:

“I gave the edition of the Septuagint, most diligently corrected many years ago, to the people of my language.”

The same is found in Letter 71 to Lucinius:

“I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, which many years ago I most diligently corrected and handed over to those eager to learn.”

Finally, to pass over other passages, in Letter 106 to Sunnia and Fretela, where he explains how great the difference is between the Common and the Hexaplar edition, he says:

“But that edition which is contained in the *Hexapla*, and which we translated, is the very one …” [Column 0013]

Therefore he translated not merely those little books which scarcely make up the smallest part of the canon, but the entire edition, as it existed in the Hexapla—or else he restored the Greek to the Latin by comparison.

Yet, as we said, the holy Interpreter himself caused great damage in this matter during his lifetime. As for restoring the books that have long been missing, the matter is virtually hopeless. Certainly neither others, so far as I know, nor I myself have been fortunate enough to find even some portion of them among ancient manuscripts in libraries, although I examined those collections with the greatest diligence possible.

Nevertheless, unless I am deceived, so large a part of that edition survives in the Commentaries of the holy Father himself that nearly all the prophets, certainly the twelve Minor Prophets, and Ecclesiastes, could almost be restored to their original completeness.

I am convinced that the version from the Septuagint which he continually places beneath the corresponding sections of the version from the Hebrew, and which he so often expounds according to another meaning, is that very version which he had revised according to the Greek exemplar—not, as is commonly thought, the Old Latin version in a corrected form.

I recognize what everyone will immediately object: that almost no visible sign of Jerome’s labor is presented there, since most of the marks by which it alone can be identified—the asterisks and obeli—are absent.

Yet I think the matter should be inferred otherwise. From the few such marks that survive here and there, one may conclude that the edition must be regarded as none other than one that proceeded from Jerome’s pen; for no other Latin edition was ever equipped with those signs.

The fact that they occur more rarely than the circumstances would seem to require, especially in the Major Prophets, is explained by the purpose and character of his work. The holy Father did not intend there to publish the text of Scripture, but to expound and elucidate it. Indeed, he wished the Hebrew truth to have the Septuagint serve it—*τοὺς LXX*—and therefore considered it sufficient to note the more important differences of words and meanings either by those signs or, as he does elsewhere, in explicit words, since he preferred to adhere to the Hebrew text as the more genuine one.

Otherwise, the day would fail me if I wished merely to point out word for word the more noteworthy passages in which obeli or asterisks are used. They are more readily encountered in the Commentaries on the Minor Prophets.

Let us therefore seek examples elsewhere, and from Isaiah alone. Chapter 40, verse 1:

“What is added by the Septuagint—‘Priests’—is marked beforehand with an obelus.”

And verse 7:

“This which is marked with asterisks—‘because the spirit of God blew upon it; truly grass is the people; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen’—was added from the Hebrew and from the edition of Theodotion.”

In chapter 45, in the text itself, he marks the words “Renew yourselves to me, islands” with a transverse obelus.

Chapter 51, verse 10:

“The name ‘Jerusalem,’ which has been added here by the Septuagint and is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the three interpreters, must therefore be marked beforehand with an obelus,” and so forth.

And a few verses later:

“But that which is said above, ‘And it shall not fall into corruption, and its bread shall not fail,’ was added from the edition of Theodotion, from the Hebrew.”

In the following chapter:

“In this passage the name ‘Zion’ has been added by the Septuagint, and for that reason it has been marked with the spit [obelus].”

Finally, chapter 55:

“And what follows, ‘and your captives shall be subject to you in it,’ we have marked beforehand with an obelus.”

If these passages represent an edition other than the one corrected by Jerome, let the impartial reader decide.

What more should be said when Jerome marks Latin codices as erroneous, while elsewhere he reads differently—or correctly—in the passage under discussion? At the beginning of Jeremiah 31 he says:

“Ridiculously, the Latin codices in this passage, because of the ambiguity of the Greek word, have interpreted *lupinos* [lupins] instead of *calidum* [hot].”

Yet in the Septuagint version that he himself sets forth he had preferred *calidum*. Therefore he praises not the recension of the Old Latin version that was commonly in circulation and that incorrectly had *lupinos*, but the recension that he himself had prepared. Similar examples can often be encountered elsewhere.

Now, what the method of his labor was, and whether that work should properly be called a translation or, as seems to us, a recension, each person can judge for himself from what has been said, and much more correctly from the surviving monuments themselves.

When the holy Father says in the Letter to Sunnia and Fretela cited above that he translated the edition contained in the *Hexapla*—for I do not know whether he uses this verb elsewhere to signify his labor—we should understand him to be referring to the additions made beneath the asterisks, which he also rendered into Latin whenever they were supplied from the Greek Hexaplar text. He also refers to passages in which corruption had extended through several verses and which he provided with a new translation.

But this does not mean that the work should be counted among translations of the kind represented by his version from the Hebrew. It belongs among corrections and revisions, as he himself consistently calls it elsewhere.

Natalis Alexander is mistaken when he says that the surviving books—Job and the Psalter, as well as the three books of Solomon and Chronicles—were newly translated by the holy Father according to the Greek, while he merely corrected the other books that have perished.

It is enough to compare the second correction of the Psalter with the first to establish that neither was adorned with the character and finish of a new translation. [Column 0015]

There are learned men, among them Simon in Book II, chapter 10, who maintain that the words added beneath the asterisks were translated directly from the Hebrew into Latin by the holy Interpreter.

This is true if they are speaking of the book of Chronicles. St. Jerome testifies that in that very recension according to the Septuagint he compared it from beginning to end, as the saying goes, with a teacher of the Law who was held in admiration among the Hebrews. The Greek and Latin codices were so corrupt that the book seemed to contain not so much Hebrew names as a collection of barbarous and Sarmatian ones.

Accordingly, he expressly warned:

“Wherever you see asterisks—that is, stars—shining in this volume, know that there has been added there from the Hebrew what is not found in the Latin codices.”

But this does not appear to have been done in the remaining books, in which the holy Interpreter himself again indicates that he translated the Greek from the edition of Theodotion, just as it had been inserted by Origen into the *Hexapla*.

We shall cite one passage on this matter from Letter 112 to Augustine:

“Wherever there are strokes—that is, obeli—it signifies that the Septuagint has said more than is found in the Hebrew. But wherever there are asterisks—that is, shining little stars—what was added from the edition of Theodotion by Origen is present; and there we translated the Greek.”

The words immediately following these have misled those who hold the contrary opinion:

“Here we have expressed what we understood from the Hebrew itself, preserving sometimes the truth of the meanings rather than the order of the words.”

For these words do not refer, as they think, to the recension according to the Greek; the context of the passage proves that they refer to the other translation without these signs, from the Hebrew, which he had mentioned immediately before in the preceding sentence.

But let us not spend more time contending over testimonies of this kind. Each person will be able to judge the matter for himself by comparing the texts of the two versions against each other.

## A Few Remarks on the Individual Books

Tobit and Judith are the first to appear. They were translated into Latin not from the Greek but from a Hebrew or Chaldaic exemplar. Perhaps enough has already been said about them in the notes to the prologues, and it does not seem worthwhile to repeat that material here.

The first book distinguished by the signs of asterisks and obeli, and properly belonging to this series, is Job. It is scarcely possible to say how many errors—not merely introduced through the fault of scribes but also through that of critics—we have removed from this book.

I may truly say with Jerome:

“Job still lay among the Latins in the dung, and teemed with the worms of error.”

And again:

“Just as everything was restored to him twofold in proof and victory, so I have made him possess in our language—let me speak boldly—what he had lost.”

St. Augustine’s book of *Annotations*, and the recent edition of the Alexandrian codex, provided great assistance in repairing the text and in restoring, to the places marked by the obelus and asterisks, what was missing or incorrectly represented in innumerable passages. I would prefer that you learn these things from reading the work itself rather than suppose that I am asking you to admire our diligence.

The Book of Psalms, which follows, is presented according to the holy Father’s two editions, as was also noted above, in accordance with the Greek. The notes have explained once and again—and many others before us have taught the same thing—why the earlier and less accurate recension is called the Roman Psalter, while the second is called the Gallican Psalter. These names preserve a useful history of the matter.

Yet, following Walton in *Prolegomena* X.5, Natalis Alexander is also mistaken in Question III on the Latin Vulgate, where he supposes that Jerome labored over the Psalter four times, and consequently invents a second correction from the Greek after those two, although it never existed.

Peter Pithoeus errs in the opposite direction in his work on the Latin interpreters of the Bible. He wants our present edition of the Psalms—which, apart from the marks of obeli and asterisks, is entirely the same as the Psalter called Gallican, as will be clearer than daylight to anyone who compares the texts—to be nothing other than the Old Latin version that existed before Jerome, derived from the edition called Lucian’s. He further maintains that Jerome’s only translation from the Greek exemplar is the one presented by the Roman Psalter.

The circumstance that some readings in printed copies of the Vulgate, although rarely, are not approved by Jerome deceived this learned man. Such is the reading at Psalm 5:9:

“Direct my way in your sight,”

instead of which the holy Interpreter orders that it be rewritten:

“In my sight, your way.”

But that reading belongs to the printed codices, not to the manuscripts, which, just as Jerome’s notation indicates, read the better form.

Other examples of the same kind, which seem contrary to Jerome’s judgment, were caused especially by the absence of obeli in the commonly circulated books. Since the obeli are properly placed in the old handwritten codices, they entirely remove the difficulty.

We have been especially fortunate that we have not lacked such codices, of the greatest antiquity and not without excellent correction—above all, the Vatican codex, once belonging to the Queen of the Swedes, which is written almost entirely in what are called uncial letters. You will appreciate how useful these manuscripts have been to us when you come to read the work itself. [Column 0017]

We have also made the so-called Roman Psalter, the other exceedingly ancient recension of the same book, especially rich in places where it differs from Jerome’s version.

We received it from a remarkable manuscript preserved in the library of the chapter at Verona. It is written in what is called square script, reflects approximately the sixth century, and is of the best quality among manuscripts of its kind.

On each facing page it has a Greek text corresponding to the same number of verses of the Latin version, though the Greek text is written not in Greek but in Latin letters. Lest you think this a unique feature of the book, know that I have encountered not a few manuscripts of this kind in the libraries of Italy, and that they were once praised by Luke of Bruges.

But to speak now of the Latin version, which is chiefly relevant to our purpose: unless it is itself the Augustinian recension, it appears for the most part to have been prepared after its model by some learned person, perhaps Cassiodorus.

It is well known that the Bishop of Hippo undertook the correction of the Psalter. He relates this in Letter 261 to Audax, §5, where, after saying that he lacked Jerome’s version from the Hebrew, he adds:

“We did not translate it, but corrected some corruptions of the Latin codices from Greek exemplars. As a result, we may have made it somewhat better than it was, but not such as it ought to have been. For even now, if anything that perhaps escaped us at that time troubles readers, we correct it by collating the codices.”

The Latin version of the Veronese codex agrees almost constantly with Augustine’s reading—not only in those passages where it differs from the other editions of the Psalter, both those that exist now and those that once existed, but also wherever it seems to have a less correct reading than they do.

There are only a few places—more precisely, approximately ten—in which it departs in a different direction. These cannot at all be regarded as readings belonging to the Old Latin edition that were corrected by Augustine. For it is neither likely that the labor of the Bishop of Hippo was confined to so few corrections, nor—and this is the essential point—that he devoted himself only to the latter part of the book. Our manuscript begins to differ from that point onward.

It must therefore be inferred, on the contrary, that the holy Bishop’s diligence did not extend that far in the same measure in which it had extended through the earlier portions, and that those psalms were corrected in those passages by the Veronese editor either according to other exemplars or—what I would rather believe—according to Augustine’s later work. Augustine had noted these later corrections in his own copy after the *Enarrationes* delivered to the people:

“For even now, if anything that perhaps escaped us at that time troubles readers, we correct it by collating the codices.”

Moreover, it seems that our manuscript has in some places reproduced a reading from Augustine’s own *Enarratio*, rather than from the text of the psalm as it was set forth.

The Roman Psalter also often reads more correctly than that earlier correction of Jerome, and it bears the mark of a genuinely learned critical mind.

Can the great Jerome, if the reading in the Veronese codex is older, be thought to have introduced a new and inferior reading in place of the good and generally accepted one? The matter would be different if, while correcting rapidly, he allowed certain readings to remain—perhaps for good reasons—which he would otherwise have judged less satisfactory.

If the version contained in the Veronese codex is the version that existed before the holy Father’s correction, then whoever says that Jerome corrupted the old reading whenever it differs from and is better than his version, rather than correcting it, must be accused of outrageous slander. Such a person would be attributing to that book a record of antiquity so great that it would have to have been drawn from the treasury of Jerome’s own donations.

But in order that you may clearly understand with what blindness—or rather with what complete lack of judgment—someone has commonly forced this version upon us as the Itala, recall the example we often observe in the notes, at Psalm 127:2:

“You shall eat the labors of your hands.”

No one who has read how much difficulty that passage once caused the ancient interpreters, and especially Hilary of Poitiers, could be persuaded to believe that this was the old version before Jerome, and that it was the Itala. The Latin books before Jerome had *labores fructuum* (“the labors of fruits”) in place of *labores manuum* (“the labors of hands”).

The matter would have been settled and straightforward if this interpretation had been known to those writers. Nor was there any reason for that distinguished bishop, after offering various opinions, to approach the passage from another direction and, as Jerome reports in Letter 34 of our recension, to Marcella, assert that the meaning stands better if one writes “to eat a fruit of labors,” rather than “the labors of fruits.”

But this could not at all be discovered by collating the Latin codices. For, as the holy Doctor continues, the Latins, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, interpreted *καρπούς* (*karpous*, “fruits”) rather than “hands,” even though *καρποί* (*karpoi*) can also mean “hands,” which is what is written in the Hebrew, **CHAPHACH**.

The reading of the Itala—or, as they call it, the Old Vulgate—was therefore *fructuum* (“of fruits”). It alone was so prevalent in all the books that even Jerome retained it in the first correction of the Psalter. He substituted *manuum* (“of hands”) in the fuller second edition, which he adorned with obeli and asterisks.

It follows, and is perfectly clear, that the version contained in the Veronese codex, which prefers *manuum*, cannot be imposed on anyone as the Itala or Old Vulgate, since it is even later than Jerome’s second correction—namely, the Gallican Psalter and the present Vulgate.

In fact, this passage is among those in which our manuscript differs from the Augustinian recension. Augustine himself was unaware of that reading, at least at the time when he was expounding that psalm. He read it according to the common Latin version and treated it almost exactly as Hilary had done:

“You shall eat,” he says, “the labors of your fruits. O you, O you many who are one, you shall eat the labors of your fruits.”

To those who do not understand, he seems to be speaking perversely; for he ought to have said: “You shall eat the fruit of your labors.”

Moreover, there are many other such examples in the Verona codex, readily apparent, which there is no time to produce one by one; they have been indicated incidentally in the notes. Finally, they will leap to the eye if you compare them with Jerome’s letter to Sunnias and Fretela, where certain readings of his old Vulgate are praised. If, nevertheless, some words remain in that book which bear the flavor of that more ancient version, such as *amaricare* (“to make bitter”), *ignire* (“to set on fire”), and similar expressions, these are among the words which the recent reviser judged it preferable to retain and which, moreover, conveyed a more suitable sense to St. Augustine, although they may have seemed less Latin.

Otherwise, if one may draw an inference from this, the Itala Version is that which retains certain words peculiar to it. The present-day Itala, therefore, should also be called our Vulgate, which consists to a considerable extent of its wording, and especially the Roman Psalter, that is, Jerome’s first revision, which departs from the old reading in far fewer places. For I indeed think that the Itala is to be sought here more than in the other various Greek translations of the Psalms, whether printed or in manuscripts; and that those words may finally be called its surviving remains in which nearly all the ancient Psalters of the other Churches agree.

The Verona Psalter is one of these. It was formerly adapted to the use of our Church, apparently in the seventh century, or in the age of Cassiodorus. I give it precedence because of its selection of exceptionally excellent readings, its division of the verses, and the utmost care of the copyist in transcribing it. I also hope to earn considerable gratitude from learned men for having appended it to the Hieronymian texts—especially because, by noting only the places in which it differs from the Roman Psalter, I have represented the whole work in not many verses, with great savings of time and parchment.

Even without my saying so, those who love a deeper knowledge of Scripture know how much light is added thereby to the industry of the holy Father, and how admirably it has been done that one may inspect the variations of the readings, together with, in almost every case, the causes and dispositions of the translators, and enjoy such venerable records. But we had another reason for publishing this Version: namely, to rescue it, insofar as lay within the power of our side, from the adverse fortune with which it had been contending.

In the recent Roman edition of Anastasius, this book—written out in Greek and Latin, throughout the text in cola and commas—was serving, if the gods please, as *Prolegomena to the Lives of the Popes*, with a new author even enlisted for itself. Then, forced by a second title to deceive the reader, it was labeled *Itala Version*; finally, covered in rags of readings from languages which the editor did not know at all, it appeared to have been deliberately brought onto the stage to make the common people laugh, as when, for example, at Psalm CXVII, a feminine case is noted in place of the feminine gender.

But let us set these matters aside. Like six hundred others, I would have intended to conceal them had the purpose of the work allowed it. To the Psalms we append the prefaces to the books of Chronicles and of Solomon; enough has already been said about them shortly before. Finally, in their proper order, we have added the books of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and Maccabees, although they are Deuterocanonical and were not revised by Jerome, simply so that the complete body of Scripture, according to the present Canon, would not be lacking. We give notice of this at the head of that section, lest anyone be misled by the sequence of the text.

Next follows the New Testament, which the holy Father himself testifies in the catalogue of his works to have been brought by him into conformity with the Greek text. In these words, as I understand them, he most clearly shows what the undertaking was and what task he had taken upon himself. Nevertheless, there are those who agree that the Gospels were brought by him into conformity with the Greek text, but doubt this concerning the remaining books; indeed, they would have them revised by someone else who was imitating Jerome’s example.

I too, to conceal nothing, am influenced by the fact that these books lack a preface, whereas it was customary for the holy Translator to place a preface before all the works he translated. The one preface we possess, addressed solely to Damasus, explicitly promises only the four Gospels. It is also significant [Col. 0021] that Augustine, in Letter 104 among the Hieronymian letters, written in the year 403, knew of no labor undertaken by Jerome other than this work, whatever he may have thought of it, on the book of the Gospels. “We give,” he says in section 6, “no small thanks to God for your work, by which you translated the Gospel from the Greek, because there is almost no offense anywhere when we compare it with the Greek Scripture.” Jerome received this letter as Letter 112, in which he finally replied to him, as though Augustine had spoken about the New Testament.

“And if,” he says in section 20, “as you say, you accept me in the revision of the New Testament, and explain the reason why you accept me,” and so forth. Yet perhaps someone will wish to maintain that, by the name “New Testament” itself, the Gospels are sufficiently designated, on the basis of other expressions of this kind. Nevertheless, Jerome’s constant and unvarying manner of speaking of the New Testament *without qualification*—not only in the passages cited, but also in Letter 71 to Lucinius, where he says, “I rendered the New Testament into conformity with the Greek authority,” and in the corresponding passage of Letter 106 to Sunnias and Fretela—will absolutely not allow us to think that he means only the book of the Gospels.

In fact, when he wished to designate that one book alone, he used its proper name, as in the preface to Damasus. There he indicates that he had not yet turned his attention to the remaining parts of the same Testament, although he immediately afterwards took them in hand and examined them with the same diligence. Letter 27 to Marcella leaves scarcely any room for doubt. In it, replying to the detractors of his translations from the New Testament, he takes nearly all his examples from Paul’s Epistles.

“They read, ‘rejoicing in hope, serving the time’; we read, ‘rejoicing in hope, serving the Lord.’ They think that an accusation against a presbyter must be received without qualification; we read, ‘Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter,’ and so forth. Let them prefer, ‘A human saying, and worthy of all acceptance’; let us, together with the Greeks, be mistaken in reading … ‘A faithful saying,’ and so forth.”

From this an argument is also drawn concerning the remaining books, and indeed concerning the whole Canon of the New Testament, which the holy Father brought into conformity with the authority of the Greek manuscripts—although he furnished only the Gospels with a preface, since that section is the first and most distinguished of all, and perhaps also because he applied his corrective hand and assistance to it in far more places.

Richard Bentley, who, in order to prepare such a Hieronymian edition, had solicited the judgments of learned men by means of a prospectus published to the public, based on manuscript codices of various peoples from the earliest periods, preferred to present a specimen of the great work from the final chapter of the Apocalypse. In this way he wished to show that he did not doubt even this book—which appears exposed to the reproaches of many critics—having been revised by Jerome in accordance with the Greek. That labor could have benefited us greatly, had not the editor’s death intervened after long delays.

Meanwhile, even without him, we have omitted nothing that concerned our purpose. Before the Canons of the Gospels we have placed, in Greek and Latin, Eusebius’s letter to Carpianus, which was lacking in the preceding edition of Martianay but was altogether necessary for understanding the arrangement of the Canons. We have collated the Gospels, the Epistles of Paul, and the rest of the text of Scripture against the most ancient manuscript codices and those of the best quality, paying little or no attention to more recent copies. These are indeed abundant in the libraries of Italy, but they do not possess equal authority when the restoration of Jerome’s original reading is at issue. You will learn the rest from the annotations.

## THE SECOND PART OF THE DIVINE LIBRARY OF ST. EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON

Containing several books which are not found in the Canon of the Hebrews, or which, although included in the Hebrew Canon, were nevertheless translated again from the Greek text of the Septuagint.

## THE FINAL ORDER OF THE OLD TESTAMENT

[Col. 0023]

## [THE BOOK OF TOBIT]

### JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF TOBIT

Jerome, presbyter, sends greetings in the Lord to the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus.

[Note: Chromatius, namely, of Aquileia; Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum.]

I never cease to wonder at the urgency of your demands. You require me to render into Latin style a book written in the Chaldean language—specifically, the book of Tobit, which the Hebrews, cutting it away from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, have assigned among those books which they call *apocrypha*.

[Note: Thus reads the manuscript codex of the Great Bible of the Carthusian monastery of Villeneuve near Avignon. Learned men agree that it should be read this way, Leander of Saint-Martin and all the others who are certain that the Jews recognize no other Hagiographic books except those which constitute the third order of the Hebrew Canon. Most printed editions corruptly read, together with very many manuscripts, *Hagiographa*. For Tobit’s book could not have been cut away from the Canon, or catalogue, of the divine Scriptures—if I may use the words of the holy Doctor—without at the same time being cut away from the order of the Hagiographa and placed among the apocrypha by the Hebrews.

But lest spiteful envy or some hostile person object to us here, let him remember that all and each of the Hebrews’ Hagiographic books were mentioned and numbered by Jerome in the preface to the books of Kings. Among them he absolutely refused to include either Tobit or Judith:

“The third order, *Hagiographa* [ἁγιόγραφα], contains: the first book begins with Job, the second with David … The third is Solomon, having three books: Proverbs … Ecclesiastes … Song of Songs. The sixth is Daniel. The seventh is *Dabreajamim* … which book among us is entitled First and Second Chronicles. The eighth is Ezra, which likewise among the Greeks and Latins is divided into two books. The ninth is Esther. And thus the books of the Old Law altogether number twenty-two: five of Moses, eight of the prophets, and nine of the Hagiographa.

“Although some write Ruth and Lamentations among the *Hagiographa* and think that these books should be counted in their number, and consequently hold that the books of the ancient Law number twenty-four … This prologue of the Scriptures, like a helmeted beginning, may be applied to all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, so that we may know that whatever lies outside these is to be placed among the *apocrypha* [ἀπόκρυφα]. Therefore Wisdom … the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the Shepherd are not in the Canon.”

How inconsistent Jerome would be with himself if, after deciding here that the book of Tobit is to be placed among the apocrypha, he later said in the preface to Tobit itself that among the Hebrews it had been counted among the Hagiographa. Therefore, lest the holy Doctor be thought to have taught contradictory and mutually opposed things, the error of the ancient copyists must be corrected according to the manuscript exemplar praised above. For it was first copied out with the greatest care and then made more accurate by a second revision, and it is of better quality.

But concerning these matters again in the preface to Judith, where another manuscript codex of the Bible, from the library of the Avignon college of the Society of Jesus, supports our reading, *apocrypha*, and confirms it.]

**MART.**—Most other books, both ancient and recent, read *Hagiographa*. Critics otherwise well educated prefer this reading chiefly because, although this book was not admitted into the earlier Hebrew Canon, which contains only books written in Hebrew, it nevertheless continually possessed divine authority both among the Jews themselves and among the Fathers of the Church, as is clear from the testimonies of both sides and, moreover, from the arguments of Grotius and Sixtus of Siena.

Nevertheless, the printed reading, *apocrypha*, which Martianay long ago restored from the manuscripts and supported with sound arguments, is uniquely the true one. It is uniquely supported both by the matter itself and by Jerome’s context—not only here, but much more clearly in the *Galeate Prologue*, and finally in the prologue to the books of Solomon and another to Jonah. A greater number of manuscript codices, and codices of greater authority, also stand on its side: they found it written thus in their exemplars. Such are the author of the Ordinary Gloss, Comestor, Cardinal Hugh, the *Marmotrectus*, Abulensis, and the author of the Preface to the Bible edited together with the Ordinary Gloss and Lyra; they are also supported by Driedo, Catharinus, Garzia Galarza, and formerly by Simonius, among others.

Indeed, among those manuscripts which prefer *Hagiographa*, some, either here or below in the prologue to Judith—which corresponds to this passage—note *apocrypha* in the margin of the book. Thus the interlinear gloss reads at this place; and so Humphrey Hody testifies that it is found in a certain Lambeth manuscript at the prologue to Judith, where an ancient hand, more than two hundred years old, has written in the margin: “*Apocrypha* is the more correct reading.”

He says the same thing: in another Bodleian manuscript (NE. A. 2.1), an ancient hand has noted at the prologue to Tobit, “or rather, among the apocrypha.” Thus *apocrypha* is read in the prologue to Judith in another excellent two-volume Lambeth Bible of very large format; and in the Bodleian Bible (NE. F. 3.25), *apocrypha* is read in both prologues.

Among the older writers who believed the reading *Hagiographa* to be correct, they determine that it must be taken in a broader sense. Thus Dionysius the Carthusian; and in a third Bodleian biblical manuscript (F. 107), opposite the word *Hagiographa* in the prologue to Tobit, is written: “that is, *apocrypha*; for *Hagiographa* is used broadly.” In the prologue to Judith, beside the same word, an interlinear note is added: “broadly.”]

I have satisfied your wish, though not my own inclination. For the studies of the Hebrews accuse us and charge us with transferring these things into Latin ears against their Canon. But judging it better to displease the judgment of the Pharisees and to serve the commands of bishops, I persisted as best I could.

And because the language of the Chaldeans is close to the Hebrew language, I found an eloquent man thoroughly skilled in both languages and undertook a day’s labor. Whatever he expressed to me in Hebrew words, I, having summoned a secretary, set forth in Latin speech. I shall repay the reward of this work with your prayers, once I learn that I have gratefully completed what you deemed worthy of commanding.

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF TOBIT

[Note: This book, which Martianay was content faithfully to reproduce from the Vatican edition, we have continuously collated against the most ancient Palatine manuscript codex of the same Vatican library, numbered 24. We also consulted another Vatican manuscript, formerly belonging to the Queen of Sweden, numbered 7; we had found it fruitful in reviewing the books of the preceding volume as well.

It is also said that another manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés bears the following title: “The Book of the Acts of Tobit son of Ananiel, son of Gabriel, of the tribe of Naphtali.” But the Chaldean text from which the holy Father produced this translation appears to have contained no genealogy of Tobit, although other texts, and the Greek editions whose model that manuscript follows, provide fuller genealogies, differing among themselves.]

## TOBIT

[Col. 0025]

### [Chapter I]

Tobit, of the tribe and city of Naphtali—which is in Upper Galilee, above Naasson, beyond the road that leads westward, with the city of Sephet on the left—was taken captive in the days of Salmanasar, king of the Assyrians. Yet, even while held in captivity, he did not abandon the way of truth, so that every day he distributed among his fellow captives, his brothers who were of his kindred, everything he was able to possess.

Although he was the youngest of all in the tribe of Naphtali, he did nothing childish in his conduct. Indeed, while everyone else went to the golden calves which Jeroboam, king of Israel, had made, he alone fled the company of them all and went on to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord. There he worshiped the Lord God of Israel, faithfully offering all his first fruits and tithes, so that in the third year he distributed the entire tithe to proselytes [Col. 0025C] and resident foreigners. These and similar things the young boy observed according to the law of God.

When he became a man, he took Anna, from his own tribe, as his wife, and fathered a son by her. He gave the boy his own name and taught him from infancy to fear God and abstain from every sin.

Therefore, when through the captivity he came with his wife and son into the city of Nineveh, together with his entire tribe, while everyone else ate food from the Gentiles, he guarded his soul and was never defiled by their food. And because he remembered the Lord with all his heart, God gave him favor in the sight of King Salmanasar and granted him power to go wherever he wished, with freedom to do whatever he desired. Thus he went to all those who were in captivity and gave them counsels of salvation.

When he came to the city of Rages in Media and had ten talents of silver from what the king had bestowed upon him, he saw Gabelus, a needy man of his own tribe, among a great multitude of his kinsmen. Under a written bond, he entrusted him the aforementioned weight of silver.

After a long time, when King Salmanasar had died and his son Sennacherib reigned in his place, and hated the children of Israel in his sight, Tobit continued every day through all his kindred. He consoled them and divided among each person, as he was able, from his possessions; he fed the hungry, gave clothing to the naked, and diligently provided burial for the dead and the slain.

Finally, when King Sennacherib had returned from Judea, fleeing the plague which God had inflicted upon him because of his blasphemy, and in anger had killed many of the children of Israel, Tobit buried their bodies. But when this was reported to the king, he ordered Tobit to be killed and took away all his property.

Tobit, however, fled naked with his son and wife and hid, because many people loved him. After forty-five days, the king’s sons killed him, and Tobit returned to his house; all his property was restored to him.

### [Chapter II]

After this, when it was a feast day of the Lord and a good meal had been prepared in Tobit’s house, he said to his son: “Go and bring some of our tribe who fear God, so that they may feast with us.”

When he had gone out, he returned and announced to him that one of the children of Israel lay slain in the street. Immediately springing up from his couch, leaving his meal, he reached the body fasting. He took it and carried it secretly to his house, so that he could bury it carefully after sunset.

When he had concealed the body, he ate bread with mourning and trembling, recalling the saying which the Lord spoke through the prophet Amos: “Your feast days shall be turned into lamentation and mourning.” When the sun had set, he went out and buried him.

All his neighbors, however, reproached him, saying: “You were already ordered to be killed because of this matter, and you barely escaped the sentence of death, and now you are burying the dead again!” But Tobit feared God more than the king: he carried away the bodies of the slain, hid them in his house, and buried them in the middle of the night.

It happened one day that, exhausted from burying the dead, he came into his house, threw himself down beside the wall, and fell asleep. From a nest of swallows, warm dung fell onto his sleeping eyes, and he became blind.

The Lord permitted this trial to befall him so that his patience might be given as an example to later generations, just as that of holy Job. For although from infancy he had always feared God and kept his commandments, he was not angered against God because the affliction of blindness had come upon him. Rather, he remained steadfast in the fear of God, giving thanks to God throughout all the days of his life.

For just as kings insulted blessed Job, so his parents and relatives mocked his way of life, saying: “Where is your hope, for the sake of which you performed almsgiving and burials?” Tobit rebuked them, saying: “Do not speak in this way, for we are children of saints, and we await that life which God will give to those who never change their faith in him.”

His wife Anna went every day to work at the loom, and from the labor of her hands she brought home whatever sustenance she could obtain. It happened, therefore, that when she received a young goat, she brought it home. When her husband heard it bleating, he said: “See to it that it is not stolen. Return it to its owners, for it is not permitted for us either to eat anything stolen or to touch it.”

At this his wife answered angrily: “Clearly your hope has proved empty, and your almsgiving has now become evident [Alternative: has now appeared].” And with these and other words of the same kind she reproached him.

### [Chapter III]

Then Tobit groaned and began to pray with tears, saying:

“You are righteous, Lord, and all your judgments are [Note: In the Palatine manuscript: ‘your judgments are true.’] righteous, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And now, Lord, remember me, and do not take vengeance for my sins, nor remember my offenses or those of my parents.

“For we did not obey your commands [Note: The same manuscript reads: ‘and we were delivered up.’ In Greek: ‘and you gave us up,’ etc.]; therefore we were delivered into plunder, captivity, and death, and into a byword and reproach among all the nations among which you scattered us.

“And now, Lord, your judgments are great, because [Alternative: who] we have not acted according to your commands and have not walked sincerely before you. And now, Lord, deal with me according to your will, and command that my spirit be received in peace [Col. 0028A], for it is better for me to die than to live.”

On that same day it happened that Sarah, daughter of Raguel [Note: With the Palatine manuscript and the manuscript of the Queen, the reading is “daughter of Raguel in the city,” without the intervening name Rages.], in the city of Rages in Media, also heard a reproach from one of her father’s maidservants, because she had been given to seven husbands and the demon named Asmodeus had killed them as soon as they had entered to her.

When she rebuked the girl for this offense, the maidservant answered her, saying: “May we never see another son or daughter of yours upon the earth, you murderer of your husbands! Do you also wish to kill me, just as you have already killed seven men?” [Note: The same manuscripts read: “we shall never see.”]

At these words she went up to the upper room [Alternative: “in the upper room”] of her house. For three days and three nights she neither ate nor drank, but, persevering in prayer, pleaded with God with tears to free her from this reproach.

On the third day, when she completed her prayer by blessing the Lord, she said:

“Blessed is your name, God of our fathers, who, when you are angry, show mercy, and in a time of tribulation forgive sins to those who call upon you. To you, Lord, I turn my face; to you I direct my eyes [Note: Instead of *dirigo* (“I direct”), the manuscripts prefer *converto* (“I turn again”).] I ask, Lord, that you release me from the bond of this reproach, or at least remove me from the earth. You know, Lord, that I have never desired a man, and have kept my soul pure from every desire. I have never joined myself to those who play, nor made myself a companion of those who walk in frivolity. I consented to receive a husband in your fear, not in my lust.

“Either I was unworthy of them, or perhaps they were not worthy of me [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “perhaps they were not worthy of me,” etc.], because perhaps you have preserved me for another man. Your counsel is not in human power.

“But everyone who worships you knows this for certain: if his life is placed under trial, it will be crowned; if it is in tribulation, it will be delivered; and if it is under correction, it will be permitted to come to your mercy. For you do not delight in our destruction: after the storm, you bring calm; and after tears and weeping, you pour out rejoicing. May your name, God of Israel, be blessed forever.”

At that time the prayers of both were heard in the presence of the glory of the Most High God, and the holy angel of the Lord Raphael was sent to heal them both [Note: The same manuscript omits the pronoun “them” and then reads: “whose prayer had at one and the same time been recited in his presence.”], whose prayers had been recited at the same time in the presence of the Lord.

### [Chapter IV]

Therefore, when Tobit thought that his prayer had been heard so that he might die, he summoned his son Tobiah and said to him:

“Listen, my son, to the words of my mouth, and build them in your heart as a foundation. When God receives my soul, bury my body. You shall honor your mother all the days of her life; for you must remember what dangers, and how great, she endured for you in her womb. When she too has completed the time of her life, bury her beside me.

“Throughout all the days of your life keep God in mind, and beware lest you ever consent to sin and neglect the commands [Note: Here too the same manuscript omits the name “of the Lord.”] of the Lord our God. From your possessions give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for then the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you.

“As you are able, so be merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, gladly strive to distribute even a little. For you store up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity. Because almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and will not allow the soul to go into darkness. Almsgiving will be a great confidence before the Most High for all who perform it [Alternative: “for all who perform it”].

“Pay attention to yourself, my son, and beware of every fornication. Apart from your wife, never allow yourself to know the crime. Never permit pride to rule in your mind or in your speech, for from it every destruction began.

“Whoever has worked for you, immediately pay him his wages, and do not let the wages of your laborer remain with you at all. What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another. Eat your bread with the hungry and needy, and cover the naked with your garments.

“Set out your bread and wine upon the burial of the righteous, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners. Always seek counsel from the wise. Bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways [Col. 0029C] and to keep all your counsels in him.

“I also inform you, my son, that when you were still a little child I gave ten talents of silver to Gabelus in the city of Rages in Media, and I have his written bond with me. Therefore seek how you may reach him, receive from him the aforementioned weight of silver, and return his bond to him.

“Do not be afraid, my son. We lead a poor life, but we shall possess many good things if we fear God, turn away from every sin, and do what is good.”

### [Chapter V]

Then Tobiah answered his father and said: “I will do everything you have commanded me, father. But how I should seek this money, I do not know. He does not know me, and I do not know him. What sign shall I give him? Nor have I ever learned the road by which one goes there.”

Then his father answered him and said: “I have his written bond with me. When you show it to him, he will immediately repay you. But go now and find a trustworthy man who will go with you for a proper fee, so that, while I am still alive, you may recover it.”

Then Tobiah went out and found a handsome young man standing, girded and apparently ready to travel. Not knowing that he was an angel of God, he greeted him and said: “Where do you come from, good young man?”

He answered: “From the children of Israel.”

Tobiah said to him: “Do you know the road that leads into the region of Media?”

He answered: “I do. I have often traveled all its roads, and I stayed with Gabelus our kinsman, who lives in the city of Rages in Media, situated on Mount Ecbatana.”

Tobiah said to him: “Please wait for me until I tell these things to my father.”

Then Tobiah went in and reported all this to his father. His father, greatly astonished, asked that the young man come in to him.

When he had entered, he greeted him and said: “May you always have joy.”

Tobiah said: “What joy can I have, sitting in darkness and unable to see the light of heaven?”

The young man said to him: “Take courage; it is near at hand that you will be healed by God.”

Then Tobit said to him: “Can you lead my son to Gabelus in the city of Rages in Media, and, when you return, I will pay you your fee?”

The angel answered him: “I will lead him and bring him back to you.”

Tobit answered: “I ask you, tell me: of what house or tribe are you?”

The angel Raphael said: “Are you asking about the lineage of the hired man, or about the hired man himself who will go with your son? But lest I make you anxious, I am Azarias, son of the great Ananias.”

Tobit answered: “You are of a great lineage. But I ask you not to be angry that I wished to learn your lineage.”

The angel said to him: “I will lead your son away in good health and bring him back to you in good health.”

Tobit answered: “Travel well, and may God be with you on your journey, and may his angel accompany you.”

Then, after preparing everything that had to be carried on the journey, Tobiah said farewell to his father and mother, and the two of them traveled together.

When they had set out, his mother began to weep and say: “You have taken away the staff of our old age and sent him away from us. Would that the money for which you sent him had never existed! Our poverty was enough for us to count as riches the sight of our son.”

Tobit said to her: “Do not weep. Our son will arrive safely and return safely to us, and your eyes will see him. For I believe that a good angel of God accompanies him and arranges everything that happens around him, so that he will return to us with joy.”

At these words his mother stopped weeping and fell silent.

### [Chapter VI]

Tobiah set out, and a dog followed him. He stayed at the first stopping-place beside the river Tigris. He went out to wash his feet, and suddenly a huge fish came out to devour him.

Tobiah, terrified, cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Lord, it is attacking me!”

The angel said to him: “Take hold of its gill and pull it toward you.”

When he had done so, he dragged it onto dry land, and it began to writhe before his feet.

Then the angel said to him: “Open this fish and take out its heart, gall, and liver; keep them for yourself, for these are useful and necessary for medicines.”

When he had done this, he roasted its flesh, and they carried it with them on the journey; the rest they salted, enough to last them until they reached the city of Rages in Media.

Then Tobiah questioned the angel and said to him: “Please, brother Azarias, tell me what remedy there will be in those things which you ordered me to preserve from the fish.”

The angel answered him: “If you place a piece of its heart upon burning coals, its smoke drives out every kind of demon, whether from a man or from a woman, so that it will no longer approach them.” [Note: The entire passage, “And its gall is useful for anointing eyes in which there is a white film, and they will be healed,” is absent from the Palatine manuscript.]

“And its gall is useful for anointing eyes in which there is a white film, and they will be healed.”

Tobiah said to him: “Where do you wish us to stay?”

The angel answered: “There is here a man named Raguel, a kinsman of your tribe. He has a daughter named Sarah, and he has no other child, male or female, besides her. All his property is due to you, and you ought to take her as your wife. Therefore ask her of her father, and he will give her to you in marriage.”

Then Tobiah answered and said: “I hear that she has been given to seven men and that they died. I have also heard that a demon killed them. I am afraid that the same thing might happen to me; and since I am my parents’ only child, I would bring their old age down to the grave in sorrow.”

Then the angel Raphael said to him: “Listen to me, and I will show you over whom the demon can prevail. Those who enter marriage in such a way that they exclude God from themselves and from their mind, and devote themselves to their lust as a horse and mule do, which have no understanding—the demon has power over them.

“But when you have taken her and entered the chamber, keep yourself continent from her for three days [Col. 0031C], and devote yourselves to nothing except prayer. That very night, when the liver of the fish is burned, the demon will be driven away. On the second night, you will be admitted to the union of the holy patriarchs. On the third night, you will receive a blessing, so that healthy children may be born from you.

“When the third night has passed, you shall take the virgin with the fear of the Lord, led more by the love of children than by lust, so that in the seed of Abraham you may obtain a blessing in your children.”

### [Chapter VII]

They entered Raguel’s house, and Raguel received them joyfully. Looking at Tobiah, Raguel said to his wife Anna: “How like this young man is to my cousin!”

After saying this, he added: “Where are you from, our young brothers?”

They answered: “We are from the tribe of Naphtali, from the captivity of Nineveh.”

Raguel said to them: “Do you know Tobit, my brother?”

They answered: “We know him.”

While they were saying many good things about him, the angel said to Raguel: “The Tobit about whom you are asking is this man’s father.”

Raguel threw himself upon him and, kissing him with tears, wept upon his neck and said: “Blessed are you, my son, because you are the son of a good and excellent man.”

And Anna his wife, and Sarah their daughter, also wept.

[Col. 0032A] After they had spoken, Raguel ordered a ram to be killed and a feast to be prepared. When he urged them to sit down to dinner, Tobias said: “I will neither eat nor drink anything today unless you first confirm my request and promise to give me your daughter Sarah.” At these words Raguel was terrified, knowing what had happened to the seven men who had entered to her; and he began to fear that the same might happen to this man as well. While he hesitated and gave the petitioner no answer, the angel said to him: “Do not be afraid to give her to this man, for your daughter is owed as a wife to this God-fearing man; therefore no other man could have her.” Then Raguel said: “I do not doubt that God has admitted my prayers and tears into his presence. And I believe that he caused you to come to me for this very reason: that she might be joined to her own kindred according to the law of Moses. And now do not doubt that I shall give her to you.” Taking his daughter’s right hand, he placed it in Tobias’s right hand, saying: “May the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob be with you, and may he himself join you together and fulfill his blessing in you.” And after receiving the document, they drew up the marriage contract. After this they feasted, blessing God.

Raguel then summoned Anna his wife and ordered her to prepare another chamber. He brought his daughter Sarah there, and she wept. He said to her: “Be of good courage, my daughter. May the Lord of heaven grant you joy in place of the distress you have endured.”

[Note: In the Palatine manuscript: “He brought Sarah into it,” etc.; and shortly afterward, *filia mi* (“my daughter”) in place of *filia mea* (“my daughter”).]

[Cap. VIII.] After they had dined, they brought the young man in to her. Tobias, remembering the angel’s instructions, took a piece of the fish’s liver from his satchel and placed it upon live coals. Then the angel Raphael seized the demon and bound it in the desert of Upper Egypt. Tobias then encouraged the maiden and said to her: “Sarah, arise, and let us pray to God today, tomorrow, and the day after tomorrow, because during these three nights we are joined to God; after the third night has passed, we shall be united in marriage. For we are children of the saints; we cannot be joined together like the nations that do not know God.”

They rose together, and both prayed earnestly at the same time that healing might be granted to them. Tobias said: “Lord God of our fathers, may the heavens and the earth, the sea and the springs, the rivers, and all your creatures that are in them bless you. You made Adam from the clay of the earth and gave him Eve as a helper. And now, Lord, you know that I take my sister as my wife not for the sake of lust, but solely out of love for offspring, in which your name may be blessed for ever and ever.” Sarah also said: “Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us, and may we both grow old together in health.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript, together with the Vulgate manuscripts, reads: “Then Sarah also said,” etc.]

And it happened around the time of the cockcrow that Raguel ordered his servants to be summoned, and they went away with him together [Col. 0033A] to dig a grave. For he was saying: “Perhaps the same thing has happened to him as to those other seven men who entered to her.”

[Note: The word “perhaps” is probably omitted in the Palatine manuscript.]

When they had prepared the pit, Raguel returned to his wife and said to her: “Send one of your maidservants and let her see whether he is dead, so that I may bury him before daybreak.” She sent one of her maidservants. When she entered the chamber, she found them safe and unharmed, sleeping together there. On her return, she announced the good news. Raguel and Anna his wife blessed the Lord and said: “We bless you, Lord God of Israel, because what we thought would happen has not happened.”

[Note: The same manuscript adds here: “to us.”]

“For you have shown us your mercy and driven away from us the enemy who was pursuing us. You have had mercy on two only children. Make them, Lord, [Col. 0033B] bless you more fully, and let them offer you a sacrifice of your praise and of their health, so that every nation may know that you alone are God throughout the whole earth.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads *in plenius* (“more fully”). Shortly afterward, in place of *universitas*, which our manuscript and all the others restore, Martianaeus had erroneously read *universitatis*.]

Raguel immediately ordered his servants to fill in the pit they had dug before it became light. He told his wife to arrange a feast and prepare everything necessary as food for travelers. He also had two fat cows and four rams killed, and ordered a banquet to be prepared for all his neighbors and all his friends. Raguel adjured Tobias to remain with him for two weeks. Of everything Raguel possessed, he gave Tobias half; and he drew up [Alternative reading: adds *hanc* (“this”).] a document so that the half remaining after their deaths would pass into Tobias’s ownership.

[Col. 0033C] [Cap. IX.] Then Tobias summoned the angel, whom he considered to be a man, and said to him: “Brother Azariah, I ask you to listen to my words.

“Even if I were to give myself to you as a servant, I would not be worthy of your care. Nevertheless, I beg you to take servants and animals for yourself, go to Gabael in the city of Rages in Media, return his written acknowledgment to him, receive the money from him, and ask him to come to my wedding. For you yourself know that my father is counting the days: if I delay even one day longer, his spirit is saddened. And surely you see how Raguel adjured me; I cannot disregard his adjuration.”

[Note: Our manuscripts read: “I beg you to take them,” omitting *sine te* (“for yourself”), etc.]

Then Raphael took four of Raguel’s servants and two camels and went to Rages, the city of Media.

[Note: The same manuscript omits here the word “city”; shortly afterward [Col. 0034D] it reads: “and when he came to Gabael, he gave him the written acknowledgment,” instead of “and finding Gabael,” etc.]

When he found Gabael, he returned his written acknowledgment to him and received all the money from him. He told him everything that had happened to Tobias, Tobias’s son,

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “everything that had happened to him.”]

and made him come with him to the wedding.

When he entered Raguel’s house, he found Tobias reclining at table. Gabael rushed forward, and they kissed one another.

[Note: The same manuscript adds: “Then Gabael wept,” and afterward: “May the Lord God bless you,” etc.]

Gabael wept, blessed God, and said: “May the God of Israel bless you, because you are the son of an excellent and righteous man who fears God and gives alms. May a blessing also be spoken over your wife and your parents. May you see your children and your children’s children to the third and fourth generation. May your offspring be blessed by the God of Israel, who reigns for ever and ever.”

[Note: The Palatine manuscript has *nomen* (“name”) in place of *semen* (“offspring”).]

When everyone had said, “Amen,” they approached the banquet; and even the wedding feast they conducted with fear of the Lord.

[Cap. X.] But while Tobias remained because of the wedding, his father Tobias was anxious and said: “Why, do you suppose, is my son delaying, or why is he being detained there? Do you suppose that Gabael has died and that no one will return the money to him?” He himself began to grieve excessively, and Anna his wife with him; and they both began to weep because their son did not return to them on the appointed day. His mother therefore wept with irreparable tears

[Note: In the same manuscript, *incomparabilibus* (“incomparable”) is read in place of *irremediabilibus* (“irreparable”).]

and said: “Alas, alas for me, my son! Why did we send you away to travel abroad, you light of our eyes, staff of our old age, comfort of our life, hope of our posterity? Having everything together in you alone, we ought not to have let you go from us.” Tobias said to her: “Be quiet and do not be troubled. Our son is well; the man with whom we sent him is sufficiently trustworthy.” But she could in no way be consoled. Every day she would leap up, look around, and go along all the roads by which he seemed likely to return, so that, if possible, she might see him coming from afar.

[Col. 0034C] Raguel, however, said to his son-in-law: “Remain here, and I shall send Tobias your father a messenger bearing news of your safety.” Tobias replied: “I know that my father and mother are now counting the days, and that their spirit is tormented within them.” Though Raguel pleaded with Tobias at length, and Tobias was unwilling to listen to him on any account, Raguel gave him Sarah and half of all his possessions—boys, girls, livestock, camels, cows, and a great deal of money—and sent him away safe and rejoicing, saying: “May the holy angel of the Lord be with you on your journey, bring you safely to your destination, and let you find everything well with your parents. May my eyes see your children before I die.”

The parents took their daughter, kissed her, and let her depart,

[Col. 0034D] exhorting her to honor her parents-in-law, love her husband, manage the household, govern the home, and show herself blameless.

[Cap. XI.] As they were returning, they reached Charan, which lies midway along the road opposite Nineveh, on the eleventh day. The angel said: “Brother Tobias, you know how you left your father. If it pleases you, let us go ahead, while the household, together with your wife and the animals, follows our route at a slow pace.” When it was agreed that they should go, Raphael said to Tobias: “Take some of the fish’s gall with you, for it will be necessary.” Tobias took some of that gall, and they departed.

Anna was sitting beside the road every day on the brow of the mountain, from which she could look into the distance. As she watched for his arrival from that same place, she saw him far away and immediately recognized her approaching son. Running, she announced it to her husband, saying: “Look, your son is coming!”

Raphael said to Tobias: “As soon as you enter your house, immediately worship the Lord your God. After giving him thanks, approach your father [Col. 0035B] and kiss him. At once smear on his eyes the gall of this fish that you are carrying with you. For you should know that his eyes will immediately be opened, and your father will see the light of heaven and rejoice at your appearance.”

Then the dog that had been with them on the journey ran ahead. Like a messenger arriving, it rejoiced, wagging its tail affectionately. His blind father rose and, stumbling with his feet, began to run; and, placing his hand in the boy’s hand, he went out to meet his son. He welcomed him and kissed him, together with his wife, and they both began to weep for joy. After they had worshiped God and given thanks, they sat down.

Then Tobias took some of the fish’s gall and smeared his father’s eyes.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “He smeared his father’s eyes.”]

He waited for almost half an hour, and a white film began to come out of his eyes, like the membrane of an egg.

[Col. 0035C] Tobias seized it and drew it away from his eyes, and immediately he recovered his sight. He and his wife, and all who knew him, glorified God. Tobias said: “I bless you, Lord God of Israel, because you chastised me and you saved me; and behold, I see Tobias my son.”
