After seven days, Sarah also entered, the wife of his son, together with the whole household in good health, the livestock, the camels, and the wife’s considerable money; as well as the money he had received from Gabael. She told her parents all the benefits God had bestowed on him through the man who had led him. Achior and Nabath, Tobias’s cousins, came rejoicing to Tobias and congratulating him on all the good things God had shown him. For seven days they all feasted and rejoiced with great joy.

[Cap. XII.] Then Tobias summoned his son and said to him: “What can we give this holy man who came with you?” Tobias replied to his father: “Father, what reward shall we give him? Or what could be worthy of his benefits? He led me away and brought me back safely; he himself received the money from Gabael; he himself enabled me to have a wife; he himself restrained the demon from her; he brought joy to her parents;

[Note: The Palatine manuscript adds here *tribus* (“for/through three”), or reads *parentibus ejus tribus fecit* (“he did [it] for her parents three [times/ways]”; the precise force is uncertain).]

he himself rescued me from being devoured by the fish; he also enabled you to see the light of heaven; and through him we have been filled with every good thing. What worthy gift can we give him for all this? But I ask you, my father, to ask him whether he might perhaps deign to take half of everything that has been brought.”

The father and son called him and took him aside. They began to ask him to accept half of everything they had brought. Then he said to them privately: “Bless the God of heaven, and confess him before all living creatures, because he has shown you his mercy. For it is good to conceal a king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God. Prayer with fasting is good, and almsgiving is better than storing up treasures of gold, because almsgiving delivers from death, and it is what cleanses sins [Col. 0036B] and causes mercy and eternal life to be found. But those who commit sin and iniquity are enemies of their own souls.

“Therefore I reveal the truth to you, and I will not conceal from you the hidden word. When you prayed with tears, buried the dead, left your meal, hid the dead by day in your house, and buried them at night, I offered your prayer to the Lord. And because you were acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should test you. And now the Lord sent me to heal you and to free Sarah, your son’s wife, from the demon. For I am the angel Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord.”

When they heard this, they were troubled, and, trembling, fell upon the ground on their faces. The angel said to them: “Peace be with you; do not [Col. 0036C] be afraid. For when I was with you, I was there by the will of God. Bless him and sing to him. I appeared to be eating and drinking with you, but I make use of food invisible to human beings and of drink that cannot be seen by human beings. It is therefore time for me to return to him who sent me. But you bless God and recount [Note: The same manuscript omits the word “all” here.] all his wonders.”

When he had said this, he was taken from their sight, and they could no longer see him. Then they lay prostrate on their faces for three hours, blessing God; and when they rose, they recounted all his wonders.

[Cap. XIII.] Tobias the elder opened his mouth, blessed the Lord, and said: “Great are you, Lord, for ever, and your kingdom is throughout all ages, because you chastise and save; you lead down to the underworld [Col. 0036D] and bring back, and there is no one who can escape your hand. Confess to the Lord, children of Israel, and praise him in the sight of the nations, because for this reason he scattered you among nations that do not know him: so that you might recount his wonders and make them know that there is no other almighty God besides him. He chastised us because of our iniquities, and he will save us because of his mercy. Therefore behold what he has done with us, and confess him with fear and trembling; exalt the King of the ages by your works.

“But I shall confess him in the land of my captivity, because he has shown his majesty to a sinful nation. Turn, therefore, sinners, and do justice before God, believing that he will show you his mercy. But I and my soul shall rejoice in him.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “We shall rejoice in God.”]

“Bless the Lord, all his chosen ones; keep days of joy and confess him. Jerusalem, city of God,

[Note: The same manuscript has the fuller reading: “Jerusalem, city of the great God, the Lord has chastised you,” etc.]

the Lord has chastised you for the works of your hands. Give thanks to the Lord for your blessings, and bless the God of the ages, so that he may rebuild his tabernacle in you, recall all your captives to you, and you may rejoice for ever and ever. You shall shine with a splendid light, and all the ends of the earth shall worship you. Nations shall come to you from afar, bringing gifts; they shall worship the Lord in you, and they shall regard your land as a holy place. For they shall invoke the great name in you. Cursed shall be those who despise you, and condemned shall be all who blaspheme you; but blessed shall be those who build you up. You shall rejoice in your children, because they shall all be blessed and gathered to the Lord. Blessed are all who love you and rejoice over your peace.

“My soul, bless the Lord, because he has delivered Jerusalem, his city,

[Note: The Palatine manuscript omits the following entire phrase: “from all its tribulations, the Lord our God”; these words can also be absent without loss of correct meaning. Many more words are missing here in the Hebrew and Greek texts.]

from all its tribulations, the Lord our God. I shall be blessed if the remnant of my descendants live to see the glory of Jerusalem. The gates of Jerusalem shall be built of sapphire and emerald, and its entire circuit of walls from precious stone. All its streets shall be paved with white and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through its lanes. Blessed is the Lord, who has exalted it,

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “so that his kingdom may be over it”; it also does not recognize the words “for ever and ever.”]

and may his kingdom be over it for ever and ever. Amen.”

[Cap. XIV.] Thus the words of Tobias came to an end. After he had received his sight, Tobias lived forty-two years and saw the children of his grandchildren. When he had completed one hundred and two years,

[Note: The same manuscript reads “one hundred and twelve” instead of “one hundred and two.” Neither the Hebrew nor the Greek text says anything about Tobias’s burial; indeed, the latter seems to assign Tobias only ninety-six years of life.]

he was honorably buried in Nineveh. For he had lost the sight of his eyes at fifty-six years of age, and recovered it at sixty. The remainder of his life was spent in joy, and he proceeded in peace with good progress in the fear of God.

At the hour of his death he summoned Tobias his son and his seven young sons, his grandsons, and said to them: “The destruction of Nineveh is near, for the word of the Lord has not failed. And our brothers who were scattered from the land of Israel shall return to it. Its entire deserted land shall be filled, and the house of God that was burned in it shall be rebuilt. There all those who fear God shall return; the nations shall abandon their idols, come to Jerusalem, and dwell in it; and all the kings of the earth shall rejoice in it, worshiping the King of Israel.

“Listen, therefore, my sons, to your father. Serve the Lord in truth [Col. 0038B] and seek to do what pleases him. Command your children to practice righteousness and almsgiving, so that they may remember God and bless him at all times in truth and with all their strength. Now therefore, my sons, listen to me and do not remain here. On whatever day you bury your mother beside me in one grave, from that day direct your steps to leave this place; for I see that its iniquity will bring about its end.”

After the death of his mother, Tobias departed from Nineveh with his wife, his sons, and his grandsons, and returned to his parents-in-law. He found them unharmed in a good old age; he cared for them and himself closed their eyes. He himself received the entire inheritance of Raguel’s household, and lived to see the fifth generation, the children of his grandchildren. After completing ninety-nine years in the fear of the Lord, they buried him with joy.

All his kindred and every generation of his family continued in a good life and holy conduct, so that they were acceptable both to God and to human beings, and to all who dwelt on the earth.

[Col. 0037] Here ends the Book of Tobit.

[Col. 0037]

[THE BOOK OF JUDITH.]

JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF JUDITH

[Note: We also collated this book, together with its prologue, against the same manuscript codices of the Vatican Library: one Palatine manuscript, no. 24, and the other belonging to the Queen of Sweden, no. 7, which we praised in the recension of the preceding Book of Tobit. Martianaeus used no manuscripts, just as he had done when printing that work.]

[Col. 0037D] Among the Hebrews, the Book of Judith is read among the apocrypha,

[Note: The same manuscript, the biblical codex of the Carthusians of Villeneuve near Avignon, already praised in the preface to the Book of Tobit, consistently reads *apocrypha*, not *hagiographa*, as the printed books and nearly all the manuscripts have. But the manuscript copy of the Holy Bible belonging to the College of Avignon of the Society of Jesus, which in the preceding prologue retained the corrupt reading *hagiographa*, presents here the pure and genuine reading—namely, the one we have restored on the authority of those two manuscript codices. We are supported especially by the authority of St. Jerome, who, when limiting and defining the number of the hagiographical and canonical books among the Hebrews in his prefaces to the volumes of Kings, Daniel, and Chronicles, makes no mention of Tobit or Judith except when he removes these books from the number of twenty-four, or twenty-two, and determines that they are to be placed among the apocryphal writings. Origen also taught this before Jerome in his Letter to Africanus, where he testifies that the Jews do not use the books of Tobit and Judith and do not possess them except among the apocrypha. “Concerning this,” he says, “we ought to know that the Hebrews do not use Tobit or Judith. For they have them only in the apocrypha, in Hebrew, as we learned from them.” We omit further conjectures, since we have brought forward clear testimonies and arguments to confirm the matter in question, namely, our edition. MART. Perhaps we have said more than enough above about the correctness of this reading at the corresponding double passage of the prologue to Tobit. The other manuscript of ours, the Queen’s manuscript, unfortunately reads *hagiographa*, as do the earlier printed editions. See also Origen, Letter to Africanus.]

and its authority is judged insufficient for supporting those matters that come into dispute.

[Note: The Chaldean copy praised by Jerome has been lost through the ravages of time; nor does the oldest surviving version, the Greek, appear to have been translated from that copy.]

“Nevertheless, since it was written in the Chaldean language, it is counted among the histories. But because this book

[Note: Not because a new canon of Scripture was published, or a special decree was issued in favor of this book; rather, as learned men commonly suppose, the Council of Nicaea is said to have received it because its Fathers also drew testimonies and examples from this book. Those who have adopted this view assemble a long series of Fathers, including pre-Nicene writers, who occasionally praise the history of Judith. I do not deny that a great number of such witnesses can be produced, from almost every age of the Church; but I do not think that this was Jerome’s intention. Rather, I believe that he referred to a definite, written decree of the council, although it was spurious and falsely attributed to the Nicene Fathers. In Jerome’s time, there existed lists of the sacred books under the name of the Council of Nicaea and also of the Council of Chalcedon. Although these had been established by a pious fraud, they were nevertheless commonly circulated and possessed authority. We can gather this clearly from Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Letters*, chapter 14. After speaking of Jerome’s interpretation of Scripture, its division, and the number of its books, Cassiodorus adds: “Therefore, although many Fathers—that is, St. Hilary, Rufinus, Epiphanius, and the Councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon—did not contradict him but differed, nevertheless all of them, through their divisions, adapted the divine books to appropriate mysteries.” Thus monuments had long before been attributed to the Nicene and Chalcedonian councils that arranged the order of Scripture differently and reckoned the books differently.]

the Council of Nicaea is said to have counted among the number of the holy Scriptures, I have yielded to your request—indeed, to your demand—and, setting aside the occupations by which I was severely pressed, have devoted this little work to it, transferring meaning from meaning rather than word for word.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads: “and only those things,” etc. From this it may appear that the holy Translator occasionally abridged that history.]

“I have cut away the extremely corrupt variation of many codices, and expressed in Latin only what I could find in the Chaldean words with their meaning intact. Receive Judith, a widow and an example of chastity, and proclaim her with perpetual praises in triumphal honor. For she offered herself as an example not only to women but also to men,

[Note: From this passage we seem able to infer with sufficient correctness that this preface—and indeed Jerome’s version of Judith—was addressed to men, not women. Since the persons to whom it is dedicated are mentioned neither in the printed books nor in the manuscripts, Tillemont and others after him conjecture that, because of the suitability of the work, it was given to the most industrious women, Paula and her daughter Eustochium. It seems more probable to us that Jerome is again addressing the two bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus, to whom he had most recently dedicated the Book of Tobit, and that the reason he dedicates the history of so great a woman to men is that her virtue is worthy of imitation not only by women but also by men. If this is true, it also makes the time when the holy Father undertook this labor more plausible. I do not understand, however, what the scribe who copied the Queen’s codex intended when he adds at the end, “to his brother Gerard.”]

for the one who rewarded her chastity granted her such virtue that she conquered the unconquered among all men and overcame the unsurpassable.”

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “so that she might conquer him, invincible by all,” etc.]

THE BOOK OF JUDITH BEGINS

[Col. 0041]

[Col. 0041A] [Cap. I.] Now Arphaxad, king of the Medes, had brought many nations under his rule. He himself built a very powerful city, which he called Ecbatana, from squared and cut stones. He made its walls seventy cubits wide and thirty cubits high, while he set its towers one hundred cubits high. Each side of the square extended [Alternative reading: “was held” (*tenebatur*)] for a distance of twenty feet, and he set its gates as high as the towers. He gloried as though powerful in the strength of his army and in the splendor of his chariots.

[Note: Here the Queen’s manuscript prefers “height” in place of “width,” and shortly afterward “width” in place of “height.” A little later it incorrectly reads “of the neighbors” instead of “of twenty.”]

In the twelfth year of his reign, Nabuchodonosor, king of the Assyrians, who reigned in the great city of Nineveh, fought against Arphaxad and defeated him in the great plain called Ragau, near the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Jadason, in the plain of Arioch, king of the Elymaeans. Then the kingdom of Nabuchodonosor was exalted, his heart was lifted up, and he sent to all who dwelt in Cilicia, Damascus, and Lebanon, to the nations in Carmel and Cedar, to the inhabitants of Galilee in the great plain of Esdrelon, to all who were in Samaria, and across the Jordan as far as Jerusalem, and throughout all the land of Jesse, until one reaches the borders of Ethiopia.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “to the mountains” instead of “to the borders.”]

To all these Nabuchodonosor, king of the Assyrians, sent messengers. They all opposed him with one accord, sent the messengers back empty-handed, and dismissed them without honor. Then King Nabuchodonosor became angry against that entire land and swore by his throne and his kingdom that he would avenge himself on all [Col. 0041C] these regions.

[Note: Our manuscripts unanimously read only “on all,” without adding the words “these regions.” A little earlier, one Queen’s manuscript reads “against all the land” instead of “against that entire land.”]

[Cap. II.] In the thirteenth year of King Nabuchodonosor, on the twenty-second day of the first month, a decree was issued in the house of Nabuchodonosor, king of the Assyrians, concerning his vengeance. He summoned all the elders, all his commanders, and his warriors, and held a council with them concerning his plan. He declared that his intention was to bring the entire earth under his rule. When this proposal pleased everyone, King Nabuchodonosor summoned Holofernes, commander of his army, and said to him: “Go out against the whole western kingdom, and especially against those who have despised my authority. Your eye shall spare no kingdom; you shall subject every fortified city to me.”

Then Holofernes summoned the commanders and officers of the Assyrian army. He counted the men for the expedition as the king had commanded him: one hundred and twenty thousand fighting infantry and twelve thousand mounted archers.

[Note: The Palatine codex reads: “and mounted archers”; shortly afterward, where “innumerable” is omitted, it reads: “in a multitude of camels.”]

He ordered his entire expedition to march ahead with an innumerable multitude of camels, together with those things [Alternative reading: *quae* (“which”) for *qui* (“who”)] that abundantly supplied the armies, and also herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, whose number was beyond counting. He arranged for grain from all Syria to be prepared along his route. From the royal treasury he took a very great quantity of gold and silver. He himself and the whole army set out with chariots, cavalry, and archers, who covered the face of the earth like locusts.

When he had crossed the borders of Assyria, he came to the great mountains of Ange, which are to the left of Cilicia. He climbed to all their fortresses and took every stronghold. He breached the famous city of Melothi, plundered all the sons of Tharsis and the sons of Ishmael,

[Note: Another reading is “the sons of Israel.”]

who were opposite the desert, and [Col. 0042B] went southward toward the land of Cellon.

[Note: The Queen’s manuscript reads: “toward the south, the land of Caeleon”; the Palatine reads: “and toward the south of the land of Celeon.”]

He crossed the Euphrates and came into Mesopotamia. He destroyed all the lofty cities that were there, from the torrent of Mambre as far as the sea, and seized its territory from Cilicia to the borders of Japheth, which lie to the south. He led away all the sons of Midian, plundered all their wealth, and killed with the sword all who resisted him.

After this he descended into the plains of Damascus during the harvest season, burned all the crops, and had all the trees and vines cut down.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads “had them burned” instead of “had them cut down.”]

Fear of him fell upon all the inhabitants of the land.

### [Chapter III]

Then the kings and rulers of all the cities and provinces—namely, of Syria, Mesopotamia, Syria Sobal [Alternatively: the Syrians of Sobal], Libya, and Cilicia—sent envoys. When they came to Holofernes, they said:

“Let your indignation against us cease. It is better for us to serve the great king Nebuchadnezzar while alive and to submit to you than, dying, to suffer the losses of our servitude along with our destruction. All our cities, all our possessions, all our mountains, hills, and plains, our herds of cattle, flocks of sheep and goats, horses and camels, all our resources, and our households are before you: let all that is ours be under your law [Note: The same manuscript omits the pronoun ‘our’; then it reads, ‘We now and our sons,’ etc.]. We now, and our sons, are your servants. Come to us as a peaceful lord and use our service as it pleases you.”

Then he descended from the mountains with his cavalry in great force, and he seized every city and every inhabitant of the land. From all the cities he took for himself auxiliary troops, strong men selected for war. Such fear fell upon those provinces that the inhabitants of all the cities—their rulers and honored men together with the people—went out to meet him as he approached, receiving him with crowns and lamps and leading dances with tambourines and flutes [Note: The same manuscript omits the words ‘and flutes’]. Yet even while doing these things, they could not soften the ferocity of his heart; for he destroyed their cities and cut down their sacred groves. King Nebuchadnezzar had ordered him to exterminate all the gods of the earth, so that he alone might be called God by those nations whom Holofernes’s power could subjugate.

Passing through Syria Sobal, all Apamea, and all Mesopotamia, he came to the Edomites in the land of Gabaa, took their cities, and remained there for thirty days. During those days he ordered his entire army of fighting men to assemble.

### [Chapter IV]

When the Israelites living in the land of Judah heard this, they were exceedingly afraid at his approach. Trembling and terror seized their minds, lest he do to Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord what he had done to the other cities and their temples. They sent word throughout all Samaria, round about as far as Jericho, and occupied all the mountain summits. They surrounded their villages with walls and gathered grain in preparation for battle.

The priest Eliacim also wrote to all who were opposite Esdrelon—which lies opposite the great plain near Dothain—and to all those through whose territory a road might pass, ordering them to secure the mountain ascents by which there could be a road to Jerusalem and to guard the places where the route between the mountains might be narrow.

The Israelites did as the priest of the Lord, Eliacim, had ordered them. And all the people cried out to the Lord with great urgency, and they humbled their souls with fasting [Note: Again the same manuscript omits the words ‘and prayers’] and prayers, both they and their wives. The priests clothed themselves in sackcloth; the infants they cast down before the face of the Lord’s temple; they covered the Lord’s altar with sackcloth; and they cried out unanimously to the Lord [Note: Here too the same manuscript does not recognize the words ‘the God of Israel’], the God of Israel, that he might not give their infants over as spoil, their wives for division, their cities to destruction, and their holy places to defilement, so that they might become a reproach among the nations [Note: This isocolon—‘and become a reproach among the nations’—is found in none of our manuscripts. The Palatine manuscript alone has the plural ‘in defilements’].

Then Eliacim, the great priest of the Lord, went throughout all Israel and addressed them, saying:

“Know that the Lord will hear your prayers if you remain steadfast in fasting and prayer before the Lord. Remember Moses, the servant of the Lord, who overthrew Amalek, confident in his strength, power, and army [Note: The manuscript of the Queen omits this second clause, ‘and in his army’], and in [Alternatively: in] his shields, chariots, and cavalry—not by fighting with iron, but by praying with holy prayers. So shall all the enemies of Israel be, if you persevere in this work that you have begun.”

In response to this exhortation they prayed to the Lord and remained in his presence, so that even those who offered burnt offerings to the Lord, girded with sackcloth, offered sacrifices to the Lord, with ashes upon their heads. And with all their heart they prayed to God that he would visit his people Israel.

### [Chapter V]

It was reported to Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, that the Israelites were preparing to resist and had closed the mountain passes. He burned with immense fury and great anger, summoned all the leaders of Moab and the commanders of Ammon, and said to them:

“Tell me who this people is that occupies the mountains, what their cities are like, how many and how strong they are, what their military strength and numbers are, and who their king or commander is. Why, above all who dwell in the East, have these people despised us and not come out to meet us, to receive us in peace?”

Then Achior, commander of all the Ammonites, answered:

“If you are willing to listen, my lord, I shall tell the truth in your presence about this people who dwell in the mountains, and no false word will come from my mouth.

“This people is descended from the Chaldeans. It first dwelt in Mesopotamia because they refused to follow the gods of their ancestors, who were in the land of the Chaldeans. Thus they abandoned the rites of their ancestors, who worshiped a multitude of gods, and worshiped one God of heaven. He also commanded them to leave that place and dwell in Haran.

“When famine covered the whole land, they went down into Egypt. There they multiplied over four hundred years to such an extent that their army could not be counted. When the king of Egypt oppressed them and subjected them to labor in the construction of his cities, in mud and brick, they cried out to their Lord, and he struck the whole land of Egypt with various plagues.

“When the Egyptians drove them away and the plague ceased among them, but then again wanted to seize them and bring them back into their service, as they fled, the God of heaven opened the sea for them, so that the waters stood solid like a wall on either side, and they crossed through the bed of the sea on dry ground. When the innumerable army of the Egyptians pursued them there, it was covered by the waters so completely that not even one remained to report the event to posterity [Note: In the Palatine manuscript: ‘Having also gone out through the sea’; and shortly afterward, ‘they encountered,’ instead of ‘they seized’].

“After they had crossed the Red Sea, they occupied the deserts of Mount Sinai, where no human being had ever been able to dwell, nor had any child of man found rest. There bitter springs were sweetened for them to drink, and for forty years they received food from heaven.

“Wherever they entered, without bow or arrow and without shield or sword, their God fought for them and conquered. No one could attack this people except when it withdrew from the worship of the Lord its God [Note: In place of ‘worship,’ two of our manuscripts prefer ‘cultivation’; the Palatine manuscript also omits the following name, ‘of the Lord’]. Whenever they worshiped another besides their own God, they were given over to plunder, the sword, and disgrace. But whenever they repented of having withdrawn from the worship of their God, the God of heaven gave them strength to resist.

“In the end they overthrew the king of Canaan, the Jebusite, the Perizzite, the Hittite, the Hivite, the Amorite, and all the powerful inhabitants of Heshbon, and they themselves possessed their lands and cities. As long as they did not sin in the presence of their God, things went well with them, for their God hates iniquity.

“For even in former years, when they had departed from the way that God had given them to walk in, they were destroyed in battle by many nations, and many of them were led captive into a foreign land. Recently, however, they returned to the Lord their God from the dispersion into which they had been scattered; they gathered together, ascended all these mountains, and once again possess Jerusalem, where their holy places are.

“Now therefore, my lord, investigate whether there is any iniquity among them in the sight of their God. Let us go up against them, for their God will surely hand them over to you, and they will be subjected to the yoke of your power. But if this people has not offended its God, we shall not be able to resist them, because their God will defend them, and we shall become a reproach throughout the whole earth.”

When Achior had finished speaking these words, all Holofernes’s nobles became angry and considered killing him, saying to one another [Note: The manuscript of the Queen reads, ‘saying one to another, “Who …,” etc.]:

“Who is this man to say that the Israelites can resist King Nebuchadnezzar and his armies—unarmed men, without strength and without knowledge of the art of war? Let us go up into the mountains, then, so that Achior may learn that he is deceiving us. When their powerful men have been captured, he too shall be pierced with the sword along with them, so that every nation may know [Alternatively: so that all nations may know] that Nebuchadnezzar is the god of the earth and that there is no other besides him.”

### [Chapter VI]

When they had finished speaking, Holofernes became exceedingly angry and said to Achior:

“Because you have prophesied to us, saying that the race of Israel is defended by its God, I shall show you that there is no God except Nebuchadnezzar [Note: The Palatine manuscript inserts ‘you have prophesied among us’]. When we have struck them all down as one man, you too shall perish with them by the Assyrian sword, and all Israel shall be destroyed with you. Then you will learn that Nebuchadnezzar is lord of the whole earth. The sword of my army shall pass through your sides, and you shall fall pierced among the wounded Israelites; you shall not breathe again until you have been exterminated with them.

“But if you think your prophecy true, let not your face fall, and let the pallor that has taken possession of your face depart from you, if you think that these words of mine cannot be fulfilled. So that you may know that you will experience these things together with them, behold, from this hour you shall be joined to their people, so that when they have received the punishment due to my sword, you too may undergo vengeance with them.”

Then Holofernes ordered his servants to seize Achior, take him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites. Holofernes’s servants took him and set out across the plains. But when they had drawn near the mountains, slingers came out against them. Turning aside along the slope of the mountain, they tied Achior by his hands and feet to a tree and, thus bound [Note: Both of our manuscripts read: ‘They left him, or let him down, bound with ropes’], left him there with ropes. Then they returned to their lord.

The Israelites, coming down from Bethulia, came upon him. They released him and brought him to Bethulia, set him in the midst of the people, and asked why the Assyrians had left him bound. In those days the leaders there were Ozias son of Micha, of the tribe of Simeon, and Charmi, who was also called Gothoniel.

In the midst of the elders and in the presence of all, Achior recounted everything he had said when questioned by Holofernes: how Holofernes’s people had wanted to kill him because of this statement, and how Holofernes himself, enraged, had ordered him handed over to the Israelites for this reason—so that, after conquering the Israelites, he might order Achior himself to die by various punishments because he had said, “The God of heaven is their defender.”

When Achior had explained all these things, the whole people fell on their faces and worshiped the Lord. With common lamentation and tears they poured out their united prayers to the Lord, saying:

“Lord God of heaven and earth, look upon their pride, and regard our humility. Pay attention to the faces of your holy ones, and show that you do not abandon those who place their confidence in you, while you humble those who trust in themselves and boast of their own strength.”

When their weeping had ended and the people had completed a whole day of prayer, they comforted Achior, saying:

“The God of our ancestors, whose strength you proclaimed, will give you this recompense: you will see their destruction with your own eyes. And when the Lord our God has granted this freedom to his servants, may God also be with you in our midst, so that, as it pleases you, you and all your people may live with us [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript omits the word ‘so that’ [ut] and, shortly afterward, the phrase ‘with us’].”

Then Ozias, after the council had ended, welcomed him into his house and prepared a great banquet for him. All the elders were summoned, and, when the fast had been completed, they refreshed themselves together. Afterward the whole people was called together, and throughout the night they prayed inside the church, asking help from the God of Israel.

### [Chapter VII]

The next day Holofernes ordered his armies to advance against Bethulia. There were one hundred and twenty thousand infantrymen and twenty-two thousand horsemen, besides the equipment of those men whom he had taken captive and brought away from the provinces and cities, all in the vigor of youth. They all prepared themselves together for battle against the Israelites and came along the mountain ridge to the summit overlooking Dothain, from the place called Bolma [Note: In our manuscripts and printed books it is called Belma], as far as Chelmon, which lies opposite Esdrelon.

When the Israelites saw their multitude, they threw themselves upon the ground, putting ashes on their heads and praying together that the God of Israel would show mercy to his people. Then they took up their weapons of war and sat at the places leading toward the narrow path between the mountains [Alternatively: the mountainous places], and they guarded them all day and all night.

As Holofernes circled around, he discovered that a spring supplied their water channel and directed it from the southern side outside the city. He therefore ordered their water channel to be cut. There were nevertheless springs not far from the walls, from which they could apparently draw water secretly, more for restoring their strength than for drinking.

But the Ammonites and Moabites approached Holofernes and said:

“The Israelites do not trust in spear or arrow; the mountains defend them, and the hills, standing on the precipice, fortify them [Note: The Palatine manuscript has ‘the mountains and hills defend them’ instead of ‘fortify them’]. If you wish to overcome them without an engagement in battle, station guards at the springs, so that they may not draw water from them [Note: The same manuscript reads, ‘draw from them water,’ with ‘water’ not intervening between ‘draw’ and ‘from them’]. Then you will kill them without a sword; or, exhausted, they will surrender their city, which they think cannot be overcome because it is situated in the mountains.”

These words pleased Holofernes and his attendants, and he stationed companies of one hundred men around each spring. When this guard had been maintained for twenty days, the cisterns and water reservoirs failed for all the inhabitants of Bethulia [Alternatively: for those inhabiting Bethulia], so that there was not enough within the city to satisfy anyone for even one day, since water was distributed to the people by measure each day.

Then all the men, women, young people, and children gathered before Ozias and said with one voice:

“Let God judge between us and you, because you have brought evil upon us by refusing to speak peaceably with the Assyrians; and because of this, God has sold us into their hands. Therefore there is no one to help us when we fall before their eyes in thirst and great destruction.

“Now gather together all who are in the city, so that we may willingly surrender ourselves, all of us, to the people of Holofernes. It is better for us to bless the Lord as captives while alive than to die and become a reproach to all flesh, while we see our wives and children dying before our eyes.

“Today we call heaven and earth to witness, and the God of our ancestors, who requites us according to our sins: hand over the city now into the power of Holofernes’s army, so that our end may be swift beneath the sword, rather than being prolonged by the dryness of thirst.”

When they had said this, there was great weeping and wailing in the church from everyone. For many hours they cried out to God with one voice, saying:

“We have sinned with our ancestors; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity. Because you are merciful, have mercy on us, or avenge our iniquities through your scourging. Do not hand over those who confess you [Note: Again the same manuscript reads ‘those who trust in you’] to a people that does not know you, lest they say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

When they had grown weary from these cries and exhausted by these tears, they fell silent. Then Ozias rose, drenched in tears, and said:

“Be of good courage, brothers, and let us wait five more days for mercy from the Lord. Perhaps he will turn away his indignation and give glory to his name. But if, after five days have passed, help has not come, we shall do what you have said.”

### [Chapter VIII]

When Judith the widow heard these words—she was the daughter of Merari, son of Idox, son of Joseph, son of Ozias, son of Elai, son of Jamnor, son of Gedeon, son of Raphaim, son of Achitob, son of Melchiah, son of Enan, son of Nathaniah, son of Salathiel, son of Simeon, son of Reuben—

Her husband Manasses had died during the barley harvest. He had been supervising those who were binding sheaves in the field; the heat came upon his head, and he died in Bethulia, his own city, where he was buried with his ancestors.

Judith had been left a widow for three years and six months. In the upper part of her house she had made herself a secluded room, where she remained shut in with her maidservants. She wore sackcloth around her waist and fasted throughout all the days of her life, except on Sabbaths, new moons, and the festivals of the house of Israel.

She was exceedingly beautiful in appearance. Her husband had left her great wealth, a large household, and estates filled with herds of cattle and flocks of sheep. She was renowned above all others [Note: Two manuscripts read, ‘she was the most beautiful of all,’ followed by ‘because she feared the Lord greatly’; this reading is not itself without merit], because she greatly feared the Lord, and no one spoke an evil word about her.

When she heard that Ozias had promised to surrender the city after the fifth day had passed, she sent for the elders Chabri and Charmi. They came to her, and she said to them:

“What is this word by which Ozias has agreed to surrender the city to the Assyrians if help does not come to you within five days? Who are you to tempt the Lord? This is not speech that calls forth mercy [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, ‘that will prolong mercy’], but rather speech that provokes anger and kindles fury. You have set a time limit for the Lord’s mercy and, according to your own judgment, appointed a day for him.

“But because the Lord is patient, let us repent in this very matter and ask his forgiveness with poured-out tears. For God will not threaten as a human being does, nor will he be inflamed to anger as a son of man is. Therefore let us humble our souls before him, and, standing in a humbled spirit, serving him, let us say to the Lord through our tears that he should show us his mercy according to his will.

“Let us pray that, just as our hearts have been troubled by their pride, so also we may glory in our humility, because we have not followed the sins of our ancestors, who abandoned their God and worshiped foreign gods. For that crime they were given over to the sword, plunder, and confusion before their enemies.

“But we know no other God besides him. Let us humbly await his consolation. He will avenge our blood upon our enemies for the afflictions they inflict, humble all the nations that rise up against us, and the Lord our God will render them without honor.

“And now, brothers, because you are elders among the people of God and their souls depend upon you, raise their hearts by your speech, so that they may remember that our ancestors were tested, to determine whether they truly worshiped their God.

“They must remember how our father Abraham was tested and, proved through many tribulations, became God’s friend. So also Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and all who pleased God passed faithfully through many tribulations.

“But those who did not endure trials with fear of the Lord and who expressed their impatience and the reproach of their murmuring against the Lord were destroyed by the destroyer and perished by serpents.

“Therefore let us not avenge ourselves for what we suffer. Rather, considering that these punishments are less than our sins, let us believe that the Lord’s scourges have come upon us as servants are corrected—for our amendment, not for our destruction.”

Ozias and the elders said to her:

“Everything you have said is true, and there is nothing objectionable in your words. Now pray for us, since you are a holy woman and one who fears God.”

Judith said to them:

“Just as you recognize that what I was able to say came from God, so test whether what I have decided to do is from God, and pray that God may make my plan firm. Stand at the gate tonight, while I go out with my maidservant, and pray that, as you have said, the Lord may look upon his people Israel within five days. But I do not want you to investigate my action; until I report back to you, let nothing else be done except prayer for me to the Lord our God.”

Ozias, prince of Judah, said to her [Note: In the same manuscript it reads, ‘prince of Judaea’]:

“Go in peace, and may the Lord be with you for the vengeance of our enemies.”

Then they returned and went away.

### [Chapter IX]

When they had departed [Note: Two manuscripts read, ‘When they had gone up,’ etc.], Judith entered her prayer room. She clothed herself in sackcloth, put ashes on her head, prostrated herself before the Lord, and cried out to the Lord, saying:

“Lord God of my father Simeon, who gave him a sword against foreigners who had proved violators in their defilement and exposed the thigh of a virgin to her shame; you gave their women over as spoil and their daughters into captivity, and all their plunder into division among your servants, who had been zealous for your zeal: help me, I beg you, Lord my God, a widow.

“For you brought about the former things, and conceived what came after them; and this event has come to pass because you yourself willed it. All your ways are prepared, and you have established your judgments within your providence.

“Look now upon the camp of the Assyrians, just as then you deigned to look upon the camp of the Egyptians, when they ran after your servants in arms, trusting in their chariots, cavalry, and multitude of warriors. But you looked upon their camp, and darkness wearied them. The abyss seized their feet, and the waters covered them.

“Let these men also be like that, Lord, who trust in their multitude, boast of their chariots, and glory in their spears [Note: The words ‘and in their shields’ are found in none of our manuscripts], shields, arrows, and lances. They do not know that you yourself are our God, who crushes wars from the beginning, and that ‘the Lord’ is your name.

“Raise your arm as at the beginning, and shatter their strength by your strength. Let their power fall beneath your anger—those who promise to violate your holy places, defile the tabernacle of your name [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads ‘the tabernacle of your honor’ instead of ‘of your name’], and strike down the horn of your altar with their sword.

“Make their pride, Lord, be cut off by their own sword. Let him be caught by the snare of his own eyes fixed on me, and strike him by the lips of my love. Give me steadfastness of mind, that I may despise him, and strength, that I may overthrow him.

“For this will be a memorial of your name, when the hand of a woman has cast him down. Your strength is not in multitude, Lord, nor is your will in the power of horses. From the beginning, the proud have not pleased you; rather, the prayer of the humble and gentle has always pleased you.

“God of the heavens, creator of the waters and Lord of all creation, hear me, miserable as I am, praying and placing my hope in your mercy. Remember, Lord, your covenant, and put a word in my mouth; strengthen counsel in my heart, so that your house may remain in your sanctification. Let all nations recognize that you are God, and that there is no other besides you.”

### [Chapter X]

When she had finished crying out to the Lord, she rose from the place where she had lain prostrate before the Lord. She called her maidservant, went down into her house, removed the sackcloth, took off her widow’s clothing, washed her body, and anointed herself with the finest ointment [Note: This is one of those expressions which, being of Greek origin, have led learned men to suspect that this Latin version was derived not from a Chaldean archetype but from a Greek translation. The word for ‘headband’ which follows, and other expressions below, seem unlikely to have been used by the translator unless the wording of the Greek exemplar had suggested them. Hence it has also been argued that this cannot be Jerome’s version, since it was taken not from Chaldean but from Greek. Yet who could deny that Jerome might have retained these very words from an older translation because they were sufficiently clear and commonly accepted—the very reason he himself often gives in his prologues, namely, lest he appear to depart too far from an established good reading? Moreover, translating according to his own understanding rather than from another source, he wrote these same words and used them in precisely the same sense. Thus in the Galeatian Prologue: ‘You who anoint the head of the reclining Lord with the most precious myrrh of faith.’ And in Letter 38 to Marcella: ‘The little maidservants arranged the hair, and the innocent head was confined by curling headbands’].

She arranged the hair of her head, put a headband [mitra] upon it, dressed herself in her delightful garments, and put sandals on her feet. She took bracelets for her right arm, and lilies [Note: Learned critics have thought this a corruption for the word *pselia*, the Greek word ψέλια, meaning ‘bracelets.’ It could easily have been used or retained by Jerome in Latin letters as *pselia* from an earlier version, and then changed by a copyist who did not understand the foreign word into the familiar and nearly similar word *lilia*, ‘lilies.’ Since the Chaldean archetype is lacking, however, this cannot be established with certainty], earrings, and rings, and adorned herself with all her ornaments.

The Lord also granted her splendor, because all this adornment arose not from lust but from virtue. Therefore the Lord enlarged her beauty so that she appeared to all eyes with incomparable loveliness [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, ‘He enlarged her with this beauty.’ Another manuscript reads ‘in bodily beauty’ instead of ‘with incomparable beauty.’ Finally, all manuscripts read *ascopam* instead of *ascoperam*, and instead of *palathas*—which are masses of dried figs or fig cakes—they unanimously read *lapates*, apparently through a transposition error in pronunciation].

She put upon her maidservant a wineskin, a vessel of oil, parched grain, cakes of figs, bread, and cheese, and set out.

When they reached the city gate, they found Ozias and the elders of the city waiting. When they saw her, they were astonished and marveled greatly at her beauty. Yet they asked her nothing, but let her pass, saying:

“May the God of our ancestors grant you favor, and may he strengthen every purpose of your heart by his power, so that Jerusalem may glory in you and your name may be numbered among the holy and righteous.”

All who were there said with one voice, “Amen, amen.” Judith, praying to the Lord, passed through the gates, both she and her maidservant [Note: In the Palatine manuscript, ‘she passed through the gates,’ without the word ‘through’].

As she was descending the mountain around daybreak, Assyrian scouts met her and detained her, saying:

“Where are you coming from, and where are you going?”

She replied:

“I am a daughter of the Hebrews. I fled from their presence because I have learned what is going to happen: they will be given over to you as plunder, because, despising you, they were unwilling to surrender themselves voluntarily in order to find mercy in your presence.

“For this reason I considered the matter and said: ‘I shall go before the commander Holofernes, reveal their secrets to him, and show him by what approach he can seize them, so that not one man of his army will fall.’”

When those men heard her words, they examined her face, and astonishment was in their eyes, because they marveled greatly at her beauty. They said to her:

“You have preserved your life by finding such a plan as to descend to our lord. Know this: when you stand in his presence, he will treat you well, and you will be most pleasing in his heart.”

They led her to Holofernes’s tent and announced her arrival.

When she entered before him, Holofernes was immediately captivated by her appearance. His attendants said to him:

“Who could despise the Hebrew people, which possesses women so beautiful that for their sake we ought rightly to fight against them?”

Judith saw Holofernes seated beneath a canopy woven of purple, gold, emeralds, and precious stones. When she looked directly at his face, she worshiped him, prostrating herself upon the ground. At his lord’s command, Holofernes’s servants raised her up.

### [Chapter XI]

Then Holofernes said to her:

“Be of good courage, and do not fear in your heart, for I have never harmed a man who wished to serve King Nebuchadnezzar. But if your people had not despised me, I would not have raised my spear against them.

“Now tell me for what reason you have withdrawn from them and why you chose to come to us.”

Judith said to him:

“Accept the words of your maidservant, for if you follow the words of your maidservant, the Lord will accomplish a perfect deed with you. For as Nebuchadnezzar, king of the earth, lives, and as his power lives—the power that is in you for the correction of all erring souls—not only do human beings serve him through you, but the beasts of the field also obey him.

“The skill of your mind has been reported to all nations, and it has been declared throughout the whole world that you alone are good and powerful in all his kingdom, and that your discipline is proclaimed throughout every province. Nor is it hidden what Achior said, nor is it unknown what you ordered to happen to him.

“For it is certain that our God has been so offended by sins that, through his prophets, he commanded the people to be handed over because of their sins. And because the Israelites know that they have offended their God, your terror is upon them.

“Moreover, famine has overtaken them, and because of the drought they are already counted among the dead. Finally, they have resolved to kill their livestock and drink their blood. The holy things of the Lord their God—which God commanded not to be touched—grain, wine, and oil, they have considered consuming, and they intend to use what they should not even touch with their hands. Therefore, because they are doing these things, it is certain that they will be delivered over to destruction.

“When I, your maidservant, learned this, I fled from them, and the Lord sent me to announce these very things to you. For I, your maidservant, worship God even now while I am with you. Your maidservant will go out and pray to God, and he will tell me when he has returned their sin upon them. I shall come and report it to you, so that I may lead you through the middle of Jerusalem, and you will have the entire people of Israel like sheep without a shepherd, and not even one dog will bark against you. For these things have been told to me through the providence of God.

“And because God is angry with them, I have been sent to announce these very things to you.”

All these words pleased Holofernes and his servants. They marveled at her wisdom and said to one another:

“There is no woman like this on earth in appearance, beauty, or eloquence.”

Holofernes said to her:

“God has done well, who sent you before the people, so that you yourself might deliver them into our hands. Since your promise is good, if God does this for me, you will be great in the house of Nebuchadnezzar, and your name will be spoken throughout the whole earth.”

### [Chapter XII]

Then he ordered her to enter where his treasures were stored and commanded that she remain there. He also appointed what should be given to her from his own banquet.

Judith answered him:

“Now I cannot eat any of the things you have ordered to be given to me, lest an offense come upon me. I shall eat from the provisions I brought with me.”

Holofernes said to her:

“If the provisions you brought with you run out, what shall we do for you?”

Judith replied:

“As surely as you live, my lord, your maidservant will not consume all these provisions before God has accomplished by my hand what I have planned.”

And [Note: [Col. 0053D] Again the same manuscript reads, “and they brought her in,” etc.] his servants led her into the tent [Col. 0053C] which he had ordered. As she entered, she asked that she be allowed to go out at night and before dawn for prayer and supplication to the Lord. He instructed his chamberlains that she might go out and come in as she pleased to worship her God for three days. At night she went out into the valley of Bethulia and bathed herself in a spring. As she came up, she prayed to the Lord God of Israel to direct her way toward the deliverance of his people. Once inside, she remained clean in the tent until she received her food in the evening.

On the fourth day Holofernes gave a banquet for his servants and said to Vagao, his eunuch: “Go and persuade that Hebrew woman to consent willingly to dwell with me. For among the Assyrians it is disgraceful if a woman mocks a man by passing away from him as though she were immune [Col. 0053D] to his advances.”

Then Vagao [Note: [Col. 0053D] More correctly—and consistently—our manuscripts call him Bugoan.] went in to Judith and said: “Let the good young woman not hesitate to enter my lord’s presence, so that she may be honored before him, eat with him, and drink wine in pleasure.” Judith answered him: “Who am I to contradict my lord? Whatever appears good and excellent before his eyes, I shall do. Whatever pleases him shall be best for me throughout all the days of my life.”

She rose, adorned herself in her garments, entered, and stood before him. The heart of Holofernes [Col. 0054A] was shaken, for he was burning with desire for her. Holofernes said to her: “Drink now and recline in pleasure, for you have found favor before me.” Judith said: “I shall drink, my lord, because my soul has been exalted today above all my days.” She took and ate and drank in his presence what her maidservant had prepared for him. Holofernes became merry with her and drank exceedingly much wine, more than he had ever drunk in his life.

## Chapter XIII

When evening came, his servants hurried to their lodgings, and Vagao closed the doors of the chamber and departed. They were all exhausted from the wine, while Judith was alone in the chamber. Holofernes lay on the bed, overcome by excessive drunkenness. [Col. 0054B] Judith told her maidservant to stand outside the chamber and keep watch.

Judith stood beside the bed, praying with tears and silently moving her lips, saying: “Strengthen me, Lord God of Israel, and look at this hour upon the work of my hands, so that, as you promised, you may raise up Jerusalem, your city; and what I have conceived, believing that through you it can be accomplished, [Note: [Col. 0054D] The manuscript of Regina has more: ‘as I thought,’ etc.] may I complete.”

When she had said this, she approached the pillar at the head of his bed and loosened his dagger, which was tied there and hanging down. After drawing it from its sheath, she seized the hair of his head and said: “Strengthen me, Lord God, at this hour.” She struck his neck twice and severed his head. She removed his canopy from the pillars and unrolled his headless body. [Col. 0054C] Shortly afterward she went out, handed Holofernes’ head to her maidservant, and ordered her to put it into her bag.

The two women went out, as was their custom, as though for prayer. They crossed the camp, went around the valley, and came to the city gate. From a distance Judith said to the guards on the walls: “Open the gates, for God is with us, the one who has shown his power [Note: [Col. 0054D] The Palatine manuscript reads, ‘who has brought great deliverance in Israel.’] in Israel.”

When the men heard her voice, they summoned the elders of the city. They all ran to her, from the least to the greatest, for they had thought that she would not return. After lighting lamps, they all gathered around her. She climbed to a higher place and ordered silence. When everyone had become silent, Judith said:

“Praise the Lord our God, who has not abandoned those who hope in him, and who through me, his servant, has fulfilled the mercy that he promised to the house of Israel. This night he has killed the enemy of his people by my hand.”

Then she brought Holofernes’ head out of the bag and showed it to them, saying:

“Behold the head of Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army; and behold his canopy, beneath which he reclined in his drunkenness, where the Lord our God struck him by the hand of a woman. As the Lord himself lives, his angel guarded me both when I went out from here, when I remained there, and when I returned from there to here. The Lord did not permit me, his servant, to be defiled, but brought me back to you without the pollution of sin, rejoicing in his victory, in my escape, and in your deliverance. [Note: [Col. 0055D] The same manuscript has, ‘Let us all give thanks to him,’ etc.] Give thanks to him, all of you, for he is good, for his mercy is forever.”

All worshiped the Lord and said to her: “The Lord has blessed you by his power, because through you he has brought our enemies to nothing.”

Ozias, the leader of the people of Israel, said to her: “Blessed are you, daughter, by the Lord God Most High, above all women on earth. Blessed is the Lord who created heaven and earth, who guided you to the wound of the head of our enemies’ commander. Today he has so magnified your name [Col. 0055B] that your praise will never depart from the mouths of those who remember the Lord’s power forever. For you did not spare your own life because of the distress and affliction of your people, but came to the aid of their downfall in the sight of our God.” And all the people said: “Amen, amen.”

Achior was summoned and came. Judith said to him: “The God of Israel, to whom you bore witness that he would avenge himself upon his enemies, has himself cut off this night the head of all unbelievers by my hand. And so that you may know that this is true, behold the head of Holofernes, who in contempt of his arrogance despised the God of Israel and threatened you with death, saying: ‘When the people of Israel have been captured, I shall order your sides to be pierced with a sword.’”

When Achior saw Holofernes’ head, he was stricken with terror [Col. 0055C] and fell facedown upon the ground; his spirit was overcome. But after he had recovered his breath and revived, he fell at Judith’s feet, worshiped her, and said: “Blessed are you by your God in every tent of Jacob, for in every nation that hears your name the God of Israel will be magnified because of you.”

## Chapter XIV

Judith said to all the people:

“Listen to me, brothers. Hang this head upon our walls. When the sun has risen, let each man take up his weapons, and go out with force—not as though you were descending below, but as though making an assault. Then the scouts will have to flee to their commander [Note: [Col. 0055D] Two manuscripts read, ‘to rouse him for battle.’] to rouse him for battle. When their commanders run to Holofernes’ tent and [Col. 0055D] find him headless and rolling in his own blood, fear will fall upon them. [Alternative: trembling.] When you realize that they are fleeing, pursue them without fear, for the Lord will crush them beneath your feet.”

When Achior saw the power that the God of Israel had displayed [Col. 0056A] in Israel [Alternative: “among Israel”], he abandoned the practices of his gentile religion, believed in God, circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and was joined to the people [Note: [Col. 0055D] The Palatine manuscript inserts the name of God here.] of Israel, he and all the succession of his descendants, to the present day.

As soon as day broke, they hung Holofernes’ head upon the walls. Each man took up his weapons, and they went out with great noise and shouting. When the scouts saw this, they ran to Holofernes’ tent. Those who were in the tent came and made a disturbance before the entrance to the chamber, contriving by their noise to awaken him, so that Holofernes would be roused not by those calling him but by the sounds. No one dared knock upon or enter the chamber of the Assyrians’ commander. But when his commanders, tribunes, and all the [Col. 0056B] chief officers of the Assyrian king’s army had arrived, they said to the chamberlains:

“Enter and awaken him, for mice have come out of their holes and dared to challenge us to battle.”

Then Vagao entered his chamber and stood before the curtain, clapping his hands, for he suspected that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith. But when he could detect no movement of the man lying there by the sense of hearing, he approached the curtain, lifted it, and saw Holofernes’ headless corpse lying upon the ground, soaked in its own blood. He cried out in a loud voice with weeping and tore his garments.

He entered Judith’s tent, but did not find her. He rushed outside to the people and said: “A Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nabuchodonosor. For behold, Holofernes lies upon the ground, and his head is not on him.”

When the leaders of the Assyrian army heard this, they all tore their garments. An unbearable fear and trembling fell upon them, and their minds were utterly confused. An incomparable outcry arose in the midst of their camp [Note: [Col. 0055D] The Palatine manuscript reads, “in the middle of their camp.”]

## Chapter XV

When the entire army heard that Holofernes had been decapitated, their minds and counsel fled from them. Driven only by trembling and fear, they sought safety in flight, so that no one spoke with his neighbor; instead, [Note: [Col. 0055D] The Greek has otherwise: “but having poured out together with one accord,” ἀλλὰ ἐκχυθέντες ὁμοθυμαδὸν. For this reason Grotius thought that Jerome, who translates “but with bowed head,” had read, not from the Chaldean text, but from the very similar Greek expression ἐκκλιθέντες. Although I accept Grotius’ conjecture, I nevertheless do not believe that Jerome was misled by the similarity of the Greek reading, since he did not consult the Greek exemplar at all in preparing this translation. Rather, I suppose that he may have read an older Latin translator, as Grotius proposes, whose rendering Jerome retained without any loss either to the Chaldean truth or to the correct sense.] with bowed heads, abandoning everything, they hastened to escape from the Hebrews, whom they heard coming against them armed [Note: [Col. 0056D] The manuscript of Regina has, “whom they saw coming against them armed, and fleeing,” etc.], fleeing along the roads of the plains and the paths [Col. 0056D] of the hills.

When the Israelites saw them fleeing, they pursued them. They descended, sounding trumpets and shouting after them. Because the Assyrians were not assembled but were rushing headlong in flight, while the Israelites pursued them in a single column [Col. 0057A], they weakened all whom they could find.

Ozias sent messengers through all the cities and regions of Israel. Every region and every city sent its chosen armed youth after them [Note: [Col. 0057D] The Palatine codex reads, “and all the cities sent chosen young men,” etc.], and they pursued them with the sword until they came to the limits of their territories.

The survivors who were in Bethulia entered the Assyrian camp, seized the booty that the fleeing Assyrians had left behind, and were heavily laden [Note: [Col. 0057D] The same manuscript reads honestati sunt instead of onustati, “they were honored” instead of “they were laden”; shortly afterward it has abstulerunt secum, “they took away with them,” instead of attulerunt, “they brought”; and below, a minimo usque ad magnum, “from the least to the greatest,” instead of ad maximum, “to the greatest.”]

Those who returned victorious to Bethulia brought everything that had belonged to the Assyrians with them, so that there was no counting their sheep, cattle, and all their movable goods; from the least to the greatest, they all became wealthy from the plunder.

[Col. 0057B] Joacim, the high priest, came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all his elders to see Judith. When she went out to meet him, they all blessed her with one voice, saying:

“You are the glory of Jerusalem, the joy of Israel, the honor of our people. You have acted courageously, and [Note: [Col. 0057D] The manuscript of Regina reads, “your heart was strengthened,” etc.] your heart was strengthened because you loved chastity and knew no other man after your husband. Therefore the hand of the Lord also strengthened you, and [Note: [Col. 0057D] The Palatine manuscript reads, “and therefore you shall be blessed by God,” etc.] therefore you shall be blessed forever.”

And all the people said: “Amen, amen.”

For thirty days the people of Israel could scarcely gather all the spoils of the Assyrians. Everything that was proved to have been Holofernes’ personal property—gold, silver, garments, gems, and every kind of household furnishing—they gave to Judith, and all of it was presented to her by the people. All the people rejoiced with the women, virgins, and young men, with instruments and lyres.

Then Judith sang this song to the Lord, saying:

## Chapter XVI

“Begin for the Lord with tambourines; sing to the Lord with cymbals; play a new psalm to him; exalt and invoke his name.

The Lord who destroys wars—the Lord is his name.

He established his camp in the midst of his people, to rescue us from the hand of all our enemies.

Assyria came from the northern mountains with the multitude of its strength. Its multitude blocked the torrents, and its horses covered the valleys.

He said that he would burn my borders and kill my young men with the sword, give my infants over to plunder [Col. 0057D], and my virgins into captivity.

But the Lord Almighty struck him and delivered him into the hands [Alternative: “hand”] of a woman, and pierced him.

[Col. 0058A] For their champion did not fall by young men, nor did the sons of Titans strike him, nor did lofty giants [Note: [Col. 0057D] By common agreement our manuscripts read imposuerunt se, “set themselves against him,” instead of opposuerunt, “opposed.”] oppose him; rather Judith, daughter of Merari, overthrew him by the beauty of her face.

For she removed her widow’s clothing and put on the clothing of joy in the exultation of the children of Israel.

She anointed her face with perfume and bound her curls with a headdress; [Note: [Col. 0058D] All our manuscripts omit the clause “she took a new robe.”] she took a new robe to deceive him.

Her sandals captured his eyes; her beauty took his soul captive; with a dagger she cut off his neck.

The Persians were horrified by her steadfastness, and the Medes by her boldness.

[Col. 0058B] Then the camps of the Assyrians howled when my humble ones appeared, fainting from thirst.

The sons of maidens pierced them, and like fleeing children they killed them. They perished in battle before the face of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0058D] The Palatine manuscript does not add “of my God” here.] my God.

Let us sing a hymn to the Lord; let us sing a new hymn to our God.

Adonai, Lord, you are great and glorious in your strength [Note: [Col. 0058D] The Palatine manuscript omits “your” here and in the immediately following verse], and no one can overcome you.

Let every creature of yours serve you [Alternative: “serve”], for you spoke, and they came to be; you sent your spirit, and they were created, and there is no one who can resist your voice.

The mountains will be moved from their foundations with the waters; the rocks will melt like wax before your face.

But those who fear you will be great before you [Col. 0058C] in all things.

Woe to the nation that rises up against my people, for the Lord Almighty will take vengeance upon them; on the day of judgment he will visit them.

For he will give them fire and worms in their flesh, so that they may burn and feel pain forever.”

After this, the whole people came to Jerusalem after the victory to worship the Lord. As soon as they had been purified, they all offered burnt offerings, vows, and their pledged offerings. Judith offered as a devoted offering of oblivion [Note: [Col. 0058D] The same manuscript reads, “all the military equipment,” omitting “vessels”; shortly afterward it has, “she removed as a devoted offering,” instead of “she offered,” etc.] all of Holofernes’ military equipment that the people had given her, as well as the canopy that she herself had taken from his bed. The people were joyful before the holy things, and for three [Col. 0058D] months the joy of this victory was celebrated with Judith.

After those days each person returned to [Note: [Col. 0058D] Both the manuscripts of Regina and the Palatine read, “each person returned to his own home, and Judith,” etc. The Greek has ἕκαστος εἰς τὴν κληρονομίαν ἑαυτοῦ, “each person to his own possession,” etc.] his own home. Judith became great in Bethulia and [Col. 0059A] more renowned than anyone throughout the land of Israel. Chastity was also joined to her courage, so that she knew no man all the days of her life after Manasses, her husband, had died. On feast days she went out in great glory. She remained in her husband’s house for 105 years, freed her maidservant Abram, and died and was buried with her husband in [Col. 0060A] Bethulia. All the people mourned her for seven days. Throughout the whole span of her life, and for many years after her death, no one disturbed Israel.

The day of this victory is counted by the Hebrews among the holy days and has been observed by the Jews from that time to the present day.

[Col. 0059] Here ends the Book of Judith.

[Col. 0059]

# TWO VOLUMES OF THE OLD TESTAMENT: JOB AND THE PSALTER

Translated into Latin by Saint Jerome from Greek exemplars, or from Origen’s Hexaplar edition, with the signs of asterisks and obeli.

## J. MARTIANAEUS’ NOTICE ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS

The Book of Job, which Jerome formerly translated into Latin according to the Septuagint, adding obeli and asterisks, had lain in the dust for many centuries. At last R. P. Domnus Claudius Martin recovered it from the library of the monastery of Marmoutier and sent it to us without delay. We openly acknowledge that this new edition of Saint Jerome owes very much to his services and goodwill.

When that precious monument of sacred antiquity reached us, we immediately read through it in its entirety with the greatest eagerness. Examining everything with curious eyes, we discovered that it was precisely the book that Augustine valued so highly in his own time that he praised the diligence and fidelity of its translator, Jerome.

How much neglect and destruction the Book of Job had suffered before Origen among the Greeks and Jerome among the Latins restored it whole and sound is attested not only by Jerome’s own preface but also by the words of Origen Adamantius and certain other ancient writers. It therefore seemed worthwhile to place at the beginning of the volume testimonies by such authors concerning the Book of Job. With these preceding testimonies of the ancient Fathers, fair-minded judges of such matters will more readily permit us to censure manifest errors of the copyists and to restore certain omissions—namely, the signs of obeli and asterisks, which the thoughtlessness of scribes either omitted or confused in the manuscript codex. Moreover, we have sometimes taken care to supply the two heavier points and to delimit what is set under asterisks and obeli, because, if these boundaries are removed, the obeli and asterisks create greater confusion than if no such signs appeared. For how will the reader recognize the extent of what is marked by asterisks unless he sees the boundaries fixed in their proper places?

Thus, lest so distinguished a work be published by us to no purpose, we have been compelled not to fear adding in certain places a few omitted points. We are certain from other evidence that Jerome himself printed the same two points for the same purpose in his later revision of the Psalms. Let this general preliminary notice suffice; the rest will be explained below in its proper places.

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENT FATHERS CONCERNING THE BOOK OF JOB

## From Origen’s Letter to Africanus

[Col. 0059B]

“But also in Job, from the passage ‘It is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord raises’ to the end, whatever follows is absent among the Hebrews. For this reason it does not exist in Aquila either. In the Septuagint and Theodotion, however, those passages are found which are equivalent to one another.

“We also find a thousand other passages in Job in our copies that contain either less or more than the copies of the Jews. They contain less, for example, where Job rose in the morning and offered sacrifices for them according to their number [one calf as a sin offering for their souls]. And when the angels of God came to stand before God, the devil also came with them; and this: ‘Going around the earth and walking through it.’ In addition, after the words ‘The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away,’ the Hebrews did not have: ‘As it pleased the Lord, so it happened.’

“Our copies contain more in the passage where Job’s wife speaks to him, from: ‘How long will you persist [saying: “Behold, I shall remain a little longer, still awaiting the hope of my salvation,” up to these words: “so that I may rest from my troubles and pains, which now constrain me”].’ For these are the only words of the woman [understand: ‘written in Hebrew’]: ‘Say a word against the Lord and die.’

“Again, very many passages are found throughout the middle of the entire Book of Job in the Hebrew copies, but not likewise in ours—often four or three verses, and sometimes fourteen, sixteen, or nineteen. Why should I enumerate these? We collected them with much labor so that the difference between the Jewish copies and ours would not escape us.”

## From Hesychius, or whoever was the author of the unpublished *Hypotheses* on the Sacred Books, in Usserius of Armagh’s letter to Ludovicus Capellus

Hesychius, or whoever was the author of the unpublished *Hypotheses* on the Sacred Books, notes, by means of a distinction, that the Book of Job contained 1,600 στίχοι (*stichoi*, lines) without asterisks, but 2,200 with asterisks.

## From Letter 71, formerly 10, of Saint Augustine to Jerome

[Col. 0061A]

“In this letter I add what we learned later: that you translated Job from the Hebrew after we already possessed a certain translation of the same prophet rendered into Latin from the Greek language. In that translation, however, you marked with asterisks what is present in the Hebrew but absent from the Greek, and with obeli what is found in the Greek but not in the Hebrew, with such remarkable diligence that in certain places we see individual stars assigned to individual words, indicating that those same words exist in Hebrew but not in Greek.”

The reader should note that Augustine used this translation of Jerome in his *Book of Annotations on Job*, while omitting these signs of asterisks and obeli.

## From Jerome’s Preface to His Translation of the Book of Job from the Hebrew

[Col. 0062A]

“Let my detractors, then, accept in its entirety what they have accepted in part—or let them erase my translation together with its asterisks. For it is impossible that, after they have seen that those translators omitted more, they will not also admit that they erred in certain places, especially in Job. If you remove what has been added under the asterisks, the greater part of the volume will be mutilated—and this only among the Greeks. Among the Latins, however, before the translation that we recently published with asterisks and obeli, nearly seven hundred or eight hundred verses are missing, so that the shortened, torn, and gnawed book displays its ugliness publicly to its readers.”

# JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF JOB

[Col. 0061]

[Col. 0061B]

“If I were weaving a little basket from rushes, or folding palm leaves, so that I might eat my bread in the sweat of my face and attend anxiously to the work of my belly, no one would bite at me and no one would criticize me. But now, because in accordance with the Savior’s saying I wish to work for food that does not perish, and to clear the ancient path of the divine Books of thorns and brambles, a genuine tooth is fixed into me [Note: [Col. 0061C] Through the error of copyists, seven manuscripts or more read this way: ‘a double tooth is fixed into me.’ In the canon of Saint-Germain-des-Prés the word error has been added: ‘a genuine error is fixed into me.’ The printed editions retain the corruptions of all the manuscripts, for Erasmus and Marianus read: ‘a double error is fixed into me.’ But this expression, ‘to fix a genuine tooth into someone,’ was familiar to Jerome, as is clear from this passage in Book One of his *Apology against Rufinus*: ‘He says that I am a malicious man, a detractor of everyone, always fixing a genuine tooth into my predecessors.’ Similar expressions seem to have been drawn from Satire 1 of Persius and Satire 5 of Juvenal. MART. —Some manuscripts read ‘double.’ Jerome uses this expression frequently, as Martianaeus notes. In some places he adds ‘and a tooth,’ as in the Preface to the *Chronicle*. I am not unaware that many will fix a genuine tooth into this volume.] I am called a falsifier who corrects errors, and accused not of removing errors but of sowing them.

“For the habit of antiquity is so powerful that many prefer even acknowledged faults, choosing to have more beautiful codices rather than corrected ones.
