Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0061C] Here one encounters the astonishing audacity of ancient scribes, who dared in almost all manuscript codices to remove the words ‘O Paula and Eustochium’ and replace them with ‘O dearest brothers,’ as though offended that Jerome had dedicated his nocturnal studies to women. The same rancorous envy appears in the preface to the books of Solomon, which we promised above to print more accurately at the end of the Bibliotheca, when discussion of these volumes was undertaken. Moreover, the fan of which Jerome speaks here, counting it among the little gifts of monks, was an instrument chiefly for stirring a fire or driving away flies. Eustochium held such a fan in her hand while attending her mother Paula, lying in bed and about to die. See Jerome’s Epitaph of Paula. MART.] O Paula and Eustochium, the unique exemplar of nobility and humility, accept these spiritual and enduring gifts in place of the fan, baskets, and little hampers—the small gifts of monks—and rejoice that blessed Job, who still lay among the Latins in dung [Col. 0062B] and swarmed with the worms of errors, is now whole and undefiled.

“For just as everything was restored to him twofold through his testing and victory, so I have made him possess in our language—[Note: [Col. 0062C] Many manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read ‘so that I may speak boldly.’ MART.] I say it boldly—what he had lost.

“Therefore I warn you, and every reader, with the customary Preface, and by always attaching the same notice at the beginnings of the books I ask you: wherever you see the preceding virgules ÷, know that what follows is not found in the Hebrew volumes. But wherever the image of a star + shines, know that it has been added from Hebrew into our language.

“Also, those passages which we thought were present, but which had been so corrupted that they deprived readers of their meaning, I corrected with great labor at your request. [Note: [Col. 0062C] In several manuscripts and in the printed editions the reading is ‘which seemed to be present.’ Consequently, ten manuscripts read ‘from my hatred’ instead of ‘from my leisure.’ MART.] [Note: [Col. 0062C] He took this from Sallust’s statement in *Jugurtha*, chapter 4: ‘A greater benefit will come from my leisure than from the public affairs of others,’ etc. Jerome calls his literary studies ‘leisure,’ as they are commonly called. I mention this so that you may not, perhaps following the judgment of a more recent critic, think that the names here have been displaced through the fault of copyists and that one should read, ‘from my business … rather than from the leisure of others,’ etc.] For I judged that something more useful would come to the Churches of Christ from my leisure than from the business of others.”

# THE BOOK OF JOB BEGINS

[Col. 0061]

[Col. 0061A] **[Chapter I.]** There was a man in the land of Ausitis, whose name was Job. That man was truthful, blameless, righteous, a worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil. He had seven sons and three daughters. And his livestock numbered [Col. 0062A] [Col. 0063A] [Note: [Col. 0063B] The words we have enclosed in brackets after Martianaeus—“very numerous”—are altogether absent from the Hebrew and the Greek. Nevertheless, they are not marked with an obelus in the Latin manuscript, so that a careful student can easily see that they are a gloss rashly inserted into the text. We shall designate below by the same notes such interpolations as, by good arguments, we conclude to have been absent not only from the Hebrew but also from Origen’s Hexaplar edition. Martianaeus marked them with a smaller asterisk.] [very numerous]; sheep, seven thousand; camels, three thousand; yoke of oxen, fifty; and five hundred she-asses in herds, [Note: [Col. 0063C] Chrysostom, explaining this passage in the Catena of the Greek Fathers on Job, observes as follows: Since “very abundant service” is marked with an obelus, one must know that whatever is marked with an obelus is not found in the Hebrew—ὅτι ὅσα ὠβέλισται, ἐν τῷ Ἑβραϊκῷ οὐ κεῖται—but was placed by the Septuagint for the sake of clarity. Chrysostom must here have followed the error of some copyist; for “very abundant service” is read in the Hebrew source, *va-‘avuddah rabbah me’od*, that is, “and a very great household,” or “very abundant service.” Aquila likewise translated it so, as Olympiodorus testifies in the Catena already mentioned. He says “service” because it was rendered by servants. Aquila: “very abundant servitude”; Symmachus, more clearly, “household.” Thus Olympiodorus: from this we are certain that Chrysostom was misled by a copyist’s ignorance, since the latter had wrongly placed an obelus before the words of Scripture. MART. — We have prefixed an obelus to these words, “and very abundant service,” in accordance with the Greek manuscript, and because the actual facts require it. The single sentence in the Hebrew text, “and a very great household,” is here explained twice through the Greek translation: first by the phrase we cut out, and then by this other phrase, “and great works were his upon the earth.” It is obvious that one or the other is redundant. Although the former adheres more closely to the Hebrew, we have pierced it with an obelus because of the authority of the ancient writers, especially Chrysostom in the Catena of the Greek Fathers on Job, who says: ὅτι ὠβέλισται τὸ, Καὶ ὑπηρεσία πολλὴ σφόδρα, “because the phrase ‘and very abundant service’ is marked with an obelus.” Martianaeus, who did not notice that these two expressions were explanations of one and the same sentence, approved both at once and even dared to accuse Chrysostom of error, saying that “we are certain that he was misled by a copyist’s ignorance, who had wrongly placed an obelus before the words of Scripture.” In fact, he himself is thoroughly mistaken because he did not understand the holy Doctor.] ÷ and very abundant service, ** and great works were his upon the earth. That man was distinguished among the sons of the East.

His sons used to come together each day and hold a feast; they summoned their sisters also to eat and drink with them. When the days of the feast had ended, Job sent for them and purified them. Rising early, he offered sacrifices for them according to their number, [Note: [Col. 0064B] We supplied this sign, having been advised by Origen in his letter to Africanus. [Col. 0064C] See Origen’s testimony above. MART. — The Greek also places an obelus here, though it has the fuller reading, μόσχον ἕνα περὶ ἁμαρτίας ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν, “one calf for sin on behalf of their souls,” and so forth. Origen, in his letter to Africanus, section 3, reads περί instead of ὑπέρ in another place as well. In either case, it seems that the Latin should be rendered: “one calf for sin on behalf of their souls.”] ÷ and one calf for the sin of their souls. ** For Job said: “Perhaps my sons have sinned and cursed the Lord in their hearts.” Thus Job did every day.

**NOW ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE ANSWERED AND SAID:**

**NOW JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:**
## [Chapter VI]

If anyone were to weigh my anger and place my words on the scales together, they would find them heavier than the sand of the seashores. [Note: “Pains” (*dolores*) should be read, as Martianay himself observed; and the Greek indeed has *odynas* (“pains”).] But, as it seems, my words are evil. For the arrows of God [alt. the Lord] are in my body; their fury drinks my blood. When I begin to speak, they spur me on. Why? Will the wild ass bray for no reason unless it is seeking food? Or will an ox bellow when it has fodder in its manger? Can bread be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in empty words? So my soul too cannot remain silent. For I see my food as foul, like the odor of a lion.

But if my petition should be granted and the Lord should fulfill my hope, let the Lord, having begun, wound me, but not kill me forever. Let the city be my tomb, upon whose walls I was leaping. I will not spare. For I have not lied [Note: In Saint Augustine: “For I have not lied: they are the words of my holy God.” The Greek adheres more closely to our printed reading.] in the words of my holy God.

For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my allotted time, that my soul should sustain it? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh made of bronze? Or was I not trusting in this very thing [Note: Augustine further adds, “when it was well with me.” He interprets these as genuine words of the sacred text, that is, “when I was immortal in the image of God.” They are absent, however, from the Hebrew and Greek texts.]? But help has departed from me. Mercy has been turned away from me, and the visitation of the Lord has disregarded me.

My kinsmen did not look upon me, like a torrent that fails, or like waves that have passed over me. Those who feared me have now rushed upon me. As snow or ice, once congealed, disappears when it has melted in the heat, and no trace remains of what it was, so I too have been abandoned by everyone. I have perished and have been made an exile from my house.

Look at the ways of the Temanites; observe the paths of the Sabaeans [Note: Another recension joins the words differently: “Observe the paths of the Sabaeans.” But the Greek text also differs, and contains more.]. Observe them, because those who trust in cities and riches will meet with confusion.

But now you too have risen up against me without mercy; yet, when you see my wound, be afraid [Note: This complete verse, verse 21—“But now you too have risen up against me without mercy; yet, when you see my wound, be afraid”—was missing from Martianay’s edition through the carelessness of an earlier copyist. We have supplied it from Saint Augustine, in exactly these words. It was not one of those passages that should be slaughtered with an obelus or supplied beneath asterisks on the pretext of variation among copies or notes; rather, it occurs continuously both in the Hebrew and especially in the Greek text: “But now you too have attacked me without mercy, so that, seeing my wound, you may fear.” The Latin translation we have restored corresponds word for word to this. See, if you wish, Saint Augustine’s own Annotation.].

Why? Did I ask anything of you? Or do I need your strength to save me from enemies or rescue me from the hand of the mighty? Teach me, and I will be silent. If I have erred, tell me. But, as I see it [Note: Augustine reads *parva* (“small”) rather than *prava* (“wicked”), and explains it in the following annotation: “He calls the true human being one who signifies the person performing repentance by conversion to God, whose words they called small.” Nevertheless, the Greek word *phaula* properly means “worse,” “evil,” “worthless,” and words unworthy of a true human being.], you say that they are the wicked words of a true man.

For I am not asking help from you, nor does your rebuke impose silence upon me. I cannot endure the expression of your speech. Yet you have attacked the orphan [alt. the insignificant] and leapt upon your friend.

But now [Note: The Greek has: “But now, looking upon your faces, I will not lie.” This agrees with the Hebrew printed here and with Augustine, who differs by one word, reading “looking” rather than “beholding.”]—look at me; + give heed to me. I will not lie to your face. Sit down, and let there be no injustice; then once again stand for justice. For there is no injustice in my mouth.

## [Chapter VII]

And do not my jaws meditate upon wisdom [alt. “were meditating”]? Is not human life upon the earth a trial, and his life like that of a day-laborer? Or like a servant fearing his master and obtaining shade? Or like a laborer awaiting the wages of his work? So I too waited for empty months, and nights of pain were allotted to me.

If I sleep, I say, “When will it be day?” And if I rise again, “When will it be evening?” [Note: Martianay’s edition less accurately reads “I shall be filled.” Saint Augustine reads “I am filled at once,” and the Greek likewise has *plērēs de ginomai* (“I become full”); we therefore prefer their reading.]

But I am filled with pains from evening [Col. 0072C] until morning, and my body thickens with the corruption of worms. I pour out clods of earth, scraping away pus, and my life [Note: We have supplied the pronoun “my,” which was missing, from Augustine and the Greek.] is more fragile than speech, and hope has perished into emptiness.

Remember, then [alt. “therefore”], that my life is a breath, and my eye will not return again to see good things. + [Note: Martianay erroneously read *nonne* (“is it not?”) as one word in place of *non me* (“will not recognize me”), which we have restored from Augustine and also from the Greek text. Likewise, in place of *cognoscet* (“will recognize”), *cognoscit* (“recognizes”) had previously been read, less accurately.] The eye of the beholder will not recognize me. + Your eyes are upon me, and I do not remain **, like a cloud swept away [from heaven].

For if a human being descends to the underworld, he will not ascend again; he will not return any longer to his house, and his place will not know him any longer. Therefore I too will not spare my mouth. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will open [Note: The Greek contains more: “I will open my mouth in bitterness,” and so forth. The Hebrew does not. In the following passage, marked with an obelus, an asterisk formerly stood; Martianay himself, however, rejected it.] the bitterness of my soul ÷ being constricted **.

Am I perhaps the sea, or a dragon, that you have appointed a guard over me? + For I said **, “My bed will comfort me, and on my couch I will bring consolation back to myself.” You terrify me through dreams and stupefy me through a vision. [Note: We have again corrected *absolvens* (“releasing”) to *absolves* (“you release”), in accordance with Augustine and the Greek verb *apallasseis*.] You release my soul from my spirit, and my bones from death. + [Note: Saint Augustine joins this differently: “I drove my bones away from death.” In the Greek manuscript this final verb is not found, not even beneath an asterisk.] I drove them away. For I shall not live forever ÷ so that [Col. 0073B] I may endure patiently **.

Depart from me, for my life is vanity. What is a human being, that you have magnified him? Or why have you directed your attention toward him? So that you visit him in the morning and judge him in his repose? How long will you not release me or leave me until I swallow my saliva [in pain]?

[Note: We have supplied the conditional particle “if,” which was missing, from the Greek manuscript—“If I have sinned”—and from Augustine’s reading, confirmed by his own annotation: “If I have sinned, I can do nothing to you …” A little later: “But if a human being’s sin harms you neither by deed nor by word,” and so forth.]

If I have sinned, what can I do to you, you who know human understanding? Why have you set me up to speak against you, making me a burden to you? And why have you not forgotten my iniquity and cleansed my sin? [Note: Saint Augustine reads this in the third person: “and he has made forgetfulness”; the Greek likewise has *lēthēn epoiēsō* (“you have made forgetfulness”).] But now I shall go into the earth.

[Note: In place of “In the morning I shall awake,” which is also what the Greek text says—*orthrizōn*—the Augustinian books wrongly prefer “For I shall awake.” Minor matters below are likewise corrected.]

In the morning I shall awake, and I shall be no more.

## BALDAD THE SAUCHITE SPOKE IN RESPONSE:

## [Chapter VIII]

How long will you speak such things? A verbose spirit is in your mouth. Does the Lord act unjustly when he judges? Or will he who made all things pervert what is just? If your sons sinned before him, he sent them into the hand of their iniquities.

But you, rise early before the Lord Almighty and pray. If you are pure and truthful + **, he will hear your prayer and restore to you the life of righteousness; your former state will be very small, but your latter state will be immeasurable.

For inquire of the former generation and investigate the lineage of the ancestors. [Note: In the manuscript there is a copyist’s error here: he reads “and we are outsiders,” that is, “outsiders” instead of “yesterday’s people.” MART.] We are people of yesterday and do not know; our life upon the earth is a shadow.

Or will they not teach you and tell you, and bring words forth from their heart? Does the rush grow green without water, or does the reed grow unless it is irrigated? It still stands in its root, and it will not be harvested. Before every plant drinks, does it not wither?

[Note: Through a careless error, Martianay read *vivat* (“may it live”) instead of *bibit* (“may it drink”), which we have restored with the support of the Greek text, *pro tou pien* (“before it drinks”). Augustine puts it very elegantly: “Unless it drinks; for the impious has never flourished.”]

Thus, then, will be the end of those who forget the Lord. For the hope of the impious will perish, and his house will not be habitable; his tent will be filled with spiders. Even if he supports his house, it will not stand; and when he begins, it will not endure.

For it is moist before the sun, and its shoot will rise from its decay. [Note: We have supplied the pronoun “its,” which both Augustine and the Greek text itself contain—*autou*.] It sleeps among gatherings of stones and will live in the midst of pebbles. If the place swallows him, it will deny him.

[Note: Previously the reading was *si deglutietur* (“if he is swallowed”); following Augustine, we have rewritten it as *deglutierit* (“if he swallows”), as does the Greek: *ean katapiē*.]

For you have not considered these things, because overthrow is imputable. But from the earth another will spring up. [Note: Here too we have rewritten *germinavit* (“it sprang up”) as *germinabit* (“it will spring up”), in accordance with the Greek *anablēsei* and Augustine’s testimony. Previously, through the customary error of ancient copyists, *germinavit* was read.]

For the Lord will not reject the innocent. [Note: The Greek likewise has *apopoiēsetai* (“he will reject”), although Augustine reads *probabit* (“he will approve”); he adds: “Or: will he not reject? Or: will he approve the impious as innocent?”] Nor will he accept any gift from the impious. But he will fill the mouth of the truthful with laughter and their lips with confession. Their enemies will be clothed with confusion, and the tent of the impious will not remain [alt. “will not endure”].

## AND JOB RESPONDED:

## [Chapter IX]

Truly I know that it is so. For how can anyone be righteous before the Lord? If he wishes to contend with him in judgment, he will not answer him one thing out of a thousand. For he is wise in understanding, strong, and great. Who has been hard before him and remained?

He is the one who brings mountains to old age [Note: Martianay reads *perducet* (“will bring”) in accordance with antiquity, but less accurately; the Greek has *ho palaiōn* (“he who makes old”).], and they do not know it; who overturns them in his anger; who shakes the world from its foundations, and its pillars tremble.

He commands the sun, and it does not rise, and he seals up the other stars. He alone stretches out the heavens and walks as though upon the earth, upon the sea. He makes the Bear, and the Evening Star, and the Pleiades, and the inner chambers of the South. He does great and unsearchable things, glorious and immense things whose number has no end.

If he passes over me, I shall not see him; and if he passes by me, even then I shall not know him. [Note: Augustine reads this second parallel clause differently: “If he is higher than I” (or “if he brushes past me swiftly”), “I shall not recognize him.” I do not know whether the words placed in parentheses are being quoted as part of the text itself. In any event, our reading agrees sufficiently with the Greek.]

For if he hands someone over to death, who will turn him aside? Or who will say to him, “What have you done?” For his anger is unturnable. Under him are subjected [Note: Although Augustine reads this way too, and although Benedictine editors, who explain him precisely at this point, have no doubt about the Latin reading and concern themselves only with correcting the Greek, I suspect the Latin itself of corruption all the more because it is certain that it derives from the Greek exemplar they regard as corrupt. In place of *caetera*, the Septuagint has *kētē*, that is, “the sea monsters that are beneath heaven.” Even if we grant the corruption they posit in the Greek version—which perhaps once ought to have read *kēthoi tēs hyperēphanias*, “the helpers of pride,” in agreement with the Hebrew text—it must nevertheless be admitted that this corruption is extremely ancient, and far older than Jerome. Jerome plainly read *kē tē*, not *kēthoi*, as the rest of the interpretation of the clause—“which are beneath heaven”—demonstrates. The word *caetera* agrees neither with the Hebrew reading nor with the restored Greek *kēthoi*, but betrays itself as corrupted by scribal error because of its similarity to *cete* (“sea monsters”). I therefore maintain that Jerome did not write *caetera* here, but *cete*: for he could not have produced that interpretation from any exemplar, whereas the proposed Hexaplaric text, or even the common text of the Seventy, readily supplied *kētē*, “sea monsters,” in exactly those letters. The sense also is excellent, for Virgil likewise speaks of “huge sea monsters” in Book V of the *Aeneid*, where Servius is to be consulted as he gives the Greek declension; and Statius speaks of “rocky sea monsters” in Book I of the *Achilleid*, to say nothing of others. Conversely, whoever wrote *caetera* could not have been the translator at all, but only an ancient copyist who rashly supplied two little letters according to his own judgment and discretion. Since the result made reasonable sense—or so it perhaps seemed to him as a critical emendation—he easily imposed it upon all his readers down to the present day. Indeed, the corruption began already in the translator’s own age, for Augustine himself, whom we know to have used Jerome’s translation in his book of Annotations, was already using such a corrupted copy. This is clear both from his reading and especially from the annotation he adds there: “Under him are subjected all things beneath heaven. Except heaven itself,” he says, “that is, the rational creation; for if it had subjected all other things to itself, it would never be punished through the things it had subjected.” See how quickly and widely the fraud prevailed. We ourselves attribute such value to venerable antiquity that, although we have shown the reading to be false, we do not dare to alter it.]

all things beneath heaven. If he should hear me and distinguish my words, + with himself **. Even if I should be righteous, he will not hear me. + I shall plead his judgment **.

But if I call, and he should hear me [Note: Saint Augustine reads and interprets this with the opposite sense: “and if he should not hear me.” The Greek text itself, however, contradicts him, since it does not contain that negative particle.], I shall not believe that he has heard my voice. Perhaps he would crush me in a whirlwind. For he has brought many tribulations upon me without cause. He does not allow me to breathe, but has filled me with bitterness. Indeed, because he can, he prevails. For who can oppose his judgment?

Even if I am righteous, my mouth will speak impiously. Even if I am blameless, I shall be found perverse. For even if I acted impiously against my soul [Note: The word “my” is to be marked with an asterisk, as in the Greek. In place of the following adverb *verumtamen* (“nevertheless”), Martianay incorrectly read *verum autem* (“but truly”). Finally, another asterisk should again be prefixed to the words that follow, “There is one thing,” and so forth. Augustine reads simply *haplōs*, “what I said,” not “because of what I said,” although the latter agrees better with the Greek.], I do not know. Nevertheless, my life is taken away.

There is one thing for which I have also spoken: anger destroys the great and powerful [alt. “destroyed”], because worthless people [Note: Martianay had read, with very little sense, *neque homines* (“nor people”) instead of *nequam homines* (“worthless people”), which we have corrected.] will be in great death, while the righteous are mocked.

+ The earth has been handed over into the hands of the impious. + He covers the faces of its judges. [Note: As we have shown elsewhere, Saint Augustine here too used a corrupt copy, which reads and interprets “making judgment” instead of “the faces of its judges.”] + But if this is not so, who is he, then? +

Now my life is lighter than a runner. [Col. 0076A] + They have fled and have not seen goodness. ** [Note: Martianay had placed the asterisk before only the final word, “goodness,” omitting even the final punctuation. We have moved it back to the beginning of the verse in accordance with the Greek manuscript. The following word, “They went away,” occurs in Hebrew but not in Greek.] They went away like the track of a ship, or like a flying eagle seeking food. [Note: Martianay incorrectly read in the nominative “flying and seeking eagles,” which is an error arising from an ancient pronunciation.]

But if I speak also, I forget while I am speaking. Turning my face aside [alt. “toward my face”], I groan. I am shaken in all my limbs. For I know that you will not leave me unpunished. And since I am impious, why am I not dead, but suffer?

But even if I were purified in snow and cleansed with clean hands, you have dipped me deeply in filth, and my garment has loathed me. [Note: Again Martianay had read *tinxi* (“I dipped”) instead of *tinxisti* (“you dipped”), and shortly afterward, “For a human being is not,” instead of “For you are not a human being,” and so forth. After Augustine’s support, we have restored these readings from the Greek *bapsas* (“having dipped”) and *ou gar ei anthrōpos* (“for you are not a human being”). Minor matters are corrected below.]

For you are not a human being like me, with whom I could dispute, so that we might come together for judgment. Would that there were an arbiter for us, one who might reprove and hear between the two of us [alt. “between both”]! Let him turn away from me his rod + ** and let his fear not terrify me. I will speak and not fear him. For I am not now with myself. [Note: The word “now” is absent from the Hebrew, Greek, and the Augustinian books themselves.]

## [Chapter X]

My soul has fainted in my life. I will bring forth words against myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul, ÷ being constricted **, and I will say to the Lord:

Do not teach me to be impious. Why have you judged me in this way? Or is it good for you if I act unjustly, since you despise the work your hands have made and have paid attention to the counsel of the impious? Or do you see as a human being sees? + Or will you see as a human being sees? [Col. 0077A] Or is your life human, or are your years [Note: We have prefixed an asterisk to the word “like,” which Martianay had wrongly placed after it, and we have added the final punctuation.] + like the days ** of a human being? For you have searched out my iniquity and investigated my sins.

You know that I have done nothing impious [alt. “impiously”]. But who is there who can snatch me from your hands [alt. “be snatched away”]? Your hands made me and fashioned me; afterward, having changed, you struck me. Remember that you fashioned me from clay and will turn me back into the earth again. [Note: Martianay again wrongly read “only” in place of “again.” The Greek has *palin* (“again”). Minor matters are corrected below.]

Did you not milk me like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh; you inserted me among bones and sinews. You gave me life and mercy, and your oversight guarded my spirit.

Although these things are in you, I know that you can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you. Even if I sin, you will watch me; but you will not hold me innocent of iniquity. And if I act impiously, woe to me; and if I am righteous, I cannot breathe.

For I am full of disgrace, and I am seized like a lion for slaughter. Again, having changed, you torment me most cruelly. You restore my torments within me [alt. “You renew my torments”]. You have used great anger against me and brought trials upon me.

Why, then, did you bring me out of the womb, and why was I not dead, so that no eye might see me? I would have been as though I had never existed. Why, then, was I not buried immediately from the womb? Or is the time of my life not short?

[Note: Through a careless error, Martianay read *attere* (“crush”) in a contrary sense instead of *patere* (“allow”). The Greek has *eason me* (“allow me”). Augustine likewise reads and explains it thus: “Allow me, then, to rest in you.” He further has “until” instead of “so that,” and soon appears to heighten the sense in his own words rather than quote the actual text, when he adds: “Before I go into punishments from which it is not possible to return.”]

Allow me to rest a little, before I go where I shall not return: into a land dark and gloomy, into a land of eternal night, where there is no light and no seeing of human life.

## [Col. 0077C] SOFAR THE MINAEAN SPOKE IN RESPONSE:

## [Chapter XI]

He who says many things ought also to hear. Or will an eloquent man be considered righteous? Blessed is the human being who is born, a human being of short life. [Note: This second occurrence of “human being” is superfluous; neither Saint Augustine nor the Greek repeats it.]

Do not be excessive in words when there is no one to contradict you. Nor should you say, “I am righteous in my deeds and was blameless before him” + **. But how the Lord might speak to you, + and open his lips with you, ** and teach you the power of wisdom, for it will be doubled upon you; then you will know that what you deserve has been duly repaid to you by God for the things you have done wrong. [Note: Saint Augustine reads: “that what you sinned has been repaid to you by the Lord.”]

But will you find the Lord’s trace, or have you reached the furthest limits of what the Almighty has made? He is higher than heaven; what will you do? He is deeper than the underworld; what do you know? Or longer than the expanse or the height of the sea.

But if he overturns all things + or gathers them together, ** who will say to him, “What have you done?” For he knows the works [Note: The same manuscript contains more: “the works of unjust men”; and shortly afterward it has the more correct reading: “But a human being is otherwise unstable.”] of the impious, and when he sees unjust things, he will not neglect them.

A human being is otherwise unstable in his words, and a human being born of woman is like a wild ass in the desert. For if you have set your heart aright and stretch out [alt. “stretching out”] your hands toward him, if there is anything unjust in your hand, put it far away ÷ from you **, and let no iniquity remain in your house.

For then your face will shine like pure water, and you will strip yourself [perhaps “you will be stripped”] of filth, and you will not fear. You will forget your labor like a wave that passes by, and you will not be terrified. [Note: Here too, apparently from a corrupt manuscript, he read with the negative particle “a wave that does not pass,” and then “you are terrified” instead of “you will be terrified.”]

Your prayer will be like the morning star, and life will rise for you from noon. You will trust because you have hope. And peace will appear to you in place of anxieties and cares. For you will rest, and there will be no one to attack you, and many will entreat your face.

+ But the eyes of the impious will waste away, ** while salvation will leave them; for their hope is the destruction of their soul.

## JOB RESPONDED:

## [Chapter XII]

“So you alone are human beings? Will wisdom die with you? I too have a heart, just as you do; yet the righteous and blameless man comes **[Note: Martianus has less correctly, ‘comes to laughter.’]** to be mocked. For he was prepared for a fixed time, so that another might fall and his house be laid waste by the wicked. Indeed, let no one who is wicked trust that he will go unpunished when he provokes God to anger, as though no investigation were to be made into them.

“But nevertheless, ask the four-footed creatures whether they will answer you, or the birds of heaven whether they will declare it to you; and tell the earth, if it will speak to you. + And the fish of the sea will report it to you. + Who does not know, among all these things, that the hand of the Lord made them? **If the life of every living thing and the spirit + of every **human** flesh are not in his hand. [Note: The same editor again wrongly has *hands* instead of *hand*. Greek: ἐν χειρί, ‘in the hand.’]

“For the ear tests words, and the palate, when tasting food, [tests] it for itself. + With much time comes wisdom, and with long life comes knowledge. With him are wisdom and strength; his are counsel and understanding. If he destroys, who will build? [Note: Here too, following the Greek and Saint Augustine, we read ‘will build’; Martianus has ‘builds.’ Moreover, we removed the obelus which he himself, against his will, had placed before the words ‘who will open,’ taken from his corrupt manuscript.]

“If he shuts around a man, [Note: The preceding obelus wrongly cuts off ‘who opens?’ because these two words are found in the Hebrew; without them the sentence would remain incomplete in one member. MART.] who opens? If he withholds the water, he will dry up the earth; but if he releases it, [Note: Saint Augustine inserts the conjunction ‘and’: ‘But if he also releases it.’ We have corrected ‘will go out,’ corruptly read by Martianus, to ‘will destroy,’ on the authority of his testimony and the Greek ἀπολέσει.] he will destroy, overturning the earth.

“With him are dominion and might, discipline and understanding. He leads counselors [Al. advisers] captive and throws the judges of the earth into terror [Al. throws them]. He establishes kings upon thrones + and girds their loins [Al. hips] with a belt. ** He sends priests away captive and overthrows the powerful of the earth. He changes the speech of the faithful and recognizes the understanding of the aged; he pours ignominy upon princes and heals the humble. He reveals the depths from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light. [Note: Martianus has ‘led forth,’ less suitably; and, as often elsewhere, shortly afterward he omitted the terminal points that mark the end of the material enclosed by asterisks.] + He deceives nations and destroys them, ** laying nations low and leading them along the way [Al. leading them into the way]. He reconciles the hearts of the princes + of the people ** of the earth; but he leads them astray along a way [Al. into the way] they did not know. He handles darkness and not light, and they wander like a drunkard.

## [Chapter XIII]

“Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard it, and I know what you also know. And + indeed ** I am not more foolish than you; rather, I too will speak to the Lord and, if he wills, rebuke him in his presence. But you are physicians of iniquity, all of you healers of evils. Would that you might fall silent! It would be counted as wisdom for you.

“Therefore hear the rebuke of my mouth, **and attend to the judgment of my lips. Do you speak before the Lord’s presence and utter deceit before him? Or do you withdraw so as to become judges yourselves? It will be best if he examines you. For if, while doing everything, you attach yourselves to him, he will nevertheless rebuke you. [Note: The asterisk and the following word are superfluous here. Once *quia* is removed, the sense is complete; nor is it found in the Hebrew scroll. MART. —Martianus, with an asterisk prefixed, adds *quia*, although he himself acknowledges that the mark and the word are additions recklessly inserted in his manuscript. Perhaps *via* should be read instead of *quia*, and the variant *via ejus* for *ei* had been written in the margin, corresponding to the Alexandrian Greek, ὁδῷ αὐτοῦ, ‘in his way,’ instead of αὐτῷ, ‘to him.’]

“But if you have secretly shown partiality to persons, will not his condemnation terrify you, and will not his fear fall upon you? Your boasting will be ashes, and your body will be clay.

“Be silent, so that I may speak + myself ** and rest from anger, taking my flesh in my teeth and placing my life in my hand. [Note: The pronoun ‘my’ appears to need supplying; it is present in both the Hebrew and Greek text.] Though he who is mighty should kill me, because [Al. ‘he who’] he has also begun, nevertheless I will speak and rebuke him before his face, and this will become salvation for me. For deceit will not enter before him.

“Hear, hear my words, which I shall recount to you while you listen. Behold, I draw near to my judgment. I know that I shall be found righteous. Who is he who will be judged with me? + so that I may now be silent and cease. ** Grant me two things + then I shall not hide myself from your face **: withdraw your hand from me, and let your terror not frighten me. Then you will call, and I will answer; you will speak, and I will reply to you. How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make them known to me. Why do you hide from me? Or do you think me your adversary, and do you fear me as a leaf moved by the wind? Or are you hostile to me as to hay that is carried away? For you have written bitter things against me, laid upon me the sins of my youth, put my foot in fetters [Al. fetters], and watched all my deeds. You have examined the roots of my feet, while I grow old like a wineskin or like a garment eaten by moths.

## [Chapter XIV]

“For a human being, born of woman, is short-lived and full of anger; like a flower, when it has blossomed, he falls, and he flees like a shadow and does not remain. Have you not also cared for him and brought him to judgment before you? For who will be clean from defilement? Not even one, even if his life should have been but a single day. [Note: Here we found an asterisk in place of an obelus, through the copyist’s ignorance. Who could be unaware that Jerome marked with obeli, not asterisks, what was read in the Septuagint but absent from the Hebrew scrolls? We therefore readily permit ourselves similar corrections and changes wherever we are certain what derives from Jerome and what from sleepy copyists in the Latin manuscripts. MART.] + upon the earth. ** For his months have been counted [Note: The Septuagint has ‘with him’ or ‘from him,’ παρά αὐτοῦ, but the manuscript more correctly has ‘with you,’ according to the Hebrew *ittach*, that is, ‘with you’ or ‘before you.’ MART.] before you. You have appointed his time, and it does not pass.

“Withdraw from him; let him rest and enjoy his day as a hired laborer. [Note: Olympiodorus notes that some copies read: ‘Withdraw from me, so that I may rest and be content with food or wages, like a hired laborer.’ MART.] There is hope for a tree: if it is cut down, it will flower again, and its shoot will not fail. For if its root has grown old in the earth, [Note: Polychronius says that the Hebrew has ‘in ashes’ rather than ‘in the rock,’ as required by the continuation of the preceding verse and by the nature of the matter itself. Aquila has ‘in dust’ and Theodotion ‘in earth,’ agreeing with the Hebrew source; for the word ῥάδαμνος, ‘shoot,’ they rendered κορμός, that is, ‘trunk,’ instead of ‘sprout.’ Again, the Greek says ‘will make a harvest’ at the end, while the Hebrew, attending to the matter itself, says ‘will produce fruit.’ In both cases the sense is the same. The manuscript agrees with the Hebrew in the final expression, ‘will produce fruit.’ MART.] and its trunk has died in the rock, it will flower at the scent of water and produce fruit like a young plant.

“But when a man dies, he departs; and when a human being falls, he is no more. For in time the sea diminishes, the river is abandoned and dries up. A human being, when he sleeps, will not rise again. As long as heaven exists, it will not be stitched together, + and he will not be raised from his sleep. ** Would that you would keep me in the underworld, hide me until your anger should rest, and appoint me a time when you would remember me! For if a human being dies, will he live again after the days of his life have been completed? I will wait until I do it again; then you will call, and I will answer you. Do not reject the works of your hands. You have counted my thoughts, and nothing of my sins has escaped you. You have sealed my iniquities in a pouch; you have marked down if I have erred unwillingly.

“And indeed [Al. ‘certainly’] a falling mountain flows away, + and a rock grows old in its place. [Note: Here too we have restored the marks of the asterisks and the terminal points, as often elsewhere.] Stones are worn away by water, + and by the flooding of frequent torrents the sand of the earth is diminished, ** but you have destroyed the hope of a human being. For you have driven him to the end, and he has departed; you have changed his face and dismissed him. When his children are many, he does not know; and if they are few, he does not know + about them. ** But his flesh [Note: Here the copyist had placed an obelus, ÷, instead of an asterisk, +, through an obvious error; we have corrected it according to the Hebrew manuscript. It should also be noted that in the following phrase, ‘upon him,’ no mark appears in the Alexandrian manuscript at the end of this chapter, although these words are not found in the Roman edition of the Septuagint. MART.] + upon him [Note: Martianus had joined these words after inserting a point: ‘upon him. They melted,’ which is not satisfactory.] will ache over him, and his soul will grieve over him.”

## Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

## [Chapter XV]

“Will a wise man answer with a spirit of knowledge and fill his belly with sorrow, reproving with words that are unsuitable, with speeches that will be of no benefit + in them? Have you not rejected fear and spoken such words before the Lord’s presence? For you are guilty because of the words of your mouth, and you have chosen the tongue of the wicked. Let your own mouth, not I, condemn you, and let your lips contradict you.

“What? Were you the first human being born, or were you formed before the hills? [Note: Olympiodorus and Polychronius, in the chain of the Greek Fathers, read: ‘Nor were you formed before the hills,’ or, as the Hebrew has, ‘conceived.’ ‘Nor did you hear the Lord’s constitution,’ for which Aquila has ‘secrets,’ Theodotion ‘mystery,’ and Symmachus more clearly ‘conversation.’ Jerome agrees with Aquila when he translates, ‘or did you hear the secrets of the Lord,’ and so forth. MART.] Or did you hear the secrets of the Lord, or is wisdom found only in you? What do you know that we do not know, or what do you understand that is not also with us? + Yet both the aged and the very old are among us, + older than your father’s days.

“Have you committed so little sin, and have you been wounded so grievously? ** You have spoken with excessive arrogance. What did your heart dare, and what did your eyes endure, that you broke out in fury against the Lord and uttered such words from your mouth? [Col. 0081C] For what is a human being, that he should be without guilt, or that one born of woman should be righteous? If there is no faith in his holy ones + ** and heaven is not clean before him, how much more abominable is a man who drinks iniquity like water!

“I shall tell you; listen to me. I shall declare what I have seen, what the wise have said and have not concealed from their fathers. To them alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them. All the life of the wicked is in solitude; the numbered years allotted to the mighty are filled with fear in his ears. When he thinks that he is already at peace, then destruction will come upon him. He does not believe that he will return from darkness. For he has already been delivered into the hands of iron and appointed as food for vultures, and he knows within himself that he is being kept for ruin.

“The day of darkness will terrify him. Distress and tribulation will hold him. Like a commander in the front line, he will fall—[Note: Augustine asks about *qui*, ‘who’; the Greek supports the neuter, because it has ὅτι, ‘because.’] he who raised his hands against the Lord [Al. God], who was rebellious against the Lord Almighty, and ran insolently against him + with the thick neck of his shield, + because [Note: The Hebrew has ‘heart,’ as though it said: ‘The faculty of the soul has been blinded by visible luxury and delights.’ Instead of *peristomium* [manuscript: *capistrum*], it has ‘fatness’ and ‘double cloak,’ and so forth. Thus Olympiodorus in the chain of the Greek Fathers. MART.] he covered his face with his fat + and made a bridle over his thighs.

“Let him dwell in deserted cities and enter houses that are uninhabited. For what he prepared, others will take away, and he will not become rich, nor will his substance remain. He will not cast a shadow upon the earth, nor will he escape darkness; rather, the wind will dry up his branch, and his flower will fall. Let him not hope that he will endure, for empty things will come upon him. His cutting off will decay before its time, and his shoot will not be seen. He will be harvested like an unripe grape before its time; let him fall like the flower of an olive tree. For the testimony of the wicked is death, and fire will consume the houses of those who accept gifts. He will conceive groaning in his womb; empty things will come upon him, and his belly will bear deceit.”

[Note: These words are omitted in the manuscript, where the copyist left enough blank space to write them in red ink and capital letters. We see the same practice in other manuscripts, for many frequently lack headings and initial letters. MART.]

## Job answered and said:

## [Chapter XVI]

“I have heard many such things. All are comforters of evils. [Note: We have restored this according to the Greek exemplar and Augustine’s reading, ‘all of you are comforters of evils,’ instead of ‘you are all evil comforters.’ —Aquila, says Olympiodorus, has ‘comforters of troubles’; Theodotion, ‘comforters of vexations’; Symmachus renders it more clearly: ‘You are all hateful comforters.’ MART.]

“What then? ** Is there order in the words of the spirit? + Or what will trouble you if you answer? ** And I shall speak as you do [Al. ‘I speak’]. If your soul were in place of mine, I would speak to you in words and shake my head over you. There would be strength in my mouth; I would move my lips and would not spare you.

“For if I speak, I will not grieve over my wound. [Note: Martianus had falsely read ‘I will not erase my wounds,’ instead of ‘I will not grieve over my wound,’ according to the Greek οὐκ ἀλγήσω τὸ τραῦμά μου, as Saint Augustine also reads it.] But if I am silent, I shall nevertheless be pierced. Now pain has wearied me [Note: The noun ‘pain,’ which is not properly present in the Greek, is not known even to Augustine]; you have made me foolish and corrupt; + you have seized me, and I have been made a witness, + and my lie has risen against me, + it will answer against my face. [Note: Augustine has ‘I answered,’ and more correctly omits the adverb ‘then’; he also reads ‘he cast me down’ in accordance with the Greek μετέβαλλέ με, as we have restored it. Martianus had printed ‘he failed me’ from his corrupt manuscript, with almost no sense. MART.]

“For he used anger and cast me down; he gnashed his teeth against me. His pirates’ arrows fell upon me; with the sharpness of his eyes he rushed upon me. He struck me severely [Note: I would prefer ‘on the cheeks,’ which the Hebrew also favors, and I could readily suppose that Origen’s exemplar once also had εἰς σιαγόνια, ‘on the cheeks.’ Yet since Augustine too found ‘on the knees’ in his Latin manuscript, and the Greek has εἰς τὰ γόνατα, ‘on the knees,’ it is more faithful to suppose that from Jerome’s time the Greek words εἰς σιαγόνια had been corrupted by copyists, because of the similarity of the letters, into εἰς τὰ γόνατα, and that Saint Augustine used such an exemplar, since there was scarcely any loss of good sense. Accordingly, although we had long resolved to restore ‘on the cheeks,’ we have finally approved Augustine’s reading more strongly. The reading which Martianus printed from his manuscript as one word, *ingens*, whether intended for *in genas* (‘on the cheeks’) or *in gentibus* (‘among the nations’), is plainly corrupt and false through the carelessness of scribes.] on the knees, and they rushed together against me.

“For the Lord delivered me into the hands of the wicked and cast me among the impious. When I was at peace, he tore me apart; he seized my hair and pulled it out [Al. tore it away]. He set me up like a target. [Note: Martianus’s reading, ‘they surrounded me with spears,’ was again plainly erroneous. We have corrected it on Augustine’s testimony and with the continual support of the Greek text, ἐκύκλωσάν με λόγχαις, ‘they surrounded me with spears.’] They surrounded me with spears, shooting into my kidneys, and they did not spare me. They poured out my gall upon the earth and cast me down with a great prostration.

“The powerful ran at me; they sewed sackcloth onto my skin. [Note: Martianus had wrongly marked this verse, ‘For my strength has been extinguished in the earth,’ with an obelus, as though it were a Greek addition absent from the Hebrew archetype. Yet it is a most splendid sentence in the Hebrew, literally: ‘And he weakened my horn in the dust,’ which the Greeks more suitably render, Τὸ δὲ σθένος μου εἰς γῆν ἐσβέσθη, ‘My strength has been extinguished in the earth.’ We have therefore removed the obelus in accordance with the Hebrew text.] For my strength has been extinguished in the earth; my belly has been burned by weeping, and the shadow of death is upon my eyelids. [Note: The word ‘of death’ appears to require an asterisk according to the Alexandrian manuscript.] There was no iniquity in my hands, but my prayer was pure.

“May the earth not cover the blood of my flesh, and may there be no place for my cry. And now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my confidant is on high. May my supplication ascend to the Lord, and may my eye drip tears before him. Let a man be judged with the Lord + as a human being’s son with his neighbor. ** For my years have been counted, and I shall enter a way from which I shall not return [Al. ‘through which I shall not return’].

## [Chapter XVII]

“I am exhausted and troubled in spirit. I ask to be buried, and it does not happen for me. I offer prayers with difficulty. And what have I done? Outsiders have stolen my goods. + Who is this? Let him be bound to my hand. + Because you have hidden their heart from prudence, + for this reason you will not exalt them +. Let evils be announced to a portion, and let their eyes grow faint over their children. [Note: Martianus has ‘they are announced,’ less suitably, and he had omitted the final asterisk, which we have supplied. MART.]

“But you have made me a byword among the nations, and I have become a laughingstock to them. My eyes have been darkened by anger [Al. ‘on account of anger’], and I have been greatly assaulted by all; yet the truthful have marveled at this. Let the righteous rise against the enemy and let the faithful hold to his way. [Col. 0084A] Let the pure of hands take courage.

“Therefore turn, all of you, and come. For I do not find truth in you. [Note: Augustine’s manuscript less suitably has ‘he found truth in you.’ A little later, it has ‘shaken’ instead of ‘tossed about.’] My days have passed in calamities, and the joints of my heart have been shaken. They have turned night into day; light is near the face of darkness. If I wait, the underworld will be my house. In darkness my bed has been spread. I have called corruption my father, and my mother and sister, the worm. What hope do I have now? Or shall I see my good things? Or will they descend with me to the underworld? Or shall we descend together into ashes?”

## Baldad the Shuhite answered and said:

## [Chapter XVIII]

“How long will you not be silent? Restrain yourself, so that we too may speak. Why have we been silent before you like four-footed creatures? Anger abuses you. What then? [Col. 0084B] If you should die, would no one dwell under heaven? Or would the mountains be overturned from their foundations, and the light of the wicked extinguished, so that their flame would no longer shine? His light will be darkness in his house, and the lamp over him will be extinguished.

“Let the least take his substance captive. [Note: Saint Augustine has ‘let them receive,’ which means the same. But the reading ‘the least,’ which we have found, instead of Martianus’s corrupt ‘the weak,’ must be supported by his testimony and by the Greek text, ἐλάχιστοι; several minor corrections below are made according to it.] Let his counsel go astray. For his foot has been thrown into a snare, and he will be entangled in a net. Let snares come upon him; + he will strengthen [Al. ‘strengthened’] those thirsting for him **. His cord is hidden upon the earth, + and his trap is on the path [Al. paths]. All around, ** let pains destroy him, and let many come in anguish of hunger around his feet. For great ruin has been prepared for him. Let the branches of his feet be eaten, and let ripe death devour his beauty + **.

“Let health be torn from his dwelling, and let royal necessity seize him. + Let him dwell in his tent, [Note: Olympiodorus not without reason noted the following: Some copies have ‘in his night’ instead of ‘in his tent’; others have ‘in his body.’ Theodotion has: ‘Poverty of all things will dwell in his tent.’ The Hebrew, saying something more, has: ‘He will dwell in tents not his own,’ that is, he will live as a wanderer in other men’s houses. Those who interpret ‘in his night,’ removing the *mem* from the current Hebrew *mibbeli-lo*, read *ballajelo*, which means ‘in his night.’ MART.] in his night. + His beautiful things will be sprinkled with sulfur. + His roots below will dry up, + and from above his harvest will rush down. ** May his memory perish from the earth [Note: We restored the preceding three asterisks, with the terminal point added after the heavier punctuation, according to the rule of the Alexandrian manuscript, where this asterisk is prefixed only to the negative particle *non*, ‘not.’ This, it seems, is what we wished merely to point out. After the word ‘streets,’ Augustine adds ‘where it was,’ but these words are found in no original text. MART.] + and may his name not be upon the face of the streets. Let him be driven from light into darkness, and let him not be recognized among his people; nor let his house be restored beneath heaven, but let others live among his people. The least have generated against him, and astonishment has seized the great. These are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of those who do not know God.”

## Job answered and said:

## [Chapter XIX]

“How long will you weary my soul and destroy me with words? Know only that the Lord [Al. God] has done this to me. [Note: Instead of ‘you tear me away,’ Martianus found ‘you drag me ten times’ in his manuscript, which he himself rejected.] You tear me away, and you are not ashamed to press upon me. But suppose that I truly have erred, and that error dwells with me—+ so that I spoke a word I should not have spoken, + and my words were, but are no longer, timely. ** Why then do you exalt yourselves against me and reproach me with disgrace?

“Know therefore that it is the Lord [Col. 0085B] who has troubled me and surrounded me with his rampart. Behold, [Note: We freed the words ‘I laugh at reproaches, and I will not speak,’ which were plainly and undeservedly pierced by Martianus with an obelus, since they are clearly present in the Hebrew, literally: ‘I will cry out reproaches, and I will not be heard.’ The Greeks translated them somewhat more freely: γελῶ (or λαλῶ) ὀνείδη, καὶ οὐ λαλήσω, ‘I will laugh at—or speak—reproaches, and I will not speak.’ We then corrected Martianus’s own reading: he had read *rideor*, ‘I am laughed at,’ instead of *rideo*, ‘I laugh,’ which produces almost the opposite sense; and *opprobrio*, ‘with reproach,’ instead of *opprobria*, ‘reproaches,’ although the two amount to the same thing, and some Greek copies likewise read ὀνείδη instead of ὀνείδει. Augustine’s reading is preferable; he also has ‘I speak’ at this point instead of ‘I will speak.] I laugh at reproaches and will not speak; I will cry out, and there is judgment nowhere.

[Note: An obelus, ÷, had been placed here instead of an asterisk, +. Martianus substituted an asterisk from his own copy for the false obelus in the manuscript. We think it better, according to the Alexandrian manuscript, to remove both marks. MART.]

“I am surrounded and cannot go on. He has put darkness upon my face; he has stripped me of glory, removed the crown from my head, torn me apart on every side, and [Note: Martianus had falsely read ‘he departed.’ All books have the first person, as we have restored it.] I departed. He cut off my hope like a tree. He used me most savagely in anger and regarded me as an enemy. His trials came together; + they made their way through me, + and they surrounded my tent. ** My brothers have withdrawn. They have recognized strangers more than me, and my friends have become merciless. My neighbors did not care for me, and those who knew my name forgot me. The neighbors of my house and my maidservants + regarded me as a stranger; + I was foreign in their sight. I called my servant, and he did not answer. My mouth pleaded, and I begged my wife. I called upon [Al. ‘he called upon’], flattering, ÷ the children + of my womb, ** and they despised me forever. When I rise, they speak to me. Those who knew me abhorred me, and those whom I loved rose up against me.

“My flesh has rotted on my skin, and my bones are in my teeth. Have pity on me, have pity on me, my friends! For the hand of the Lord has touched me. Why do you persecute me as the Lord does? Are you not satisfied with my flesh?

“Who will grant me that my words may be written and placed forever in a book, + with an iron stylus ** and lead; or + as a testimony [Al. ‘of testimony’] ** may they be carved in rocks? For I know that he who will release me is eternal. Upon the earth my skin, which suffers these things, will rise again. For these things have come upon me from the Lord; I am conscious of them, which my eye has seen and no other, and all these things have been completed for me in my bosom.

“Even if you say, ‘What shall we say against him? Shall we find the root of the word in him?’ Fear the sword yourselves +. For wrath will come upon the wicked, and then you will know + that there is judgment.”

## Sophar the Naamathite answered and said:

[Note: The heading ‘SOPHAR MINAEUS’ was omitted in the manuscript through the copyist’s carelessness; we have supplied it from the Septuagint, which calls him the Minaean instead of the Naamathite. MART.]

## [Chapter XX]

“I did not expect you to answer these things in this way. Nor do you understand [Al. ‘understand not’] more than I do. [Note: Martianus reads the singular ‘you understand’; the Greek and Augustine, whom we follow, have the plural.] + I shall hear the instruction of my confusion, + and the spirit of wisdom will answer me. + Do you know this from ancient times, from when the human being was placed upon the earth?

“The joy of the wicked is great ruin, and the gladness of the lawless is destruction. If his gifts ascend to heaven and his sacrifice touches the clouds, [Note: These words are not marked with an obelus because nothing in the Hebrew corresponds to them; rather, the Hebrew contains the same thought in a single word, כְּזֶבֶל, ‘like dung.’ Jerome translated it ‘like a dung heap.’ The Greeks, however, seem to have read the passage differently, and therefore do not mark it with an obelus in the Alexandrian manuscript.] ÷ when he thinks that he is already secure, ** in the end he will perish; and those who knew him will say, ‘Where is he?’ Like a sound flying away, he will appear nowhere; he will fly away like a nocturnal phantom.

“An eye will see him, and will not add to it, + and his place will no longer behold him. + May the wicked destroy his children, + and may his hands be set on fire [Al. ‘his hand be set on fire’] with pains. + His bones are full of his youth, + and with him they will sleep in the ashes. + If wickedness is sweet in his mouth, + he will hide it beneath his tongue. He will spare it and not abandon it; he will hold it in the middle of his throat, and he will not be able to help himself. The gall of asps is in his belly. Ill-gotten riches will be vomited out.

“An angel will drag him from his house, [Note: This reading of nearly all the Greek copies, including the Hexaplaric copies from which Jerome translated—ἐξ οἰκίας, ‘from the house’—has been corrupted by copyists, whether through carelessness or misguided correction, in place of ἐκ κοιλίας, ‘from the belly,’ corresponding to the Hebrew בטן, which Jerome himself knew from his translation out of the Hebrew. Olympiodorus likewise states here that the other translators rendered it ἐκ γαστρός, ‘from the belly.’ MART.] [Col. 0087A] and [Note: The copy used by Augustine less suitably has ‘the fury of dragons will shine’; nor was ‘he will soothe’ satisfactory here. We have changed it to ‘he will milk,’ as the sense requires; the Greek is θηλάσει. Shortly afterward, we have restored ‘milking trough’ from Augustine instead of ‘milking.’ MART.] he will milk the fury of dragons. Let the tongue of the serpent kill him; let him not see the milking trough of cattle, nor the pastures of honey and butter.

“He labored for riches in vain and without purpose, riches of which he will not taste—things that will be expelled like something hard, which cannot be chewed or swallowed. For he has broken down the houses of many strong men, destroyed dwellings, and not rebuilt them.

“There is no safety for his substance. + He will not be saved by his desire. + No remnants of food will remain; therefore his prosperity will not flourish. ** When he thinks that he is filled, he will be constricted, and every necessity will come upon him. If he fills his belly in any way, he will send forth against him the fury of wrath. He will rain anguish upon him, and he will not escape the hand of the sword. Let a bronze arrow wound him and a missile pierce [Col. 0087B] his body. [Note: Here the asterisk was changed into an obelus because, through the copyist’s ignorance or carelessness, this sign + had been placed in the manuscript instead of ÷; we have substituted the latter. MART.] ÷ ** Let lightning fall upon his dwellings [Al. tents], + let it run over him terribly, and let all darkness remain in him. Let an inextinguishable fire consume him; let the stranger injure his house and let heaven reveal his iniquities. Let the earth oppose him; let destruction drag his house to the end. Let the day of wrath overtake him.

“This is the portion of the wicked man from the Lord, and the inheritance of his possessions from the overseer.”

## Job answered and said:

### [Chapter XXI]

“Listen, listen to my words, and let this consolation from you not be a consolation to me. Bear with me, and I shall speak; then, at last, you will laugh at me. What then? Is my rebuke human? Or why should I not be angry? Look at me, and be astonished, and put your hand beneath your chin. For if I remember, I am troubled, and my flesh is seized by pains.

“Why do the impious live and grow old in riches? [Col. 0087C] Their offspring are according to the ÷ desire [Note: [Col. 0087D] I would prefer to pierce with a single obelus the word *desire*, but not also the following word *soul*. I conjecture, however, that the Seventy read the Hebrew differently and, instead of [uncertain Hebrew], meaning ‘before them,’ read a very similar spelling [uncertain Hebrew], which they translated κατὰ ψυχὴν, ‘according to the soul’; for they do not seem otherwise able to have devised the word *soul* here.] of their soul ** and their descendants are before their eyes. Their houses are abundant, and there is no fear anywhere, nor is the scourge of the Lord upon them. Their cows conceive and do not miscarry; [Col. 0088A] their herd is safe and gives birth. + And they send forth their young like [Note: [Col. 0087D] If I am not mistaken, the copyist omitted the word *cattle* or *flocks*, which is read in the Hebrew; without this word the sense is nonexistent or incomplete. Moreover, the second asterisk in this verse may seem superfluous, since this entire sentence, added from the Hebrew books to the Septuagint translation, is sufficiently marked by a single asterisk. MART. —The passage marked here by two asterisks is not preserved in the Greek copy. Martianaeus has learnedly observed that the word *cattle* or *flocks* seems to have dropped out, a word which corresponds to the Hebrew, and without which the sense is nonexistent or incomplete. He also rightly observed that this sentence, added from the Hebrew—or from Theodotion—to the Septuagint edition, could be indicated by a single asterisk. In place of *their old sheep*, Augustine appears to have read, from an apparently uncorrected manuscript, *sheep grown old*.] + their young **, and they remain like their old sheep. Their little ones provoke one another to play. They hold the psaltery and the lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. ** And they finish their life in good things, and sleep in the repose of the underworld.

“But they say to the Lord, ‘Depart from us. We do not wish to know your ways. + What is the Lord, that we should serve him? + Or what advantage is there, that [Note: [Col. 0088D] From the Greek word ἀπαντήσωμεν, *let us meet him*, I conjecture that *we shall obey him* is an error of the Latin copyists for *we shall meet him*, the writing of which is nearly similar. Augustine passes over this passage.] we should obey him?’ ** Yet good things were in their hands. But he does not regard the works of the impious. Rather, the lamp of the impious will be extinguished, and destruction will come upon them. Pains will hold them because of wrath, and they will be like straw in the wind, and like dust carried away by a whirlwind. [Note: [Col. 0088D] The name *God*, which is still lacking in the Greek, appears to require an asterisk. We correct certain other minor matters below.]

“God, may his children + lack ** his goods. Repay him, and he will know. May his eyes see his own death, and may he not be saved by the Lord. + For there is no desire of his in his house after him, + even though the number of his months has been cut in half. Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge? Is it not he himself who judges even murderers? + Here ** he will die in the strength of his simplicity, wholly in abundance and prosperity. His inward parts are full of fat, and their marrow is diffused.

“But another dies in the bitterness of his soul, eating nothing good. And together they will sleep in the earth, and corruption will cover them.

“Therefore I know that you boldly press me, + because you say, ‘Where is the house of the prince, + and where is the covering in the tents of the impious?’ + Ask those who pass along the road, + and you will not fail to recognize their signs. + For the wicked man is spared on the day of destruction, + and they are led to the day of wrath. + Who will announce his way before him, + and who will repay him for what he himself has done? + He too has been led to the graves [another reading: *grave*], + and he kept watch over the burial mound. + The pebbles [another reading: *stones*] of the torrent were sweet to him, + and after him every person follows, + and before him are countless others.

“How then do you console me in vain? For there is no rest for me from you.” [Col. 0088C]

### ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### [Chapter XXII]

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding [Note: [Col. 0089C] This passage diverges considerably from the Hebrew. The Greek, however, does not preserve the words that follow under the asterisk. Compare the two texts; we have supplied the terminal points immediately.] and knowledge, + and makes understanding dwell above us? ** For what does it concern the Lord if you are in works + without guilt? ** Or what benefit is it to him that your way is blameless? Or will one who fears you rebuke you, and will he come with you into judgment?

“Is not your wickedness [Note: [Col. 0089C] The words marked under the asterisk are read in the Hebrew. The obelus ÷ was therefore wrongly placed in the manuscript in place of the asterisk +. MART. —The manuscript of Martianaeus also retained the obelus that we restore here, and rightly so: it marks one word, *is*. Since he failed to notice this, he replaced the deleted word with an asterisk, contrary to the intention of the holy Translator. Shortly afterward we supplied the terminal points after the asterisk, which applies only to the adverb *because*.] ÷ is ** great, and your sins innumerable? + Because ** you took your brothers’ pledge without cause, and stripped the poor of their clothing; you did not give water to the thirsty, and you deprived the hungry of bread. [Note: [Col. 0089C] The order of these verses is reversed in the Septuagint. [Col. 0089D] MART.] You caused someone to dwell upon the earth, or did you show regard for anyone’s person? You sent widows away empty, and crushed orphans.

“Therefore snares surrounded you, and a great war crushed you. Your light has been turned into darkness [Note: [Col. 0089D] Martianaeus has it incorrectly as *in darkness*. Below, several minor points are corrected from Augustine.] ; water covered you while you slept. [Col. 0089B] Is it not he who dwells on high who looks down and humbles those who commit injustice? And you said, ‘What does God know? Does he judge through the clouds [another reading: *distinguish*]? + Clouds are his hiding place, and he will not be seen. + He travels around the circuit of heaven. + Do you then keep watch over the path of the age + which wicked men have trodden, + men who were taken prematurely? Their foundations are those of a flowing river. ** They say, ‘What will the Lord do to us, or what will the Almighty bring upon us?’ Yet he himself filled their houses with good things. And the thought of the impious is far from him.

“The righteous saw this [Note: [Col. 0089D] Augustine has, very corruptly, *the more righteous will be*, contrary to the Greek text, Ἰδόντες δίκαιοι ἐγέλασαν, ‘the righteous saw and laughed’.] and laughed, and the blameless mocked them. + Has not their substance been destroyed, + and has not fire consumed their remnants? ** Be firm [Note: [Col. 0089D] Here *firm* means steadfast and patient, not soft or effeminate.] ; if you endure [Note: [Col. 0089D] Saint Augustine adds *patient*, which is not found in the Greek. Its origin can be understood from an old scholion written in the margin of the book.] , then your fruit will be good. Receive rather the decree from his mouth, and take his words into your heart. If you return and humble yourself before the Lord, you will remove injustice far from your tent. + And you will place it upon a mound, upon a rock, + [Note: [Col. 0089D] The damaged Alexandrian edition places no asterisks here. Augustine reads *placing* rather than *you will place*; finally, where the Latin has *and in the rocks*, the Greek has *and as rocks*, or *as a rock*, καὶ ὡς πέτρα.] and upon the rocks of the torrent of Ophir.

“The Almighty will be your helper against your enemies, and he will make you like pure silver tested by fire. Then you will have confidence before the Lord, receiving heaven with gladness. When you pray to him, he will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows. He will restore to you the conduct of righteousness, + and in your ways there will be light ** [Note: [Col. 0089D] The words marked here with obeli are found in the Hebrew; therefore the copyist wrongly inserted such obeluses, whose use is pointless when the sentences exist in the Hebrew source. The asterisks + may have stood in Jerome’s text, not obeli ÷. MART. —We have removed, on the authority of other books, the obeli prefixed to this and the following paired clause; they are plainly false and were themselves disapproved by Martianaeus. On Augustine’s testimony we have also restored *he was lifted up in pride*, in place of Martianaeus’s *you were lifted up in pride*. The recent corrected edition of the Alexandrian codex has ὑπερηφανεύσατο, ‘he became proud’; the following clause, *and he will save the one who is downcast in his eyes*, is marked with an asterisk.] because he humbled himself, and you will say, ‘He was lifted up in pride.’ And he will save the one who is downcast in his eyes. Rescue the innocent, and you will be saved through the purity of your hands.” [Col. 0090A]

### JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### [Chapter XXIII]

“Indeed I know that the rebuke comes from my hand, and that his hand has become heavy upon my groaning. [Note: [Col. 0090C] Augustine incorrectly has *my hand*, instead of *his*.] Who will make me know and find him, and come as far as his throne, so that I may set forth my case before him, fill my mouth with accusations, and learn the arguments he will speak to me, and understand what he announces to me? Will he contend with me in great strength? Certainly not. [Another reading: *Nevertheless.*] Only let him not abuse me with terror. For truth and rebuke come from him. He brings my judgment to its end.

“For even if I go first, I shall no longer be. And at the end, how shall I know + him? + [Note: [Col. 0090D] On Augustine’s testimony we have restored, *What will he do on the left?*, which gives a more coherent sense and is especially supported by the Greek, Ἀριστερὰ ποιήσαντος αὐτοῦ. Martianaeus, using the first person and even an interrogative mark, had read, *What shall I do on the left?*] What will he do on the left? I shall not apprehend him. + He will turn to the right, and I shall not see **; but he himself knows my way, and [Note: [Col. 0090D] Martianaeus incorrectly had the future *will test*, which, with Augustine’s agreement, we have corrected to *he tested*, from the Greek διέκρινε. We silently correct other minor matters above and below.] he tested me like gold.

“I shall go forth in his commandments. + My foot held fast to [Note: [Col. 0090D] This passage seems to require restoration according to the Greek, with the terminal points supplied here and a new στοιχεῖον, or textual unit, beginning thereafter: *I kept his ways; I shall not turn aside*, etc. Ὁδούς γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἐφύλαξα, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐκκλινῶ.] his ways. I kept watch; I shall not turn aside. I shall not depart from his commandments. In my bosom I have hidden his words.

“But if he himself judges in this way, who is there that can contradict him? For whatever he wished, he also did [Note: [Col. 0090D] The fourteenth full verse, which the holy Father translated from the Hebrew as, *when he has fulfilled his will in me*, and many similar words, is absent both from the Greek exemplar and from this Latin version.] . Therefore I hastened to him, and, being admonished, I was anxious about him [Note: [Col. 0091C] This passage, marked with asterisks, is another version of the immediately preceding fifteenth verse; it is a double translation, as will become clear from comparison with the Hebrew archetype. It would therefore more properly have been marked with obeli, unless it also possessed asterisks in the Greek.] +. Therefore I shall be troubled at his presence. I will consider him and fear him **. And the Lord has softened my heart, and the Almighty has troubled me. For I did not know that darkness would come upon me, and that obscurity would cover my face. [Col. 0091D]

### [Chapter XXIV]

“Why have the times not been hidden from the Lord, while the impious have not known his days? They have crossed the limits. Seizing the flock with the shepherd, + they prepared **; they drove away the orphan’s animal and took the widow’s ox in pledge. They turned the poor aside from the right way ÷, ** and the meek of the earth hid themselves together. And they rushed upon me + like wild asses ** in the field, going out to their work. [Col. 0091D]

“Bread became sweet to them in their youth ** [Note: [Col. 0091D] The clause *They reaped a field before its time*, etc., is not found in the Greek Alexandrian codex and therefore appears to require an asterisk. What follows, *They cultivated the vines of the weak*, diverges considerably from the Hebrew; but there is no room here to pursue the matter.] They reaped a field that was not theirs before the proper time. They cultivated the vines of the impious without payment and without food. They caused many naked people to sleep without clothing, and took away their covering in the cold. + They became wet from the mountain drip **; since they had no covering, they were covered by the rock. They snatched the orphan from the breast, and humbled the one who had fallen. They unjustly made the naked sleep, and took away the bread of the hungry. They lay unjust ambushes in narrow places, but they did not know the way of justice.

“By force they were driven from the city and from their houses [Note: [Col. 0091D] Augustine also omits the little word *by force*, which the Greek likewise does not properly have.] . The souls of the little ones were in great lamentation. Yet did God himself not take care of them? Though they were upon the earth and did not know the way of justice, they did not walk in his paths. Knowing their deeds, he handed them over to darkness.

+ And at night he will be like a thief. + The eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, + saying, ‘No eye will see me,’ + and he placed a hiding place for his face. + He digs beneath houses in darkness. By day they seal themselves up. + They did not know the light, + because morning is, together with them, the shadow of death [Note: [Col. 0091D] Augustine incorrectly has *remains*; *in the morning* is to be read.] [Note: [Col. 0091D] Another half-verse seems to require supplementation. Because of the repetition of the words *shadow of death*, it may easily have fallen out of the Latin manuscript. It is clearly present not only in the Greek, ὅτι ἐπιγνώσεται ταραχὰς σκιᾶς θανάτου, but also in the Hebrew. From the Greek it can be translated almost word for word and supplied after the asterisk: *because he will know the troubles of the shadow of death*. Martianaeus had incorrectly read the following word *light* in another sense.] + he is light upon the face of the water **. Let their portion be cursed upon the earth. Let their plantations appear dry upon the earth. For they seized from the bosom of orphans. Then his sin was remembered. Like a mist of dew, he appeared nowhere.

“Let it be repaid to him as he acted. Let every wicked man be crushed like an incurable tree. For he did not do good to the barren woman, and he did not show mercy to the widow.
