In anger he overthrew the weak. When he rises, therefore, he does not trust his own life. When he begins to grow weak, let him not hope for health, but let him fall [another reading: *he falls*] into sickness. For his exaltation afflicted many. He withered like mallow in the heat, or like an ear of grain falling from the stalk + of its own accord ** [Note: [Col. 0092D] Augustine may have read more accurately, *of its own accord*. The Greek is αὐτόματος. We have supplied the final asterisk from the recent edition of the Alexandrian codex.] . Otherwise, who is there who can speak and make me speak falsely, and reduce my words to nothing?”

### BALDAD THE SAUCHITE ANSWERED AND SAID:

### [Chapter XXV]

“What beginning is there except fear of him who does all things on high? Let no one suppose that there is delay for pirates. Against whom will there not be ambushes from him? Or how will a human being be righteous before the Lord, or how will one born of a woman cleanse himself, if he commands the moon and it does not shine, and the stars are not pure before [another reading: *with*] him? How much more is a human being corruption, or a human son a worm!” [Col. 0092A]

### JOB ANSWERED AND SAID:

### [Chapter XXVI]

“Whom are you helping, or whom will you assist? Is it not the one who has great strength and a strong arm? Whom are you advising? Is it not the one who possesses all wisdom? Or whom are you following? Is it not the one whose strength is great? To whom have you announced words, or whose breath is that which comes forth from you?

+ Will the giants be reduced to nothing + beneath the water, and their neighbors? + The underworld is naked before him, + and there is no covering for destruction. + He stretches the north over nothing +, suspending the earth over nothing (in the air) +, binding it in his clouds, + and the cloud beneath him is not torn [Note: [Col. 0092D] Martianaeus has *from him*; Augustine incorrectly has *the face of the sun*, instead of *of the throne*, Greek θρόνου.] . + He holds the face of the throne + and stretches [another reading: *he stretched*] his cloud over it, + he set a command around the face of the water + until the completion of the light. + The pillars [Note: [Col. 0092D] Here we have removed the word *light*, which neither Augustine nor the other original books recognize; it plainly reveals itself as a gloss rashly intruded from the margin into the text. Moreover, we have supplied asterisks to the individual half-verses and finally added the heavier terminal points which were lacking.] of heaven trembled [another reading: *quaked*] + and were stunned at his rebuke **.

“By his power he calmed the sea. By his understanding the sea-monster was wounded, and the bars of heaven fear him. At his command he killed the deserting dragon. Behold, these are parts of his way [Note: [Col. 0092D] We have removed here the pronoun *his*, falsely repeated and absent from all the other books.] . And we have heard only a drop of his word. But who will understand the power of his thunder, when he acts?” [Col. 0092C]

### JOB ADDED TO HIS PROEMIUM AND SAID:

### [Chapter XXVII]

“As the Lord lives, who has judged me in this way, and the Almighty, who has made my soul bitter: for as long as my breath is in me and the divine spirit is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak injustice, nor shall my soul meditate wickedness. [Col. 0093A]

“Far be it from me to call you righteous until I die. For I shall not remove my innocence [Note: [Col. 0093C] Augustine has *I shall not separate the innocent from me*. In the Greek itself, although *innocence*, or ἀκακία, is preferred, *my* is nevertheless not added.] from me. I will hold fast to my righteousness and will not let it go. For I am not conscious of having committed anything unjust.

“Therefore my enemies are like the overthrow of the impious, and those who rise up against me are like the destruction of the wicked. For what hope is there for the impious, since he waits and trusts in the Lord, in case he might be delivered, or the Lord might hear his prayers? Or if distress comes upon him [another reading: *happens to him*], does he have any confidence in his presence? Or when he calls upon him, will he hear him? [Note: [Col. 0093C] Augustine likewise has *he had confidence*, without *any*; and shortly afterward, *if he calls, he will hear*, without *him*.]

“Therefore I shall announce to you what is in the hand of the Lord. What comes from the Almighty I shall not lie about. Behold, you all know that you speak empty things [Note: [Col. 0093C] We have added *empty things* from Augustine, in accordance with the Greek, which repeats the word with a slightly different sense, κενὰ κενοῖς ἐπιβάλλεσθε. Earlier it had *you speak vainly*. Minor matters are corrected below.] . This is the portion of the impious person from the Lord. The possession of the powerful, however, will come upon them from the Almighty.

“If his sons are many, they will be for slaughter. And if they become young men, they will be in need. Those around him will die by death, and no one will pity their widows [another reading: *their widows will not be pitied*].

“If he gathers silver like earth and prepares gold like clay, the righteous will obtain all these things, and the truthful [Note: [Col. 0093C] The obelus, as very often elsewhere, had been marked in place of an asterisk; we restore the asterisk on the authority of the Hebrew books, where the word *truthful*, or *innocent*, is read. [Col. 0093D] MART.] + will possess his substance **.

“For their houses will be like a moth [another reading: *moths*] and a spider [another reading: *spiders*] that has stored up. The rich man sleeps and will add no more. + He opened his eyes, and he is not. + Pains will meet him like water; + in the night darkness will carry him away. + Heat will take him, and he will depart; + it will toss him from his place ** and cast upon him, and will not spare him. For flight will flee from his hand. He will clap his hands over him and drag him from his place.

### [Chapter XXVIII]

“For silver [another reading: *of silver*] has a place from which it comes, and gold has a place where it is refined. Iron is made from the earth, and bronze is likewise cut out like stone [Note: [Col. 0093D] Augustine has *is mined like stones*; the Greek is ἴσα λίθῳ λατομεῖται, *it is quarried like stone*.] . [Col. 0094A]

“He appointed an order for darkness, + and he himself found every limit, + the stone of darkness and the shadow + of death, + the breaking of the torrent from the ashes **.

“But those who forget the way of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0093D] Previously, and with the opposite sense, the text had *they were strengthened* instead of *they were weakened*. We did not hesitate to restore the latter from the Greek ἠσθένησαν. What follows, *by human beings*, Augustine applies to the subsequent clause, *they were shaken*, which is closer to the Greek.] were weakened by human beings, + and they were shaken. [Note: [Col. 0093D] All the following eight verses, marked with asterisks, are found in Saint Augustine’s *Book of Annotations on Job*. It is therefore certain that Augustine used this translation of Jerome, not the old and Vulgate version, in which seven or eight hundred verses were missing before Jerome’s hand supplied them. MART.]

+ The earth from which bread came forth [Note: [Col. 0093D] We have corrected *beneath* from the Greek ὑποκάτω, in place of Martianaeus’s erroneous reading *above*. Saint Augustine reads differently: ‘and he will burn it.’] + was turned beneath it as if by fire. + The place of sapphire is its stones, + and its gold [Note: [Col. 0094C] Augustine’s reading, *and heaps of gold for him*, is all the more convincing because it adheres more closely to the Greek exemplar, καὶ χῶμα χρυσίον αὐτῷ. It would be tedious to repeat that here, as almost everywhere else, we have restored the asterisks and terminal points to their proper places.] is a heap +. The path which the bird did not know, + nor the vulture’s eye see, + nor the sons of the arrogant tread, + nor the lion pass over it. + Upon the hardest stone he stretched out his hand; + for he overturned mountains from their roots ** and broke apart the banks of rivers. But his eye saw every precious thing [Note: [Col. 0094C] Saint Augustine reads *my eye*, although the Greek text does not support this, having *his*, αὐτοῦ.] ; he uncovered the heights of rivers and displayed his power in the light. [Col. 0094B]

“But where was wisdom found, and what is the place of knowledge? A mortal does not know its way, nor will it be found among human beings. + The abyss said, ‘It is not in me,’ + and the sea said, ‘It is not with me.’ + Gold will not be given ÷ [Note: [Col. 0094C] In the Hebrew we read *Segor*, which Jerome translated as *refined gold*, that is, the purest gold. The Septuagint interpreted it as συγκλεισμόν, *a closure*. The word *closed*, which is not in the Hebrew, was therefore marked with an obelus in the manuscript. MART.] enclosed ** in exchange for it, + and silver will not be weighed as its price. + It will not be inferior to the gold of Ophir, + to precious onyx, or sapphire. + Gold and glass will not be equal to it, + and its exchange will be golden vessels [Note: [Col. 0094D] The text previously had, with the opposite sense, *and there is no exchange*. We restored *and its exchange*, in accordance with the Greek and Augustine. We also supplied several missing asterisks and terminal points.] .

+ And the heights [Note: [Col. 0094D] The manuscript has *heavy*, corruptly, instead of *Gabis*, a Hebrew word; for in Hebrew it is written *ramoth ve-gabis*, that is, *corals and pearl*, as some prefer.] and Gabis will not be remembered. + You will draw wisdom from hidden places. + The topaz of Ethiopia will not be compared with it. + It will not be compared with pure gold. + Where, then, was wisdom found? + And what is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of every human being, + and concealed from the birds of heaven.

+ Destruction and death said, ‘We have heard its glory **.’ The Lord established its way, and he himself knows its place. For he himself sees everything under heaven [Note: [Col. 0094D] Martianaeus incorrectly retained *he completed* from a corrupt manuscript, contrary to the Greek text, ἐφορᾷ, and Augustine’s reading *he sees*, which we restore.] , and he knows what is on the earth—he who made all things: the balances of the winds and the measures of the waters. [Col. 0094D]

“When he made these things, as he saw them, he numbered them [Note: [Col. 0094D] Martianaeus had read, *because he made this, as he saw it and made it*. Since these words diverged considerably from the Greek text and smelled of a glossator’s invention, we preferred Augustine’s reading, *when he made it, he counted it as he saw it*, which is sound enough and corresponds closely to the Greek, Ὅτε ἐποίησεν, οὕτως ἰδὼν ἠρίθμησε.] + and the way of the storm [another reading: *storms*] with voices. + Then he saw it, explained it, prepared it, and investigated it **. [Col. 0095A]

“But he said to the human being: ‘Behold, piety is wisdom, while abstaining from evil is knowledge.’”

### JOB ADDED TO HIS PREFACE, SAYING:

### [Chapter XXIX]

“Who will restore me to the months of former days, in which the Lord guarded me? When his lamp shone over my head [Note: [Col. 0095C] The text previously had, evidently through an error, *thus through*, instead of *over*. We correct it from the Greek ὑπέρ and from other books.] ; when I walked in his light through darkness; when I flourished in my ways; when the Lord looked upon my house [Note: [Col. 0095C] Augustine has *when he looked upon the word of the Lord*, etc. [Col. 0095D] Nevertheless, the Floriac manuscript should be followed, since it reads, in agreement with the present edition, *when the Lord looked upon*, etc. —Thus the Divine Library of Saint Jerome can serve to correct or restore many other passages in Augustine’s writings. MART.] ; when I was in great abundance and my children were around me; when butter flowed along my roads; when my mountains abounded in milk.

“When I went out early into the city [Note: [Col. 0095D] The text had corruptly read *in the mornings into the city*.] , and a seat was set for me in the streets. [Col. 0095B] When young men saw me, they hid themselves, but all the elders rose up [another reading omits *all*], and the powerful ceased speaking, putting a finger to their mouths. When they heard me, they called me blessed, and their tongues clung to their throats; for the ear that heard blessed me, and the eye that saw me turned aside.

“For I delivered the poor from the ÷ hand ** of the powerful [Note: [Col. 0095D] Martianaeus had marked the solid words *from the hand of the powerful* with an obelus, although only the word *hand* is present in the Hebrew, with the others corresponding to it. Although this word has a different meaning from that translated by the Septuagint, it is nevertheless the same word that they rendered by δυνάστου; and, in my opinion, they were deceived by the similarity of the words, which differ from one another by a single letter. We therefore mark only that word with an obelus. Below too, as we often note, we have added terminal points in their proper places to distinguish the ends of the supplied readings.] , and I brought help to the orphan who had no helper. + The blessing of the perishing came upon me **, and the mouth of the widow blessed me.

“I clothed myself in righteousness, and I dressed myself in judgment like a cloak. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the weak. I sought out the judgment I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the unjust and tore plunder from between their teeth. [Col. 0095C]

“For I said, ‘My age will grow old; like a palm tree I shall live for a very long time.’ + My root is spread out by the waters, + and dew will remain upon my harvest. + My glory will be new with me, + and my bow will walk in my hand **.

“Those who heard me looked toward me and kept silent at my counsel; they added nothing to my speech, but rejoiced when I spoke to them. As thirsty earth waits for rain, so they waited for my speech. And when I returned to them, they did not believe it, + and the light of my face did not fall. + I chose their way and sat as prince, + and I dwelt like a king surrounded by warriors, + like one consoling mourners **.” [Col. 0096A]

### Chapter XXX

“But now the least of them mock me; now those younger in age than I admonish me, whose fathers I scorned [Note: Martian., *spernens parentes* (‘scorning their fathers’), nevertheless not without learning observes that another hemistich ought to follow here, approximately in this form: ‘whom I did not consider worthy to be with the dogs of my flocks,’ as it stands in the Greek, Οὓς οὐχ ἡγησάμην ἀξίους εἶναι κυνῶν τῶν ἐμῶν νομάδων (‘whom I did not consider worthy even of the dogs of my flocks’), and that this seems to have fallen out of the Latin manuscript.]; and [Note: Some manuscripts lack certain words, namely, ‘whom I did not consider worthy of the dogs of my flocks,’ or ‘I did not deign to place them with the dogs of my flock.’ These words, however, are not found in the book of Saint Augustine’s *Annotations*; nor can we infer from his exposition of this passage that he read them in his copy. MART.] the strength of their hands was as nothing to me. + In them [Note: Augustine has *in eo* (‘in it’); it was rightly disappearing, instead of which Martianus corruptly had *periebat*. The following asterisk, as well as another shortly afterward in the recent recension of the Codex Alexandrinus, is not actually present; nor do they seem to us to clarify anything except the words immediately preceding them, *In* and *Qui*. A few other minor matters are corrected below, and especially the larger points are placed in their respective locations.] all life was perishing. + In want and hunger they were unstable; those who fled [Note: We have restored this passage, prompted by Saint Augustine, who after the Septuagint reads *heri* (‘yesterday’), not *heremi* (‘of the wilderness’), as the copyist of our manuscript had written. MART.] into the wilderness yesterday [Alternative: of the wilderness] because of straits and miseries. + They gnawed the bark of trees; their food was the root of plants. Dishonored and subjected [Alternative: abject], and lacking every good thing. Those who ate the roots of trees because of great hunger. Thieves rose up against me [Alternative: over me], whose houses were caves of rocks, + and they shouted among the trees ** Those who dwelt beneath the roots of the earth. Sons of fools, [Col. 0096B] + and of the baseborn; their name and honor were extinguished from the earth.

“But now I am their lyre, and they have me as a byword [Alternative: for a byword]. They abhorred me and withdrew far away; nor did they spare my face from spitting. For opening his quiver, he afflicted me; and they put a bridle in my face. They bound my feet with fetters and opened over me the paths of their destruction. My paths were broken up. For he stripped me of my robe and wounded me with his arrows. He used me as he wished. I am wrapped in pains, and my pains are renewed. My hope departs like a breath, and like a cloud + my salvation has passed away ** And now my soul will be poured out over me ** The days of affliction have taken possession of me. At night my bones were broken, and my sinews dissolved. With great force he seized my robe, + and like the hem of my garment he encircled me ** I have regarded myself as clay. My portion is in earth and ashes. But I cried out to you, and you did not hear me. + They stood and looked upon me ** You attacked me without mercy. With a powerful hand you struck me and appointed me to sufferings, + and cast me away from salvation ** For I know that death will crush me. For earth is a house for every mortal.

“And if only I could kill myself, or ask [Note: In Augustine: ‘I would ask another, and he would do it for me.’] another to do this for me! But I wept [Col. 0097A] over every invalid, and sighed when I saw a man in need. I was expecting good things. Behold, days of evils have come upon me instead. + [Note: We have supplied this asterisk and the one that follows according to the practice of the Codex Alexandrinus.] My belly boiled, and it will not be silent. + Days of poverty have taken hold of me ** Groaning, I walked without [Note: The Greek has ἄνευ θυμοῦ or φιμοῦ, that is, ‘without anger’ or ‘without a bridle’; hence I do not know where our text derived *sine silentio* (‘without silence’), unless the passage is corrupt and perhaps *sine confidentia* (‘without confidence’), or something similar, ought to be read. Nor does Augustine correctly have *et stetit* (‘and he stood’) instead of *steti* (‘I stood’), and so forth.] silence, and I stood in the assembly crying out. I became a brother to sirens, and a friend to the daughters of ostriches. My skin became exceedingly black, and my bones + were roasted ** by the heat. My lyre was turned into mourning, and my song into weeping.

### Chapter XXXI

“I made a covenant with my eyes, + [Note: Augustine has a different reading, and more than one clause: ‘that I would not think of a virgin, and I will not think of a virgin.’ Although this is not from the original books, even if he read *cogitabo*, we have judged it preferable on the basis of the Greek συνήσω (‘I will understand’), whereas Martianus read *cogitavi* (‘I thought’).] and I will not think of a virgin. + And what other portion is there from God above, + and the inheritance of the Almighty from the heights? Is not destruction for the unjust, and alienation for those who commit iniquity? ** Does he not himself see my way, and number all my steps?

“If I have walked with mockers, or if my foot hastened to deceit, let him weigh me in a perfectly just balance. But the Lord knows my innocence. If my foot has turned aside from the way, and if my heart has followed my eye. If my hands have touched gifts, may I sow and let others eat my fruits; may I be without a root upon the earth. If my heart has followed a woman, or if I have lain in wait at her doors, may my wife also please another, and may my children be humbled. For it is an unbridled passion of the mind [Note: Nor is Augustine’s manuscript correct here in reading *animae meae* (‘of my soul’) in place of merely *animi* (‘of the mind’).] to defile a man’s wife. It is a burning fire in all the limbs. Wherever it enters, it will destroy to the roots.

“But if I have despised the judgment of my male servant or my maidservant, [Note: Here we have supplied the remaining words of the present verse, *cum judicarentur apud me* (‘when they were judged before me’), and then the entire following verse, which is the fourteenth in those books where the verses are marked in numerical sequence: *Quid enim faciam, si judicium meum faciat Dominus? quod si et visitationem, quod responsum dabo?* (‘For what shall I do if the Lord brings my judgment? And if there is also an inquiry, what answer shall I give?’). This substantial and most notable passage was absent from the Latin edition before us, which had been produced from an abridged and defective exemplar. There is no doubt that it fell out through the mere carelessness of an ancient copyist. Indeed, if any part of the sacred text is more certain than another, this is so: it is found not only in the Hebrew archetype from which Jerome afterward translated it into Latin himself, but also in the Greek, from which he prepared this earlier translation. The words are: κρινομένων αὐτῶν πρὸς ἐμὲ, τί γάρ ποιήσω, ἐὰν ἔτασίν μου ποιήσῃ ὁ Κύριος, ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἐπισκοπήν; τίνα ἀπόκρισιν ποιήσομαι; (‘when they are judged before me, for what shall I do if the Lord makes an examination of me, and if there is also an inquiry? What answer shall I give?’). The Latin words supplied by us correspond to these word for word; and their strongest mark of authenticity is that, except for the words enclosed in parentheses, Augustine himself cites them and transcribes them in precisely the same words. We therefore have no doubt that these are the same words which Saint Jerome placed in his translation from the Greek. Only the words enclosed in brackets—*Quid enim faciam, si judicium meum faciat Dominus* (‘For what shall I do if the Lord brings my judgment?’)—have been supplied by us in accordance with the Greek text, with the utmost fidelity, as can be seen. It is also highly probable that, if genuine copies existed, they would not differ from these even verbally. They have been inserted into the text because otherwise scarcely any sense would remain, and the structure of the sentence restored by us could not be adequately understood by the reader.] when they were judged before me (for what shall I do if the Lord brings my judgment?), and if there is also an inquiry, what answer shall I give?

“Were not they conceived in the womb as I was, and were we formed alike in the belly? I did not deny the weak anything they needed. I did not torment the eye of the widow. Or if I ate my bread alone and did not give any of it to the orphan + (because from my youth I nourished them as a father + [Note: We have restored the particle *et* (‘and’) and the final points that were missing. Other such marks of asterisks and points are restored below according to the example of the Codex Alexandrinus.] and from my mother’s womb I was their guide ** or if I looked down on one who was naked and perishing, and did not cover one + who had no garment ** If the shoulders of the weak did not bless me, and if they were not warmed by the shearing of my sheep. If I raised my hand + over the orphan ** trusting that my help was great, may my shoulder depart [Note: In the Roman edition of the Septuagint, *my shoulder from its joint*. Augustine, like our manuscript, has *from my neck*. MART.] from my neck, and my arm be crushed from my elbow. For the fear of the Lord [Alternative: the word *Lord* is absent] restrained me, + and I shall not endure because of its weight. + If I made [Note: Saint Augustine also has this reading. Others have: ‘If I made gold my measure.’ Let the diligent reader compare this edition of Job with the text of Saint Augustine’s *Annotations*: he will immediately see that it is precisely the version Augustine uses in that work. MART.] gold my strength ** and if I trusted in a precious stone; if I also rejoiced when my wealth was great, if I placed my hand among [Note: Previously it was falsely read *in numerabilibus*. The Greek has ἐπ’ ἀναριθμήτοις (‘among innumerable things’), in accordance with which we correct the text.] innumerable things.

“Do we not see the shining sun fail and the moon diminish? For it is not in them, [Col. 0098B] + and my heart was secretly deceived ** And if I kissed my hand, putting it to my mouth, let this also be reckoned to me as great injustice, because I lied before the Lord Most High. And if I rejoiced over the ruin of my enemy, and my heart said, ‘It is well done,’ let my ear hear my curse; may I be proclaimed in disgrace among my people.

“And if my maidservants often said, ‘Who will grant us that we may be satisfied with his flesh?’ although I was sufficiently good. No stranger remained outside. My door was open to every newcomer. And if, sinning willingly, I hid my sin—for I was not ashamed of the multitude of the people, so as not to confess it before them—or if I sent away the weak from my door with empty hands. + Who will grant me an auditor? + If I did not fear the hand of the Lord, ** [Note: Saint Augustine says at this passage: ‘If I have any written document; and if I did not tear it from my shoulders, and, crowned, read it while lifting it upon my shoulders,’ and so forth.] lifting upon my shoulders any written document I might have, and reading it publicly as one crowned; and if I did not tear it up and return it, taking nothing from the debtor.

“If the earth ever groaned over me, or its furrows wept together; [Col. 0099A] or if I alone ate its produce without payment; or if, by deceiving the soul of the lord of the land, I grieved him: may it produce nettles for me [Note: Martianus has *germinet mihi urticam* (‘may it produce nettles for me’), and shortly afterward *spinam* (‘a thorn’).] instead of wheat, and a thorn instead of barley.”

### And the words of Job came to an end.

### Chapter XXXII

“But the three friends of Job also ceased to answer him further, for Job was righteous in his own sight. And the wrath of Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, from the kindred of Ram, of the land of Ausitis, was kindled against Job. For he was exceedingly angry because he had said that he was righteous before God. And he was exceedingly angry with his three friends because they could not answer Job’s objections, and they considered him impious. But Elihu waited to answer Job, because they were older than he in days. And Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of the three men, + and his wrath was kindled.

### And Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said:

“I am young in age, but you are older; therefore I kept silent, fearing to declare my learning to you. But I said: It is not age that speaks, nor do they know wisdom through many years; rather, it is the spirit in human beings, and the breath of the Almighty that teaches them. For the long-lived are not necessarily wise, nor do the aged understand judgment. Therefore I say: Listen to me, that I may declare to you what I know.

“Behold, I waited patiently for your words, + and I listened to your understanding until you had examined the arguments, + and until I understood you; + and behold, there is no one among you who reproves Job, + or answers his words. [Col. 0099C] + Do not say: ‘We have found wisdom [Note: We have deleted *Domini* (‘of the Lord’), which Martianus added here. It is found in no original manuscript and preserves neither the genuine force of the text nor of the sentence; moreover, because it immediately recurs below in the same form, it may easily appear to have been repeated through the error of an ancient copyist. The Hebrew does indeed contain the words that follow from this point to the end of the section, except for the final sentence; but in the Greek some of these are entirely absent, while others are expressed with shorter and almost different meanings.] + The Lord cast him aside, and not a man.’ + He has not yet spoken to me, + and I will not answer him in your speeches.”

They were astonished and did not answer further. Their words failed them. + For since I waited and they did not speak, + and they stood and did not answer further, + I too will answer with my share, + and I will declare my knowledge. + [Note: Rather, this final sentence should be marked with an obelus, not illustrated by an asterisk, since the Hebrew text does not know it. Moreover, it is displaced and not placed in its proper location if compared with the Greek, where, three verses earlier, it appears somewhat more correctly as: Ἀνθρώπῳ δὲ ἐπετρέψατε λαλεῖν τοιαῦτα ῥήματα (‘But you allowed a man to speak such words’).] But you allowed a man to speak such words.

### And Elihu continued and said: “I will speak again.”

“For I am full of words, and the spirit of my belly constrains me. For my belly is like a wineskin full of new wine, fermenting and tightly bound, and like a ruptured smith’s bellows. I will speak and find relief; opening my lips, I will answer. For I will not be ashamed before the face of a man, nor will I be embarrassed before a mortal. For I do not know how to flatter a face; otherwise the moths would also devour me [Alternative: will devour me].

### Chapter XXXIII

“Now therefore, Job, hear my words, and perceive my speech with your ears. Behold, I have opened my mouth, and my tongue has spoken + in my throat. ** My heart is pure in my words, and the understanding of my lips comprehends what is pure. The divine spirit that made me, and the breath of the Almighty that teaches me. If you can, answer me concerning these things. Take your stand against me, and I against you. From clay you were made, just as I was; from the same material we were made. Neither my fear will terrify you, nor will my hand be heavy upon you. + Nevertheless, you said: ‘In my ears ** I heard the sound of your words,’ by which you say: ‘I am pure from sin, and without guilt. I have not transgressed. Behold, he has found a complaint against me, and considers me as though I were opposed + to him. ** For he placed my foot in the stocks and watched all my ways.’

“How then [Note: The missing word *dicis* (‘you say’) has been supplied here in accordance with the Greek text and Augustine’s reading.] do you say, ‘I am righteous,’ and he has not heard me? For the One who is above human beings is eternal. But you will say: ‘Why did he not hear the judgment and every word?’ For God speaks once, and in the second time + he does not consider it. ** In a dream, or in a nocturnal vision; or as a savage fear falls upon human beings when they sleep in their bed [Alternative: beds]: then he opens the ears of human beings, terrifying them with such fearful images, so as to turn a person away from iniquity, rescue his body from destruction, and spare his soul from death. [Note: This should be supplied from the Greek text: τοῦ μὴ πεσεῖν αὐτὸν ἐν πολέμῳ (‘so that he may not fall in battle’). Saint Augustine read it differently: ‘because war is coming.’] And again he will rebuke him in sickness on his bed, and the multitude of his bones will waste away; and he will not be able to eat any food. + And his soul will long for food ** until his flesh wastes away and his bones are exposed, empty. His soul draws near to death, and his life to the underworld.

“But if there are + death-dealing angels + he will not answer them. Not one of them will wound him if he understands in his heart that he should turn to the Lord, and declares his way to a man—[alternative or marked passage: displays his folly]—[Note: This obelus seems to be removable and should be deleted; the sentence is indeed found in the Hebrew, although in somewhat different words, or at least this material does not exceed what the Hebrew contains. The word *renovabit* (‘he will renew’), which follows, had been placed afterward; we have moved it before, in accordance with the Greek edition.] he will help himself so that he does not fall into death, + and he will renew his body like plaster on a wall, + and fill his bones with marrow, soften his flesh like that of a child, and restore himself as a strong man among human beings.

“He will pray to the Lord, and he will be received with favor; and he will enter [Alternative: entered] with a cheerful face and confession, and will render righteousness to human beings. Then a man will reproach himself, saying: ‘What things I was doing!’ and ‘I did not chastise myself as I deserved,’ and ‘I sinned.’ + Save my soul, so that I may not enter corruption, + and my life shall see the light. + Behold, God will do all these things + three times with a man ** But [Note: In Martianus: ‘But he will rescue’; this is less suitable.] he rescues my soul from death, so that my soul may praise him in the light.

“Give ear, Job, and hear me. Be silent, and I will speak. + If you have an argument, answer me; + speak, for I wish to justify you. + Otherwise hear me, be silent, and I will teach you wisdom.”

### And Elihu answered and said:

### Chapter XXXIV

“Hear my words, you wise men; and you who possess wisdom [Alternative: knowledge], perceive them with your ears. + For the ear tests words [Alternative: speeches], + and the throat tastes food. + Let us choose judgment for ourselves, + [Note: I would certainly prefer that *sententiam* be rewritten as *sentiamus* (‘let us understand’), since the Greek has Γνῶμεν (‘let us know/understand’), and Jerome himself, interpreting from the Hebrew, rendered it accordingly; finally, the correct order of the context requires this. As for the asterisks and terminal points that we so often restore, it is tiresome to repeat the matter.] an opinion among ourselves as to what is good. ** For Job said: ‘I am righteous, and the Lord has removed my judgment, and in my judgment he has lied. + My arrow is violent, without iniquity. + Who is a man like Job, + drinking mockery like water? ** not sinning, nor acting impiously, nor at all sparing [Note: The Greek has οὐδὲ κοινωνήσας μετά, etc. (‘nor sharing with those who…’), from which I suspect that the words *omnino parcens* (‘entirely sparing’) are corrupt. Rather, read, at my suggestion, *particeps* (‘a participant’) instead of *parcens*. But the lack of original books prevents me from introducing that reading into the text.] those who practiced iniquity, so that he might go with + impious men ** For he said: ‘A man who walks with God will not be visited.’” [Note: Saint Augustine omits the word *vir* (‘man’).]

“Therefore, you who are wise in heart, hear me. Far be impiety from the Lord, and from the Almighty, injustice. For he repays a man for his work, + and each person finds according to his way. ** Do you suppose that the Lord will do wrong, and that the Almighty will pervert judgment, who made the earth? Who is he that restores the world beneath the heavens, and all that is in it? For if he should wish to restrain and hold back his spirit within himself, all flesh would die together, and every human being would return to the earth ÷ from which he was formed. ** But if you have not been moved, hear these things; perceive the sound of my words. See the One who hates iniquities and destroys the wicked, who is eternal and righteous. + The impious person is the one who says to a king, ‘You act unjustly’ [Alternative: ‘wrongly’], + and to rulers, ‘You act most impiously,’ ** who did not respect the face of the dishonored; they do not know how to show honor to rulers or to admire their faces. Empty things will come upon them, so that they cry out and plead with a man. For they acted unjustly when the weak were excluded.

“For he himself sees the works of human beings, and nothing of what they do is hidden from him. Nor will there be a place; + and there is no shadow of death ** where those who practice iniquity may hide, + because it is no longer established in human power ** For the Lord looks upon all, who comprehends things unsearchable, glorious, and wondrous, whose number is beyond counting. + He knows their works + and [Note: Augustine has, instead of this clause, ‘they seemed to him to shine.’ The Greek manuscripts likewise disagree among themselves.] will overturn the night, and they will be humbled. + And he extinguished the wicked, [Note: ‘And he extinguished the wicked; they seemed to him to shine.’ Thus Saint Augustine in the frequently mentioned book of his *Annotations on Job*. The Vulgate, following the Hebrew, has: ‘As wicked men he struck them, in the place of those who see.’ But our Latin manuscript seems to follow the Greek Alexandrian Septuagint, for it reads καὶ ὁρατοὶ ἐγένοντο ἐναντίον τῶν ἐχθρῶν, ‘and they became conspicuous before their enemies.’ MART.] + and made them conspicuous before their enemies, + because they turned aside from the law of God, + and did not understand his righteous acts, + so that the cry of the poor might reach him, and he would hear the cry of the poor. + He himself will give quiet, and who can condemn? + He will hide his face, and who will see him? + Both against a nation and against a person alike. + He makes a hypocrite reign because of the perversity of the people.

“Because I began to speak to the Lord, I will not cease. + But what I see less clearly, show me. If I have acted unjustly, I will not do so again. + Will he demand it from you because you rejected it? You chose, and not I. And if you know anything, speak. ** Therefore the wise in heart will say these things: And a wise man will hear [Note: Martianus continued this passage under asterisks, which we have ended after the preceding half-verse by placing larger points. Here, however, the opposite mark, the obelus, seems to belong before *verbum* (‘the word’), since the Hebrew lacks it and reads only *audiat me* (‘let him hear me’).] my word. But Job did not speak in wisdom, and his words are not of knowledge. Rather, learn, Job, and do not [Col. 0102C] answer any longer like fools, lest we add to our sins, and injustice be reckoned against us because we speak many words before the Lord.”

### And Elihu answered and said:

### Chapter XXXV

“Why [Note: This entire chapter seems to have been absent from the Septuagint interpretation called the *koinē*, that is, the common or Old version. It is no objection that the individual verses are not marked with an asterisk, since copyists omit many signs in the middle of pages, contenting themselves with noting them at the beginning and end. In this way, four or five obelisks are found marked at the beginning in the Royal manuscript of the Bible, no. 3564, although each page of the prophet Daniel, where the hymn of the three youths is written, requires more than forty such signs. Whoever wishes may consult that manuscript and compare it with our edition of Daniel, so as to be convinced by experience that we have said nothing except the truth. MART. — Martianus maintains that this entire chapter was absent from the Greek common edition, and therefore that each verse, or hemistich, ought here to be marked with an asterisk. He gives no reason, however, for proving his conjecture; and the appearance of truth forbids us to accept such an assertion literally without further evidence. On the contrary, since some of these verses—those marked by number—are said to have been supplied from Theodotion in the Hexaplaric books, as in one Colbertine manuscript cited by Montfaucon, one may very reasonably infer from that note that only those particular verses, and not all of them equally, were absent.] did you think this in judgment? [Col. 0103A] + Who are you, that you said, ‘I am righteous before the sight of God’? + Or do you say, ‘What benefit is it to you?’ or, ‘What shall I do if I have sinned?’ ** Therefore I will answer you and your three friends.

“Look toward heaven and see; gaze upon the clouds, how high they are above you. If you have sinned, what will you do [Alternative: what are you doing]? Or if you have committed many unjust acts, what can you do? And if you are righteous, what will you give him? + Or what will he receive from your hand? Your impiety concerns a man like yourself, + and your righteousness a son of man. + From the multitude of those who slander, they will cry out, + they will shout because of the arm of the many. ** [Note: Martianus had an asterisk here in place of the final point; it was better to delete it according to the recent edition of the Codex Alexandrinus. Other such matters are corrected below.] And he did not say: ‘Where is God who made me? Who assigns the watches of the night, who separates me from the four-footed creatures of the earth and from the birds of heaven. + He made me wiser.’ + There they will cry out, and he will not hear [Alternative: you will not hear] ** because of the injuries of the wicked.

“For the Lord does not wish to see vanity. For the Almighty himself observes those who practice righteousness, and he will save me. Judge against him, therefore, if you can. Praise him as he is, + and now because he does not visit his anger, nor + has he known sins with sufficient severity, + and Job vainly [Note: Augustine has *aperuit* (‘opened’) and shortly afterward *in ignorantia sua* (‘in his ignorance’).] opens his mouth, + he multiplies words in his ignorance.”

### And Elihu added and said:

Source/review notes: The source’s alternate readings, critical signs and scopes, column anchors, editorial attributions, and bibliographic witnesses are retained in English. Fragmentary or grammatically ambiguous printed readings remain visibly fragmentary rather than receiving an invented subject.

## [Chapter XXXVI]

[Col. 0103D] Bear with me a little, so that I may teach you. [Note: We have supplied the little word “me” from Augustine and the Greek text.] For there are still words within me. [Note: Previously it was incorrectly written “near are”; it should be “there are.”] I shall draw my knowledge from afar, but I shall speak of my works, which are just. In truth—and you will understand that the words are not unjust—[Note: It was again incorrectly written “not in justice,” instead of “not unjust,” as the Greek οὐκ ἄδικα (“not unjust”) requires; we have corrected it in accordance with Augustine, who reads likewise. The preceding passage also rests on the same authorities.] know that God will not reject the innocent. The mighty in the strength of his heart will not preserve the wicked alive, but will give [Col. 0103C] judgment to the poor. He will not take his eyes from the just, and with kings he places them upon a throne. He makes them sit forever, and they will be exalted.

[Note: Augustine reads “he made them sit”; he considers these words to be supplied and attached immediately to the preceding isocolon.]

Those who are bound in fetters will be captured in the cords of poverty; he will announce to them their works [Col. 0104A] and their sins when they have grown strong; but he will hear the just. And he said: “For they will turn away from iniquity, if they hear you and serve you; they will complete their days in prosperity and their years in glory.” **

But he does not save the ungodly, because they were unwilling to know the Lord; and when they were admonished, they were disobedient. [Note: Augustine reads “will not give life,” and shortly afterward “in his ignorance.”] And hypocrites will harbor anger in their hearts. [Note: We have supplied the word “heart” (*corde*), omitted in our manuscript, from Augustine, who reads: “and hypocrites of heart will harbor anger.” MART.] They will not cry out, because [Col. 0104C] he has bound them. [Note: Previously “he will bind” was written, contrary to the other books and the Greek ἔδησεν (“he bound”); the final punctuation was also missing, and we have restored it below in its proper place. We have corrected several other minor matters as well.] Therefore let their soul die in youth, and let their life be wounded by angels, because they have afflicted the weak and powerless. But he will establish the judgment of the meek. And because the abyss deceived you from the mouth of the enemy: poured out beneath it; and your table descended, full of fatness **.

The judgment of the just will not fail; and [Col. 0104B] anger will be upon the ungodly because of the wickedness of the gifts they were receiving in their iniquities. Do not let the inclination of your mind turn you away from the prayers of the weak when they are in distress. And do not draw out all who possess strength through the night, so that the peoples may rise on their behalf; but take care that you do nothing improper, for this is what you have chosen in preference to poverty. [Note: “To draw out” was incorrectly read as “to exalt.” Augustine warned us of this, and especially the Greek μὴ ἐξελκύσῃς (“do not draw out”).] **

Behold, God will be strengthened in his power. [Note: Augustine cites a double variant here: “Behold, God will comfort,” or “will be strengthened in his power.” See the book of the *Annotations on Job*. MART.] For who is like him in might? Or who can examine his works? Or who can say, “He has acted wickedly”? Remember that his works are great, which men have praised. Every human being looks toward him. All people are pierced with compunction. Behold, God is great, and we shall not know him. The number of his years is infinite. [Col. 0104D] But the drops of rain are numbered for him. [Note: Instead of the true reading, which we supplied from Augustine—“But for him they are countable”—Martianay’s edition had, with nearly the opposite and unsuitable meaning, “innumerable.” The Greek text itself contradicts that reading: Ἀριθμηταὶ δὲ αὐτῷ ὑετοῦ σταγόνες, “But the drops of rain are numbered for him.”] Rain will be poured out along its paths. Clouds will flow and grow dark over very many people.

He appoints a time for the beasts, and they know the order of their lair. [Note: In Greek there is οὐκ ἐξίστατο (or ἐξίσταται), “he was not astonished” or “is not astonished,” a reading which Augustine also prefers and which we ourselves would rather follow, instead of “is numb.” But where the text has “his spirit,” he reads “your spirit.” The old note of the Colbertine manuscript, preserved by Montfaucon, says of these four half-verses: Οὗτοι οἵδε οὐ κεῖνται ἐν τῷ Ἑβραϊκῷ, διὸ καὶ ὠβελίσθησαν, “These four verses are not found in the Hebrew, and therefore they have been marked with obeli.”]

In all these things your spirit is not numb, nor is your heart changed from your body **. If he should think of extending a cloud, he spreads it out equally over the tabernacle. [Note: Augustine has the fuller reading: “equally over the tabernacle.”] **

[Col. 0105A] Behold, he pours out his light over it, and covers the roots of the sea. In them he will judge the peoples; he will give food to many. In his hands he conceals the light, and he commands it concerning its opposite, so that it may announce to his friend above it the possession of the one who strives to ascend.

## [Chapter XXXVII]

[Col. 0105C] But at this my heart was astonished, and it was torn from its place. Hear the sound of terror and the noise issuing from his mouth. [Note: Augustine has more here: “and the sound of his voice”; he reads “with the tumult,” instead of “the tumult.” Since the Greek text differs from both readings here and also below, we venture nothing.] Beneath the whole heaven he circles, and his light reaches the ends of the earth. After him the voice will roar. He will thunder with the sound of his majesty, and when his voice is heard it cannot be investigated. The Mighty One will thunder wondrously with his voice **.

[Note: Augustine’s exemplar, apparently mistakenly, preferred “cloud” (nubi) instead of “snow” (nivi); the Greek has χιόνι (“snow”). We have rightly taken from it shortly afterward “of his power,” in accordance with the Greek δυναστείας, whereas Martianay read “power”; and likewise “he marks,” instead of “is marked,” with the Greek κατασφραγίζει. We have appended the missing final dots to this word.]

For he does great things that we did not know, commanding the snow, “Be upon the earth.” And the storm of rain and [Col. 0105B] the storm of showers are his power. In the hand of every human being he marks it. [Note: Augustine and the Latin Vulgate read the verb actively, ‘he marks,’ rather than passively, ‘is marked.’ MART.] Thus every person may know his own weakness. The beasts entered their shelter and rested in their lair. From the storehouses comes the storm, and from the storehouses the cold; and ice will be given by the Spirit of God. He governs, as it pleases him, the water, and he will water the grain with clouds. [Note: Augustine reads “he watered the cloud.” “He scattered the cloud” is not quite correct, unless the preceding noun, “clouds,” is excepted; that noun agrees better with the Greek νέφελη (“cloud”) of the current text. We have also placed the following asterisks in their proper positions and limits.] He spreads his light through the clouds, and they themselves turn about under his direction, to accomplish everything that he has commanded them. These things have been established by him over the earth, whether in a tribe, or in his own land, or wherever he wishes it to be found in mercy **.

[Col. 0105D] Hear these things with your ears, Job. Stand and admonish by the strength of the Lord. [Note: The text in Augustine’s book of *Annotations* must be corrected; it has the corrupt reading “and move the power of the Lord.” MART.] We know that God established his works when he made light from darkness. [Col. 0106A] Do you know the distinction of the clouds and the great falls of evils? But your garment is strong, while the earth rests from the south. [Note: The manuscript and Augustine read “so strong,” instead of “warm,” as does the Hebrew canon of truth and the Latin Vulgate. This is not a recent error of copyists but an ancient one, for Saint Augustine also read it that way in his exemplar, interpreting “a strong garment” as “proud dignity.” MART.] [Note: It should be rewritten as “warm”; the Greek word θερμή (“warm”) demands this, although Augustine himself preferred “strong.” Shortly afterward he also reads “you will strengthen” instead of “you will have strengthened.” Greek manuscripts support either reading.] Will you strengthen the heavens with him, which have been spread out evenly for life? **

Therefore teach us what we should say to him, and let us rest, though saying much. [Note: Augustine’s reading “me” is preferable, in agreement with the Greek, instead of “us.”] Is there a book or a scribe standing beside me, so that, standing here, I may make a person keep silent? [Note: He likewise reads *assistis* (“you stand beside me”); the Greek has παρέστηκεν (“has stood beside”). We have corrected the next word with the aid of both authorities: where the text had the corrupt “or,” it should read “so that.”]

But the light that shines in the clouds is not visible to all. And a passing spirit will cleanse them. [Note: We have not found in the Greek what corresponds to “and a passing spirit will cleanse them.” It is nevertheless present in the Hebrew archetype, from which Jerome himself translated: “and a passing wind drove them away.” Augustine also reads it, though somewhat differently: “the spirit passes and will cleanse,” and so forth.]

From the north comes a cloud of golden color. In it there is great glory and honor of the Almighty, and we find no one equal to his power. Do you not think that the one who judges justly will hear him? Therefore human beings will fear him; the wise in heart will also fear him.

## [Chapter XXXVIII]

After Elius had ceased speaking, [Col. 0106B] the Lord spoke to Job from the whirlwind of a cloud: Who is this who hides my counsel, keeping words in his heart, and thinks that I am [Col. 0106C] hidden? [Note: Augustine has “to give” (*dare*) for “to be hidden” (*latere*). I do not know whether he himself read this obvious error in his exemplar, or whether it was introduced by later copyists transcribing the Saint’s book of *Annotations*: he himself indicates quite clearly in the attached annotation, “because they are not hidden from God,” that the text he read or cited has a verb of hiding, not of giving. Moreover, he reads *Accingere* (“gird yourself”) for *Accinge* (“gird”).] Gird your loins like a man; I shall question you, and you shall answer me. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have knowledge. Who set its measurements [Note: The editor observes that an obelus had here been copied as an asterisk; copyists easily interchange signs whose use and meaning they do not understand. MART.], if you know, or who stretched the measuring line over it? Or upon what were its [Col. 0106D] circles fixed? [Note: Augustine likewise has “its circles were fixed,” instead of “were spread out,” and the Greek has πεπήγασι, “were fixed.”] Who is it that placed the cornerstone upon it ** when the stars were made together? [Note: We supplied the words “upon it,” which were missing in Martianay’s edition, from Augustine’s exemplar, and marked them with an obelus, although they occur in the Greek text, ἐπ’ αὐτῆς (“upon it”), but are not added in the Hebrew. In the manuscript from which Martianay copied this edition, an obelus also stood here, although the words that should have been marked were omitted. This misled him into marking, quite improperly, the words “when they were made,” which clearly correspond to the Hebrew and which Jerome translated from that source as “when they praised me.” The Greeks, following a different etymology of the word, have Ὅτε ἐγενήθη, “when they were made,” and so forth.] All my angels praised me with a loud voice.

I closed the sea with gates when it roared from its mother’s womb, wishing to come forth. I made a cloud its covering and wrapped it in mist; I set boundaries for it, placing [Col. 0107A] bars and gates. And I said: “Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond; but within yourself your waves shall be shattered.”

Or did you appoint the morning light with me? Or did Lucifer know his order? [Col. 0107C] Seize the extremities of the earth and shake the wicked out of it. [Note: Augustine has “grasp” and “shake out”; I think that “punishments,” where “wings” or “feathers” should be read, is a typographical error. For the following word, Martianay incorrectly read “soul” instead of “animal,” supported by Augustine and the Greek ζῷον (“animal”); shortly afterward he likewise read “you did” instead of “you placed,” in agreement with the Greek ἔθου. Augustine, following the Septuagint, reads ‘fashioned an animal.’ MART.] You took earth’s clay and fashioned an animal, and set the famous creature upon the earth. You took light away from the wicked; you shattered the arm of the proud; you came to the source of the sea; you walked in the tracks of the abyss. Are the gates of death opened to you through fear? Did the gatekeepers of hell, seeing you, fear? Have you understood the breadth beneath heaven?

Tell me, then, how great each thing is, and in what land the light dwells, or what [Col. 0107D] place belongs to darkness. [Note: We supply “each” (*quaeque*) from Augustine, as the Greek requires, πόση ἥτις ἐστίν (“how great each is”). Martianay knew this reading of the bishop of Hippo but, remarkably, rejected it: “The manuscript, following the Hebrew, reads better Hullah, that is, ‘the whole of it,’ namely the earth.” He forgot that this version derives from Greek, not Hebrew; nor did he understand that the observation aids neither his case nor the reader.] If you lead me to their boundaries—and if you know [Col. 0107B] their paths—do you know that you were then born, and that the number of your years is great? [Note: This is, I think, a copyist’s error: he wrote the substantive verb *sit* (“is”) for the conditional particle *si* (“if”). It should therefore be read: “or what place belongs to darkness. If you lead me,” etc. The Septuagint and Augustine agree. MART. — Previously the corrupt reading was “place is”; then, after a full stop, “Lead me,” etc. We have corrected it not only on the authority of all the books, especially the Greek, but also in accordance with Martianay’s own stated intention.]

Or have you entered the treasuries of snow? Or have you seen the treasuries of hail, which have been stored for the time of enemies and for the day of battle and war? [Note: Augustine adds “to you”; although the word occurs in Greek manuscripts and may be adopted into Latin, it should be marked with an obelus because it is absent from Hebrew. Several minor corrections are made below.] From where does frost proceed, and the south wind scatter beneath heaven? Who prepared a channel for the mighty rain and a way for the sounds of the storm, so that it might rain upon a land where there is no man, in the desert where there is no human being, to saturate the pathless and uninhabited place, and to make the green of grass sprout? **

[Col. 0108C] Who is the father of rain? Or who generated the drops of dew? [Note: Augustine has a different reading: “And who is it that gave birth to the clods of dew?” The Greek text also has a variant reading: “clods,” βώλους, instead of “drops,” συνοχάς. The Alexandrian codex retains both, but I would not dare say which Saint Jerome preferred, or whether he himself noted one of them in the margin.] From whose womb does ice proceed? Or who gave birth to the frost in heaven, which descends like a stream of water? Or who melted the face of the wicked? Did you understand the bonds of the Pleiades and open the enclosure of Orion? Or will you bring forth Mazuroth in its season and bring [Col. 0108A] evening over its construction? **

Do you know the changes of heaven, or all the things that occur together beneath heaven? [Note: Martianay incorrectly read “movements,” contrary to the Greek τροπάς, “changes,” as Augustine also reads. He likewise had “of all things,” instead of “all things,” contrary to the same authorities.] Will you call the cloud with your voice, and will the clouds obey you in the trembling of mighty water? [Note: Augustine reads here: “You will send by force rivers, and they will go,” which plainly deprives the Scriptural sentence of its meaning. We must therefore adhere wholly to our edition and to the Latin Vulgate, lest the errors of copyists impose upon us as they did upon the holy Doctor. MART.]

You will send out lightning by force, and it will go; or will they say to you, “What is this?” Who gave women wisdom in weaving and knowledge of varied work? Or who is it that numbers the clouds in wisdom and bends the instruments of heaven down to the earth? [Note: We supplied the words “is it,” from Augustine, in agreement with the Greek text τίς δὲ ὁ ἀριθμῶν (“who is it that numbers”). The asterisk that follows, I think, marks the single word “instruments,” which I believe was supplied from Symmachus; in the other Greek books there is only οὐρανόν, “heaven.” Finally, instead of “he bends,” Martianay had “he may bend”; we have restored the former on the authority of Augustine and the Greek text.]

[Col. 0108D] Ash is spread out like earth, and he has cemented it like a cube with stones. [Note: This passage is corrupt both in our manuscript and in Saint Augustine. The manuscript reads “like stones of citizens,” while Augustine’s annotations have “like stones of food.” Each of the ancient writers wrote what he understood, not what he found. We therefore restore “a cube,” in accordance with the reading in the Septuagint, ὥσπερ λίθῳ κύβον, “like a cube with a stone.” MART.]

Will you catch food for lions, or fill the souls of dragons [or cubs]? For they are timid in their lairs, and they sit in the forests lying in wait. Who prepared food for the raven? For its young cry out to the Lord, wandering and [Col. 0108B] seeking food.

## [Chapter XXXIX]

Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth upon the rocks, or have you watched over the births of the does? Have you counted the months of their pregnancy, released their pains, and nourished their young without fear? Will you send forth their offspring? Their young will break away; they will multiply in the grain; they will go out and not return to them. [Note: Martianay less well had the two words “and they will go.” With Augustine we read “they will go out” (ἐξελεύσονται); afterward we have likewise restored “to them” (*eis*) in place of “to them” (*ad eas*).]

Who is it that set the wild ass free, and who loosened its bonds? For I made its tent a desert and its dwellings salty ground. [Note: Augustine has “its deserted dwelling,” and “its dwellings,” and so forth.] It mocks the multitude of the city and does not hear the complaint of the taskmaster. It looks upon the mountains of its pasture and seeks every green thing.

Will the unicorn be willing to serve you, or to sleep upon your manger? Will you bind its yoke with straps, or will it plow furrows for you in the field? Do you trust in it because its strength has been changed, or will you leave [Col. 0109A] your works to it? Will you believe it because it will return your seed and bring it into your threshing floor? [Note: Martianay incorrectly had “into the ark,” contrary to the Greek text εἰς ἅλωνα (“into the threshing floor”), and also contrary to Augustine.]

The wing of the ostrich is mixed with the wings of the heron and the hawk. It leaves its eggs upon the earth, and they grow warm in the dust. It forgets that a foot may scatter them, and the beasts of the field will trample them. [Note: We have restored this passage partly from Augustine and partly from the Greek text. The word “field,” retained by both—and indeed by all the books—was missing. Augustine prefers the singular: “the beast of the field will trample.” We have also supplied several preceding asterisks and removed one that had been added below.]

It hardens itself against its young, as though they were not its own. It labored in vain, without any fear, because the Lord disregarded it in his wisdom and did not grant it understanding. When the time comes, it will lift itself high [or fly away], and it will laugh at the horseman and the rider [or mock them]. **

Did you surround the horse with strength, insert neighing into its neck, and clothe it with armor? And did you give glory to its breast and boldness? [Note: The correct reading was “glory,” not “of glory,” as Augustine and the Greek δόξα (“glory”) unanimously support.] It exults as it goes out into the field and advances [Col. 0109B] into battle with strength. Meeting the spear, it despises it and does not turn away from the iron. Above it the bow and sword rejoice, together with the trembling of spears and lances. ** Anger overturns the earth, and it will not believe until the trumpet sounds. When the trumpet has sounded, it will say, “Well done!” From afar it smells the battle, the thunder of commanders, and the shouting.

Does the hawk grow feathered through your wisdom, spreading its wings motionless and looking toward the south? [Note: Martianay incorrectly read “with spread feathers,” with almost no intelligible sense, instead of “with extended wings,” in agreement with Augustine and the Greek sense. We have also removed the conjunction after the asterisk.] ** Or does the eagle rise at your command? And will the vulture, sitting upon its nest on the rock, remain on the summit of the rock and in the cave? ** When it is there, it seeks food; its eyes see from afar, and its young wallow in blood. [Col. 0109C] Wherever corpses are, there they are immediately found.

[Note: Augustine has a different reading: “The Lord answered and said, ‘Does he who disputes with the Almighty rest?’” He also reads “will rest” instead of “rests,” and “God” instead of “Lord.”]

[Col. 0109D] The Lord continued and spoke to Job: Will the one who disputes with the Almighty remain silent? Let the one who reproves the Lord answer this.

## JOB ANSWERED THE LORD AND SAID:

[Col. 0110D] What, then, am I judged—admonished and rebuked by the Lord—when I hear such things, though I am nothing? [Note: I would prefer “I” instead of “therefore,” in agreement with the Greek ἐγώ. Augustine reads “that I may be judged,” instead of “I am judged.” An obelus is placed before these words in the recent edition of the Alexandrian codex. We have placed the final punctuation, which had incorrectly been postponed until after the words “since I am nothing,” before those words, in accordance with the Hebrew truth.] What answer shall I give? I shall place my hand upon my mouth. Once I have spoken, I will not add again.

## THE LORD ANSWERED JOB FROM THE WHIRLWIND AND SAID:

## [Chapter XL]

By no means. But gird your loins like a man. I shall question you, and you shall answer me. Do you reject my judgment? Or do you think that I spoke to you in such a way [Col. 0110A] that you might appear just? Do you have an arm against the Lord, or do you thunder against him with your voice? Then assume height and strength; clothe yourself with glory and honor. Send out angels in anger, and humble every insolent person. Seeing every proud person, extinguish him. Crush the wicked at once, hide them together beneath the earth, and fill their faces with disgrace. Then I shall confess that your right hand can save you.

But behold the beast that I made with you; it eats grass like cattle. Behold, its strength is in its loins, and its power is above the navel of its belly. ** [Note: The final punctuation was missing, and the pronoun “its” was indicated by an asterisk. We have supplied the punctuation in both places.]

It raises its tail like a cypress, and its sinews are intertwined; its ribs are bronze ribs, and its spine is molten iron. This is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, which he made. Let it be mocked by his angels. As it climbs [Col. 0110B] the steep mountain, it makes joy for the four-footed creatures in Tartarus. It sleeps beneath every kind of tree, beside reeds, rushes, and sedge; great trees with their roots and the shrubs of the torrent shade it.

If there is a flood, it will not fear; it is secure even when the Jordan crashes against its mouth. ** [Note: These two later asterisks and the final punctuation were missing; we have supplied them from the recent edition of the Alexandrian codex.] In its eye it will receive him. With its twisted crest it pierces the nostrils. **

Bring the dragon in with a hook. Will you put a halter around its nostrils, seal a ring in its mouth, and pierce its lip with a clamp? [Note: Instead of “you will seal,” I would prefer to read the words separately, “if you bind,” or something similar, with one particle marked by an asterisk. In Greek it is εἰ εἰλήσεις (“if you bind”). Minor matters below are corrected.] **

Will it speak prayers and supplications to you gently? Will it make a covenant with you, and will you take it as an eternal servant? Will you play with it as with a bird, or bind it like a sparrow for a child? Nations are fattened upon it, and the [Col. 0110C] Phoenician peoples divide it among themselves. Even if all the ships came together, they would not carry the skin of its tail, nor its head in fishermen’s boats. **

Will you lay your hand upon it, remembering the battle that takes place in its body, so that it may not happen again?

## [Chapter XLI]

You have not seen it, nor have you been amazed at what is said; you have not feared what has been prepared for me. For who is it that can resist me? Or who will resist me and endure? If everything beneath heaven is mine? I will not be silent on its account, and the speech of its powers has compassion on its equal. **

Who will uncover the face of his clothing? Or who will enter into the fold of his breastplate? Who will open the doors of his face? Fear surrounds his teeth, and bronze shields are in his inward parts. His binding is like [Col. 0111A] a smyrites stone. [Note: The Septuagint has ὥσπερ σμυρίτης, “like smyrites.” Others read σιδηρῖτις, “sideritis.” I believe that the copyist, instead of *smyrites*, read *zirimitis*. MART.] [Note: It seems that “smyrites” should be restored, in accordance with the Greek σμυρίτης, as Martianay himself conjectured. The asterisks that follow have been placed by us in their proper positions.]

One adheres to another; and breath will not pass between them. A man will be joined to his brother; they will be held together and will not be torn apart. **

[Col. 0111C] At his sneezings light shines, and his eyes are like the appearance of the morning star. From his mouth burning lamps go forth, and fiery grates are scattered. [Note: The Greek more correctly has ἐκπορεύονται, “they go forth,” and διαριπτοῦνται, “they are scattered.” We note these points in passing, for there is no time to pursue them all.] Smoke comes from his nostrils, like smoke from a furnace burning with fire and coals. His soul kindles coals, and flame proceeds from his mouth. [Note: The Greek does not add the verb “kindles.” I would rather read “it kindles,” as well as “it proceeds,” instead of “it will proceed.” The asterisk below is supplied from the Greek edition of the Alexandrian codex.]

Strength dwells in his neck, and destruction runs before him. The flesh of his body adheres to him, poured around him and immovable. ** His heart is hardened like a stone, and stands like an untiring anvil. When he turns himself, fear comes upon the four-footed beasts raging over the earth. If spears meet him, they will do nothing to him—the lifting of the spear and the breastplate. **

[Col. 0111B] He considers iron to be straw, and bronze like rotten wood; a bronze arrow will not wound him. He draws the bow as though it were hay; he considers the hammer like stubble.

[He considers the waters stones, and the sling’s cast as hay.]

[Note: This pericope, which we have enclosed in brackets—“He considers waters stones, the cast of a sling as hay”—is, if I see rightly, a duplicate rendering of the preceding statement: “a bronze arrow will not wound him; he draws the bow as though it were hay.” It arose from variant manuscript readings of this passage and interpolation of several words. Certainly it occurs only once in either the Hebrew or Greek text and in translations made from them; nor can corresponding words for this second fragment be found in the original books. It is easily an old pre-Jerome Latin interpretation, first written in the margin by some student for private scholarly use, then rashly inserted and sewn into the text by an unskilled copyist. We judged it permissible only to enclose the interpolator’s words in brackets.]

[Col. 0111D] He laughs at the trembling spear.

His lair is made of sharpened iron stakes, and all the gold of the sea is beneath him, like immeasurable mud. He makes the abyss boil like a bronze vessel; he considers the sea like an alabaster vessel. [Note: The Greek has ὥσπερ ἐξάλειπτρον, which may be rendered in Latin as “like an alabaster vessel,” or “like a vessel for perfume.” Thus the ancient lexicographers interpret it, especially Pollux more than once: “The vessel in which the perfume was kept, resembling a phial, was called an *exaleiptron*.” The ancient Greek translators of Scripture agree, especially Aquila, who translated it as μυρεψητήριον, “a vessel for perfume”; and Jerome himself, in his translation from the Hebrew, where he renders it “like a pot.” The reason this text has “erased” is simply that ἐξάλειπτον, from the verb ἐξαλείφω, “to erase,” was read instead of ἐξάλειπτρον, a word very similar in sound and writing—whether this was an error by the Greek copyist in the exemplar in question or a slip by the translator’s eye while reading.] He counts the abyss as a promenade **. Nothing upon the earth is like it, made to be mocked by my angels. It sees every high thing, and it is king of all that are in the waters.

## [Chapter XLII]

Job answered the Lord and said: I know that you can do all things, and that nothing is impossible for you. Who is it that hides counsel from you, thinking that, by sparing words, he can conceal you? [Col. 0112A] Who, then, announced to me what I did not know—[Col. 0112C] great and marvelous things that I did not understand? [Note: We marked the words “great and” with an obelus, since only “marvelous things” is found in the Hebrew. The frequently praised recent edition of the Alexandrian codex gives preference to our reading.]

Hear me, Lord, and I too shall speak; I shall question you, and you shall teach me. Previously I heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I despised myself and wasted away, and I regarded [Col. 0112D] earth and ashes. [Note: The Greek text inserts, or repeats, ἐμαυτόν, “myself,” more correctly. The complete clause that follows—“And it came to pass after the Lord had spoken…”—was missing from Martianay’s manuscript exemplar; he supplied it from the Greek.] [Note: The words from here up to the name “Job” were omitted through the carelessness of the scribe in our Latin manuscript. MART.]

And it came to pass after the Lord had spoken all these words to Job.

## THE LORD SAID TO ELIPHAZ THE TEMANITE:

You have sinned, you and your two friends. For you have not spoken anything true before me, as my servant Job has. Now therefore take for yourselves seven calves and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and he will offer sacrifices for you. My servant Job will pray for you, because unless his face were acceptable to me—and unless it were [Col. 0112B] on his account—I would have destroyed you. For you have not spoken truthfully to me against my servant Job. [Note: The Greek has specifically “anything good,” οὐδὲν ἀγαθόν.]

** [Note: We have supplied these heavier points, which indicate by an asterisk only the pronoun “for yourselves,” and which were missing in Martianay’s edition.]

### Source-critical apparatus

The supplied edition uses `+` to open or divide text marked with an asterisk, `÷` for text marked with an obelus, and `**` to close the marked range. The following register translates every marked scope rather than silently dropping the signs:

- **Chapter XXXVI.** Asterisked: “The mighty in strength of heart will not preserve the wicked alive … will be exalted”; “those bound in fetters … years in glory”; “and hypocrites of heart will harbor anger”; “and because the abyss deceived you … your table descended full of fatness”; “so that peoples may rise for them … you chose this rather than poverty”; “the works which men praised … clouds darken over very many people”; and “if he should think to extend a cloud … the possession of one striving to ascend.” Obelized: “He appoints a time for the beasts, and they know the order of their lair; in all these things your spirit is not numb, nor is your heart changed from your body.”
- **Chapter XXXVII.** Asterisked: “At this my heart was astonished … the Mighty One thunders wondrously with his voice”; “the storm of rain and storm of showers are his power; in every person’s hand he marks it”; “and ice will be given by the Spirit of God”; “whether in a tribe, in his own land, or wherever he wishes it to be found in mercy”; and “from the south; will you strengthen the heavens with him, spread out evenly for life?”
- **Chapter XXXVIII.** Obelized: “and thinks that I am hidden” and “upon it” after the cornerstone. Asterisked: “if you know”; “so that it may rain where there is no man, in the desert where there is no human being, saturate the pathless and uninhabitable place, and make green grass sprout”; “will you bring forth Mazuroth in its season and bring evening over its structure?”; and the supplied word “instruments” in “instruments of heaven.”
- **Chapter XXXIX.** Asterisked: “if you know the time when wild goats give birth on the rocks”; “will you send out their offspring? … they will go out and not return to them”; “and its dwellings [are] salty ground”; “it looks upon the mountains of its pasture and seeks every green thing”; the sequence from “because it will return your seed” through the ostrich’s rising and laughing at horse and rider; “the trembling of spears and lances”; “looking toward the south”; “on the summit of the rock and in the cave”; and “its eyes see from afar.” In Job’s answer the printed sequence begins an asterisked reading at “What, then, am I judged?” and obelizes “admonished and rebuked by the Lord, hearing such things” before closing the range.
- **Chapter XL.** Asterisked: each supplied pronoun “its” in “its strength” and “its power”; the flood/Jordan clause through “with its twisted crest it pierces the nostrils”; and the sequence from the disputed “seal/bind a ring in its mouth” through “nor its head in fishermen’s boats.”
- **Chapter XLI.** Asterisked: “I will not be silent on its account, and the speech of its powers has compassion on its equal”; the joined armor-scales from “one adheres to another” through “they will not be torn apart”; “the flesh of its body … poured around it and immovable”; “the lifting of the spear and the breastplate”; and “he counts the abyss as a promenade.”
- **Chapter XLII.** The editorial note identifies “great and” before “marvelous things” as obelized because Hebrew has only “marvelous things.” The pronoun “for yourselves” is asterisked. The final printed sign sequence places a critical boundary around “to me” in “you have not spoken truthfully to me against my servant Job”; the accompanying note records Greek “anything good.”

The edition also records these alternate readings in place:

- **Chapter XXXVI:** “the Lord” for “God”; “gives life to the wicked” for “will not preserve the wicked alive”; “judgment to the poor” for “judgment of the poor”; “his eyes” with the alternate pronoun “his”; “their works are announced” for “he will announce their works”; omission of “you” in “if they hear you”; “were unwilling” for the subjunctive “may have been unwilling”; “has established” for “will establish”; “will descend” for “descended”; singular “to the righteous” for plural “the righteous”; and omission of “in” before “iniquities.”
- **Chapter XXXVII:** “at these things” for “at this”; and singular “that which is to be done” for plural “things to be done.”
- **Chapter XXXVIII:** “which” for “upon which” concerning the earth’s circles; “in its mother’s womb” for “from its mother’s womb”; “you walk” for “you walked” in the abyss; “the light dwells” for “may dwell”; “you are” for “you were”; “on the day of battle” for “for the day of battle”; “and so that it may rain” for “so that it may rain”; feminine “a pathless and uninhabitable land” for the neuter “pathless and uninhabitable place”; “equally like a river” for “like a river of water”; present “obey” for future “will obey”; “food” for “a cube”; singular “for a lion” for plural “for lions”; and “crying out and seeking food” for “wandering and seeking food.”
