- **Chapter XXXIX:** accusative “the rocks” for “on the rocks”; “and” for “or” before binding the unicorn; present “you leave” for future “you will leave”; “and will you trust” for “or will you trust”; “left its eggs” for “leaves its eggs”; “will scatter them” for “scatters them”; “God” for “the Lord”; “will fly away” for “will lift itself high”; “will mock” for “will laugh at”; “in battle” for “into battle”; “turns the earth” for “overturns the earth”; “when the trumpet has cried out” for “when the trumpet has sounded”; “and at your command” for “or at your command”; “the eyes look back” for “the eyes look ahead/from afar”; and “at once” for “immediately.”

The translated editorial notes retain the source’s authorities and witnesses: Augustine’s *Annotations on Job*, the Greek Septuagint, the recent Alexandrian-codex edition, the Colbertine manuscript reported by Montfaucon, the Latin Vulgate, the Hebrew text, Martianay, Pollux, Aquila, and Jerome. Notes signed `MART.` preserve that editorial attribution.

And Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Minaean departed; and they did as the Lord had commanded them. And he forgave their sin for Job’s sake. The Lord, moreover, increased Job’s possessions. And when he had also prayed for his friends, he forgave them their sin. And the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had possessed before. And all his brothers and sisters, and all who had known him from the beginning, heard everything that had happened to him, and they came to him. And when they had drunk and eaten bread with him in his house [Note: These words seem to reflect the version from the Hebrew, not the Greek, where the wording is different: “and, eating and drinking with him, they consoled him,” etc. Greek: *φαγόντες δὲ καὶ πιόντες παρ’ αὐτῷ· παρεκάλεσαν αὐτόν*.], they consoled him and expressed astonishment at all the evils that the Lord had brought upon him. [Col. 0112C] And each one gave him one lamb; and [Note: This passage again departs considerably from the Greek text, which has “and a four-drachma gold coin without a mint-mark” (*καὶ τετράδραχμον χρυσοῦν ἄσημον*). From the Hebrew, however, the holy Father translated it as follows: “and each one [gave him] one golden earring.”] each man gave him one golden earring.

But the Lord blessed Job’s latter days more than his former ones. And his livestock consisted of fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and one thousand grazing she-asses. And seven sons and three daughters were born to him. And he named the first Day, the second Cassia, and the third Horn of Amalthea. And no women like Job’s daughters were found under heaven. And their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.

And Job lived after the affliction [Note: The Septuagint has “one hundred and seventy years.” But the Alexandrian manuscript agrees with our edition in the final clause, “and all the years he lived were two hundred and forty-eight.” In addition, an obelus should have been placed before this total of Job’s years; for that verse is not read in the books of the Hebrews. MART.] one hundred and forty years. ÷ And all the years of his life were two hundred and forty-eight ** + And Job saw his sons, + and his sons’ sons to the fourth generation ** [Note: This total of Job’s years is found neither in the Hebrew nor among the other translators, as the note of the Colbertine manuscript and another Royal Hexaplar manuscript cited by Montfaucon bears witness: “It is not found in the Hebrew, nor among the others.” We have therefore marked it with an obelus.]. And Job died an old man, full of days.

[Note: Here the Hebrew archetype ends, as do the Greek interpreters who translated from it. The passages that follow, marked verse by verse with obeli in the Septuagint and Theodotion, are understood to have been taken from the Syriac. Since there is room on the page, it is pleasing to append here the interpretation of this continuation from the Greek in the old Vulgate edition: “And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord will raise.” The following passages are drawn from the Syriac: “Job lived in the land of Uz, between the borders of Edom and Arabia, and previously he was called Jobab. He took a foreign wife (an Arab woman), and a son was born to him, named Ennon. Job was the son of Zerah, a descendant of Esau, and of Bozrah; and he was the fifth after Abraham (in the Arabic version, the sixth). These are the kings who reigned in Edom, where Job also reigned. The first was Balac, son of Beor; and the name of that man’s city was Dennaba. After him came this Jobab, who is called Job; and after Job, Asom, who was ruler in the land of Teman. After him came Adad, son of Barac, who killed and routed Midian in the plain of Moab; and the name of his city was Gethem. Among Job’s friends who came to him was Eliphaz, of the sons of Esau and king of Teman; Bildad, king of the Saucheans; and Zophar, king of the Minaeans.”]

÷ And it is written that he will rise again with those whom the Lord will raise.

÷ [Note: Let the reader remember Origen’s words, with which we were told at the beginning of this book that this entire section, although retained by the Septuagint translators together with Theodotion, is absent from the Hebrew books and is marked throughout with obeli. Moreover, all learned men agree that this addition is extremely ancient, since Aristeas, Philo, and Polyhistor mention it, as Spanheim testifies in *History of Job*, chapter 4. Its authority among the Greeks may be learned from the preface to the Greek Fathers’ *Catena on Job*. Concerning the same addition Saint Jerome writes in his *Hebrew Questions*: “Some wrongly suppose that Job was of the race of Esau; for what is found at the end of the book itself—namely, that he was fourth from Esau, and the other details contained there—are not found in the Hebrew books, since it was translated from the Syriac.” Polychronius should also be added to Jerome, for he likewise diminished the credibility of the addition in these words: “Some reject the genealogy at the end because it is not found in the Hebrew . . .” [Col. 0114C] They assert that the similarity of names in the genealogy of Esau found in the book of Genesis, where Jobab is mentioned, gave certain people a pretext for error and for a note of this kind; and that, with the passage of time, what had been written in the margin was afterward incorporated by others into the text of the book. MART.]

This is interpreted from the Syriac book as follows: he lived in the land of Ausitis, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia, and his former name was Jobab. And he took an Arab woman as his wife. And she bore a son whose name was Ennon. He himself was the son of Zerah, a son of the sons of Esau, and on his mother’s side of Bosram, so that he was fifth from Abraham.

And these are the kings who reigned in Edom, in the land where he too reigned. First, Balaac, son of Boor, whose city was called Dennaba. After Balaac came Jobab, who is called Job. After him came Casus, who was ruler of the region and of the Temanites. After this came Adad, son of Barad, who destroyed Midian in the plain of Moab; and the name of his city was Gethem.

Those who came to him as friends were Eliphaz, king of the Temanites, from the sons of Esau; Bildad, tyrant of the Saucheans; and Zophar, king of the Minaeans. **

*The Book of Job according to the Septuagint ends here.*

[Col. 0113]

# [The Book of Psalms]

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Work

The Psalter according to the Septuagint translators, revised once and again by Jerome, was first published at Rome about ten years ago through the study and labor of the priest J. Carus, with obeli and asterisks added in the Psalter which ancient and more recent writers call the Gallican Psalter.

In order to imitate the diligence of the learned Carus in publishing Jerome’s two Psalters, and to make our edition somewhat more carefully corrected and more complete, we searched through a great many very ancient manuscript codices to supply whatever seemed to be lacking both in the text and in the signs of the obeli and asterisks. With the considerable assistance provided by this abundance of ancient manuscripts, we fulfilled the wishes of Carus, who, deprived of the same assistance from manuscript books, admits that he handed over the work he had begun for others to complete.

He writes: “The titles of these Psalms have been excerpted from manuscript codices and from Cassiodorus, insofar as was possible, though not as much as was necessary or desired—for that would have required several men of keener sight, and the manuscript codices themselves, to be available to us. We frankly admit that greater diligence was desirable in adding obeli, asterisks, and *diapsalmata*, and in dividing the verses in both editions. We have at least provided a specimen, so that, with the way thereby opened, others might more accurately accomplish what was desired through more thorough care and labor.”

Accordingly, while readily forgiving with sincere goodwill whatever he may have done poorly in this edition of the Psalter, we shall devote ourselves to one purpose: that the Hieronymian Psalter, which we said above was partly published and partly unpublished, may now appear as accurately corrected and as complete in every respect as possible, for the public benefit of the Church and of students.

The holy Doctor mentions the two revisions of the Psalms according to the Septuagint that he undertook in the preface that follows shortly. In the second book of his *Apology against Rufinus*, he also testifies that the Psalter corrected by his efforts had formerly been undertaken at Rome, in these words: “The Psalter also, which certainly, most carefully corrected according to the Septuagint translators through our labor, Rome received some time ago, while I was translating it anew according to the Hebrew, and so forth.”

Which revision he has in mind here, however—whether the earlier one he produced while at Rome, or the later one issued during his retreat at Bethlehem with obeli and asterisks—we can scarcely determine. Certainly, the first revision, which he says below was produced hastily at Rome, cannot be meant here, although not a few writers claim that it is. For how could the Roman Church have received from Jerome a Psalter that was “most carefully corrected,” when he had corrected it hastily and only for the most part?

It therefore seems most probable that both of Jerome’s editions, the earlier and the later, were received in the city of Rome, and that Jerome referred indiscriminately to both revisions when he charged Rufinus with his most carefully corrected Psalter according to the Septuagint. The words of Walafrid, quoted shortly below, strongly support our opinion; from them we are certain that the Gauls borrowed even the later revision of the Psalter from the Romans.

The earlier edition came to be called the Roman Psalter because it was used by the Roman Church from ancient times, and its use continues today in the Vatican Church. The later and more accurate edition was called the Gallican Psalter because our Gauls were the first of all to employ it in ecclesiastical services.

Let the reader therefore remember that in this edition of the two Psalters—the Roman and the Gallican—we have marked the former at the head of the columns with the letter R, and the latter with the letter G. With these letters prefixed, no confusion between the versions can subsequently creep in.

[Note: In our edition the versions will be distinguished by differences in type. Roman type will designate the Roman codex; italic type will designate the Gallican codex.]

# Testimonies Concerning Jerome’s Two Psalters According to the Septuagint Translators

[Col. 0115]

## Jerome, Letter 71 to Lucinius Boeticus, §5

“I do not doubt that you possess the edition of the Septuagint translators, and many years ago I carefully corrected it and delivered it to students.”

## The Same, Book II Against Rufinus, §30

“The Psalter also, which certainly, most carefully corrected according to the Septuagint translators through our labor, Rome received some time ago, while I was translating it anew according to the Hebrew, and so forth.”

## Likewise, Letter 106 to Sunnia and Fretela

“I shall briefly explain the meaning of this matter to you. Wherever something is lacking in the Greek in comparison with the Hebrew truth, Origen added it from Theodotion’s translation and placed an asterisk, that is, a star, as a sign—one that illuminates and brings into the midst what previously seemed hidden. But wherever something is found in the Greek codices that is not in the Hebrew, he prefixed an obelus, that is, a lying-down stroke, which we may call in Latin a spit; by it he shows that what is not found in the authoritative books ought to be struck out and pierced through. These signs are also found in the poems of Greek and Latin writers.”

## The Same, in the Same Letter

“And from this an error arises among you and among many others: because, through the carelessness of scribes, the entire distinction is confused when the strokes and asterisks are omitted. Again: ‘You say that in the Greek it does not have *sibi*.’ It does not have it in the Hebrew either, and among the Septuagint translators it is marked beforehand with an obelus. When these signs are left aside by many as though superfluous through the carelessness of scribes, a great error arises in reading.”

[Col. 0116A] In the same place:

“Another edition of the Septuagint translators, which is also found in the *Hexapla* codices, and which I faithfully translated into Latin.”

A little later in the same place:

“Those things that are found in the *Hexapla*, and which I translated, are the very version of the Septuagint translators preserved incorrupt and unstained in the books of the learned.”

## The Same, Letter 112 to Augustine, §19

“You ask why my earlier translation in the canonical books has asterisks with strokes prefixed.”

## Then, in the Same Author’s Letter 134 to the Same Person, at the End

“We could not obey your instructions, especially in the edition of the Septuagint, which is marked with asterisks and spits. For we lost much of our earlier labor through the fraud of a certain person.”

## The Same, in the Preface to the Psalter from the Hebrew, Addressed to Sophronius

“Nor do I say this in order to attack my predecessors, or because I think anything should be taken away from those whose translation I once carefully corrected and gave to the people of my own language.”

## From Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, Chapter 25

“As for the Psalms, while the Romans still have them according to the Septuagint translators, the Gauls and some Germans sing the Psalter according to the revision which Father Jerome composed from the Septuagint edition. Gregory, bishop of Tours, is said to have brought it from the Roman regions into the churches of Gaul.”

## From the Threefold Psalter in the Sorbonne Manuscript, No. 2783

“The Psalter which, according to the Septuagint translators, was sung in all the churches was corrected by Jerome. When it had again become corrupted, he composed a new Psalter, which would not differ greatly from the edition of the Septuagint translators and would agree substantially with the Hebrew. To make this clear to everyone, he distinguished the Psalter by asterisks, that is, stars +, and by obeli, that is, a lying-down stroke ÷, teaching that what is contained between the asterisk and the two dots ** is not found in the Hebrew but was added by the Septuagint translators. [Note: Something seems to be missing here. Compare Jerome’s following preface.] It was corrected solely according to Theodotion’s edition.

Pope Damasus, at Jerome’s request, instituted the singing of this Psalter in the Gallican churches, and for this reason it is called Gallican; while the Romans retained the Psalter according to the Septuagint, for which reason it is called Roman.

Since these two Psalters were insufficient for presenting testimonies concerning Christ against the Jews, who accept only what is found in the Hebrew, he added a third, called the Hebrew, because, at the request of the wise man Sophronius, he translated it from the Hebrew truth into Latin word for word. Sophronius translated this Psalter, as well as other works of Jerome, from Latin into Greek.”

[Note: Martianaeus seems to have copied this preface from some commonly circulated volume of the Bible, not from manuscript codices, which he does not mention. It is found in the edition published with the ordinary and interlinear glosses and the commentaries of Nicholas of Lyra, as well as in Hugh of Saint-Cher’s *Postilla*. Finally, it is also found in the old edition of several works of Jerome, often cited by us, from the year 1496; but it escaped other editors, especially Erasmus and Victorius. We have transcribed it from the manuscripts that we shall cite in the following annotation, and compared it with the commonly circulated editions.]

# Jerome’s Preface to the Book of Psalms

[Note: Accordingly, we collated this book, together with the preface just mentioned, against two manuscript codices of the Vatican Library, both of the highest antiquity and especially excellent quality. One had formerly belonged to the Queen of Sweden and is marked No. 24; the other is Palatine, under No. 39, written almost entirely in uncial letters and so accurately corrected that I would scarcely wish you to find any equal to it. Besides this preface, the book contains Jerome’s preface to Sophronius, which is prefixed to his other translation from the Hebrew, as well as another piece concerning the praises of the Psalms. Finally, it contains this rubric in red ink: “The copyist: know with complete certainty that this is the Psalter according to Jerome, corrected according to the Septuagint and sent from Jerusalem to Rome” (the manuscript reads “sent at Rome”). Many lines follow, in bound verse, explaining the form of the fourfold Psalter. We thought it worthwhile to transcribe at least the following, correcting them in places.]

The page speaks in four double columns,  
For each column displays what the Hebrew source  
Most truly gives, which Jerome,  
Revealing it, expressed in Latin speech.  
Here too the Greek sense and wording properly appear,  
Written in our little letters and our character;  
Yet this page, translated from Greek into Latin speech,  
Retains what I said above in written form.  
The Roman Church also continually uses it,  
And it is called the common and Vulgate edition.  

From these columns the venerable translator  
Of the Hebrew language marks what must be rejected  
And also indicates what must be retained.  
But a fourth translation is written in this column,  
Which the aforesaid man, faithfully following the Septuagint,  
Strived to transfer from Greek into this language  
And revealed with complete fidelity.  
The peoples of the East also sing this version,  
As do those whom Gaul has produced  
And those whom the North brings forth.  

Therefore, reader, look carefully now upon  
The fourfold form of the Psalter, brought together  
In varied speech; and do not allow yourself  
To be deceived by any model,  
When you see before your eyes the authors’ truthful teachings.  

The first column, written above on the page,  
Which the Gauls recite, retains faithfully  
The language of Jerome, as I said,  
Its faithful translator.  
Remember that whatever differs from this edition  
Also differs equally from the Hebrew.  

But the Vulgate contains a second,  
Less carefully corrected, which the Romans sing  
And the Italians use.  
The third contains what was truly translated  
By the Hebrew master, and this will reveal  
All these things to us more clearly.  
The last is marked in the proper Greek language;  
As I said, since it is less common,  
We approve it less.

# Psalms (C)

[Col. 0117B] When I was formerly at Rome, I had corrected the Psalter and, according to the Septuagint translators, although hastily, had corrected a large part of it. But because you see it again corrupted through the fault of scribes, and the old error carrying greater force than the new [Col. 0118B] correction [Note: The Palatine manuscript omits the word *valere* (“to prevail”); it then reads something resembling *novalis*.], you compel me, as though with a new ploughing, to cultivate a field already torn apart and to uproot the thorns that grow again in crooked furrows. You say that it is right that what repeatedly sprouts badly should be cut down still more often.

[Note: The words “whence the customary” are also absent from the Palatine manuscript.]

Therefore, in my customary preface I admonish both you, for whom this labor may perhaps be wearisome, and those who may wish to possess copies of this kind, that what I have carefully corrected be transcribed with care and diligence. [Note: The old edition of 1496 has *transcribant* (“let them transcribe”), which is probably more correct.] Let each person note either the lying-down line or the radiant signs—that is, the obeli ÷ or the asterisks +. Wherever he sees a preceding stroke ÷, from it up to the two dots ** that we have printed, he should know that the Septuagint translators [Alternative: interpreters] have more. But wherever he sees the likeness of a star +, he should know that it has been added from the Hebrew books, likewise up to the two dots, solely according to the edition of Theodotion, who in the simplicity of his language does not differ from the Septuagint translators. [Note: The Palatine manuscript omits the Greek article *to* (“the”) up to this point.]

Knowing that I have done this for you and for every devoted student, I do not doubt that there will be many who, whether through envy or disdain, would rather regard what is excellent with contempt than learn it. [Note: The same manuscript reads *videre* (“to see”). In the preface to the Psalter from the Hebrew addressed to Sophronius, we stated that we think one should read *et invidere* (“and envy”); these are Pliny’s words, which the holy Father transferred into his own work. Indeed, in another preface to the books of Chronicles according to the Septuagint, to be reprinted below, the holy Doctor himself supports this reading at the end of the passage, where he cites Pliny by name: “For, as Pliny says, most people would rather despise the best things and envy them than learn.”]

They would rather drink from a turbid stream [Alternative: brook] than from the purest spring.

## Roman Psalter

[Note: This is called Roman because it was certainly prepared by Jerome at the request either of Damasus or of other friends from the city, for the benefit and use of that Church, as we learn immediately from the first words of the prologue: “When I was formerly at Rome, I had corrected the Psalter and, according to the Septuagint translators, although hastily, had corrected a large part of it.” The other, distinguished by obeli and asterisks and corrected by the holy Doctor in a later and more careful effort against the Greek of the Hexapla, is called Gallican because the Gallican Church long ago used it in divine services. When the holy Father therefore says of this very revision of the Psalter in Book XI against Rufinus, “The most carefully corrected Psalter according to the Septuagint translators was received at Rome through our labor some time ago,” this should not be understood as though he said that this edition too had been received for the use of that Church—which, content with the earlier correction, still retains it in the Vatican basilica—but merely that he sent this labor of his to Rome, as the note of the Palatine codex mentioned above also indicates. This Gallican Psalter with obeli and asterisks was first published in print, together with the commentary of Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, in 1694, and afterward reprinted in 1618 in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, volume XI, from the revision of John Cochlaeus. Usserius praises another edition, from 1539, in chapter 9 of his work on the Septuagint version. Finally, the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, under the name of Joseph Maria Carus the priest, prepared another edition from the Vatican manuscripts with the greatest care and diligence; Martianaeus used it, and we have continuously examined it word for word.]

[Note: [Col. 0147C] Here the Palatine codex marks *Diapsalma*; it also reads *subdes* (“you put under”) for *subdis* (“you subject”).]

God, who gives me vengeance and subdues peoples beneath me, my deliverer from my enemies ÷ [Note: [Col. 0147C] Saint Jerome, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, speaks as follows of this passage; Martianus also praises these words as a distinguished testimony of sincere and modest character: “Because we are devoted to the truth once and for all, if something has been corrupted either through the haste of the translator or through the fault of copyists, we ought simply to confess and correct it. In Hebrew you have nothing else except this: ‘My deliverer from my enemies.’ But the Septuagint added *the angry ones* (*iracundis*). This is the reason why that word is marked with an obelus.

“Nevertheless, if the matter may be examined more attentively, the Septuagint can easily defend themselves against the holy Father’s accusation and show that they did not add something of their own. The word that immediately follows *my enemies* in the Hebrew text, if one begins the second half-verse with it, also means ‘and yet’; if it is joined to what precedes, it is a noun denoting anger; and if it is joined to another substantive, it functions as an adjective and means ‘angry.’ Thus, in Proverbs 22:24, it means ‘an angry man,’ and in 29:22, ‘an angry man,’ as Jerome himself translates it. These are the passages that the recent editor of the Alexandrian codex has noted before us.

“Therefore the Septuagint did not append *orgilous* (ὀργίλους), that is, ‘angry ones,’ from their own invention; rather, they correctly understood that Hebrew word as a noun, not as an adverb. In fact, the following half-verse does not begin with καί, ‘and,’ or with any other particle or adverb, but simply with Ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπανισταμένων, ‘from those who rise up,’ and so forth. Jerome preferred to take it as *and*, or as an adverb meaning *also*; that was entirely open to him. But it was not permissible to accuse the Septuagint’s literal translation of interpolation.

“Nevertheless, in Martianus the holy Father’s edition was truly [lacuna; the supplied text resumes with the ending *-sa*] corrupt at this point, for he marked with a new obelus not only the word *angry ones* but also the following *and*. Carus and the Palatine manuscript, by contrast, correctly placed an asterisk before that small word, and we have restored it in accordance with the mind of the holy translator, who otherwise would not be consistent with himself.

“Yet I do not think it was written that way in the Origenian exemplar. Rather, the word may have been inserted into the Latin afterward by Jerome, or perhaps by others who had noticed the passage from his letter to Sunnia cited above.

“Moreover, I think that formerly the obelus was placed not before the word *angry ones* but before the preceding *my*. The Palatine manuscript certainly presents it as: ‘from my enemies ÷ my ** angry ones,’ and so forth. Augustine too, in his *Correction*, which the Veronese manuscript carefully reproduces, rejects the pronoun *my*, since it was absent from better Greek exemplars. Other Latin manuscripts of Jerome also reject it, including the most distinguished manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, which we cite in the notes to that letter.

“Finally, the Hebrew text itself, with different points supplied beneath the letters, can be read more suitably in the construct state with the following word, namely ‘from angry enemies,’ rather than in the absolute state. The teachers of that language will not deny this.”] the angry ones **

+ And ** from those who rise up against me you will exalt me; you will deliver me from the unjust man.

Therefore I will confess you among the nations, Lord, and I will sing praise to your name.

He magnifies the salvations of his king and shows mercy to his anointed one, to David and his seed forever.

## PSALM XVIII

### FOR THE ENDING, A PSALM OF DAVID

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.

Day pours forth the word to day, and night makes knowledge known to night.

[Col. 0149A] There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.

Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world ÷ [Note: [Col. 0149C] See what we have said above, and not only once: the Hebrew expression signifies not simply “the world,” but “the world of the earth.” The obelus that follows is missing in the Palatine manuscript and in Carus.] ** of the earth.

÷ In ** the sun he placed his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.

He rejoiced like a giant to run the course [Note: [Col. 0149C] Here he had found the pronoun “his” added beneath the obelus. Jerome’s Chartres manuscript still has the same obelus, or dagger, with a blank space in this form: “to run the course ÷: from the summit,” and so forth. Perhaps the holy Doctor removed this word while correcting the Psalter, because the Hebrew and Greek manuscripts read without the pronoun “his.” MART. —In Jerome’s own time, copies added the pronoun “his.” Concerning this matter, in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, he says: “And you say that the Greek does not have ‘his’; but we found it added beneath an obelus, and it is clear that it is absent from the Hebrew.” The Palatine manuscript likewise preserves an erasure here, of the obelus and the pronoun that had been inserted; but a certain Chartres manuscript in Martianay’s possession restores the obelus and leaves a blank space for the pronoun. Finally, opposite the following verse, the same Palatine manuscript notes “Diapsalma.”] His going forth is from the summit of heaven.

And his course reaches to its summit; no one is hidden from his heat.

The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the little ones.

The ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.

[Col. 0149B] The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever ÷ unto ages **; the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.

They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

And [Note: [Col. 0149D] The Palatine manuscript omits this obelus; Carus also strikes through the word [Col. 0150D] “for.” In the margin of the book, the same manuscript again writes “Diapsalma.”] for ** your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.

Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden ÷ ** faults, and spare your servant from those belonging to another.

If they do not rule over me, then I shall be undefiled, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.

÷ [Note: [Col. 0150C] The Palatine manuscript and Carus again omit this obelus less correctly.] And ** they shall be such that the sayings of my mouth may please, and the meditation of my heart before you ÷ always **

O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

### FOR THE ENDING, A PSALM OF DAVID

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands.

Day pours forth the word [Note: [Col. 0148D] The same manuscript has “pours forth” and “announces,” instead of “makes known,” following Augustine’s correction; likewise the readings that follow.]

and night makes knowledge known to night.

[Col. 0150A] There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.

Their sound has gone out into all the earth [Ms. has gone forth], and their words to the ends of the world.

In the sun he placed his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.

He rejoiced like a giant to run the course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven [Note: [Col. 0150C] The same manuscript has “like a giant to run the course, from the summit [Col. 0150D] of heaven,” and so forth, “to the summit of heaven, and there is no one,” and so forth, following Augustine.]

and his course reaches to its summit; there is no one who can hide from his heat.

The law of the Lord is irreproachable [Ms. undefiled], converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, granting wisdom to the little ones.

The ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0150D] Augustine, and the Veronese manuscript that copies him, read “heart” in the singular; shortly afterward, “pure, enduring” instead of “holy, endures,” and “justified in the same thing” instead of “in themselves.” As for what is then read in the same manuscript, “a clean precious stone” instead of “much,” that is an error of the editor rather than of the manuscript in reading. Finally, “for your servant will keep them,” and so forth.] hearts; the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes.

[Col. 0150B] The fear of the Lord is holy, endures forever; the judgments of God [Ms. of the Lord] are true, justified in themselves.

They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

For your servant also keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.

Who understands his offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord; spare your servant from those belonging to another.

If they do not rule over me [Note: [Col. 0150D] Augustine very correctly emended this to “rule,” that is, “the offenses,” as the Veronese manuscript also recites; then, “and I shall be cleansed from a great offense,” from the same source.] then I shall be undefiled, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.

And they shall be such that the sayings of my mouth may please, and the meditation of my heart before you may always please.

O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

This testimony of the holy Father is very well known. The editor of the Veronese Psalter does not derive it from that letter, but from the preface to the Books of Chronicles addressed to Chromatius, in which there is neither any mention of it nor any mention of this Psalm, as though it had never existed. For *feneratur* in Latin can be said both of one who lends at interest and of one who receives a loan; but it is expressed more clearly if we say “he lends at interest.” What concern is it to us what the grammarians want? You understand one another better in our barbarism than you would be eloquent to one another in our eloquence. Thus this righteous man has mercy all day and lends at interest. The editor of the Veronese Psalter did not overlook this passage; nevertheless, even with such a clear testimony, he could not be taught that this was the Augustinian recension, not the old edition which he himself presents as the Itala.], he will not be disturbed, because the Lord strengthens his hand.

[Note: [Col. 0184D] This manuscript alone, together with Augustine, has “will perish together,” and “the remnants of the impious will perish.” Thus in the final verse: “he will rescue them and withdraw them from sinners.”]

[Col. 0184C] And the Lord will help them and deliver them; he will rescue them from sinners and save them, because they have hoped in him [Ms. “in him”].

Shortly afterward, instead of “may they insult me,” the Verona manuscript prefers “may they rejoice over me,” closer to the Greek ἐπιχαίρωσί μοι, “may they rejoice over me.” Augustine, however—to conceal nothing—differs from this, at least in the commonly circulated copies, where the old reading “they insult me” is retained. Thus the editor of the Verona manuscript falsely says that Augustine too read “may they at some time rejoice” in his exposition of this psalm, section 22. I can scarcely suppose that Augustine knew this reading from the parallel testimony which he cites: “those who attack me will rejoice if I am shaken.”]

In what follows Augustine also retains “those who hate me unjustly”; the Verona manuscript, however, prefers *injuste* rather than *inique*: both are rendered “unjustly,” but the Latin wording differs, a point its editor ought to have noted, since he diligently pursues even the smallest matters. Then, in agreement, they read: “Those who repay evil for good,” and “because I pursued righteousness,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0186C] The Verona manuscript adds the old gloss: “And they cast me away, the beloved one, as a dead man who has become abominable.” It copied this from Augustine, who recites it twice in his exposition. Nevertheless, it may be thought that he did not regard it as part of this verse, but adopted it as a testimony from elsewhere for the sake of his interpretation or allegory. We do not, however, fail to recognize that it flowed from Greek copies, from which Theodoret quotes it in exactly these words: Καὶ ἀπέῤῥιψάν με τὸν ἀγαπητόν, ὡς νεκρὸν ἐβδελυγμένον, “And they cast me away, the beloved one, as a dead man who has become abominable.” Hence some Oriental versions derived from the Greek, as well as certain Latin codices, also received it.]

Do not forsake me, Lord my God; do not depart from me. Attend to my help, Lord God of my salvation.

Yet this is very different from the Greek reading δυνατέ, “mighty one.” Still, the Veronese codex reproduces Augustine even where he is less correct.] O mightiest one; peoples shall fall beneath you into [Note: The Veronese manuscript has “in the sight of,” instead of “in the heart of”; and, more surprisingly, in the facing Greek column it consistently reads *enopion* in Latin letters, corresponding to ἐνώπιον, instead of ἐν καρδίᾳ, “in the heart,” as all other books known to me, and the witnesses in every language, prefer. This therefore cannot be used as evidence for the old Latin version, since there is no Greek exemplar that reads ἐνώπιον. I would rather regard it as the bold alteration of a glossator. You should also know that *enopion* was written by the first hand in our codex; immediately afterward, however, another hand—apparently equally ancient—crossed out the letters *epion* with a transverse stroke and marked them with an obelus in the margin of the book, writing *cardia* above them. As we have said, this is the reading of all the Greek exemplars.] the heart of the king’s enemies.

You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.

Myrrh, drop, and cassia from your garments, from [Note: The older reading is commonly thought to have been “from the heavy things,” which was itself an error in certain Latin books before Jerome. They suppose that it arose from the scribes’ mistake, because of the great similarity between *gravibus* and *gradibus*, and that the reading which seemed better suited to the context was substituted for the other in later Latin books. The editor of the Veronese Psalter also adopted this transferred opinion. I think quite otherwise, and would not have the variant reading arise from a nearly identical Latin spelling, but rather from a different reading in the Greek codex, from which a different Latin interpretation likewise flowed; thus neither reading need be attributed to a scribal error. One Greek reading—and the genuine one—is ἀπὸ βάρεων, “from the houses,” from the native Palestinian word βάρις, meaning a large house. Those who translated “from the heavy things” also read this, but derived it from βαρύς, “heavy.” Those who translate “from the steps,” however, I maintain read βάσεων instead of βάρεων, with one letter changed, and thus translated the Greek quite properly rather than being deceived by the similarity of Latin words. If no Greek exemplars now produce this reading, the reason must be that the Latin interpreter read it in this form, while it was not written down in the same way by the Greek scribes. In reality, since the same noun occurs below in other cases—for example, in Psalm XLVII, in the penultimate verse, τὰς βάρεας—those who interpret it as “steps,” as most do, clearly did not take that word to mean “heavy things.” First, the difference between the two words is greater than could readily cause confusion; and, above all, no interpreter has translated “heavy things” in that passage. It is therefore perfectly clear that they read τὰς βάσεις instead of τὰς βάρεις there, and consequently that here also, and below where they write “from the steps” instead of “from the heavy things,” they received the wording not from an error in the Latin books but from the reading or emendation of their Greek exemplar. Those who think that these books are erroneous are themselves greatly mistaken. See what we explained in the note to Letter 65, to Principia, column 388. The Veronese book and Augustine read “from the houses.”] ivory steps: from them the daughters of kings have delighted you, in your honor.

For behold, [Note: Both the Roman and Gallican Psalters read “the kings of the earth have assembled.” This certainly cannot be permitted by those who have undertaken to restore Jerome’s works: for who would tolerate in his books what he declares he removed? “In the forty-seventh psalm,” he says, “you read, ‘For behold, the kings have assembled,’ whereas you say that in the Greek you have read, ‘For behold, its kings have assembled.’ The text of the reading itself shows that this is superfluous; and in the ancient Latin books it was written ‘the kings of the earth,’ which we removed because it is found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint.” Thus he writes in the letter praised hundreds of times. [Col. 0203A] We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple.

[Col. 0208A] If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world of the earth and its fullness are mine.

But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant through your mouth?

Yet you hate [Note: In these same books alone: “You hated instruction”; and shortly afterward: “If you saw a thief, you ran together with him”; and “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue embraced deceitfulness.” A little below, “you suspected” instead of “you thought.”] discipline and have cast my words behind you.

If you saw a thief, you ran together with him; and with adulterers you placed your portion.

[Col. 0208B] Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit.

That this is faulty and does not stand in our language is clear even to fools . . . . We cannot say, ‘You slandered against your brother,’ but ‘You slandered your brother,’ and so forth.” MART.] you slandered your brother, and against the son of your mother you placed a stumbling-block.

[Col. 0212B] TO THE END, FOR MELETH [Note: [Col. 0212C] Through the error of copyists, many manuscripts read “Amalech” for “Meleth.” Everyone knew the name “Amalech.” Therefore they changed the Hebrew “Meleth,” wholly unknown to them, into the word “Amalech.” The holy Doctor frequently complains of this exchange of names while illuminating the sacred volumes in his commentaries. This psalm, moreover, is identical with the preceding Psalm 13, except without any intermixture of the eight verses added there. See above. MART. — Through the customary error of copyists, “Amalech” for “Meleth” is also written in the Verona book. ## TO THE END, “DO NOT DESTROY,” DAVID, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE, WHEN SAUL SENT AND GUARDED HIS HOUSE IN ORDER TO KILL HIM

Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me.

Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood.

For behold, they have hunted my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me. There is neither my iniquity nor my sin, O Lord.

Without iniquity I ran and was guided; rise up to meet me and see—and you, O Lord, God of hosts, God of Israel.

Attend to visiting all the nations; do not have mercy on all who work iniquity. DIAPSALMA.

*Note:* The same books read: “to visit all the nations; do not have mercy on all,” etc. Then: “They shall return toward evening,” as below. Augustine, however, has “Let them return,” and immediately afterward “let them suffer,” etc.

[Col. 0222A] They shall return toward evening, and suffer hunger like dogs, and **they shall** go around the city.

Behold, they themselves shall speak with their mouth, and a sword is in their lips.

For who has heard? And you, O Lord, shall laugh at them and **hold all the nations as nothing**.

I shall keep my strength toward you, because **you**, God, are my protector; my God’s mercy shall go before me.

*Note:* The same books omit the pronoun “you” here. In the following verse they likewise read: “My God has shown me among my enemies: do not,” etc. A little later Augustine has “lead down” for “destroy,” and below: “And from curse and deceit completions shall be proclaimed,” **in anger**, etc.

My God, show me good things among my enemies; do not kill them, lest my people at some time forget your law.

Scatter them by your strength, and destroy them, my protector and Lord.

The sins of their mouth, the word **[manuscript: words]** of their lips; and let them be caught in their pride. And because of cursing and deceit, let them be driven into the anger of completion, and let them not be.

And they shall know that God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth. DIAPSALMA.

They shall return toward evening, and suffer hunger like dogs; and they shall go around the city.

*Note:* Omitting the words “Behold, they themselves,” Augustine and the Veronese manuscript have the remainder as follows: “They shall scatter to eat; but if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.” Augustine more correctly has: “But if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.” “But I shall sing of your power,” etc.

Behold, they themselves shall scatter to eat; but if they are not satisfied, they shall murmur.

But I shall sing of your strength, and rejoice in the morning in your mercy.

For you have become my protector and my refuge in the day of my tribulation; my helper, to you I shall sing psalms.

For you, God, are my protector; my God, my mercy.

## PSALM LIX

[Col. 0221]

## TO THE END, FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE: DAVID, FOR INSTRUCTION, WHEN HE BURNED MESOPOTAMIA OF SYRIA AND SOBAL, AND JOAB TURNED BACK AND STRUCK EDOM IN THE VALLEY OF THE SALT PITS—TWELVE THOUSAND

*Note:* The same manuscript reads: “He burned Syria of Mesopotamia and Syria of Sobal,” and then: “and he struck Edom in the valley,” etc.

God, you rejected us and **destroyed** us; you were angry, **and** you had mercy on us.

*Note:* The Palatine manuscript also causes the word “are” to be preceded by an obelus. Most correctly, however, in the following verse, where it says “and you troubled it,” it marks with an obelus the conjunction “and,” which is not in the Hebrew text.

You shook the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.

You showed your people hard things; you gave us wine of compunction.

[Col. 0223A] You gave a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from the face of the bow. DIAPSALMA.

So that your beloved might be delivered, save with your right hand and hear me.

God spoke in his holy place: I shall rejoice **and divide** Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents.

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head.

Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope.

Into Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal; the foreigners are subjected to me.

*Note:* Here the same manuscript less correctly adds “Diapsalma.”

Who will lead me into a fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?

Are you not the God who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, **for human salvation is vain**.

*Note:* More correctly, in accordance with the Greek and the Hebrew exemplar itself, the Palatine manuscript reads “and vain” instead of “for vain.”

In God we shall act with strength, and he himself will reduce to nothing those who trouble us.

## TO THE END, FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED, IN THE INSCRIPTION OF THE TITLE: DAVID, FOR INSTRUCTION, WHEN HE BURNED MESOPOTAMIA OF SYRIA AND SYRIA OF SOBAL, AND JOAB TURNED BACK AND STRUCK THE VALLEY OF THE SALT PITS—TWELVE THOUSAND

*Note:* The title is the same in Augustine and the Veronese manuscript, except for the word “for,” which the latter omits, or which may result from a minor scribal error: “To the end, for those who shall be changed, in the inscription of the title, to David for instruction, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Sobal, and turned back Joab (the manuscript mistakenly has Moab), and struck Edom in the valley of the Salt Pits,” etc. In the text: “you had mercy on us,” instead of “on us”; and “you showed hard things to your people,” “you gave us wine” (or “wine of”) “stimulation.”

God, you rejected us and **destroyed** us; you were angry, **and** you had mercy on us.

You shook the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for **[manuscript: since]** it has been shaken.

You showed hard things to your people; you gave us wine of compunction.

You gave a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from the face of the bow. DIAPSALMA. So that your chosen might be delivered.

Save me with your right hand and hear me. God spoke in his holy place: I shall rejoice, and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of tents.

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head.

Judah is my king; Moab is the pot of my hope. Into Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal; the allophyli—foreigners—are subjected **[manuscript: subject]** to me.

Who will lead me into a fortified city? Or **[manuscript omits “or”]** who will lead me as far as Idumea?

Are you not the God who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, and human salvation is vain.

In God we shall act with strength, and he himself will reduce to nothing those who trouble us.

## PSALM LX

[Col. 0223]

## TO THE END, IN HYMNS, DAVID

*Note:* Here and below the same manuscript customarily marks the preposition of the verb “hear” with an obelus.

Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer.

From the ends of the earth I cried to you; when my heart was in anguish, you lifted me up upon a rock.

You led me, because you became my hope; a tower of strength against the enemy.

I shall dwell in your tabernacle forever; I shall be protected under the shelter of your wings. DIAPSALMA.

For you, my God, heard my prayer; you gave an inheritance to those who fear your name. You shall add days upon days to the king, his years until the day of generation and generation.

He remains forever in the sight of God; who shall seek **his** mercy and truth?

*Note:* The Palatine manuscript indicated that the pronoun “his,” which is not heard here in the Hebrew, should be struck with an obelus.

Thus I shall sing a psalm to your name forever **and ever**, so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.

## TO THE END, IN HYMNS, DAVID **[manuscript: TO DAVID]**

*Note:* Through a scribal error, the title of the following Psalm, LXI, was substituted here in the Veronese manuscript, and this one was placed before that one, contrary to all the other witnesses and to the Greek in the facing column.

Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer. From the ends of the earth I cried to you.

When my heart was in anguish, you lifted me up upon a rock.

*Note:* The same manuscript as Augustine has “when they were increased,” and from this verse: “I am a sojourner in your tabernacle forever” (Augustine: “I shall be”), “Diapsalma. I shall be covered under the shelter of your wings, for,” etc.

You led me, because **[manuscript: since]** you became my hope; a tower of strength against the enemy.

I shall dwell in your tabernacle forever; I shall be protected under the shelter of your wings. DIAPSALMA.

For you, God, heard my prayer; you gave an inheritance to those who fear your name.

*Note:* Apart from a transposition of one noun, “king” after “you shall add,” the Veronese book differs from Augustine only in obvious scribal errors: “you shall add years to his years until the day of generation and generation.” A little later: “and his truth, who shall seek it?” “Thus I shall sing,” etc.

Days upon days you shall add to the king; years until the day of the age and the ages. He shall remain forever in the sight of God.

Who shall seek their mercy and truth? Thus I shall sing to your name, O God, forever and ever, so that I may fulfill my vows from day to day.

## PSALM LXI

[Col. 0223]

## TO THE END, FOR IDITHUN, A PSALM OF DAVID

Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him is my salvation.

[Col. 0225A] For he himself is my God, my savior, and my protector; I shall not be moved any further.

How long will you rush upon a man? You all kill, like a leaning wall and a pushed-down fence?

Yet they planned to repel my honor; I ran in thirst. With their mouth they blessed, and with their heart they cursed. DIAPSALMA.

Yet be subject to God, my soul, for from him is my patience.

*Note:* In the Palatine manuscript and in Carus it is given in this form: **“For he is my God and my savior,”** etc. This is not quite correct, although the Hebrew has it differently word for word: “Only he is my rock.” But that expression is frequently taken metaphorically for God, and the Septuagint translates: **θεός μου**—“my God.”

For he himself is my God and my savior, my helper; I shall not depart.

In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, **and my hope is in God**.

*Note:* We prefix an obelus to this conjunction also, according to the Palatine manuscript, since it is not heard in the Hebrew. Saint Jerome himself bears witness in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela regarding the obelus of the following verse.

[Col. 0225B] Hope in him, all the assembly of the people; pour out your hearts before him, for God is our helper **forever**. DIAPSALMA.

*Note:* Jerome likewise approves the obelus here, saying: “Therefore ‘forever’ is an obelus.”

Yet the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may deceive themselves through vanity into the same thing.

Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies. If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.

God spoke once; I heard two things: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy; for you will repay each according to his works.

## TO THE END, FOR IDITHUN, A PSALM OF DAVID

Will not my soul be subject **[manuscript: subjected]** to God? For from him is my salvation.

*Note:* The earlier reading in the Veronese codex was: “for from him is my patience”; and on the facing Greek page in Latin letters: *hoti par autu estin e ypomone mu*—“because from him is my patience.” This, however, is the wording proper not to this verse but to the sixth verse in all the other books. I do not know whether any Greek manuscripts or commentators have ever treated the passage in this way. Among Latin witnesses I know only the Carnutensian codex, which gives it thus and is based on the Greek. I attribute this easily to scribal error, not to the authority of any archetype, since it was corrected so accurately in the Veronese codex by an ancient hand—perhaps the same hand that wrote the rest of the text on both pages—for the text itself reads: “For from him is my salvation,” *par autu gar te sotirion mu*.

[Col. 0226A] Indeed, he himself is my God and my savior, **[note: the Veronese, with Augustine, has “protector” instead of “helper”; in the following verse, “How long will you place upon a man? killing,” Augustine: “kill,” “all like,”** etc.] my helper; I shall not be moved any further.

How long will you rush upon men? You kill them all, like a leaning wall and a pushed-down fence?

Yet they planned to repel my honor; I ran in thirst. With their mouth they blessed, and in their heart they cursed. DIAPSALMA.

Yet my soul shall be subject to God **[manuscript: shall be subjected]**, for from him is my patience.

Indeed **[manuscript: since]** he is my God and **[manuscript omits “and”]** my savior, my helper **[manuscript: protector]**; I shall not depart.

In God is my salvation and **[manuscript omits “and”]** my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God.

[Col. 0226B] Hope in him, every assembly of the people, and pour out your hearts before him, for God is our helper **[manuscript omits “is”]**. DIAPSALMA.

Yet the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, so that they may deceive themselves through their own vanity into the same thing.

Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire robberies.

If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them. God spoke once; I heard two things.

For power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, mercy; for you will repay each according to their works.

## PSALM LXII

[Col. 0225]

## A PSALM OF DAVID, WHEN HE WAS IN THE DESERT OF IDUMEA

God, my God, I keep watch for you from the light of dawn.

*Note:* Jerome reads in his letter, “My soul thirsted for you”; in place of this, he says, the Greek has, “My soul thirsted in you.” He further says that the Hebrew has LACII (), which means “for you,” and which all the translators rendered. Thus the verse was translated into Latin according to the idiom of the language. MART. — The Palatine manuscript omits the obelus. In the Greek text itself, without a preposition, it is *ἐδίψησέ σοι*—“it thirsted for you.” See the letter to Sunnia and Fretela. The same Palatine manuscript, however, shortly afterward errs by inserting an asterisk.

My soul thirsted **in** you; how greatly did my flesh thirst for you!

In **the desert**, a dry and pathless land without water, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary, to see your power and your glory.

For your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you.

Thus I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift up my hands.

[Col. 0227A] As with fat and richness my soul shall be filled, and my mouth shall praise you with lips of rejoicing.

*Note:* The Palatine manuscript adds “Diapsalma” here.

If I remembered you upon my bed, I shall meditate on you in the morning, because you have been my helper.

And under the shelter of your wings I shall rejoice; my soul clung to you, and your right hand received me.

But they sought my soul in vain; they shall enter the depths of the earth. They shall be handed over to the hands of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes.

But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.

## A PSALM OF DAVID **[manuscript: TO DAVID]**, WHEN HE WAS IN THE DESERT OF IDUMEA

God, my God, I keep watch for you from the light of dawn.

My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsted for you!

*Note:* The Veronese manuscript has: “In the desert, dry and pathless **[Augustine: and without a road]**, and without water, so,” etc.

In the desert, and in a pathless and waterless place, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary, to see your power **[manuscript: might]** and your glory.

For your mercy is better than lives.

*Note:* The editor of the Veronese Psalter omitted the words “better than lives,” saying that they were absent from that codex. Rather, they escaped his diligence: they are present there, although several letters are somewhat worn by age, and we read them in that very exemplar.

My lips shall praise you.

Thus I shall bless you in my life, and in your name I shall lift up my hands.

[Col. 0228A] As with fat and richness my soul shall be filled, and lips of rejoicing shall praise your name.

*Note:* According to Augustine, the same manuscript has: “As with fat,” etc.; “my soul has been filled” (Augustine: “shall be filled”). And: “If I remembered you,” etc. In the final verse: “Everyone who swears by him shall be praised, because the mouth,” etc.

If I remembered you upon my bed, I shall meditate on you in the morning, because you have been my helper.

And under the shelter of your wings I shall rejoice; my soul clung to you, and your right hand received me.

But they sought my soul in vain; they shall enter the depths of the earth. They shall be handed over to the hands of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes.

But the king shall rejoice in the Lord; all who swear by him shall be praised, because the mouth of those who speak iniquity has been stopped.

## PSALM LXIII

[Col. 0227]

## TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID

Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.

You protected me from the assembly of the wicked, from the multitude of those who work iniquity.

For they sharpened their tongues like a sword; they bent a bitter matter as a bow, so that they might shoot the blameless in secret.

Suddenly they shall shoot at him and shall not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil word.

They recounted things in order to conceal snares; they said: Who will see them?

They examined iniquities; those who searched with scrutiny failed.

*Note:* A later hand in the same codex rewrote “He shall approach,” and “Diapsalma” is written at the end of the verse.

A man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted.

[Col. 0227C] The arrows of children have become their wounds, and their tongues have been weakened against them.

All who saw them were troubled, and every man was afraid.

And they proclaimed the works of God, and understood his deeds.

The just man shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him; all upright in heart shall be praised.

## TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID **[manuscript: TO DAVID]**

Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead **[note: According to Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has “when I am troubled.” Immediately afterward Augustine has “deliver,” and the Veronese “free.”]**; from fear of the enemy deliver my soul.

You protected me from the assembly of the wicked and from the multitude of those who work iniquity.

For **[manuscript: who]** they sharpened their tongues like **[manuscript: as]** a sword; they bent a bitter matter as a bow, so that they might shoot the blameless in secret.

*Note:* With common agreement, the same witnesses have: “so that they might shoot the blameless in secret. Suddenly they shall shoot,” etc.; “they strengthened” (or “made firm”) “for themselves an evil word”; “they recounted things in order to conceal snares,” etc. Then: “They examined,” and “those who searched with scrutiny failed.” “A man shall approach the deep heart,” etc.; and: “The arrows of children became their wounds, and their tongues were weakened against them.” Finally: “And they proclaimed … all who are upright **[or: upright ones]** in heart.”

Suddenly they shall shoot at him and shall not fear; they have strengthened for themselves an evil word. They debated in order to conceal snares; they said: Who will see them?

They examined iniquity; those who searched with scrutiny failed.

A man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted.

The arrows of children have become their wounds, and they have regarded their tongues against them as nothing.

All who saw them were troubled, and every man was afraid.

They proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds.

The just man shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him; all upright in heart shall be praised.

## PSALM LXIV

[Col. 0227]

## TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, **[added: A SONG]**

*Note:* Many words are added in manuscript codices. The Carnutensian reads as follows: “To the end, a psalm of David, **a song of Jeremiah and Haggai**, concerning the word of the pilgrimage, when they began to depart.” Others have the name Ezekiel instead of Haggai, but without any sign of an asterisk or obelus in the rest. We retained what is read in the Hebrew and among the Septuagint, but rejected what was added by scribes. MART. — Omitting the asterisk, the Palatine manuscript adds the remainder of the title in the form of the Roman Psalter: “A song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel concerning the word of the pilgrimage, when they began to depart.” Martianaeus found “of Haggai” instead of the name “Ezekiel” in the Carnutensian manuscript, in which the remaining words were also marked with an obelus. Carus reads nearly the same as the Veronese manuscript: “of the people of the transmigration, when they began to depart.”

A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be rendered to you **in Jerusalem**.

*Note:* The same Palatine manuscript, according to its custom, strikes the preposition of the verb “hear” with an obelus. On its authority we also mark with an obelus the conjunction “and” in the following verse, since it is not heard in the Hebrew.

Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come.

[Col. 0229A] The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, **and** you shall be gracious toward our impieties.

Blessed is the one whom you chose and took up; he shall dwell **in** your courts.

*Note:* The same manuscript marks with an obelus the first preposition from which the verb is formed, not the one that follows. Carus has neither. In the following verse both witnesses, with equal agreement, unjustly strike the same preposition before “good things” with an obelus; likewise a little later the conjunction “and” in “**and** in the sea,” etc.

We shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is holy, wondrous in righteousness.

Hear us, O God, our savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea.

You prepare the mountains by your strength, girded with power; you disturb the depth of the sea and the sound of its waves.

The nations shall be troubled, and those who inhabit the boundaries shall fear at your signs; you shall delight in the departures of morning and **evening**.

*Note:* It seems that the genitive case, “of evening,” should be restored; its case is also “in the evening” in the facing Roman version and in other Latin translations. Arnobius has: “At the departure of morning and evening God shall be delighted.” The Septuagint likewise has *hesperas*—“of evening.”

You visited the earth and made it drunk; you greatly enriched it.

The river of God is filled with waters; you prepared their food, for thus is its preparation **[that is, the earth’s]**.

Water its furrows; multiply its growth; in its showers it shall rejoice as it sprouts.

You shall bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields shall be filled with abundance.

The beautiful places of the desert shall grow fat, and the hills shall gird themselves with rejoicing.

The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys shall abound in grain; they shall shout, and indeed they shall sing a hymn.

## TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, A SONG OF JEREMIAH AND HAGGAI, CONCERNING THE WORD OF THE PILGRIMAGE, WHEN THEY BEGAN TO DEPART

*Note:* The Veronese manuscript has: “and Ezekiel, from the people of the transmigration, when they began to depart,” according to Augustine. See what we note on the facing column.

A hymn is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and a vow shall be rendered to you in Jerusalem.

Hear my prayer; to you all flesh shall come.

[Col. 0230A] The words of the wicked have prevailed against us, and you shall be gracious toward our impieties.

Blessed is the one whom you chose and took up; he shall dwell in your tabernacles.

We shall be filled **[manuscript: he shall be filled]** with the good things of your house; your temple is holy, wondrous **[manuscript: admirable]** in righteousness.

Hear us, O God, our savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea.

You prepare the mountains by your strength, girded with power.

*Note:* The books consistently agree on “in his strength, girded about with might,” and immediately afterward: “Who can endure the sound of his waves?” The Veronese manuscript has the faulty “endures.” Before Jerome, it was read: “Who will sustain?” Jerome taught in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela that this was superfluous.

You disturb the depth of the sea; but who can endure the sound **[note: In the Greek, Jerome says to Sunnia and Fretela, “you write ‘who can endure?’” That is superfluous, for the sense is: ‘You disturb the depth of the sea and disturb the sound of its waves.’]** of its waves?

The nations shall be troubled, and all who inhabit the ends of the earth shall fear at your signs.

At the departures of morning and evening you shall be delighted; you visited the earth and made it drunk, **[Col. 0230B]** and greatly enriched it.

*Note:* The Veronese book agrees throughout with Augustine: “The departures of morning and evening shall delight you”; “you multiplied it to enrich it.” “The river of God is filled,” etc. “Water its furrows, and multiply its generations,” etc.; and “when it rises.” At the end: “they shall abound in grain, they shall shout, and indeed they shall sing a hymn.”

The river of God is filled with water; you prepared their food, because **[manuscript: for]** thus is your preparation.

Watering its furrows and multiplying its generations, it shall rejoice in its showers as it sprouts.

You shall bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields shall be filled with abundance.

The borders of the desert shall grow fat, and the hills shall gird themselves with rejoicing.

The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys shall abound in grain; indeed, they shall shout and sing a hymn.

## PSALM LXV

[Col. 0229]

## TO THE END, **[note: The Palatine manuscript, as in the Roman edition, has: “To the end, a psalm of David, a song of the resurrection.”]** A SONG OF THE PSALM **OF THE RESURRECTION**

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.

Say to God: How awesome are your works, **O Lord**; because of the greatness of your strength your enemies shall lie to you.

Let all the earth adore you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name. DIAPSALMA.

Come and see the works of God, awesome **in** his counsels over the sons of men.

**He** turned the sea into dry land; they shall cross the river on foot. There we shall rejoice in him.

[Col. 0231A] He rules in his strength **forever**; his eyes look upon the nations. Let those who provoke him not exalt themselves in themselves. DIAPSALMA.

*Note:* The manuscripts of Sagensis and Regius, together with Carus’s printed text, place an image of a star here instead of an obelus: “He rules in his strength **+ forever**.” We followed the Sorbonnic manuscript, which strikes only the preposition “in” with an obelus, because it is not read in the Hebrew. Our Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 8, marks “forever” with an obelus. MART. — The Palatine manuscript reads without an obelus, and also omits “Diapsalma” at the end of the following verse. It immediately errs by adding a superfluous obelus, although its first hand gives: “Bless, nations, our God,” and its second corrections likewise have “our God.”

Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard:

He placed my soul in life and did not allow my feet to be shaken.

For you tested us, O God; you examined us by fire, as silver is examined.

You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back; you set men upon our heads.

We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment.

I shall enter your house with burnt offerings; I shall render my vows to you, which my lips distinguished.

And my mouth spoke in my tribulation.

I shall offer you rich burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I shall offer you **cattle** with goats. DIAPSALMA.

Come, hear, and I shall recount to all who fear God how much he has done for my soul.

*Note:* We removed the obelus that Martianaeus prefixed to the preposition, and that the Palatine manuscript itself placed there; for it is sufficiently present in the Hebrew. The same manuscript, according to its custom, strikes the preposition of the verb “hear” in this verse and the next.

To him I cried with my mouth, and I exalted him under my tongue.

If I saw iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not hear.

Therefore God heard, and attended to the voice of my supplication.

Blessed be God, who has not removed my prayer or his mercy from me.

## TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID, A SONG OF THE RESURRECTION

*Note:* The title in Augustine and the Veronese manuscript is the same as in the Gallican Psalter on the facing page. In the text they prefer “sing psalms” instead of “sing a psalm,” as also in the third verse “let him sing”; likewise “things to be feared” instead of “awesome,” and “of power” instead of “of strength.”

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name; give glory to his praise.

Say to God: How awesome are your works; because of the greatness of your strength your enemies shall lie to you.

Let all the earth adore you and sing psalms to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, Most High. DIAPSALMA.

Come and see the works of the Lord; how awesome he is in his counsels over the sons of men.

*Note:* The same books omit the word “how.” Then they read: “They shall cross the river on foot; there we shall rejoice in him”; and shortly afterward “they embittered,” or “they make bitter,” instead of “they provoke to anger.” This is a barbarous expression, unknown to Latin ears, but Augustine did not dislike it as an expression of the force of the verb. Above, at Psalm IV.11, where it occurs, he approved it with his own judgment: “They therefore embittered God, who by sinning came into that distress.” In its proper sense below, in Psalm CXXXIV: “The Amorites are interpreted as ‘those who make bitter.’” Here, then, see whether we can understand how those who make bitter have a king who is a temptation of the eyes. And shortly afterward: “What wonder is it if those who make bitter have such a king, a lying king? For unless falsehood and pretense come first, they are not those who make bitter in the Church; for they make bitter because they pretend. The temptation of the eyes comes first; bitterness follows,” etc.

He turned the sea into dry land, and they shall cross the rivers on foot; there we shall rejoice together.

[Col. 0232A] He rules in his strength forever; his eyes look upon the nations. Let those who provoke him to anger not exalt themselves in themselves. DIAPSALMA.

Bless our God, you nations, and **hear** the voice of his praise.

*Note:* Augustine and the Veronese manuscript have: “Hear; he placed my soul in life, and did not allow my feet to be moved. For you tested us, O God; you burned us as silver is burned.” Prudentius also used this verb in the hymn on Saint Romanus the martyr near the end:

> They thrust small needles into the furnaces;  
> with these they go on burning the limbs, until they have been fired.

He placed my soul in life and did not allow my feet to be moved.

For you tested us, O God; you examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire.

You brought us into a snare **[manuscript: trap]**; he placed tribulations upon our back **[manuscript: our backs]**; you set a man upon our heads.

*Note:* The Veronese codex contains a faulty transposition of words—due, however, to the error of a single scribe—which its editor did not even note verbally: “you set men upon the heads,” instead of “you set men upon our heads.” Yet this one alteration overturns the whole meaning, and no other book agrees with it.

We passed through fire and water, and you led us into refreshment.

I shall enter your house with burnt offerings; I shall render my vows to you, which my lips distinguished.

*Note:* What follows from here through the final verses of Psalm LXVII has been supplied in the Veronese manuscript by a more recent hand. It is clear from quite evident indications that the calligrapher who undertook this task copied not from the old preceding leaves, but from another exemplar, as chance allowed. He therefore differs frequently from Augustine, even in those places where Augustine differs from the other witnesses. Nor may one infer his date from the script: he deliberately tried to imitate the ancient form and strokes of the letters so that it would not conflict with the rest of the codex, rather than displaying the form of characters current in his own age.

And my mouth spoke in my distress: I will offer you sacrifices of marrow, with [Note: [Col. 0232D] Jerome criticizes this passage, saying: “You say that you found: ‘with incense and rams’; but incorrectly. Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone: [Note: [Col. 0243D] In the Verona manuscript: “You taught me, O God, from my youth; and until old age and the extremity of old age.” I do not at all understand why the Psalter’s editor declares the latter two words to be proper to the Old Latin version, instead of *and old age*, and still less how he thereby proves that version to have adhered more closely to the Greek words; finally, how he derives the whole matter from Augustine. “These two,” Augustine says, “are names of old age (*senecta* and *senium*), and they are distinguished by the Greeks: for the condition of gravity after youth has one name among the Greeks, and the final age that comes after that gravity has another. For *πρεσβύτης* means one who is grave, and *γέρων* an old man. Since, however, in the Latin language the distinction between these two names is lacking, both have been used of old age, *senecta* and *senium*; but you know that there are two ages.” Clearly, from this passage the contrary of the praised editor’s arguments seems to us to emerge plainly and exclusively. First, the words *the extremity of old age* are not from the older Latin—or, as he calls it, the Old Latin—version, since the holy Father teaches that in Latin the distinction between the two names, γῆρος and πρεσβείου, is lacking; and thus he persuades us that this “extremity of old age,” which is a sufficiently clear distinction from simple old age, did not exist in the Latin books before him, and still less in that Version which, as they wish, he himself praises as more faithful to the words while preserving clarity of meaning—one whose very common reading he certainly could not have failed to know. The second point is equally contrary: from Augustine’s own meaning it follows that the reading of the Verona codex, or the Version that has *the extremity of old age*, is not more faithful to the Greek expression, but rather departs farther from it. For Augustine says that *πρεσβύτης* means one who is grave, and *γέρων* an old man; whereas in this interpretation *γέρων* corresponds to “grave,” and *πρεσβύτης* to “old man.” The Greek text has ἕως γήρους καὶ πρεσβείου, corresponding to *until old age and the extremity of old age*. But I am reluctant to pursue these matters, which, if our purpose permitted, we would much rather pass over entirely. If anyone wishes to know what I think of this reading, I suspect that it was later fashioned from that very exposition of Augustine by a diligent collector of his Psalter.]
