They said in their heart, their whole kindred together: [Note: [Col. 0251C] This passage is too important for us to omit anything Jerome wrote to Sunnia and Fretela: “In the same passage,” he says, “we read, ‘Let us burn all the feast-days of God from the earth’; whereas in Greek it is written καταπαύσωμεν, and we translated it, ‘Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth.’ And I wonder how some reckless person thought our annotation should be written into the text, although we wrote it on the margin for the reader’s instruction, in this form: ‘It does not have καταπαύσωμεν, as some think, but κατακαύσωμεν,’ [Col. 0251D] that is, ‘let us burn.’ And because the holy presbyter Firmus, who supervised this work, reported to me that this question had been debated by many, it seems necessary to discuss it more clearly. In Hebrew it is written SARPHUCHOL MOE DAU EL BAARES [the Hebrew characters are absent in the supplied text]: Aquila and Symmachus translated this as ἐνεπύρισαν πάσας τὰς συναγωγὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ, that is, ‘they burned all the solemn feasts of God in the land.’ The Fifth translated it κατέκαυσαν, that is, ‘they burned up.’ The Sixth, κατακαύσωμεν, that is, ‘let us burn’; and it is clear that the Septuagint likewise translated it according to the truth of the Hexapla. Theodotion also translated ἐμπυρίσωμεν, that is, ‘let us set on fire.’ From this it is clear that it should be sung as we translated it; yet one must know what the Hebrew truth has. For what the Septuagint translated should be sung in the Church because of its antiquity, while the other reading should be known by the learned for knowledge of the Scriptures. Therefore, if anything has been added in the margin out of scholarly zeal, it ought not to be placed in the text, lest the earlier translation be disturbed by the will of copyists. Reader, you see how far I am from the mind of the holy Doctor, who with great indignation and the full force of his spirit strives to prove that the Church of Christ has rejected the truth of the Hebrew chronology of the book of Genesis because, once a year, the chronology of the Septuagint interpreters is sung in the churches on account of its antiquity—the chronology that passed from Eusebius’s *Chronicle* into the Roman Martyrology.” MART.—The Palatine manuscript and Carus mark *let us cause to cease* with an obelus.] “Let us cause all the solemn feasts of God to cease from the earth.”

# PSALM 74

[Col. 0253]

[Col. 0253B] **FOR THE END, DO NOT DESTROY** [Note: [Col. 0253D] The title of this Psalm is corruptly read in the printed and manuscript books as *For the end, do not corrupt*, etc., except in the threefold Psalter of Chartres, where the true and genuine reading of Jerome is still retained: *For the end, do not destroy*, etc. I marvel at the carelessness of scribes who, in Jerome’s works, introduce not only foreign and spurious material, but—what is even more astonishing—do not hesitate to publish in his translations examples of the corruptions themselves that he had noted and corrected. Here we catch those careless men in the very act, and we call Jerome himself as witness, since he says this concerning verse 38 of Psalm 77: “But if anyone thinks that διαφθείρει means not destruction but corruption, let him recall that title in which it is written, εἰς τὸ τέλος μὴ διαφθείρῃς, that is, ‘For the end, do not destroy,’ and not, as many perversely imitate it, ‘Do not corrupt.’ We do not press this passage against the editors of St. Jerome’s works, lest it arouse against us the ignorant malice of envy—something we experienced in the widely circulated *Prodrome* of our edition.” MART.—The Palatine manuscript is entitled: *For the end, a Psalm of Asaph, a song; do not corrupt*.] **A PSALM OF ASAPH, A SONG**

He made a path for the way of his anger, and did not spare their souls from death [Note: [Col. 0263C] The same manuscript has *animarum* (“of souls”), which agrees more closely with the Greek τῶν ψυχῶν. In the following verse, instead of *in* ÷ *terra* ** Aegypti (“in the land of Egypt”), it was corrected by a later hand, without an obelus, to the Hebrew reading *in Aegypto* (“in Egypt”). It then reads “the first fruits of their labors,” as we have also said is found in the Veronensis; finally, it adds *Interlude* at the end of the verse.] and enclosed their cattle in death.

He struck every firstborn in ÷ the land ** of Egypt, the first fruits of all their labor in the tents of Ham.

And [Note: [Col. 0263D] In Martianaeus’s edition the verb *abstulit* was wrongly marked with an obelus, whereas in the Palatine manuscript only the preposition *abs* is marked, as usual. The verb is plainly present in the Hebrew, as also in the edition of the Greek Alexandrian manuscript, Καί ἀπῇρεν (“And he took away”), without an obelus, which Carus himself also did not prefix.] he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the wilderness.

And he brought them out in hope, and they did not fear; the sea covered their enemies.

And he brought them to the mountain of his holiness, the mountain [Col. 0263C] which his right hand acquired.

And he drove out the nations before them, and apportioned the land to them by lot, by the cord of distribution.

And he caused the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.

They tested and embittered the Most High God, and did not keep his testimonies.

They turned away and did not keep the covenant, just as [Col. 0265A] their fathers turned into a crooked bow.

They provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they provoked him to jealousy.

God heard, and despised them, and utterly reduced Israel to nothing.

And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle ÷ ** [Note: [Col. 0265D] The adverb *ubi* (“where”) itself also appears to require an obelus, since in Hebrew there is only “the tabernacle; he dwelt.” The Palatine manuscript and Carus less correctly mark the initial conjunction of the following verse with an obelus.] where he dwelt among human beings.

Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows [Col. 0265B] were not wept for.

And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine.

And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim [Ms. *Effrem*].

But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.

And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns, in the land which he founded forever.

And he chose his servant David, and ÷ sus ** took him from the sheepfolds; he took him from following the nursing ewes.

To shepherd Jacob his servant, and Israel, his inheritance.

[Col. 0265C] And he fed them in the innocence of his heart, and led them by the understanding of his hands.

[Col. 0258C] **AN UNDERSTANDING OF ASAPH.**

Attend, [Note: [Col. 0258D] Again, in agreement with Augustine, the same manuscript has *populus* (“people”), then *eloquar* (“I shall speak”) instead of *loquar* (“I will speak”); at the end of the verse it omits the word *saeculi* (“of the age”). Shortly afterward: “They were not hidden from their sons,” etc. And: “Declaring the praises and powers of the Lord,” etc.] my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth.

I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak propositions from the beginning of the age.

How many things we have heard and known: our fathers told us.

They were not hidden from their sons, in the succeeding generation [Ms. *the succeeding generation*].

They recounted the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders, which he performed.

[Col. 0260A] He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel.

Which he commanded our fathers [Note: [Col. 0259D] The copyist’s error, as elsewhere in the Veronensis, is *notam facere a* in place of *eam*, not *ea*, as that manuscript’s editor thinks; or perhaps he did not intend to write *notam*, but *nota*, which I consider more probable, since *et exsurgent* (“and they will rise up”) follows, [Col. 0260C] “and they will tell it to their sons,” etc. Further: “That they may place their hope in God,” and shortly afterward *Domini* (“of the Lord”) instead of *Dei sui* (“of their God”). Then: “Let them not become like their fathers, a perverse generation, embittering”—Augustine has “making bitter”—“a generation that did not correct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.”] to make it known to their sons, so that the succeeding generation might know it.

The sons who will be born will rise up and tell it to their sons.

So that they may place [Al. *I may place*] their hope in God, and not forget the works of their God, and seek out his commandments.

Let them not become like their fathers, a perverse and exceedingly bitter race, a race that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God.

The sons of Ephraim, bending the bow and shooting their arrows [Note: [Col. 0260C] The same manuscript omits *suas* (“their”) and reads *in diebus belli* (“in the days of battle”). [Col. 0260D] It also again omits *tui* (“your”) after the name of God, and in the following verse reads “his benefits and wonders, which he showed them before their fathers.” Then: “He performed wonders,” etc., and shortly afterward: “He led them across; he set the waters as in a wineskin.” Finally: “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great abyss.” There too, instead of *Dirupit* (“he split”), the book’s editor says that he corrected the reading to *Disrupit* (“he broke apart”).

A fine and wise correction, by heaven!] turned back on the day of battle.

They did not keep the covenant of their God, and they were unwilling to walk in his law.

They forgot his benefits and his wonders, which he showed them before their fathers.

He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the plain of Tanis.

He split the sea and led them through, and set the waters as in a wineskin.

He led them in a cloud by day, and throughout the night by the illumination of fire.

He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great abyss.

And he brought water from the rock, and brought out waters like rivers.

Yet they continued [Note: [Col. 0260D] Through a copyist’s error the same manuscript has *peccatores* (“sinners”) and *in iram* (“to anger”) instead of *peccare ei* (“to sin against him”), etc. Below it has “they drew down upon God” instead of “they spoke evil of God,” and then *induxerunt* (“they brought in”) instead of *inundaverunt* (“they flooded”). Two verses later it omits *et* (“and”) and adds above the line: “Finally, it reads, ‘They believed in the Lord, and they did not hope in his salvation.’”] to sin against him, provoking the Most High to anger in a waterless place.

They tested God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls; [Col. 0260C] they spoke evil of God and said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?”

For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed.

“Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?”

Therefore the Lord heard and delayed; then he added to this, and fire was kindled in Jacob, and anger rose against Israel.

[Col. 0262A] For they did not believe in their God, nor did they hope in his salvation.

He commanded the clouds above and opened the gates of heaven; [Note: [Col. 0262C] In the Veronensis manuscript: “He opened the doors of heaven and rained manna for food. And bread from heaven,” etc.; then, “He sent them abundance by grain.” “He stirred up the south wind,” etc. And below: “in the midst of their camps, around their tents,” and in the following verse: “their desire was not denied them. While the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them.”] he rained manna upon them to eat.

He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels. He sent them grain in abundance.

He stirred up the south wind from heaven, and brought in the southwest wind by his power.

He rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea.

They fell in the midst of their camps, around their tents.

They ate and were filled exceedingly, and what they desired came to them; [Col. 0262B] they were not deprived of their desire.

While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them.

He struck down many of them, and hindered the chosen of Israel.

In all these things they continued to sin, and they did not believe in [Ms. omits *in*] his wonders.

Their days came to an end in vanity, and their years in haste [Ms. *with haste*].

When [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Veronensis manuscript reads: “When he slew them, they sought him, turned back, and kept vigil at dawn before God” (the manuscript has “at dawn before him”). “And they remembered that God,” etc. Then, omitting the final word of the following verse, it continues: “But their heart was not right with him, nor was his covenant believed by them. Yet he is merciful and will be propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them. And he added to turn away his indignation, and he did not kindle all his anger.” Some of these readings agree exclusively with Augustine.] he slew them, they sought him and turned back, and before dawn they came to God.

And they remembered that God was their helper, and that the Most High God was their deliverer.

But their heart was not right with him, nor was faith found in them concerning his covenant.

Yet he is merciful, and he will be propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them.

And he multiplied his efforts to turn away his anger from them, and he did not kindle all his anger.

And he remembered that they were flesh, a passing spirit that does not return [Ms. *does not turn back*].

How often they embittered him in the wilderness! They provoked him to anger in a waterless land!

[Col. 0264A] They turned back and tested God; they embittered the Holy One of Israel.

They did not remember his hand, on the day when he delivered them from the hand of the oppressor.

[Note: [Col. 0263D] The Veronensis manuscript reads: “They did not remember his hands, on the day when he delivered them.” Two verses later: “And he turned their rivers into blood”; on this passage, recall Augustine’s exposition. It then has *Immisit eos cynomia* (“He sent upon them a cynomyia”) instead of *cynomyiam*, or more correctly *coenomyiam*. This word may perhaps belong not to the old Latin translation but to a more recent revision. I infer this from Jerome: first, from this very passage, where in his more accurate second revision he changed *muscam caninam* (“dog-fly”) to *coenomyia*; and more clearly from Letter 106 to Sunnia and Fretela, at the end, where he notes that the Latin translators before him rendered the word as “dog-fly” because of an incorrect reading of the Greek. “Κοινόμυια,” he says, “is not called *musca canina* [“dog-fly”], as the Latins translated it, with the Greek letter upsilon, but according to the Hebrew understanding it must be written with the diphthong *oi*, so that it is Κοινόμυια, meaning ‘every kind of fly.’ The old reading, therefore, was *musca canina*; afterward Jerome substituted *coenomyia*, which copyists again corrupted into *cynomyia*, restoring the earlier sense. However the matter may stand, it is clear from this that the old translation is to be sought in the Roman Psalter rather than in the Veronensis manuscript. The manuscript continues: “and it devoured them, and the frog, and it corrupted them.” Then: “He gave their fruits to the little dog,” etc.; and, plainly through the boldness of an ignorant copyist, “their walls in ruin” instead of “their mulberry trees in frost.” It also reads: “He delivered their cattle to the hail”; finally: “He sent upon them the anger of his indignation, fury, anger, and tribulations,” etc. These readings often agree with Augustine.]

As he set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis.

He turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink.

He sent upon them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; the frog, and it exterminated them.

He gave their fruits to rust, and their labors to the locusts.

He killed their vines with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.

He delivered their cattle to the hail, and their possessions [Col. 0264B] to the fire.

He sent upon them the anger of his indignation: indignation, anger, and tribulation; emissaries through evil angels.

He made a path for the way of his anger, and [Ms. omits *et*] did not spare their souls from death; he enclosed their cattle in death.

He struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt [Ms. *in Egypt*], the first fruits [Note: [Col. 0264D] The same Veronensis manuscript has “the first fruits of their labor.” Below it has *deduxit* (“he led”) instead of *eduxit* (“he brought out”), and later *perduxit* (“he led through”) instead of *induxit* (“he brought in”). In the following verse it reads: “He distributed the lot to them by the cord of distribution,” and “He settled them in tents,” etc. It also reads: “They turned away and despised, like their fathers, and they turned into a crooked bow.”] of all their labor in the tents of Ham.

And he took away his people like sheep, and led them like a flock in the wilderness.

And he brought them out in hope, and they did not fear; the sea covered their enemies.

And he brought them to the mountain of his holiness, [Col. 0264C] this mountain which his right hand acquired.

And he drove out the nations before them, and apportioned the land to them by lot, by the cord of distribution.

And he caused the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents; they tested and embittered the Most High God, and did not keep his testimonies.

They turned away and did not observe the covenant, [Col. 0266A] just as their fathers turned into a crooked bow.

They provoked him to anger on their hills, and with their carved images they rivaled him.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] The Veronensis manuscript reads “they provoked him to jealousy,” then *valde* (“greatly”) instead of *nimis* (“exceedingly”), and below “in which he dwelt among human beings.” It also has “he delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty.”]

The Lord heard, and despised them, and utterly reduced Israel to nothing.

And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh [Ms. *Selom*], his tabernacle, in which he dwelt among human beings.

And he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy.

And he shut up his people in the sword, and despised his inheritance.

Fire consumed their young men, and their virgins were not mourned.

Their priests fell by the sword; their widows [Col. 0266B] were not wept for [Ms. *will not be wept for*].

And the Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine.

He struck his enemies in their rear; he gave them everlasting disgrace.

And he rejected the tabernacle of Joseph, and did not choose the tribe [Ms. *and the tribe*] of Ephraim; but [Ms. *and*] he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved.

And he built his sanctuary like that of unicorns [Note: [Col. 0265D] The same manuscript reads: “He built his sanctuary like a unicorn, and founded it forever on the earth.” On this passage the holy Father himself, in his letter to Sunnia, from our recension, says: “On the earth, which he founded forever.” In place of this, you say that you found written: “On the earth he founded it forever.” In Hebrew it is written as Symmachus translated it: ὡς τὴν γῆν ἣν ἐθεμελίωσεν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, “like the earth which he founded forever.” But if it is not the earth that is said to have been founded, but some other thing that appears to have been founded upon the earth, let them prove from what precedes and follows what the sense is, so that something not actually stated may appear to have been founded upon the earth. If, however, they think that the sanctuary was founded upon the earth, it ought to have been written: “On the earth he founded it forever.”]—his sanctuary; he founded it upon the earth forever.

And he chose [Note: [Col. 0266D] The same manuscript inserts *sibi* (“for himself”) here. Then it reads: “To rule Jacob his servant,” etc., and “He raised them up in the simplicity of his heart and in the understanding of his hands,” etc.] his servant David, and took him from the sheepfolds; and [Ms. omits *et*] from following the nursing ewes he took him.

To feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.

[Col. 0266C] And he fed them without deceit in his heart, and led them by the understanding of his hands.

# PSALM LXXVIII

[Col. 0265]

[Col. 0265C] [Note: [Col. 0265D] In the Palatine manuscript: “For the end, a psalm of Asaph.”] **A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple and made Jerusalem a guardhouse for fruit trees.

They gave the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.

They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

We became a reproach to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those around us. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The same manuscript adds *Interlude*.]

[Col. 0267A] How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?

Pour out your anger upon the nations that did not know you, and upon the kingdoms that did not invoke your name.

For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling.

Do not remember our former iniquities [Note: [Col. 0267D] Here too the Palatine manuscript wrongly marks *antiquarum* (“former”) with an obelus; and at the end of the verse after this one it again adds *Interlude*.]; may your mercies quickly anticipate us, for we have become exceedingly poor.

Help us, O God our savior, and for the glory of your name ÷ Lord ** deliver us; and be propitious toward our sins for the sake of your name.

Do not let the nations say: “Where is their God?” [Col. 0267B] Let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been poured out enter your presence; let the groaning of the bound come before you.

According to the greatness of your arm, take possession of the sons of those put to death.

And repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom for the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord.

But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever.

From generation to generation we will proclaim your praise.

[Col. 0266C] **A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

O God, the nations have entered your inheritance; they have polluted your holy temple.

They made Jerusalem like a fruit-tree enclosure [Ms. *a guardhouse*]; they gave the dead bodies of your servants as food [Ms. *food*] to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth.

They poured out their blood like [Ms. *as*] water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

We have become a reproach to our neighbors: [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Verona manuscript, swarming with copyists’ errors, has *derisio et substantia* (“derision and substance”) for *subsannatio* (“mockery”), “to those who …,” etc.; but in the following verse [Col. 0267D], “shall blaze like fire,” etc., together with Augustine.] a mockery and scorn to those around us.

[Col. 0268A] How long, O Lord, will you be angry unto the end? Will your zeal burn like fire?

Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you, and upon kingdoms that have not called upon your name.

For [Ms. *quoniam*, “because”] they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling-place.

Do not remember [Ms. *memoreris*, “may you remember”] our former iniquities; let your mercy speedily forestall us, because [Ms. *quoniam*, “because”] we have become exceedingly [Ms. *valde*, “very”] poor.

Help us, O God [Note: [Col. 0267D] In the Verona manuscript: “O God our Saviour, for the glory of your name,” etc.; and three verses after this, again together with Augustine, “receive into adoption the sons of those put to death”; and at the end, “O God, for ever, from generation to generation we shall proclaim your praise.”] of our salvation; and, for the honour of your name, O Lord, deliver us; be merciful to our sins for your name’s sake.

Let not the nations say, “Where is their God?” [Col. 0268B] Let it be made known [Ms. *innotescat*, singular: “let it be made known”] among the nations before our eyes.

Avenge the blood of your servants which has been shed; let the groaning of the fettered come into your presence [Ms. *conspectum tuum*, “your presence”].

According to the greatness of your arm, take possession of the children of those punished by death.

Repay our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom, the reproach which they reproached [Ms. *improbaverunt*, “disapproved of”] you with, O Lord.

But we, your people and the sheep of your flock, will give thanks to you for ever; from age to age we shall recount your praise.

## PSALM LXXIX

[Col. 0267]

[Col. 0267C] **FOR THE END; FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED; A TESTIMONY OF ASAPH; A PSALM** [Ms. “A PSALM OF ASAPH”].

Give heed, you who shepherd Israel, you who lead [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Palatine manuscript, as usual, marks with an obelus the prefix *de-* of the verb *deducis* (“you lead”).] Joseph like a sheep.

You who sit upon the Cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

Stir up your power and come, that you may save us.

O God, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved.

O Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?

You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us tears to drink in measure.

You have made us a contradiction to our neighbours; and our enemies have mocked us.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] The Palatine manuscript reads “to our enemies” for “to our neighbours,” etc., contradicting the Greek itself, which has *geitosin* (γείτοσιν), “neighbours.”]

[Col. 0269A] O God of hosts, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved.

You brought a vine across from Egypt [Critical sign: the printed obelus marks only the prefix *trans-* (“across”) in *transtulisti* (“you brought across”)]; you drove out nations and planted it.

You were a guide on its journey before it; [Note: [Col. 0269D] From the Palatine manuscript and other original books we have supplied the missing conjunction *et*, “and.”] and you planted its roots, and it filled the earth.

Its shadow covered the mountains, and its boughs the cedars of God.

It stretched its branches as far as the sea, and its shoots as far as the river.

Why have you destroyed its hedge, so that all who pass along the road pluck it?

The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it.

O God of hosts, turn back; look down from heaven and see, [Col. 0269B] and visit this vine.

And make perfect that which your right hand planted, and concerning the son [Note: [Col. 0269D] The Palatine manuscript omits *hominis*, “of man”; the Hebrew text itself has no such noun here. Yet, since the Greek has *huion anthrōpou* (υἱὸν ἀνθρώπου), “son of man,” it is reasonable to believe that Jerome had marked it with an obelus. The first two words of the following verse, *Incensa igni*, “burned with fire,” are not marked with an asterisk in that manuscript or in Carus; it would have been preferable to mark only the latter word, *igni*, “with fire.”] of man whom you strengthened for yourself.

Burned with fire and dug up, they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance.

Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.

And we shall not depart from you; you will give us life, and we shall call upon your name.

O Lord God of hosts, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved.

[Col. 0268C] **FOR THE END; FOR THOSE WHO SHALL BE CHANGED; A TESTIMONY OF ASAPH; A PSALM OF THE ASSYRIANS.**

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Together with Augustine, the Verona manuscript has “shall be changed,” “a testimony to Asaph himself,” and “a psalm for the Assyrians.” But “Assyrians,” which is read in that manuscript, is one of the copyists’ errors with which it abounds, and which it would make no difference to burden the reader with at every third word. The text has “You who feed Israel,” and “like sheep,” in the plural number.]

Give heed, you who shepherd Israel; you who lead Joseph like a sheep.

You who sit upon the Cherubim, [Note: [Col. 0268D] “Therefore,” Jerome says in his *Commentary on Isaiah*, book III, chapter 6, “those who customarily say in their prayers, ‘You who sit upon the Cherubim and Seraphim,’ are mistaken, since Scripture has not taught this.” Moreover, for *apparare*, “to appear,” the Verona manuscript, with nearly all other books, more correctly reads *appare*, “appear.” In the second verse after this the same manuscript has, “O God, turn us back and illumine your face.” Here the often-praised editor of the Verona Psalter both errs and misleads: he says that *illumina*, “illumine,” agrees with Augustine alone, whereas Augustine exclusively has *ostende*, “show.” Below, the same manuscript has “you will give us drink” for “you will give us drink in tears,” and “they mocked us” for “they derided us,” etc.] appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh.

Stir up your power and come, that you may save us.

O Lord God of hosts, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved.

O Lord God of hosts, how long [Ms. *usquequo*, rather than *quousque*: both “how long”] will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?

You will feed us with bread [Ms. *panem*, accusative, for *pane*, ablative] of tears and give us tears to drink in measure.

You have made us a contradiction to our neighbours, and our enemies have derided us.

[Col. 0270A] O Lord God of hosts, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved. **DIAPSALMA.**

You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it.

You made a road before it; you planted its roots, and the earth was filled [Ms. *impleta*, “filled,” for *repleta*, “filled up”].

Its shadow covered the mountains, and its boughs the cedars of God.

You stretched its branches as far as the sea, and its shoots as far as the river.

[Note: [Col. 0270D] Again, in accordance with Augustine, the same manuscript has: “Why have you destroyed its hedge, and all who pass along the road, the boar has laid it waste,” etc. It further omits *Domine*, “O Lord,” in the following verse; reads *vero*, “indeed,” for *nunc*, “now”; and shortly afterward *perfice eam*, “make it perfect,” for *dirige*, “direct it.” Likewise, a little later, *succensa*, “set on fire,” for *incensa*, “burned”; and in the next-to-last verse *vivificabis*, “you will give life,” for *vivificasti*, “you gave life.”]

Why have you removed its hedge, so that all who pass along the road pluck it?

The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it.

O Lord God of hosts, turn back now; look down [Col. 0270B] from heaven, see, and visit this vine; direct that which your right hand planted, and concerning the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself.

Burned with fire and dug up by hand, they shall perish at the rebuke of your countenance.

Let [Ms. *faciat*, “let it make,” for *fiat*, “let it be”] your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself; and we shall not depart from [Ms. *abs*, “away from,” for *a*, “from”] you.

You gave us life, and we shall call upon your name.

O Lord God of hosts, turn us back; show us your face, and we shall be saved.

## PSALM LXXX

[Col. 0269]

[Col. 0269B] **FOR THE END; FOR THE WINEPRESSES; ASAPH.** [Note: [Col. 0269D] The Palatine manuscript adds: “The fifth day of the Sabbath.”]

[Col. 0269C] Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.

Take up the psalm, and give the tambourine, the delightful psaltery with the lyre.

Blow the trumpet at the new moon, on the celebrated day of your solemn feast.

For it is a commandment in Israel, and a judgment for the God of Jacob.

He placed ÷ **it** [Note: [Col. 0269D] Martianay unjustly marks this pronoun with an obelus, although it is manifest in the attached form of the Hebrew word, as it is called. The Palatine manuscript has advised us against removing it.] as a testimony in Joseph when he went out from the land of Egypt; he heard a language which he did not know.

He turned his back aside from burdens; his hands served at the basket.

In tribulation you called upon ÷ **me** [Note: [Col. 0269D] This obelus, however, the same manuscript wrongly omits.] and I delivered you; I answered you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction. **DIAPSALMA.**

[Col. 0271A] Hear, my people, and I shall testify against you; Israel, if you will hear me, there shall not be a new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god.

For I am [Critical signs: *Ego ÷ enim sum ***, “I—for, am”; the obelus covers “for” and “am,” not “I.”] [Note: [Col. 0271C] Formerly, in Martianay and the others, only the adverb *enim*, “for,” was marked with an obelus, although the substantive verb also is absent from the Hebrew text.] the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; open your mouth wide, and I shall fill it.

But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me.

And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own devices.

If my people had heard me, ÷ **if** Israel had walked in my ways,

I might ÷ **perhaps** have humbled their enemies to nothing, and laid my hand upon those afflicting them.

[Col. 0271B] The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall be for ever.

And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.

[Col. 0270B] **FOR THE END; FOR THE WINEPRESSES; A PSALM OF ASAPH; THE FIFTH DAY OF THE SABBATH.**

[Col. 0270C] Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.

[Note: [Col. 0270D] From Augustine and the Verona manuscript: “Receive the psalm”; and in the following verse, “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the celebrated day,” etc. The manuscript’s *insignis*, “celebrated,” is corrupt; its editor further compounds the error by proposing *insignes dies*, “celebrated days,” and errs in claiming that our codex has *dies* for *die*. The manuscript continues with Augustine: “For it is a commandment for Israel”; in the next verse, “he turned away from burdens” for “he turned his back aside,” etc.; and finally, “I rescued you” for “I delivered you,” and “I tested you in water” for “at the waters.”]

Take up the psalm and give the tambourine, the delightful psaltery with the lyre.

Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the celebrated day of your solemn feast.

For it is a commandment in Israel, and a judgment for the God of Jacob.

He placed him [Ms. omits *eum*, “him”] as a testimony in Joseph, when they went out [Ms. *exirent*, plural: “they went out”] from the land of Egypt.

He heard a language which he did not know [Ms. *noverant*, plural: “they did not know”]; he turned his back aside from burdens, and his hands served at the basket.

In tribulation you called upon me and I delivered you; I answered you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the waters of contradiction. **DIAPSALMA.**

[Col. 0272A] Hear, my people, and I shall speak, Israel; and I shall testify to you.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] The Verona manuscript, again with Augustine, first omits the name Israel and, three verses later, the pronoun *ego*, “I.” It then reads “I shall fill it,” and “my people did not obey,” etc. Then: “I dismissed them according to the inclinations of their heart, and they shall go in their inclinations.” And: “Israel, if it had walked in my ways.” Finally, in the last verse: “and he fed them with the fat,” etc.]

Israel, if you hear me, there shall not be a new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god.

For [Ms. *autem*, “but,” for *enim*, “for”] I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

Open your mouth wide, and I shall fill it; but my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me.

And I dismissed them according to the desires of their heart, and they shall go in their wills.

If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, I would have humbled their enemies to nothing, and laid my hand upon those afflicting them.

[Col. 0272B] The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time shall be for ever.

He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.

## PSALM LXXXI

[Col. 0271]

[Col. 0271B] **A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

God stood in the assembly of gods; ÷ **but** in their midst he judges gods [Note: [Col. 0271C] The Palatine manuscript, as usual, marks with an obelus the prefix *di-* of *dijudicat*, “he judges among.”].

How long will you judge iniquity and accept the persons of sinners? **DIAPSALMA.**

Judge for the needy and the orphan; vindicate the humble and poor.

Rescue the poor and needy; deliver them from the hand of the sinner.

[Col. 0271C] They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness: all the foundations of the earth shall be shaken.

I said: “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” [Note: [Col. 0271D] The same Palatine manuscript adds *Diapsalma*.]

But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes.

Arise, O God; judge the earth, because you shall inherit among all nations.

[Col. 0272B] **A PSALM OF ASAPH.**

God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he distinguishes among gods.

[Note: [Col. 0271D] Following Augustine, the Verona manuscript reads *discernere*, “to distinguish.” In the second verse after this: “Take away the helpless and needy” (Augustine: “the poor”); “rescue [them] from the hand of the sinner.”]

How long will you judge iniquity and accept the face of sinners [Ms. *faciem peccatorum*, singular “face,” genitive “of sinners,” for *facies peccantium*, plural “faces,” participial “of those sinning”]? **DIAPSALMA.**

Judge for the orphan and needy; vindicate the humble and poor.

Rescue the poor, and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner.

[Col. 0272C] They have not known, nor understood; they walk in darkness: all the foundations of the earth shall be shaken.

I said: “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.”

But you shall die like human beings [Note: [Col. 0271D] At this point the Verona manuscript has *morimini*, “you die,” and immediately afterward *caditis*, “you fall,” closer to the Greek. At the end it has *haereditaberis*, passive, “you shall be inherited,” for *haereditabis*, active, “you shall inherit”; Augustine has “you shall destroy.” Augustine says: “It should not be passed over that some codices have, ‘because you shall inherit among all nations’; for this also is not improperly understood, nor is anything opposed if both are taken together. Thus he becomes an inheritance through charity.” From these words the editor of the Verona Psalter argues that in Augustine’s testimony also one should read *haereditaberis*, as in the Verona codex, rather than *haereditabis*, which all Augustinian books report. I would scarcely believe it: no book supports it, and especially the rest of the context, with its active sense, opposes it—through charity, by cultivating his own mercifully through commandments and grace, he destroys earthly substance. Indeed, I do not sufficiently understand what he means, nor, I think, will anyone else understand his assertion that Augustine read *haereditaberis* in the passive, not merely in sense but in tense.] and fall like one of the princes.

Arise, O God; judge the earth, because you shall inherit among all nations.

## PSALM LXXXII

[Col. 0271]

[Col. 0271C] **A PSALM-SONG OF ASAPH.**

O God, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.

[Col. 0273A] For behold, your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their head.

They have devised malicious counsel against your people, and plotted against your holy ones.

They have said: “Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.”

For they have plotted unanimously; together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites,

Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.

Assyria also came with them; they became a help to the sons of Lot. [Critical signs: the source brackets *in* (“for/as”) in *÷ in ÷ adjutorium*, “as a help,” with the two obeli printed there.] [Note: [Col. 0273D] In the same manuscript and in Carus the obelus is absent.] **DIAPSALMA.**

Deal with them as with Midian and Sisera, as with Jabin at the torrent Kishon.

[Col. 0273B] They perished at Endor; they became like dung upon the earth.

Make their princes like Oreb, Zeb, Zebee, and Salmana.

All their princes [Note: [Col. 0273D] A later hand in that codex has rewritten the passage: “Their princes who said, ‘Let us possess by inheritance,’” etc.—not very satisfactorily. Nor do we approve what is marked with an obelus before *haereditate*, “by inheritance.” Jerome explains in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela why he did not add *nobis*, “for ourselves,” to the next verb *possideamus*, “let us possess”: “And you say that in Greek ‘let us possess for ourselves’ is written. This is a superfluous question; for when it is said, ‘let us possess,’ ‘for ourselves’ is understood.”] who said: ÷ **By inheritance** let us possess the sanctuary of God.

My God, make them like a wheel, and like chaff before the wind;

Like fire ÷ **which** burns the forest, and like flame burning the mountains.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] The Palatine manuscript omits the obelus; in the verse following this it has improperly prefixed it to the conjunction *et*, “and,” in “and they shall seek,” etc.]

Thus you shall pursue them in your storm, and trouble them in your anger.

Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord.

Let them be ashamed and troubled for ever ÷ **of ages**, and be confounded and perish.

[Col. 0273C] And let them know that your name is the Lord: you alone are Most High over all the earth.

[Col. 0272C] **A PSALM-SONG OF ASAPH** [Ms. “OF ASAPH HIMSELF”].

O God, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor [Note: [Col. 0272D] The Verona manuscript has *mitescas*, “be gentle,” for *compescaris*, “be restrained.” “For,” Augustine says, “some have interpreted what is here written, ‘nor be restrained, O God,’ by saying, ‘nor be gentle, O God.’” In the following verse it has *sonuerunt*, “sounded,” for *sonaverunt*, “made a noise,” and *levaverunt*, “lifted,” for *extulerunt*, “raised.” Then: “They cunningly devised counsel against your people”; shortly afterward: “Let us destroy them from the nations, and the name of Israel shall not remain in memory any longer.” Augustine also mentions manuscripts which have “from the nations,” where translators followed the sense rather than the word, etc.] be restrained, O God.

[Col. 0274A] For behold, your enemies have sounded, and those who hate you have lifted up their head.

They have cunningly devised counsel against your people, and plotted against your holy ones.

They said: “Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and the name of Israel shall be remembered no longer.”

For they have plotted [Ms. adds *in*: “in agreement into one”] in united agreement; they have made a covenant against you.

The tents of the Edomites and Ishmaelites [Ms. *Ismaelitum*, genitive plural form], Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, and foreigners with the inhabitants of Tyre.

Assyria came together [Ms. *fuit*, “was,” for *venit*, “came”] with them; they became a support for the sons of Lot. **DIAPSALMA** [Ms. omits it].

Deal with them as with Midian [Ms. *Mazia*] and Sisera, and as with [Col. 0274B] Jabin at the torrent Kishon; they perished at Endor and became like [Ms. *ut*, “as,” for *sicut*, “like”] dung upon the earth.

Make their princes like Horeb, Zeb, Zebee [Ms. *Zebe*], and Salmana—all their princes who said: “Let us possess by inheritance [Note: [Col. 0274D] “And you say,” Jerome says to Sunnia and Fretela, “that in Greek it is written, ‘Let us possess for ourselves.’ This is a superfluous question; for when ‘let us possess’ is said, ‘for ourselves’ is understood.” MART. — Why the holy Father omitted *nobis*, “for ourselves,” in his later revision will be discussed at this place in the Gallican register. Moreover, for “sanctuary” the Verona manuscript prefers “altar”; in the following verse it has *succendit*, “sets alight,” for *comburit*, “burns,” and conversely *comburat*, “burns,” for *incendat*, “sets fire.” Below: “Fill their face with shame, and let them seek,” etc.; finally: “Let them be confounded and reverence [God] for ever,” etc.] for ourselves the sanctuary of God.”

My God, make them like a wheel and [Ms. omits *et*, “and”] like chaff before the wind; and like fire which burns the forest, as though flame should set mountains alight.

Thus you shall pursue them in your storm, and trouble them in your anger.

Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek your name, O Lord.

Let them be confounded and troubled for ever and ever, and reverence, and perish; and let them know that [Col. 0274C] your name is the Lord.

You alone are Most High over all the earth.

## PSALM LXXXIII

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273C] **FOR THE END; FOR THE WINEPRESSES; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM.**

How beloved are your dwelling-places, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and fails away in the courts of the Lord.

My heart and my flesh has rejoiced in the living God.

[Note: [Col. 0273D] The same manuscript and Carus’s edition have the plural, *exsultaverunt*, “have rejoiced.” “There is no dispute in this,” the holy Father says to Sunnia and Fretela: “if we read *exsultavit*, ‘has rejoiced,’ it is understood that both my heart has rejoiced and my flesh has rejoiced; but if *exsultaverunt*, ‘have rejoiced,’ both have rejoiced together, that is, heart and flesh.”]

For the sparrow has found ÷ **for itself** a house, and the turtledove a nest for itself, in which to place its young.

Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my king and my God.

[Col. 0275A] Blessed are those who dwell in your house: for ever ÷ **of ages** they shall praise you. **DIAPSALMA.**

Blessed is the man whose help ÷ **is** from you; he has disposed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he appointed.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] The Palatine manuscript and Carus omit this obelus. In the following verse the manuscript reads *benedictiones*, plural “blessings”; in the next it marks, as usual, the prefix of *exaudi*, “hear”; and finally it omits the appended *Diapsalma*.]

For the giver of the law shall give blessing; they shall go from strength to strength: the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.

O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. **DIAPSALMA.**

Look, O God, upon our protector; and look ÷ **upon** the face of your anointed.

For a day ÷ **one** in your courts is better than [Col. 0275B] thousands.

I chose to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners.

For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord shall give grace and glory.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] The Hebrew text has another sense: as the holy Father himself translated it, “For the Lord God is sun and shield; he shall give grace and glory,” etc. How the Septuagint produced from this, *hoti to eleos kai alētheian agapa Kyrios* (ὅτι τὸ ἔλεον καὶ ἀλήθειαν ἀγαπᾷ Κύριος), “For the Lord loves mercy and truth,” I do not know; nor, if I did know, would I dare discuss it here at greater length. It is certain, meanwhile, that they read the words differently in order to render “mercy and truth,” while in the Hebrew text there is nothing corresponding to the verb “loves.” Accordingly, that word seems rightly to be marked with an obelus, as has been done in several manuscripts and in the recent edition of the Alexandrian codex. Carus marks with an obelus the following word, *Deus*, “God.”]

He shall not deprive of good things those who walk in innocence. O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.

[Col. 0274C] **FOR THE END; FOR THE WINEPRESSES; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM.**

How lovely are your dwelling-places, O Lord of hosts! My soul has longed and failed away [Ms. *deficit*, present “fails,” for *defecit*, perfect “has failed”] in the courts of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0274D] The Verona book alone, with Augustine, has “How most beloved are,” etc.; then in the next verse, “the turtledove a nest for itself, where …”; two verses later, “whose support is from you,” etc.; “in the valley of weeping, in the place which he appointed.” Then, “For he who gave the law shall give blessing,” etc.; and “the God of gods shall appear,” for “shall be seen,” etc.]

My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God; for the sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest in which to place its young.

Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my king and my God.

[Col. 0276A] Blessed are those who dwell [Ms. *ambulant*, “walk”] in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever [Ms. *saecula saeculorum*, “ages of ages”] they shall praise you. **DIAPSALMA.**

Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; he has disposed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which you appointed for him.

For he who gave the law shall give blessing; they shall walk from [Ms. *a*, “from,” for *de*, “from/out of”] strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.

O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer [Ms. *orationem*, “prayer,” for *precem*, “petition”]; give ear, O God of Jacob. **DIAPSALMA.**

Look, O God, upon our protector, and look upon the face of your anointed.

For [Ms. *quoniam*, “because,” for *quia*, “because”] one day in your courts is better than [Col. 0276B] thousands.

I chose to be cast aside in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners.

For [Ms. *quoniam*, “because,” for *quia*, “because”] the Lord loves mercy and truth [Note: [Col. 0276D] Here again the Verona manuscript adds *Deus*, “God,” but omits that name at the end of the verse.]; God shall give grace and glory.

The Lord shall not deprive of good things those walking in innocence. O Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.

## PSALM LXXXIV

[Col. 0275]

[Col. 0275B] **FOR THE END; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM.** [Note: [Col. 0276D] The Palatine manuscript adds “of David.”]

You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob.

You have forgiven iniquity to your people; you have covered all [Col. 0275C] their sins. **DIAPSALMA.**

You have softened all your anger; you have turned from the wrath of your indignation.

Turn us back, O God of our salvation, and turn away your anger from us.

Will you be angry with us for ever? [Note: [Col. 0276D] Here the Palatine manuscript less correctly omits the obelus.] ÷ **Or** will you extend your anger from generation to generation?

÷ **O God**, when you turn back, you will give us life, and your people shall rejoice in you.

Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

I shall hear what ÷ **in me** the Lord God will speak, because he will speak peace to his people,

and to his holy ones, and to those who turn to the heart.

[Col. 0277A] Nevertheless, his salvation is near those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land. [Note: [Col. 0277D] As usual, the Palatine manuscript marks the prefix *in-* (“in”) in *ut ÷ in ** habitet*, “that it may dwell in.”]

Mercy and truth have met ÷ **one another**; righteousness and peace have kissed one another.

Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.

For the Lord shall give goodness, and our land shall give its fruit.

Righteousness shall walk before him, and he shall set his footsteps in the way.

[Col. 0276B] **FOR THE END; FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM.**

You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned back [Note: [Col. 0276D] The same manuscript inserts *Deus*, “God.” Soon afterward its editor mistakenly reads *plebis tuae*, “of your people,” for *plebi tuae*, “to your people.” With Augustine, the manuscript has “You have calmed all your wrath,” for “You have softened,” etc.; and “Turn us back, O God of our salvations.” The reading *sanitantium*, “of those healing,” preferred by the editor is a most obvious copyist’s error. It further reads, with *ut*, “that,” omitted: “Will you not be angry with us for ever?” Or, “Will you extend your anger from generation to generation?”] the captivity of Jacob.

You have forgiven iniquity to your people; you have covered all [Col. 0276C] their sins. **DIAPSALMA.**

You have softened all your anger; you have turned from the wrath of your indignation.

Turn us back, O God of our salvation, and turn away your anger from us, that you may not be angry with us for ever.

Nor extend your anger from generation to generations. O God, when you turn us back, you will give us life, and your people shall rejoice in you.

Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.

I shall hear what [Ms. *loquetur*, future “will speak,” for *loquatur*, subjunctive “may speak”] the Lord God speaks in me, because he shall speak peace over [Ms. *super*, “over,” for *in*, “to/in”] his people, and over his holy ones, and to those who [Note: [Col. 0276D] The Verona manuscript has “who turn from the heart.” “Nevertheless, his salvation is near those who fear him,” etc. In the following verse it has *cucurrerunt*, “ran together,” for *obviaverunt*, “met,” and *osculatae sunt*, “kissed,” for *complexae [sunt]*, “embraced.” Finally, below it agrees exclusively with Augustine in “he shall give sweetness,” for “goodness,” and “he shall go before him,” for “shall walk.”] shall turn to him.

[Col. 0278A] Nevertheless, his salvation is near those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.

Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have embraced one another.

Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven.

For the Lord shall give goodness, and our land shall give its fruit.

Righteousness shall walk before him, and he shall set his footsteps in the way.

## PSALM LXXXV

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277A] **A PRAYER OF DAVID HIMSELF.** [Critical sign: *÷ ipsi ***, “himself,” in the title *ipsi David*, “to/of David himself.”] [Note: [Col. 0277D] The same manuscript lacks the pronoun *ipsi*, “himself,” and consequently also this obelus.]

[Col. 0277B] Have mercy on me, O Lord, because I have cried to you all day; gladden the soul of your servant, because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.

For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and of abundant mercy to all who call upon you.

There is none like you among gods, O Lord; nor is there anything according to your works.

For you are great and work wonders; you ÷ **are** [Col. 0277C] God alone. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Palatine manuscript appends *Diapsalma* here, and again attaches it three verses later.]

Because your mercy ÷ **is** great over me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell.

O God, the wicked have risen against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul; and they have not set you before their eyes. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The same manuscript, as usual, marks *non ÷ pro ** posuerunt*: the prefix *pro-* (“before”) of “they have set before.”]

[Col. 0279A] But you, O Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true.

Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your authority to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid.

Do with me a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded, because you, O Lord, have helped and comforted me.

[Col. 0278A] **A PRAYER OF DAVID** [Ms. “TO DAVID HIMSELF”].

Incline your ear to me, O Lord, [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Verona manuscript omits the words *ad me*, “to me,” which the other original books likewise lack. In the third verse after this it reads, with Augustine: “Gladden the soul of your servant, because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul. Because you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and very merciful to all who call upon you. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my prayer.”] and hear me, because I am needy and poor.

[Col. 0278B] Have mercy on me, O Lord, because I have cried to you all day; gladden the soul of your servant, because to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.

For you, O Lord, are sweet and gentle, and abundant in mercy to all who call upon you.

Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my supplication.

In the day of my tribulation I cried to you, because you heard me.

There is none like you among gods, O Lord; nor is there anything according to your works.

All nations, whatever [Ms. *quas*, “which,” for *quascumque*, “whatever/all which”] you have made, shall come; and worship before you, O Lord, and honour [Ms. *glorificabunt*, “will glorify,” for *honorificabunt*, “will honour”] your name.

For you are great and work [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Verona manuscript has *misericordias*, “mercies,” through a copyist’s error, for *mirabilia*, “wonders”; then, with Augustine, “you alone are the great God.” “Lead [me],” etc.] wonders; you [Col. 0278C] are God alone.

Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.

Let [Ms. *delectetur*, “be delighted,” for *laetetur*, “rejoice”] my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name; I shall give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and honour [Ms. *glorificabo*, “I shall glorify,” for *honorificabo*, “I shall honour”] your name for ever.

Because your mercy is great over me, and you delivered [Ms. *eruisti*, “you delivered,” for *eripuisti*, “you snatched away”] my soul from the lower hell.

O God, [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Verona book, as with most things noted in the margin, has this together with Augustine: “O God, transgressors of the law have risen against me; the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul, and have not set you before their eyes.” Then: “But you, O Lord God, compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and very merciful,” etc. See also Jerome’s letter to Sunnia and Fretela, where he teaches that the pronoun *meus*, “my,” added to *Deus*, “God,” here is superfluous, occurring neither in Hebrew nor in the Septuagint.] unjust men rose against me, and the assembly of the powerful sought my soul; they did not set you before their sight.

[Col. 0280A] But you, [Note: [Col. 0279D] Saint Jerome teaches that the word *meus*, “my,” is excessive and superfluous, because it occurs neither in Hebrew nor in the Septuagint. MART.] O Lord my God, are compassionate and merciful, patient and very merciful and true.
