Do with me, O Lord [Ms. omits *Domine*, “O Lord”], a sign for good, that those who hate me may see and be confounded.

For you, O Lord, have helped me and comforted me.

## PSALM LXXXVI

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279A] **FOR THE SONS OF KORAH; A PSALM-SONG.**

Its foundations are upon the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob.

Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Here the Palatine manuscript omits *Diapsalma*; in the following verse it reads *scientibus*, dative “to those knowing,” for *scientium*, genitive “of those knowing.”] **DIAPSALMA.**

I shall remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me.

[Col. 0279B] Behold foreigners and Tyre, ÷ **and** [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Palatine manuscript and Carus wrongly mark with an obelus the noun *populus*, “people,” rather than the preceding conjunction *et*, “and.”] the people of the Ethiopians: these were there.

Will Zion say, “A man, and a man, was born in her”? And the Most High himself founded her.

The Lord shall recount [Ms. *narravit*, perfect “recounted,” for *narrabit*, future “shall recount”] in the writings of peoples and of these princes who were in her. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Here the Palatine manuscript omits *Diapsalma*, and in the following verse the verb *est*, “is,” which is absent also from the Greek text.] **DIAPSALMA.**

As the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you.

[Col. 0280A] **TO THE END, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, A PSALM OF SONG.**

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The Veronese manuscript omits the words *To the end*. In the following verse it reads *Most glorious* instead of *Glorious*, a reading which Augustine himself praises; likewise *those who know me* instead of *those who know*, and so forth. Further below, more than once, the copyists’ carelessness introduces errors. At the end it again agrees with Augustine, *As the dwelling of all who rejoice in you*.]

Its foundations are upon the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwelling-places of Jacob.

Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God. **DIAPSalma.**

[Col. 0280B] I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me.

Behold, the foreigners and Tyre [Ms. *of Tyre*] and the people of the Ethiopians: these were there [Ms. omits *there*].

Mother Zion will say, “A man, and a man was made in her”; and the Most High himself founded her.

The Lord will tell it in the writings [Ms. *writings] of his peoples, and of their princes who were in her. **DIAPSALMA.**

As the dwelling of all our rejoicing is in you.

## PSALM LXXXVII

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279B] **A SONG OF A PSALM, FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, TO THE END, FOR MAELETH, TO BE ANSWERED, AN INSTRUCTION OF EMAN THE ISRAELITE.**

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The same manuscript has *Amalech*, *Carus*, and *Maeleth*. Recall what we said concerning Psalm LII.]

[Col. 0279C] Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out—and at night before you.

Let my prayer enter into your presence; incline your ear to my supplication. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Here a later hand in the Palatine manuscript supplies *Lord*, a name also found in nearly all the Greek manuscripts. In the following verse it reads, *and my life is in hell*; but in the next it omits, apparently through the copyist’s carelessness, the words *without help*.]

For my soul is full of evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.

I have been counted among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead.

Like the wounded who sleep in the tombs, whom you remember no longer; and they themselves have been driven away from your hand.

They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death.

[Col. 0281A] Your fury has been made firm against me, and you have brought all your waves upon me. **DIAPSALMA.**

You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an object of abhorrence to themselves.

I have been handed over, and I did not go out; my eyes languished from poverty.

I cried to you, Lord; all day I stretched out my hands to you.

Will you perform wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you? [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Palatine manuscript omits *Diapsalma* here, as do the Greek manuscripts; it is, however, found in the Hebrew.] **DIAPSALMA.**

Will anyone declare your mercy in the tomb, and your truth in destruction?

Will your wonders be known in darkness, and your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

[Col. 0281B] But I cried to you, Lord, and in the morning my prayer will anticipate you.

Why, Lord, do you reject my prayer? Do you turn your face away from me?

I am poor, and in troubles from my youth; but, though exalted, I have been humbled and disturbed.

Your angers have passed over me; and your terrors have disturbed me. [Note: [Col. 0281D] We have supplied the pronoun *me*, which was missing, from the Palatine manuscript, Carus, other original books, and especially the Hebrew.]

They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me together.

You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery.

[Col. 0280B] **A SONG OF A PSALM [Ms. *OF A DIAPSALM], FOR THE SONS OF KORAH, TO THE END, FOR MAELETH, TO BE ANSWERED, AN INSTRUCTION OF EMAN THE ISRAELITE.**

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Several manuscripts corruptly read *Amalech*, whereas the Greek has Μαελὲθ, *Maeleth*. For Αἰμὰν, *Aeman*, the Alexandrian manuscript has Αἰθὰμ, *Aetham*; from this, perhaps, the asterisk in a later correction of the Psalter arose. See the other Observations on Psalm LII. MART. The Veronese manuscript alone, with Augustine, has *Melech*, though less correctly. In the text itself, through an obvious copyist’s error, it reads *God, you saved me by day*, etc., instead of *God of my salvation*, etc. In the verse following this it again agrees with Augustine: *my life has drawn near to hell*; *I have been appointed among*, etc.; and in the next, *you have not remembered any longer*, and *they themselves from your hand*, etc. Likewise, two verses later: *Your indignation has been confirmed against me*, and *all your upheavals*, etc.]

[Col. 0280C] Lord, God of my salvation, by day I cried out, and at night before you.

Let my prayer enter into your presence; incline your ear to my supplication, Lord.

For my soul is full of evils, and my life has drawn near to hell.

I have been counted among those descending into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead. [Ms. *among the dead*.]

Like the wounded, sleeping and cast down in tombs, whom you remember no longer; indeed, they themselves have been expelled from your hand.

They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and the shadow [Ms. *in the shadow*] of death.

[Col. 0282A] Your anger has been confirmed against me, and you have brought all your exaltations upon me. **DIAPSALMA.**

You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an object of abhorrence to themselves. I have been handed over, and I did not go out.

My eyes have grown weak [Note: [Col. 0281D] Together with Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has *from poverty*, and *I cried to you, Lord; all day I stretched out my hands to you*. Two verses later it reads *will anyone declare in the tomb your mercy and truth*, etc.; and in the following verse, *and your righteousness in the land forgotten*.] from poverty; I cried to you, Lord; all day I stretched out my hands to you.

Will you perform wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess to you? **DIAPSALMA** [Ms. omits *DIAPSALMA*.]

Will anyone declare your mercy in the tomb? Or your truth in destruction?

Will your wonders be known in darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

[Col. 0282B] And I cried to you, Lord; in the morning my prayer will anticipate you.

Why, Lord, do you reject my prayer? Do you turn your face away from me? **DIAPSALMA.**

I am needy; I am in troubles from my youth. Though exalted, I have been humbled and confounded.

Your angers have passed over me; your terrors have disturbed me.

They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me together.

You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery.

## PSALM LXXXVIII

[Col. 0281]

[Col. 0281B] [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Sorbonne manuscript has this scholion: “In some copies it is found as *Israelite*, or *Ezraite*. In the text itself he reads *Izraite*.” MART.] **AN INSTRUCTION OF ETHAN THE EZRAHITE.**

I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever.

[Col. 0281C] From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth.

For you said: “Mercy will be built forever; your truth will be prepared in the heavens.”

I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant: “Forever I will prepare your offspring.”

And I will build your throne from generation to generation. **DIAPSALMA.**

The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones.

For who among the clouds is equal to the Lord? Who will be like God among the sons of God? [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Palatine manuscript has *Lord* rather than *God*, closer to the Greek Κυρίῳ.]

God, who is glorified in the council of the holy ones, is great and dreadful above all who surround him.

[Col. 0283A] Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is around you.

You rule the power of the sea; you still the motion of its waves.

You humbled the proud as one wounded; by the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies.

The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world—and its fullness. [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Palatine manuscript marks *is* with an obelus; the Hebrew omits not only this word but also the preceding *are*. We have spoken elsewhere of [Hebrew term], a single word meaning the earthly world. The same manuscript, however, improperly omits the obelus in the following verse.]

You created the north and the sea.

Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name; your arm is with power.

Let your hand be firm—and [Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus the Palatine manuscript has *and*, marking the conjunction beforehand; it would have been entirely preferable to insert it, since it is absent not only from the Hebrew text but from the Greek itself.] let your right hand be exalted; righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne.

Mercy and truth will go before your face; blessed is the people who knows the shout of joy.

[Col. 0283B] Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they will rejoice all day; and in your righteousness they will be exalted.

For you are the glory of their strength, and by your favor our horn will be exalted.

For the Lord is our elevation—and the Holy One of Israel is our king. [Note: [Col. 0283D] The same manuscript adds *Diapsalma*.]

Then you spoke in a vision to your holy ones and said: “I have placed help in the mighty one, and I have exalted the chosen one from my people.”

I found David my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him.

For my hand will assist him, and my arm will strengthen him. [Note: [Col. 0283D] The same manuscript has *will confirm*. Two verses later it has: *I will cut down his enemies from before him, and those who hate him*, etc.; these words were apparently restored by a later hand from the Greek.]

[Col. 0283C] The enemy will accomplish nothing against him, and the son of iniquity will not add to harming him.

And I will cut down his enemies from before him; and those who hate him I will turn to flight.

My truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted.

I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.

He will call upon me: “You are my father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.”

And I will make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.

[Col. 0285A] Forever I will keep my mercy for him, and my covenant will be faithful to him. [Ms. *faithful*.]

I will establish his offspring forever, and his throne like the days of heaven.

But if his sons abandon my law and do not walk in my judgments—

if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments—

I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges.

But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor prove false in my truth.

I will not profane my covenant, nor make void what proceeds from my lips.

Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David: his offspring will remain forever.

[Col. 0285B] His throne will be like the sun before me, and like the moon perfected forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0285D] The Palatine manuscript improperly omits the obelus here, as well as *Diapsalma* at the end of the verse.] **DIAPSALMA.**

But you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your anointed one.

You have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary on the earth.

You have destroyed all his fences; you have made his stronghold a terror.

All who pass along the way have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors.

You have exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him; you have gladdened all his enemies.

You have turned away the help of his sword and have not assisted him in battle.

You have destroyed him from purification and struck his throne to the ground.

You have shortened the days of his time; you have drenched him with shame. **DIAPSALMA.**

How long, Lord, will you turn away forever? Will your anger burn like fire?

Remember what my substance is; for have you established all the sons of human beings in vain? [Note: [Col. 0285D] Again, after the Palatine manuscript, Carus improperly places an obelus here instead of an asterisk.]

What man is there who will live and not see death? Will he rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld? **DIAPSALMA.**

Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?

Remember, Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have carried in my bosom from many nations.

[Col. 0285D] The reproach with which your enemies reproached, Lord, with which they reproached the exchange of your anointed one.

Blessed be the Lord forever; let it be, let it be.

[Col. 0282B] **AN INSTRUCTION OF ETHAN THE ISRAELITE.**

I will sing your mercies, Lord, forever; [Col. 0282C] from generation and offspring I will proclaim [Ms. *from generation I will announce*] your truth with my mouth.

For you said: “Mercy will be built forever; your truth will be prepared in the heavens.”

I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant: “Forever I will prepare your offspring, and I will build your throne for age after age” [Ms. *from generation to generation*]. **DIAPSALMA.**

The heavens will confess your wonders, Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones.

For who among the clouds is equal to the Lord? Or who will be like God among the sons of God?

God, who is glorified in the council of the holy ones, is great and feared above all who surround him. [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Veronese manuscript has: *God, who is to be glorified among the sons of the righteous, is great and dreadful above all*, etc.; so far as I know, it agrees neither exactly with Augustine nor with any other Psalter. Yet one should not suppose that this was the reading current before Jerome. In his frequently cited letter to Sunnias and Fretela he appropriately notes that at Psalm LXXXVIII *great and dreadful* was formerly read *great and horrible*, where he says: “For this you say you found φοβερός in the Greek, which means dreadful, to be feared, fearsome. I think that it means precisely *horrible* as well—not, as the common people think, contemptible and squalid,” etc.]

[Col. 0284A] Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are mighty, Lord, and your truth is around you.

You rule the power of the sea; you still the motion of its waves.

You humbled the proud as one wounded, and by the strength of your arm you scattered your enemies. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Here, together with Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has *and by the arm of your strength*; two verses later, *You, north and seas*, etc.; and in the following verse, *Let your hand be confirmed*, etc.]

The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness.

You created the north and the sea; Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name; your arm is with power.

Let your hand be firm, and let your right hand be exalted; righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne.

Mercy and truth will go before your face [Ms. *go before*]; blessed is the people who knows the shout of joy.

[Col. 0284B] Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they will rejoice all day; they will be exalted in your righteousness.

For you are the glory of their strength, and by your favor our horn will be exalted.

For the Lord’s is the elevation, and the Holy One of Israel is our king. **DIAPSALMA.** [Note: [Col. 0284D] According to Augustine and the Veronese manuscript, *reception* occurs instead of *elevation*. Concerning the following verse, where it has *sons* instead of *holy ones*, recall Jerome’s observation in his letter to Sunnias, etc.]

Then you spoke in the presence of your sons and said: “I have placed help upon the mighty one, and I have exalted the chosen one from my people” [Ms. *from my nation*.] [Note: [Col. 0284D] It should be known that the Hebrew has *LAASIDACH*, which all translated τοῖς ὁσίοις σου, that is, *to your holy ones*; only the Sixth Edition translated it *to your prophets*, expressing the sense rather than the word. In the κοινή I found *sons* instead of *holy ones*. Thus Saint Jerome. MART.]

I found David my servant; with my holy oil I anointed him. [Ms. *I anointed him in my oil*.]

For my hand will assist him, and my arm will strengthen him.

[Col. 0284C] [Note: [Col. 0284D] Again, as in Augustine and in the readings noted in the margin of the book, the Veronese manuscript has: *The enemy will not prevail*, *and will not add to harming him*, *from before him*, and *I will make those who hate him flee*. Two verses later it has: *I will make him the firstborn, exalted among the kings of the earth*; and after another verse, *his offspring instead of his throne*, etc.]

The enemy will accomplish nothing against him, and the son of iniquity will not harm him.

I will cut down his enemies from before him, and I will turn those who hate him to flight.

My truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted.

I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.

He will call upon me: “You are my father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.”

And I will make him the firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth.

[Col. 0286A] Forever I will preserve my mercy for him [Ms. *for him*], and my covenant will be faithful to him.

I will establish his throne forever, and his throne like the days of heaven [Ms. *of the age*.]

If his sons abandon my law and do not walk in my judgments—

if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments—

I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Together with Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has *and their transgressions with lashes*. It has *I will not destroy my mercy* [Augustine: *scatter*] from him, nor harm him in my truth; hence shortly afterward, *I will not reject*, instead of *I will not make void*.]

But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor harm him in my truth; I will not profane my covenant, and I will not make void what proceeds from my lips.

Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David: [Col. 0286B] his offspring will remain forever; his throne will be like the sun before me, and like the perfected [Ms. *composed*] moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven. **DIAPSALMA.**

But you have rejected and despised, and delayed your anointed one; you have turned away the covenant of your servant and profaned his holiness on the earth.

You have destroyed all his walls; you have made his fortifications a terror. [Ms. omits *in*.]

All who pass along the way have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors. [Ms. omits *a*.]

You have exalted the right hand of his enemies; you have gladdened all his enemies.

You have turned away the help of his sword and have not assisted [Col. 0286C] him in battle.

You have dissolved him from purification and struck his hedge to the ground. [Ms. omits *and*.]

You have shortened the days of his times; you have drenched him with shame. **DIAPSALMA.**

How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? [Ms. *God, you turn away*] Will your anger burn like fire?

[Note: [Col. 0286D] The books agree in reading: *Remember what my substance is; for you did not establish all the sons of human beings in vain. Who is the man who will live and not see death? Will he rescue his soul from the hand of hell? Which you swore to David in your truth. Remember, Lord, the reproach*, etc.; finally: *The blessing of the Lord forever*, etc.]

Remember, Lord, what my substance is; for you did not establish the sons of human beings in vain.

What man is there who lives and will not see death? Or who will rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld? **DIAPSALMA.**

Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, which you swore to David in your truth?

Remember the reproach of your servants, which I have carried in my bosom from many nations.

[Col. 0286D] The reproach with which your enemies reproached, Lord, with which they reproached the exchange of your anointed one.

Blessed be the Lord forever; let it be, let it be.

## PSALM LXXXIX

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287A] **A PRAYER OF MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD.**

Lord, you became our refuge—and [the manuscript marks an omitted or uncertain reading]—from generation to generation.

Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God. [Note: [Col. 0287C] In the Palatine manuscript *and* was restored in a second revision instead of *or*; the Greek likewise has καί. It also adds *Diapsalma* at the end. In the following passage the obelus that should precede the negative particle is missing. In fact, either *God*, the noun immediately preceding, or this negative particle is superfluous: the single Hebrew term [Hebrew term], according to its various vowel points, means *God* and *not*; it should not have been repeated and taken in two ways. Even the Septuagint, although Jerome understood the matter differently, took it only as *No*, or μή; they do not add *God* (ὁ Θεός) to the preceding verse, as it appears here.]

Do not turn man to humiliation; and you said, “Return, sons of men.”

For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday, which has passed.

And like a watch in the night; their years will be regarded as nothing.

In the morning, like grass, may it pass away; in the morning may it flower and pass away; in the evening may it fall, grow hard, and wither.

For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.

[Col. 0287B] You have placed our iniquities before you, our age in the illumination of your countenance.

For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.

Our years will meditate like a spider; the days of our years are in themselves seventy years.

But if they are in strength, eighty years; and more than this is labor and sorrow.

For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be chastised.

Who knows the power of your anger, and in fear of you can number your wrath? [Note: [Col. 0287C] The same manuscript adds another *Diapsalma* here.]

Make your right hand known in this way, and those instructed in heart in wisdom. [Note: [Col. 0287D] The Palatine manuscript places an asterisk before *in this way*; later it substitutes *fettered* for *learned*. Augustine likewise has *and the fettered in heart in wisdom* at this passage. Other manuscripts do not have *fettered*, but *learned*. The Greek word sounds the same in both meanings, differing slightly in one syllable.]

Turn, Lord—how long?—and be entreated concerning your servants.

We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we rejoiced and were glad throughout all our days. [Note: [Col. 0287D] The Palatine manuscript improperly marks the pronoun *your* with an obelus and reads *in all the days*, etc. More correctly, in the following verse it omits the obelus placed before the noun *work*, together with the verb *we are*.]

[Col. 0289A] We have rejoiced in proportion to the days in which you humbled us, and the years in which we saw evils.

Look upon your servants and your works, and direct their sons.

Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands for us. [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the Palatine manuscript the conjunction alone is marked with a cross instead of the asterisk that marks this entire passage. Augustine says concerning this place: “Thus far many manuscripts have this psalm—namely, *And direct the work of our hands for us*—but in some another final verse is read: *And direct the work of our hands*. Learned and careful men place a star before this verse; these they call asterisks, by which they indicate things found in the Hebrew or in other Greek interpreters but absent from the Septuagint translation.” See also what we note at the end of Jerome’s letter in our recension 140 to Cyprian.]

—and direct the work of our hands.

[Col. 0288A] **A PRAYER OF MOSES, THE MAN OF GOD.**

Lord, you became our refuge, [Note: [Col. 0287D] The Veronese manuscript and Augustine have *from generation to generation*. One Veronese manuscript has *or the earth would be formed, and the world of the earth*, etc. The bishop of Hippo himself knew this reading, saying, “Other manuscripts have what was expressed from one Greek word, *the earth would be formed*.” It then agrees with the Augustinian Psalter: *from age and to age you are*, omitting the following *God*. Concerning this Jerome says in his frequently cited letter to Sunnias and Fretela: “You say that *God* is not in the Greek; it is plainly absent from their copies. For the Hebrew has it, and all the other interpreters, and the Septuagint likewise translated it: ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος καὶ ἕως αἰῶνος σὺ εἶ ὁ θεός, which in Hebrew is *meolam ad-olam ath el*. See also what we note here and in the corresponding column of the Gallican Psalter.”] from generation and offspring.

Before the mountains were made, or the world of the earth was formed, from age to age you are God.

Do not turn man to humiliation; and you said [Ms. *you say*,] “Return, sons of men.”

For a thousand years in your eyes are like yesterday, which has passed. [Ms. *yesterday, which has passed*, masculine forms.]

And like a watch in the night; their years will be regarded as nothing. [Note: [Col. 0288C] The same books again have *like a watch in the night* and *their years will be*. In the following verse: *and besides, in the evening may it fall, grow hard, and wither*. *For we have failed*, etc.; likewise, two verses later, *and in your anger we have failed*, with the pronoun *us* omitted, and then *they meditated* instead of *they will meditate*. Finally, one Veronese manuscript has: *If they are more than eighty years in strength, and more than this is labor and sorrow*. It marks the following *upon us* as superfluous, as Saint Jerome teaches in his letter to Sunnias and Fretela. It then reads *and we shall be instructed* instead of *we shall be chastised*, etc.]

In the morning, like grass, may it pass away; in the morning may it flower and pass away; in the evening may it fall, grow hard, and wither.

For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.

[Col. 0288B] You have placed our iniquities before you, our age in the illumination of your countenance.

For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed.

Our years will meditate like a spider; the days of our years are in themselves seventy years.

But if they are in strength, eighty years; and most of them are labor and sorrow.

For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be chastised. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Here *upon us* is superfluous, as Jerome teaches. MART.]

Who knows the power of your anger? Or, in fear of you, can anyone number your wrath? [Ms. *and can number your anger*.]

Make your right hand known to us, and those instructed in heart in wisdom.

Turn, Lord, for a little while, and be entreated concerning your servants. [Note: [Col. 0288D] The Veronese manuscript has *Make your right hand known to me*, together with Augustine, who may be consulted in his exposition of this passage. In the following verse it has *how long?* instead of *for a little while*. Then: *We have been satisfied in the morning with your mercy; we rejoiced and were gladdened throughout all our days*. It also has: *And look upon your servants* [Augustine: *look upon*, etc.] *and upon your works, and direct*, etc.]

We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we rejoiced, and they were glad throughout all our days.

[Col. 0290A] They were glad for the days in which you humbled us, and for the years in which we saw evils. [Ms. omits *in*.]

Look upon your servants and your works, Lord, and direct their sons.

Let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, and direct the works of our hands for us.

## PSALM XC

[Col. 0289]

[Col. 0289A] **A SONG OF PRAISE OF DAVID.**

Whoever dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven.

He will say to the Lord, “You are my protector and my refuge; my God, I will hope in him.”

For he himself has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from a harsh word. [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the Palatine manuscript *he will deliver* is more correct; but I would prefer reading *and you* instead of *me* in what follows.]

He will overshadow you on his shoulders; and under his wings [Col. 0289B] you will hope.

His truth will surround you like a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night,

nor the arrow flying by day, nor the business that walks in darkness, nor the assault and the noonday demon. [Note: [Col. 0290D] The same manuscript adds *Diapsalma* here.]

A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; but it will not approach you.

Nevertheless, your eyes will behold, and you will see the retribution of sinners.

For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge.

Evil will not approach you, and scourging will not draw near your dwelling.

For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.

They will carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon.

For he hoped in me, and I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knew my name.

He will cry out to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation, I will rescue him, and I will glorify him. [Note: [Col. 0290D] The Palatine manuscript improperly omits this obelus; correctly, in what follows, it omits the pronoun *I*.]

I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.

From this very fact, however, its recent editor argues that the Itala, as he calls it, is plainly contained in that manuscript. “Therefore,” I reply, “the other Psalters just mentioned, differing from one another and preserving this reading, also present the Itala, if indeed they preserve this reading.” “Nonsense,” he adds. Hence he has no doubt that these words originally stood in the Hebrew text as well. This is a very slight conjecture, long ago dismissed by learned men; those who know Hebrew and handle the Hebrew codex generally know that these words were not there. But pursuing this matter is not our concern, especially since that editor has persuaded himself that the Hebrews erased these words from their own codices and also from the Greek ones—namely, all of them—out of hatred for the cross.] from the wood.

Soon afterward, instead of “toward the house,” the Veronese manuscript has “of the house.” Then, in the verse after that: “Sing psalms to the Lord on the lyre, on the lyre”; and, more closely following Augustine, “of the Lord King.” “Let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world of the earth, and all who dwell in it” (Augustine: “those”). Finally, “the mountains will exult,” instead of “exulted,” etc.] toward Jacob, and his truth toward the house of Israel.

[Col. 0300C] All the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God. Rejoice aloud to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and sing psalms.

Sing psalms to our God on the lyre, and on the lyre, and with the voice of a psalm on drawn-out trumpets, and with the voice of a horn trumpet; rejoice aloud before the King, to the Lord.

Let the sea and its fullness be moved, the world of the earth, and all who dwell in it.

The rivers will clap their hands [Manuscript: “let them clap”] together; the mountains exulted before the face of the Lord, for he comes—for he comes to judge the earth.

He will judge the world of the earth in justice, and the peoples in equity.

[Col. 0304B] ## PRAYER OF THE POOR MAN, WHEN HE IS ANXIOUS AND POURS OUT HIS PRAYER BEFORE GOD

[Note: The Veronese manuscript agrees almost entirely with Augustine: “The prayer of the poor man when he was troubled” (*taedium pateretur*; Augustine has *angeretur*), “and he poured out his prayer in the presence of the Lord.” “Hear, O Lord, my prayer,” immediately followed by *cito*, “quickly,” instead of *velociter*, “swiftly.” Then, after another verse, “He was struck as grass,” and after another, “I became like a pelican that dwells in solitude; I became like a night bird in the walls; I kept watch and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” To this passage refer Jerome’s substantial discussion of this verse, which occupies almost the whole of section 63 of his Letter to Sunnia and Fretela.]

O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.

Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am afflicted, incline your ear to me; on whatever day I call upon you, hear me swiftly.

For my days have faded like smoke, and my bones have been parched like things roasted in a frying pan.

I have been struck like grass, and my heart has withered, because [Manuscript: *quoniam*, “because”] I forgot to eat my bread; at the sound of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh.

I have become like a pelican in the wilderness, and I have become [Col. 0304C] like a night bird in a dwelling.

[Note: Jerome discusses the word *nycticorax* at greater length in his Letter to Sunnia. See the observations in our *Prodromus* on this passage. MART.]

I kept watch, and I became like a solitary sparrow in a building.

[Note: Jerome himself acknowledges that the ancient Latin manuscripts interpreted it in this way. MART.]

All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript, together with Augustine, reads: “My enemies reproached me then,” followed by “because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping. Because of your anger and indignation, because, when you lifted me up, you cast me down.” Augustine has *levasti*, “you lifted up,” instead. Then, after two intervening verses: “But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation. You, arising, will have mercy on Zion, because the time has come” (Augustine omits this verb), “to have mercy on it” (or “on him”), “because the time has come.”]

For I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping.

Because of your anger and indignation, for when you lifted me up, you dashed me down.

My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass [Manuscript: *velut*, “like”].

But you, O Lord, remain forever, and your memorial is from age to age.

[Col. 0306A] You, arising, will have mercy on Zion, because the time for showing mercy to it has come.

For [Manuscript: *quoniam*, “for”] your servants have taken pleasure in its stones, and they will pity its earth.

[Note: Augustine and the Veronese manuscript have “its dust” instead of “its earth”; and, one verse later, “he will be seen in his glory. He regarded the prayer of the humble and did not despise their supplication.” “Let these things be written for a later generation.” Immediately afterward: “For he looked down from his holy height,” and so forth. Finally: “To hear the groaning of the prisoners, to set free the children of those put to death.”]

And the nations shall fear your name, O Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.

For the Lord will build Zion [Manuscript: “built Zion”], and he will be seen in his majesty.

And he regarded the prayers of the poor, and did not despise their supplications.

Let these things be written for a later generation, and the people that shall be created shall praise the Lord.

For he looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth,

to hear the groaning of those bound, and to set free the children of those put to death.

So that the name of the Lord may be proclaimed in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem.

When peoples are gathered together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord.

He answered him on the way of his strength: “Declare to me the brevity of my days, and do not recall me in the middle of my days; your years endure forever and ever.”

[Note: Again, together with Augustine, the same manuscript has: “on the way of his strength,” “declare to me the shortness of my days,” “do not recall me” (the pronoun is missing from the Veronese manuscript), “in the middle of my days, from generation to generation” (Augustine: “of generations”), “your years.” At the beginning: “Lord, you founded the earth,” where Augustine prefers the order of the printed reading given here. The remainder agrees again: “but you remain, and all things like,” and so forth. Also: “But you are the same, you yourself.” Finally, in the last verse, that manuscript omits both *ibi*, “there,” and *saeculi*, “of the age.”]

At the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands.

They shall perish, but you shall remain, and all things shall grow old like a garment; and as a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed.

But you are the same, you yourself, and your years shall not fail.

[Col. 0306C] The children of your servants shall dwell there, and their offspring shall be established forever and ever.

## PSALM OF DAVID

Bless the Lord, O my soul. O Lord my God, you have been greatly magnified.

You have put on confession and beauty; you are clothed with light as with a garment.

[Col. 0308D] You stretch out heaven like a skin; you cover its upper parts with waters.

[Note: The same manuscript gives these two clauses more correctly in the second person: “you cover,” and shortly afterward, “you make the cloud its ascent.” Jerome would have preferred the rest to be expressed in the same way: “you walk,” “you make,” “you founded,” and so forth. See his letter to Sunnia and Fretela. Augustine, on the contrary, consistently prefers the third person. Finally, in the last place, with Augustine, the same manuscript, having removed the pronoun, reads simply “founded the earth upon firmness.” Then: “the abyss, like a garment, is its covering,” and at the end of the other verse: “nor shall they return to cover the earth.”]

He makes the cloud his ascent; he walks upon the wings of the winds.

[Col. 0310A] He makes [Note: The Carnutensis manuscript reads in the second person, “you make.” It has “you founded”; the Sorbonicus and Carus’s printed edition, however, have the third person. MART.] his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire [Manuscript: “blazing”].

He founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved forever and ever.

The abyss, like a cloak, is its covering; the waters shall stand upon the mountains.

At your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder [Manuscript: “thunderclap”] they shall fear.

The mountains rise and the plains descend to the place that you founded for them; you set a boundary for them, which they shall not cross, nor shall they return to cover the earth.

You send forth springs in the valleys; waters shall pass through the midst of the mountains.

All the beasts of the forests shall drink them; the wild asses shall await their thirst; above them the birds of heaven shall dwell, and from the midst of the rocks they shall give their voice.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript, with Augustine, reads: “All the beasts of the field shall drink; the wild asses shall receive their drink; above them the birds of heaven shall dwell; from the midst of the rocks they shall give their voice.” Then, after two additional intervening verses: “Wine gladdens the human heart. To gladden the face,” and so forth (Augustine: “to gladden the face”), “and bread strengthens the human heart.” “The trees of the field shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon that he planted; there the sparrows shall build their nests”; and: “the very high mountains are for deer, the rock a refuge for hedgehogs and hares,” together with other matters of lesser importance recorded in the book.]

You water the mountains from your upper chambers; the earth shall be satisfied with the fruit of your works.

You produce grass for cattle and plants for the service of humankind.

To bring bread from the earth, and wine to gladden the human heart.

To gladden the face with oil, and bread to strengthen the human heart.

All the trees of the forests shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon that you planted; there the sparrows shall nest.

For if we tried to translate the whole expression, we would have to say: ‘When they were in a small number, very few and sojourners in it.’ But what the Greek says, ‘that they were in it,’ is in Latin ‘when they were’; this verb cannot be followed by the accusative case, but by the nominative. In the same letter: “And they provoked [him] as they went up into the sea, the Red Sea.” “In place of this,” you say, “we found in the Greek καὶ παρεπίκραναν and think it should be rendered word for word, ‘and they embittered.’ But this translation is comparable to ‘walking’ or ‘annihilation.’ Read Ezekiel, and you will find παραπίκρασμον always expressed as ‘provocation’ and ‘exasperation,’ where it says οἶκος παραπικραίνων, that is, ‘an exasperating house.’ Yet Augustine, in his exposition of this Psalm, as also in the other passages noted above, was not at all displeased by that word: ‘Several codices,’ he says, ‘which I was able to inspect, both Greek and Latin, have this: “And they provoked,” or, more expressly from the Greek, “And they embittered [him] as they went up into the Red Sea.”’ See also what we note in the opposite column of the Gallican edition. And they made a calf in Horeb [Manuscript: “Choreb”], and [Col. 0320B] worshiped a carved image; and they exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.

And [Manuscript omits “And”] they forgot God, who delivered them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrifying deeds in the Red Sea.

And he said that he would destroy them, if Moses his chosen one had not stood in the breach before him, to turn away [Note: The same manuscript has: “to turn away from indignation, his anger, lest he destroy,” etc. The frequently mentioned editor notes that the Vatican Greek codex likewise prefers this reading, citing the words; yet he does not observe that ὀργῆς, which is read there, is genitive, not nominative, and that under a different punctuation the sense is: “from the indignation of his anger, lest …” In the following verse, the same manuscript has: “they did not believe his word.” In the next: “to cast them down in the wilderness,” etc.; and: “their seed among the nations, to scatter them throughout the lands.” It almost never agrees with Augustine.] his anger, lest he destroy them.

And they treated the desirable land as nothing, and did not believe in his words; and they murmured in their tents, and did not [Manuscript: “not”] hear the voice of the Lord.

And he lifted up his hand over them, to overthrow them [Manuscript: “those”] in the wilderness, and to cast their seed [Col. 0320C] among the nations and scatter them throughout the lands.

And they were consecrated to Beelphegor, and ate sacrifices of the dead.

And [Note: The same manuscript has: “And they exasperated him by their inventions,” etc. “And Phinehas stood,” etc. “And it was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever.” “And they provoked it to anger,” etc., “because they embittered his spirit.”] they provoked him through their practices, and destruction multiplied among them.

Phinehas stood forth, prayed for mercy, and the plague ceased; and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, from generation to generation forever.

And they provoked him at the waters of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit; and he made a distinction with his lips.

[Col. 0322A] They did not destroy the nations that the Lord had commanded them [Manuscript: “had commanded”], but mingled among the nations [Manuscript: “in the nations”], learned their works, served their carved images, and it became a stumbling block to them.

And they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, and poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, [Note: The Veronese manuscript omits the relative pronoun “whom.” In that codex, the first words of this verse had been erased through the following four complete lines by the long wear of the leaf, and a later hand restored them. It further reads: “And the land was killed by blood” (manuscript: “blood”). “And the land was polluted by their works. And they fornicated through their inventions, and the Lord was angry in wrath,” etc. We now return to Augustine, or to Cassiodorus, who follows him almost continuously. The holy bishop guarantees these readings in his exposition: “And the land was killed by blood.” “We might think,” he says, “that this was a scribal error, and say that he wrote ‘killed’ instead of ‘defiled,’ unless we had the benefit of God, who willed that his Scriptures should exist in many languages; and when we examined the Greek codices, we saw that it was indeed written: ‘The land was killed by blood.’” And shortly afterward: “And they fornicated through their inventions.” He calls these inventions what the Greeks call ἐπιτηδεύματα. For this word occurs in the Greek codices both here and above, where it says: “They provoked him through their inventions.” Finally, where it says: “The Lord was angry in wrath,” he notes the following: “Certain of our interpreters did not wish to render the anger expressed by the Greek θυμός; some rendered it ‘mind,’ some ‘indignation,’ and some ‘spirit.’”] whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.

The land was defiled by blood, and polluted by their works.

And they fornicated through their observances, and the Lord was angry in spirit against his people, and abhorred his inheritance.

[Col. 0322B] And he handed them over to the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them.

And their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands; often [Note: In the same manuscript: “he often rescued them.” “But they embittered him through their counsel, and they were humbled by their iniquities.” And: “He looked upon them when they were afflicted,” etc. Then one verse later: “And he gave them into mercy, before all those who had taken them captive”; finally: “Gather us from the nations, that we may …,” a reading also noted by Augustine there: “Gather us from the nations,” or, as other codices have it, “from the peoples.”] he delivered them.

But they provoked him by their counsel, and were humbled by their iniquities.

And he looked upon them when they were afflicted, when he heard their prayers.

And he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the multitude of his mercy.

And he gave them into mercies, before all those who had taken them captive.

Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.

[Col. 0322C] Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from age to age and forever; and let all the people say, “Let it be, let it be.”

PSALM 106.

[Col. 0321]

[Col. 0321C] ALLELUIA.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good: for his mercy is forever.

Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions,

[Col. 0323A] from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.

They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found no road to a city of habitation.

Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted: ÷ and ** he delivered them from their necessities.

And he led them by a straight road, that they might go to a city of habitation.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

For he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things.

Sitting ÷ in ** darkness and the shadow of death, bound [Col. 0323B] ÷ in ** misery and iron.

Because they embittered the words of God, and provoked the counsel of the Most High.

And their heart was humbled by hardships; they grew weak, and there was no one to help.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

[Note: Again the Palatine manuscript wrongly places an obelus before the small word; the obelus ought by customary practice to precede the preposition of the following verb, “he led out.” It also appends “Diapsalma” to this verse.] And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

For he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars.

He received them from the way of their iniquity; because of their injustices [Col. 0323C] [Note: The Palatine manuscript and Carus mark this pronoun “their” with an obelus, as they also do the adverb “even” in the following verse. The obelus prefixed to the conjunction that follows is absent from that manuscript, while “Diapsalma” is added at the end of the next verse. All these are to be regarded as scribal faults.] they were humbled.

Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near even to the gates of death.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted: ÷ and ** he delivered them from their necessities.

He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

And let them sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and proclaim his works with rejoicing.

Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters.

They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.

[Col. 0323D] He spoke, and the spirit of the storm arose, and its waves were lifted high.

[Col. 0325A] They rise ÷ even ** to the heavens, and descend ÷ even ** to the abysses; their soul was wasting away in calamities.

They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he led them out of their necessities.

÷ And ** he turned his storm ÷ into ** a breeze, and its waves were silent.

[Note: Again the Palatine manuscript and Carus less correctly pierce the conjunction “and” with an obelus. At the end of the verse the manuscript adds “Diapsalma.”] And they rejoiced because they were silent, and he led them into the harbor of their desire.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise him in the seat of the elders.

He made rivers into a wilderness, and springs of water into thirst.

A fruitful land into saltiness, because of the wickedness of those who dwell [Note: The words “in it” are again unjustly struck through with an obelus by the Palatine manuscript.] in it.

He made a wilderness into pools of water, and a dry land into springs of water.

And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city of habitation.

They sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of their harvest.

And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly, and he did not diminish their livestock.

They became few and were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrow.

Contempt was poured out [Note: The Palatine manuscript incorrectly writes “contention” for “contempt.”] upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a trackless place and not on a road.

[Col. 0325C] And he helped the poor in their poverty, and made families like sheep.

The upright will see and rejoice, and every iniquity will shut its mouth.

Who is wise and will keep these things, and will understand the mercies of the Lord?

[Col. 0322C] ALLELUIA.

Give thanks to the Lord, for [Note: With Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has: “for he is gracious.” And: “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hands of enemies,” etc. “From the east, and from the west, and from the north and from the sea.” And three verses later: “And he led them by a straight road” (manuscript: “straight”), that they might go, etc. And: “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his compassions,” etc.] he is good: for his mercy is forever.

Let those now redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, and gathered from the regions.

[Col. 0324A] From the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea.

They wandered in the wilderness, in dryness; they found no road to a city of habitation.

Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.

And they cried out [Manuscript: “called out”] to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

And he led them by a straight road, that they might go to a city of habitation.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

For [Manuscript: “because”] he satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul [Note: With Augustine, the Veronese manuscript has: “he filled with good things”; and shortly afterward, “those bound,” instead of “bound in chains.” Then: “Because they embittered the words of the Lord, and provoked the counsel of the Most High.” At the end of the following verse: “who would help them”; and in the next: “and he saved them from their necessities.” Then: “he broke their bonds.” “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his compassions,” etc.] with good things.

Sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound [Col. 0324B] in chains, in misery and iron.

Because they embittered the word of the Lord, and provoked the counsel of the Most High.

And their heart was humbled by hardships. They grew weak, and there was no one to help.

And they cried out [Manuscript: “called out”] to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and tore apart their bonds.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

For he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars.

He received them from the way of their iniquity; for because of their injustices [Col. 0324C] [Manuscript: “iniquities”] they were humbled.

Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and [Note: Augustine and the Veronese book likewise have: “and they drew near even to the gates of death.” And: “They cried out,” etc. Then the Veronese alone has “he saved them,” as above, instead of “he delivered them”; and in the following verse: “and he rescued them from their corruption.” Again, with Augustine: “Let them give thanks to the Lord for his compassions,” etc. And: “Let them sacrifice a sacrifice,” etc. Finally, “doing their work,” instead of “their works.”] they drew near even to the gates of death.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destruction.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders to the children of men.

That they may sacrifice a sacrifice of praise, and proclaim his works with rejoicing.

Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters.

They saw the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.

[Col. 0324D] He spoke, and the spirit of the storm arose, and its waves were lifted high.

[Col. 0326A] They rise to the heavens, and descend to the abysses; their soul was wasting away in calamities.

They were troubled [Note: The Veronese manuscript has: “They were greatly troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.” And: “They cried out,” etc., “and he led them out of their necessities,” agreeing with Augustine in these final words, as also in what follows: “He commanded the storm, and it became a breeze,” etc. (manuscript: “a hall”), “and they rejoiced because they were silent.” “And he led them into the harbor of their desire,” omitting the other half-verse, “and he delivered them from their necessities,” which most other Latin books also lack. As above, it has “compassions” instead of “mercy.”] and shaken like a drunken man, and their wisdom was swallowed up.

And they cried out to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their necessities.

And he made the storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent, and they rejoiced because they were silent.

And he led them into the harbor of their desire, and he delivered them from their necessities.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies, and for his wonders [Manuscript: “admirable things”] to the children of men.

And let them exalt him in the assembly of the people [Manuscript: “of the populace”], and praise him in the seat of the elders.

For [Manuscript omits “for”] he made rivers into a wilderness, [Col. 0326B] and springs of water into thirst.

A fruitful land into saltiness, [Note: The same manuscript, in agreement with Augustine, has “into salt works,” and shortly afterward, in the plural, “into pools of water.” Then: “And he caused the hungry to dwell there.” And: “the fruit of grain,” instead of “the fruit of harvest”; likewise afterward, “very much,” instead of “greatly,” and “diminished,” instead of “made less.” It continues: “And they became few, and were afflicted by the tribulation of sorrows and evils” (Augustine: “of evils and sorrow”). The rest agrees: “Contempt was poured out upon princes,” and “he led them astray,” etc. And: “He helped the poor from beggary,” etc. “The upright will see and rejoice,” etc.; finally, “and will understand the compassions of the Lord.”] because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it.

He made a wilderness into a pool of water, and dry land into springs of water.

And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city of habitation.

They sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of their harvest.

And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly; and their livestock was not diminished.

They became few, and were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrows.

And contempt was poured out upon their princes, and they led them astray in a trackless place and not on a road.

[Col. 0326C] And he helped the poor in their poverty, and made families like sheep.

The upright will see and rejoice, and every iniquity will shut its mouth.

Who is wise and will keep these things, and then will understand the mercies of the Lord?

PSALM 107.

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325C] SONG OF THE PSALM OF DAVID.

[Note: On the recto the same manuscript has “Psalm.” Carus adds “itself,” preceded by an obelus. In the text, the same manuscript rashly omits the obelus at the very first verse. Concerning what follows, see Jerome’s letter to Sunnias and Fretela, and what we observe there.]

My heart is ready, O God, ÷ my heart is ready **; I shall sing and make melody in my glory.

[Col. 0327A] Rise up, [Note: Several printed and manuscript books read before this: “Rise up, my glory.” But Sunnias and Fretela did not read this in Latin; hence Jerome writes to them: “What you say is absent from the Latin is rightly absent from this Psalm, because it is found neither among the Hebrews nor in any interpreter; rather, it occurs in the fifty-sixth Psalm, from which it seems to me to have been transferred into this passage.” Moreover, the Chartres and Colbert manuscripts, no. 2200, and the Sorbonne manuscript, no. 2784, do not read the addition “Rise up, my glory.” Nevertheless, in the Roman Psalter, which occupies the second or middle column of the threefold Psalter manuscript of the Sorbonne, it is still retained through scribal error; it is entirely absent from the ancient and excellent Chartres codex. MART.] O psaltery and lyre; I shall rise at dawn.

I shall give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and make melody to you among the nations.

For your mercy is great above the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds. [Note: The Palatine manuscript adds “Diapsalma.”]

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth, that your beloved ones may be delivered.

Save me with your right hand, and hear me; God has spoken in his holiness.

I shall rejoice, ÷ and ** divide Shechem; and I shall measure out the valley of the tents.

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the protection of my head.

Judah is my king; Moab [Note: In the same manuscript a space, erased by a later hand, is left large enough for this name. [Col. 0328D] Previously it seems to have read “pot.”] is the pot of my hope.

Upon Idumea I shall extend my sandal; the foreigners [Col. 0327B] have become my friends.

Who will lead me into a fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea?

Are you not the God who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, for the salvation of man is vain.

In God we shall perform a mighty deed, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.

[Col. 0326C] [Note: In the Veronese manuscript it is inscribed: “For the end. A Psalm of David himself.” In the text it agrees with Augustine: “I shall sing and make melody in my glory. Rise up,” etc.; and shortly afterward again: “I shall make melody to you among the nations.” “For your mercy is magnified above the heavens” (Augustine: “great”), etc.; and in the following verse: “that your beloved ones may be rescued.”] SONG OF THE PSALM OF DAVID.

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I shall sing and speak a psalm to the Lord.

[Col. 0328A] Rise, psalter and lyre; I shall rise at dawn.

I will give thanks to you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing a psalm to you among the nations.

For your mercy has been magnified up to the heavens, and your truth up to the clouds.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth, so that your elect may be delivered.

Save me [Ms. omits *me*] by your right hand, and answer me: God has spoken in his sanctuary: “I shall rejoice, and apportion Shechem, and measure out the Valley of Tents” [Ms. *I shall measure out*].

Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the stronghold of my head.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] Here, with Augustine, the Veronese manuscript reads “protection” (*susceptio*). In the following verse it has “foreigners are subject to me,” and in another following verse it omits the little word *and*; finally, at the end it has “our enemies” in place of “those who trouble us.”]

Judah [Ms. *Judas*] is my king; Moab is the cauldron of my hope. Into Edom I shall extend my sandal; the Philistines are subjected to me.

Who will lead me into the fortified city? Or who will lead me as far as Edom?

Are you not the God who rejected us? And will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, for the salvation of human beings is vain.

With God we shall perform mighty deeds, and he himself will bring to nothing those who trouble us.

## PSALM 108

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327B] **TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID.**

Do not be silent, O God, regarding my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have been opened against me.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] This second occurrence of “mouth” is deleted in the Palatine manuscript. Moreover, it reads, with an obelus placed before *and*, “÷ and ** with words,” etc.; Caro also approves this, contrary to the evidence of the original books.]

They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, and surrounded me with words of hatred; they attacked me without cause.

[Col. 0327C] In return for their loving + me **, they slandered me; but I prayed.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] Again, the Palatine manuscript wrongly omits the asterisk.]

They set evils against me in return for goods, and hatred in return for my love.

Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.

When he is judged, let him come forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin.

[lacuna]

Let his days be few; ÷ and ** let another receive his office.

Let his children become orphans, and his wife a widow.

[Col. 0329A] Let his children wander away and beg; [Note: [Col. 0329C] Here the Palatine manuscript also omits the conjunction, which the Greek likewise does not have.] and let them be cast out of their dwellings.

Let the creditor search out all his possessions + and ** let strangers plunder his labors.

Let there be no helper for him, nor anyone who will have mercy on his orphans.

Let his descendants be brought to destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out.

Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance in the sight of the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.

Let them be continually against the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth. [Note: [Col. 0329C] The Palatine manuscript and Carus wrongly mark the word *for* with an obelus.] Because he did not remember to show mercy,

he pursued the poor and needy man, and the broken-hearted, in order to put him to death.

[Col. 0329B] He loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.

He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment; it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones.

Let it be for him like a garment with which he is covered, and like a belt with which he is always girded.

This is the work of those who slander me [Note: [Col. 0329C] The words “before the Lord” are absent in that manuscript; *Diapsalma* is added at the end of the verse. Then, in the following verse, the substantive verb is deleted.] before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul.

And you, O Lord, Lord, deal with me for the sake of your name, for your mercy is sweet.

Deliver me, for I am needy and poor, and my heart [Note: [Col. 0329D] In the same manuscript it reads “is disturbed”; in the following verse the conjunction *and* is pierced with an obelus.] is troubled within me.

Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away; and I have been shaken off like a locust.

My knees have become weak through fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil. [Note: [Col. 0329D] Here too the same manuscript omits the asterisk.] + And ** I have become a reproach to them; they saw me, ÷ and ** shook their heads.

Help me, O Lord my God; save me according to your mercy.

And let them know that this is your hand; [Note: [Col. 0329D] A later hand in the same manuscript erased the obelus and the conjunction “and” itself.] ÷ and ** you, O Lord, have done it.

They will curse, but you will bless; let those who rise against me be confounded, but your servant will rejoice.

[Col. 0331A] Let those who slander me be clothed with shame, and let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak.

I will give abundant thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.

For he stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from those who pursued it.

[Col. 0328B] **TO THE END, A PSALM OF DAVID** [Ms. *To David himself*].

O God, do not be silent regarding my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful [Ms. *because the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful*] has been opened against me.

They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue [Ms. *a deceitful tongue*], and surrounded me with words of hatred, and attacked me [Ms. *defeated me*] without cause.

In return that they should love me, they slandered me; but I prayed.

They set evils against me in return for goods [Ms. *And they set*], and hatred in return for my love.

Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.

When he is judged, let him come forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin.

[Note: [Col. 0328D] This verse, which the Veronese manuscript does not have, Martianaeus found in one Sorbonne manuscript. Two verses after this, the Veronese codex reads “his wards” (*pupilli*), instead of “orphans” (*orphani*), and then, with Augustine, “let them be transferred” (*transferantur*), instead of “let them be removed” (*amoveantur*).]

Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one who inhabits it.

Let his days be few, and let another receive his office.

Let his children be orphans, and his wife a widow.

[Col. 0330A] Let his children, having been shaken, be removed, and let them beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings.

Let the creditor search out all his possessions, and [Ms. omits *and*] let strangers plunder all his labors.

Let there be no helper for him, nor [Ms. *let there not be*] anyone who will have mercy on his orphans.

Let his descendants [Ms. *his sons*] be brought to destruction; in one generation let his name [Ms. *their name*] be blotted out.

Let the iniquity of his fathers return to remembrance in the sight of the Lord, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out.

Let them [Note: [Col. 0329D] In the Veronese manuscript: “Let them be always before the Lord”; Augustine himself commends this reading among others in his *Enarration*, taking “against the Lord” as equivalent to “in the sight of the Lord.” He adds that other interpreters rendered it “Let them be in the sight of the Lord always,” while others read “Let them be before the Lord always,” etc. That manuscript continues, “and let their memory perish from the earth. Because they did not remember to show mercy, and pursued the man, and, in continuous construction, they delivered [him] to death”; but Augustine does not mention this reading, even word for word.] be continually against the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth.

Because he did not remember to show mercy, and pursued the poor and needy man, and delivered the broken-hearted to death.

[Col. 0330B] He loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him.

He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment; it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones.

Let it be for him like a garment with which he is covered, and like a belt with which he is always girded.

This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord, and who speak evil against my soul.

And you, O Lord, Lord, show me mercy for the sake of your name, for your mercy is sweet.

Deliver me, for I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me.

Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away; and [Ms. omits *and*] I have been shaken off like a locust.

My knees have become weak through [Ms. *from*] fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of [Note: [Col. 0330D] Through wrongly taking the Greek δι᾽ ἔλαιον (*because of oil*) for δι᾽ ἔλεον (*because of mercy*), a very similar word both in sound and spelling, the Veronese manuscript reads “because of mercy.” I do not know whether this reading was ever approved in any other Latin book. In the following verse, Augustine has “O my God, save me according to mercy,” etc. The Veronese alone then has “but your servant will be glad,” and, in the latter half of the next verse, “and let them be clothed about with their confusion as with a double cloak.” Augustine himself partly knew this reading in the *Enarration*, where, discussing *diploide*—a term he himself retained—he says: “*Diplois* is a double cloak. For some also translated this verse thus: ‘and let them cover themselves with their confusion as with a double cloak.’”] oil, and I have become a reproach to them.

They saw me and shook their heads. Help me, O Lord my God, and [Ms. omits *and*] save me for the sake of your mercy.

So that they may know that this is your hand, and that you, O Lord, have done it.

They will curse him [Ms. *themselves*], but you will bless; let those who rise against me be confounded, but your servant will rejoice.

[Col. 0332A] Let those who slander me be clothed with reverence, and let them be covered with their confusion as with a double cloak.

I will give abundant thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him.

For he stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from those who pursued it [Ms. *may save*].

## PSALM 109

[Col. 0331]

[Col. 0331A] **A PSALM OF DAVID.**

The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,

until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.

The Lord will send forth the scepter of your strength [Note: [Col. 0331C] As usual, the Palatine manuscript marks with an obelus the preposition of *will send forth*; it also adds *Diapsalma* at the end both of this and of the following verse.] from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies.

With you is the beginning on the day of your strength, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.
