He says: “Those who put not ‘word’ but ‘utterance’ translated more precisely: for the Greek has λόγιον, which is ‘utterance,’ not λόγος, which is ‘word.’” It continues: “The proud acted wickedly to the uttermost against the law,” etc. “I remembered,” etc., and “I was encouraged,” instead of “I was consoled,” which Augustine likewise notes: “Or, as other codices have, ‘I was encouraged,’ that is, I received encouragement.” Both could have been translated from the Greek word παρεκλήθην. It continues, in agreement with Augustine: “Weariness held me because of sinners abandoning your law.”] you gave me hope.

Zain. This has consoled me in my humiliation, because your utterance gave me life.

Zain. The proud acted wickedly to the uttermost; but I did not turn aside from your law.

Zain. I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted.

Zain. Faintness of spirit seized me because of sinners abandoning your law.

Zain. Your justifications were songs for me in the place of my sojourning.

[Col. 0348B] Zain. I remembered your name by night [the manuscript: “in the night”], Lord, and I kept your law.

Zain. This happened to me because [the manuscript: “This happened to me, because”] I sought your justifications.

**Heth.** My portion [Note: In the Veronese manuscript, “My part,” almost as in Augustine, except that it has “Lord” where this text has “O Lord.” Then: “I entreated your face,” etc.; “because I considered your ways,” etc. And: “I am prepared and not troubled, to keep your commandments,” which the bishop of Hippo considers only an interpolation among the various glosses [Col. 0348C] of translators. Finally, in the second half of the following verse: “and I have not forgotten your law,” again in agreement with Augustine’s reading.] is the Lord; I said, “I will keep your law.”

Heth. I entreated your face with my whole heart; have mercy on me according to your utterance.

Heth. Because I considered my ways, I turned my feet toward your testimonies.

Heth. I am prepared and not troubled, so that I may keep your commandments.

Heth. The cords of sinners have entangled me; but I have not forgotten your law.

Heth. At midnight I rose to confess to you, [Col. 0348C] because of the judgments of your righteousness.

Heth. I am a participant with all who fear you and keep your commandments.

Heth. Your mercy, Lord, fills the earth; teach me your justifications.

Teth. [Note: [Col. 0348C] The same manuscript has *suavitate* (“sweetness”), using the noun in place of *bonitate* (“goodness”), and likewise *suavis* (“sweet”) in place of *bonus* (“good”). Saint Augustine has there: “You have dealt sweetly with your servant, Lord, according to your word”—or rather, “according to your utterance.” But what the Greek says, χρηστότητα (*chrēstótēta*), our translators have rendered sometimes as “sweetness,” sometimes as “goodness,” etc. Hence the manuscript reads: “Teach me sweetness and instruction and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments.” In this connection, these words of Augustine should again be recalled: “He added ‘and instruction,’ or, as more manuscripts have it, ‘discipline’; but ‘discipline,’ which the Greeks call παιδεία (*paideía*), Scripture customarily places where instruction through afflictions is to be understood, in accordance with the saying: ‘For whom the Lord loves, he reproves; and he scourges,’ etc.] You have dealt well with your servant, Lord, according to your word.

Teth. Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed in your commandments.

Teth. Before I was humbled, I went astray; [Note: [Col. 0348D] In the same manuscript: “therefore I kept your word”; concerning which Augustine again says: “Or, as others have it more explicitly, ‘your utterance.’” The manuscript continues: “You are sweet, Lord, and teach me by sweetness.” Augustine says: “Or, as many have it, ‘You are sweet,’ or ‘You are good.’” Then, after one intervening verse—where Jerome teaches in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela that the words “in my heart” contain a pronoun unnecessarily added—the remainder reads thus in the same manuscript: “My heart was congealed like milk; but I will meditate on your law” (in place of “I meditated”). “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications,” etc.] therefore I kept your utterance.

[Col. 0350A] Teth. You are good, Lord, and in your goodness teach me your justifications.

Teth. The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me; but I shall search out your commandments with my whole [Note: [Col. 0349D] This is how Sunnia and Fretela read in the Greek manuscripts, but Jerome taught them that *super* (“against”) was superfluous here. MART.] heart.

Teth. Their heart has thickened like milk; but I have meditated on your law.

Teth. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications.

Teth. The law of your mouth is good for me, above thousands of gold and silver pieces.

Jod. Your hands made me and [Note: [Col. 0349D] The Veronese manuscript has *finxerunt* (“fashioned”), concerning which Augustine says: “Some translators did not wish to say *finxerunt me* (‘fashioned me’), but *plasmaverunt me* (‘formed me’), preferring to decline a Greek word in a less Latin manner rather than say *finxerunt*, which is sometimes also used of pretence. It continues: ‘They shall see me and rejoice, because I hoped in your words. I have recognized, Lord, that your judgments are just, and in your truth you humbled me. Let your mercy therefore be upon me,’ etc., ‘according to your word to your servant. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation. Let the proud be put to shame, because they acted wickedly against me; but I shall speak freely of your precepts.’ Soon afterward: ‘Those who know your testimonies’; almost everything agrees with Augustine.] formed me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments.

Jod. Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, [Col. 0350B] because I hoped in your word.

Jod. I have recognized, Lord, that your judgments are equity; and in your truth you humbled me.

Jod. Let your mercy now come upon me, so that it may comfort me, according to your utterance to your servant.

Jod. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation.

Jod. Let the proud be put to shame, because they acted wickedly against me; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments.

Jod. Let those who fear you, and who know your testimonies, turn toward me.

Jod. Let my heart be blameless in your justifications, so that I may not be put to shame.

Caph. [Note: [Col. 0350D] The same manuscript has: “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I hoped in your word. My eyes have failed for your word, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’ For I have become like a leather bottle in frost”—a thoroughly Latin expression, used by authors of the golden age of Latin, which, so far as I know, Ambrose alone retained. Then, after one intervening verse: “The wicked told me their pleasures”; but not “as your law,” etc. Augustine explains that our translators wished to render these “pleasures” as the things the Greeks call ἀδολεσχίας (*adoleschías*), which cannot at all be expressed in Latin by one word: some called them “pleasures,” others “talk.” The addition *suas* (“their”) in the Veronese manuscript is superfluous. Further, “they persecuted me unjustly,” in place of “the wicked,” etc. And after three verses: “Your truth is in a generation.” Also: “By your ordinance the day endures, because all things serve you.” Unless one reads “because your law,” etc.] My soul has failed for your salvation; and I hoped in your word.

Caph. My eyes have failed for your utterance, saying, “When will you comfort me?”

Caph. For I have become like a leather bottle in frost; I have not forgotten your justifications.

Caph. How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me?

[Col. 0352A] Caph. The wicked have told me tales, but not such as your law, Lord.

Caph. All your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me—help me.

Caph. They almost finished me off on the earth [Ms. omits *me*]; but I did not abandon your commandments.

Caph. According to your mercy, give me life; and I shall keep the testimonies of your mouth.

Lamed. Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven.

Lamed. And your truth is from age to age.

Lamed. You founded the earth, and it remains; by your ordinance the days endure, because all things serve you.

[Col. 0352B] Lamed. If your law had not been my meditation, I would perhaps have perished in my humiliation.

Lamed. I shall never forget your justifications, [Note: [Col. 0351D] The Veronese manuscript has: “your justifications, because by them you gave me life, Lord”; and, two verses after this: “Sinners waited for me,” etc.; then: “I saw the end of every consummation: your commandment is exceedingly broad”; likewise, after another intervening verse: “You have made me understand above my enemies your commandment, because it is mine forever.” Augustine says there: “Those who interpreted ‘forever’ understood better than those who interpreted ‘for an age.’” And after two further verses: “I restrained my feet from every evil way” (in place of “evil”), “so that I might keep your words”; and finally: “Your words are sweet to my throat,” in place of “utterances,” etc., which Saint Augustine says is more explicitly expressed in the Greek.] because by them you gave me life.

Lamed. I am yours; save me, because I have sought your justifications.

Lamed. Sinners waited for me, to destroy me; I understood your testimonies.

Lamed. I saw the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.

Mem. How I have loved your law, Lord! It is my meditation all day long.

Mem. You have made me wiser than my enemies through your commandment, because it is mine forever.

[Col. 0352C] Mem. I have understood more than all those who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation.

Mem. I have understood more than the elders, because I sought your commandments.

Mem. I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your word.

Mem. I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established a law for me.

Mem. How sweet your utterances are to my throat—sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!

Mem. From your commandments I gained understanding; therefore I hated every way of iniquity, because you established a law for me.

Nun. Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths [Ms. *my path*].

[Col. 0352D] Nun. I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice.

Nun. I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word. [Note: [Col. 0352D] The same manuscript has *usque valde* (“exceedingly”). Then: “Approve the voluntary offerings of my mouth” (in place of *adprobato*, or “approve, I pray,” or “well,” or “now”), Lord, etc. Where the following verse says “in your hands” in place of “in my hands,” the holy Father himself explains in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela: “It should be known that among the Hebrews, the Septuagint, and all other translators, it is written ‘in my hands,’ not ‘in your hands’; in Hebrew this is said *bachaffi*, etc.” Augustine, on the contrary, says: “Some manuscripts have ‘in my hands,’ but more have ‘in your hands,’ and this is certainly clear: for the souls of the just are in the hand of God.” The same manuscript continues: “Sinners set a snare for me, but I did not stray from your commandments, Lord.” “I possessed your land as an inheritance,” which is clearly a scribal error for “your testimonies.” Augustine likewise approves the reading “I possessed as an inheritance,” or “I acquired as an inheritance,” not “an inheritance,” but “as an inheritance.” Again, below, in the second letter Samech: “You are my defender and protector, and I hoped in your word.” “Depart from me, evil-doers,” etc., and “receive me according to your word”; in these passages Augustine often agrees, but often also disagrees.]

[Col. 0354A] Nun. Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, Lord, and teach me your judgments.

Nun. My soul is always in your hands, and I have not forgotten your law. [Note: [Col. 0353D] Thus the printed and manuscript books of the Roman Psalter read, as do the Greek copies of the Septuagint, both printed and manuscript: ἐν ταῖς χερσίν σου (*en tais chersín sou*, “in your hands”). The Sorbonne manuscript of the Septuagint edition has *en tes chersin su*. But Jerome says: “It should be known that among the Hebrews, the Septuagint, and all other translators, it is written ‘in my hands,’ not ‘in your hands.’ This is said in Hebrew *bachaffi* (), etc.” Therefore the Greek copies that we use, and those preserved in the threefold Sorbonne manuscript Psalter, are not [Col. 0354C] pure copies of the Septuagint. MART.]

Nun. Sinners set snares for me, but I did not stray from your commandments.

Nun. I acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, because they are the rejoicing of my heart.

Nun. I inclined my heart to perform your justifications forever, for the sake of recompense.

Samech. I hated the wicked and loved your law.

Samech. You are my helper and protector, and I hoped in your [Col. 0354B] word.

Samech. Depart from me, evil-doers, and I shall search out the commandments of my God.

Samech. Receive me according to your utterance, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.

Samech. Help me, and I shall be saved; and I shall meditate forever on your justifications [Ms. *I shall meditate*].

Samech. [Note: [Col. 0354C] The Veronese manuscript has: “You have brought to nothing all who depart from your justifications”—which Augustine says is more carefully expressed from the Greek—“because their transgression is unjust. I considered all the sinners of the earth transgressors; therefore I always loved your testimonies. Nail with nails because of fear of you.” Augustine should again be recalled here: “I counted, or thought, or considered, all the sinners of the earth transgressors. For our translators rendered the one Greek word ἐλογισάμην (*elogisámēn*) in many ways. At the beginning of the following sentence: ‘Transgressors,’ or rather ‘those transgressing’; for the Greek says παραβαίνοντας (*parabaínontas*), not παραβάτας (*parabátas*). Then, in section 6: ‘Some of our translators rendered “Nail with nails” more explicitly, which could be expressed in Greek by one word, namely καθήλωσον (*kathḗlōson*). Others wished to say “Nail,” and did not add “with nails”; and thus, while they wished to render one Greek word with one Latin word, they expressed the meaning less fully, because the word “nail” does not convey nails, whereas καθήλωσον cannot be understood without nails and can be said in Latin only with two words, as it has been said: “Nail with nails.”]

Samech. You have rejected all who depart from your justifications, because their thought is unjust.

Samech. I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved your testimonies.

Samech. Fasten my flesh with your fear, for I feared your judgments.

Ain. I practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over [Note: [Col. 0354D] The same manuscript has: “Do not hand me over to those who harm me.” Augustine again comments on this: “Some manuscripts have ‘do not hand me over to those who persecute me’; for what is said in Greek as τοῖς ἀντιδικοῦσι (*tois antidikoûsi*), some translated ‘those who harm,’ some ‘those who persecute,’ and some ‘those who accuse falsely.’ Yet, remarkably, among all the manuscripts I was able to consult, I nowhere read *adversantibus* (‘those who oppose’), although unquestionably what is called ἀντίδικος (*antídikos*) in Greek is called *adversarius* (‘adversary’) in Latin. The same manuscript continues: ‘Receive your servant for good, so that they may not accuse me falsely,’ etc.; and in the following verse: ‘and in the word of your justice,’ as also in the next: ‘and teach me your justices.’] to those who persecute me.

[Col. 0356A] Ain. Choose your servant for good, so that the proud may not slander me.

Ain. My eyes have failed for your salvation and for the utterance of your justice.

Ain. Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your justifications.

Ain. I am your servant; [Note: [Col. 0355D] The Veronese manuscript has: “Make me understand, and I shall know your testimonies. It is time to act, Lord; they have destroyed your law. Therefore I loved,” etc. Again: “Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity. Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul searched them out. The explanation of your words gives light and makes infants understand. I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments. Look upon me and have mercy,” etc. “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me. Redeem me from the slanders of men, and I shall keep your commandments.” Some of these readings agree with Augustine; others do not.] give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies.

Ain. It is time to act, Lord; the wicked have destroyed your law.

Ain. Therefore I loved your commandments more than gold and topaz.

Ain. Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every unjust way.

Phe. Your testimonies are wonderful, Lord; therefore my soul searched them out. [Col. 0356B]

Phe. The exposition of your words gives me light and grants understanding to the simple.

Phe. I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments.

Phe. Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name.

Phe. Direct my steps according to your utterance, and let no injustice rule over me.

Phe. Redeem me from the slanders of men, so that I may keep your commandments.

Phe. Let your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your justifications.

Phe. [Note: [Col. 0356D] It is also preferable here to transcribe the context of the Veronese Psalter: “My eyes ran down through streams of water, because they did not keep,” etc.; then, at the end, after one intervening verse: “the truth exceedingly.” Also: “Zeal for your house consumed me,” concerning which Augustine says: “Some manuscripts have ‘your house,’ and not ‘it weakened me,’ but ‘it consumed me.’ This seems to me to have been imported from another psalm, where it is written: ‘Zeal for your house consumed me,’ etc.” The manuscript continues: “because my enemies have forgotten your words. Your word is thoroughly refined by fire, and your servant loved it. I am young and despised,” etc.; and after another verse: “Tribulation and necessity found me; your commandments are my meditation. Your testimonies are justice; give me understanding, and give me life.”] Streams of water passed over my eyes, because they did not keep your law.

[Col. 0356C] Sade. You are just, Lord, and your judgment is right [Ms. adds *est*, “is”].

Sade. You commanded your testimonies to be justice, and your truth exceedingly.

Sade. Zeal for your house has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words.

Sade. Your utterance is thoroughly refined by fire, and your servant loved it.

Sade. I am younger and despised; I have not forgotten your justifications.

Sade. Your justice is justice forever, and your law is truth.

Sade. Tribulation and distress found me, but your commandments are my meditation.

[Col. 0358A] Sade. The equity of your testimonies is everlasting; give me understanding, and I shall live.

Coph. [Note: [Col. 0357D] The Veronese manuscript has: “I cried out with my whole heart,” etc., “and I shall seek your justifications. I cried out, save me”—without the intervening words “to you,” which Augustine also omits, although he notes that they occur in other Greek and Latin manuscripts: “I cried out to you,” etc.—“and I shall keep your testimonies. I came beforehand early and cried out; I hoped in your words.” Here Augustine again notes: “More manuscripts do not have *intempesta nocte* (‘in the dead of night’) but *immaturitate* (‘before dawn’). Yet scarcely one was found that had the doubled preposition, that is, *in immaturitate* (‘in before-dawnness’).” Shortly afterward: “What is therefore said in Greek as ἐν ἀωρίᾳ (*en aōría*) cannot be rendered by one word, but by two—that is, a preposition and a noun. Some of our translators said *intempesta nocte* (‘in the dead of night’), more said *immaturitate* (‘before dawn’), not with two words but with one, whose nominative is *immaturitas*; others used two words, as the Greek does, *in immaturitate*. For ἀωρία means ‘untimeliness,’ and ἐν ἀωρίᾳ means ‘in untimeliness’; as if even the translator who said *intempesta nocte* wished to express the doubled preposition in *intempesta*, so that one preposition would signify ‘in what hour,’ while the other would belong to the composition of the noun,” etc. Finally, in the same manuscript, in the following verse: “to meditate on your words,” in place of “so that I might meditate on your utterances,” etc.] I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, Lord; I shall seek your justifications.

Coph. I cried out to you; save me, so that I may keep your commandments.

Coph. I came beforehand early and cried out; I hoped in your word.

Coph. My eyes went before you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your utterances.

Coph. Hear my voice, Lord, according to your mercy, and according to your judgment give me life.

Coph. Those who persecute me unjustly have drawn near; but they are far from your law. [Note: [Col. 0358D] The same manuscript prefers: “Those who persecute me unjustly have drawn near,” a reading which Augustine also praises, except for the scribal error of repeating the pronoun *me*. It continues: “You are near, Lord, and all your ways are truth. From the beginning I have known,” etc. Augustine again comments here: “What the Greek says, καταρχὰς (*katarchás*), some of our translators rendered *ab initio* (‘from the beginning’), others *in initiis* (‘in beginnings’). Those who preferred the plural followed the Greek expression. In Latin, however, it is more customary to say *ab initio* or *initio* for what is said in Greek as καταρχὰς, which is apparently plural but functions adverbially,” etc. In the following verse the same manuscript has: “See my humiliation and redeem me, because,” etc. Then: “for the sake of your word give me life.” “Salvation is far from sinners, because they did not seek your justifications,” etc. Also: “Your mercies are many, Lord; according to your judgments give me life.” And, after one intervening verse: “I saw the faithless and wasted away, because they did not keep your words.” Augustine also approves this reading.]

[Col. 0358B] Coph. You are near, Lord, and all your commandments are truth.

Coph. From the beginning I understood concerning your testimonies that you founded them forever.

Res. See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law.

Res. Judge my judgment and redeem me; for the sake of your utterance give me life.

Res. Salvation is far from sinners, because they did not seek your justifications.

Res. Your mercies are exceedingly many, Lord; according to your judgment give me life.

Res. Many are those who persecute and afflict me; I did not turn aside from your testimonies.

Res. I saw those who did not keep the covenant and wasted away, [Col. 0358C] because they did not keep your utterances.

Res. See that I loved your commandments, Lord; in your mercy give me life.

Res. The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your justice are everlasting [Ms. *and everlasting*].

Sin. Princes persecuted me without cause, and my heart trembled at your words. [Note: [Col. 0358D] The Veronese manuscript has: “My heart trembled.” “I shall rejoice in your words,” etc. “I hated injustices,” etc. Also: “Seven times a day I shall praise you for your judgments,” etc. In the following verse it omits the name “Lord”; in the next it has “I sought” in place of “I loved.” Then: “My soul kept them,” etc., and “I loved them greatly,” in place of “it loved them,” which Saint Augustine testifies occurs in some manuscripts, with “my soul” understood. Finally: “because all my ways are before you, Lord.”]

[Col. 0360A] Sin. I shall rejoice over your utterances like one who finds abundant spoils.

Sin. I hated iniquity and abhorred it; but I loved your law.

Sin. Seven times a day I praised you for the judgments of your justice.

Sin. There is abundant peace for those who love your law, Lord, and there is no stumbling-block for them.

Sin. I awaited your salvation, Lord, and loved your commandments.

Sin. My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly.

Sin. I kept your commandments and your testimonies, because all my ways are before you, Lord.

Thav. Let my prayer draw near before you, [Col. 0359D] Lord; according to your utterance give me understanding. [Note: [Col. 0359D] The Veronese manuscript has: “Let my prayer draw near,” etc., “according to your utterance grant me understanding. Let my supplication enter before you, Lord; according to your word rescue me.” And after one intervening verse: “Let my tongue answer, Lord, your words, because all your commandments are justice. Let your hand be present to save me, because I chose your commandments.” At the end: “I have strayed like a lost sheep; give life to your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.” Augustine’s testimony must not be omitted here: “Some manuscripts do not have ‘seek,’ but ‘give life.’” For one syllable distinguishes the Greek words ζῆσον (*zēson*, “give life”) and ζήτησον (*zētēson*, “seek”), and the Greek manuscripts themselves vary.]

Thav. Let my supplication enter before you, Lord; according to your utterance rescue me.

Thav. My lips shall pour forth a hymn when you teach me your justifications.

Thav. My tongue shall proclaim your utterances, because all your commandments are equity.

Thav. Let your hand be present to save me, because I chose your commandments.

Thav. I desired your salvation, Lord, and your law is my meditation.

Thav. My soul shall live [Ms. *may it live*] and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.

Thav. I have strayed like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord, because I have not forgotten your commandments.

[Col. 0359]

[Col. 0359C] SONG OF ASCENTS.

When I was in distress, I cried to the Lord, and he heard me.

Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips [Note: [Col. 0359D] In the Palatine manuscript the obelus is placed with the conjunction itself and the conjunction is deleted, in accordance with Jerome’s view in his letter to Sunnia and Fretela, which you may consult.] ÷ and ** from a deceitful tongue.

When I was in distress, I cried to the Lord, and he heard me.

PSALM CXX.

[Col. 0361]

[Col. 0361A] SONG OF ASCENTS.

I lifted my eyes to the mountains; from where will my help come?

The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection at your right hand.

[Col. 0362A] SONG OF ASCENTS.

I lifted my eyes to the mountains; from where will my help come?

My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

May he not [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Veronese manuscript has: “May you not give [your foot] to be moved, nor may he who guards you sleep” (in place of “slumber”), almost agreeing with Augustine, as also in the repeated phrase “the Lord will guard you,” in place of “guards.”] let your foot be moved; may he who guards you not fall asleep.

[Col. 0362B] The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection at your right hand.

PSALM CXXI.

[Col. 0361]

[Col. 0361B] SONG OF ASCENTS.

I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: “We shall go into the house [Ms. *in the house*] of the Lord.”

Our feet were standing in your courts [Note: [Col. 0361D] The Palatine manuscript lacks the necessary asterisk. Immediately afterward it reads “For there” in place of “There”; finally, it attaches *Diapsalma* to the following verse.] + Jerusalem. **

[Col. 0361C] Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is united as one.

[Col. 0365]

[Col. 0365C] SONG OF ASCENTS.

[Col. 0366C] SONG OF ASCENTS.

Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.

You will eat the fruits of your labors; blessed are you, and it will be well with you. [Note: [Col. 0365D] The Veronese codex reads “the fruits of your labors.” If the many other indications that we have supplied in their proper places were lacking, I think this one reading would rightly suffice to establish that this is not the old version which the editor so often praised calls the Italic version. Jerome is an unimpeachable witness in Letter 34 of our recension to Marcella, no. 5: he says that the Latin books preferred “the fruits of your labors,” and that this widespread reading had caused interpreters before him great difficulty, especially Hilary of Poitiers. If this other reading, “the labors of your hands,” had finally become known to Hilary, it would have been easy for him to explain the passage suitably. Jerome says that Hilary, after considering various possibilities, asserted that the sense stood better if one wrote “to eat the fruits of labor,” rather than “the labors of fruits”; hence, he says, a spiritual interpretation should be sought. Entering upon a lengthy discussion on this occasion, Jerome employed as much labor in persuading his readers of what he wished them to understand as falsehood always requires in order to appear true. For in this passage it was not the translators of the Septuagint but the LATINS, deceived by the ambiguity of the Greek word, who interpreted *karpous* as “fruits” rather than “hands.” Yet *karpoi* can also mean “hands,” as does the Hebrew word written *chaphach*; and Symmachus and the Fifth Edition translated “your hands” in order to escape the ambiguity of the earlier wording. Thus the reading of the old Latin version was “the fruits of your labors,” not “the labors of your hands,” as Jerome later altered it. The rest of the Veronese manuscript agrees entirely with Augustine: “your wife like a fruitful vine,” and “your sons like young olive shoots,” and so forth. Finally, at the penultimate verse it has “the man will be blessed,” without *omnis*, “every.”]

Your wife will be like a flourishing vine within the sides of your house.

Your sons will be like young olive trees around your table.

Behold, thus will every man who fears the Lord be blessed.

[Col. 0368A] May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things that are in Jerusalem all the days of your life.

# PSALM 132

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371A] SONG OF ASCENTS, [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Palatine manuscript omits the name David together with the asterisk.] OF DAVID

Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one.

Like oil upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.

It descends upon the edge of his garment, like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion. [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Palatine manuscript has “upon the mouth,” as, we said, is also read in the Veronese. Nor should this be attributed to the copyist’s error. Although the Greek has ᾦαν, a word peculiar to the Septuagint in this passage and completely remote from the meaning “mouth,” it properly denotes, in their understanding, the fringe or border of a garment made from sheep’s wool. The corresponding Hebrew word, however, means “mouth” literally: “upon the mouth of his long garment,” as Scripture often speaks of garments. Jerome himself, in Letter 64 to Fabiola, no. 4, says that it denotes the upper part of the tunic with which the neck is clothed, left open, commonly called the *capitium*, “neck opening”: namely, the opening through which the head is inserted, which resembles a mouth and may appropriately be called the mouth of the garment.]

For there the Lord commanded blessing: [Note: [Col. 0372D] The same manuscript reads this incorrectly without the obelus.] [Col. 0371B] and life forever.

It also has “which descends upon Mount Zion,” and “For the Lord poured out for me,” instead of “there,” and so forth.]

And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, [Col. 0371D] against Pharaoh and all his servants.

[Col. 0373A] He struck many nations; he slew mighty kings:

Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan.

And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.

O Lord, your name is forever; O Lord, your memorial from generation to generation.

For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated on behalf of his servants.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.

They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see.

They have ears, but they will not hear; for there is no spirit in their mouth.

[lacuna]

[lacuna]

[lacuna]

Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them. [Note: [Col. 0373D] On the advice of the Palatine manuscript, we supplied the obelus, which had previously been missing, and the conjunction, in accordance with the Hebrew text.]

House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord.

House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.

Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.

[Col. 0372B] ALLELUIA.

Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants.

[Col. 0372C] You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.

Praise the Lord, for the Lord is gracious. [Note: [Col. 0372D] The Veronese manuscript has “for the Lord is good.” From this verse onward it reads, “For I know that the Lord is great, and our Lord above all gods.”]

Sing praises to his name, for it is sweet.

For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession.

For I know that the Lord is great, and our God is above all gods.

Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, [Note: [Col. 0372D] The Veronese manuscript has “in the sea and in all the abysses”; “raising up clouds from the end of the earth,” and so forth; “he who led forth the winds,” and so forth; finally, “he sent signs,” and so forth—almost always agreeing with Augustine, and often with him word for word.] in the sea and in the abysses.

And bringing clouds forth from the ends of the earth, he made lightning for the rain.

He brings forth winds from his treasuries; he struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast.

He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants.

[Col. 0374A] He struck many nations and slew mighty kings:

Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. [Note: [Col. 0373D] The Veronese manuscript omits the word “he slew,” which Augustine also seems to have retained. It then reads, “And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his servant. O Lord, your name is forever, your memorial from generation to generation. For the Lord judged his people,” and so forth, exactly as in Augustine. But it does not have the following three words, “they do not speak, they do not see, they do not hear,” contrary to what has often been noted by the editor praised above. It is known that the verses that follow have been brought here from the preceding Psalm 113; yet in them it reads “they will not touch” instead of “they will not feel,” and “in their throats” instead of “in their mouth.” Finally, again agreeing with Augustine: “Let all who make them become like them,” and at the end, “May the Lord bless you,” instead of “Blessed be the Lord.”]

And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.

O Lord, your name is forever; O Lord, your memorial is for age after age.

For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be consoled concerning his servants.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.

They have mouths, but they will not speak; they have eyes, but they will not see.

They have ears, but they will not hear; [Note: [Col. 0374D] The following verses have been transferred here in the Roman Psalter from the preceding Psalm 113. Thus, according to the will of the scribes, we have several kinds of mixture in the old Greek and Latin Vulgate. MART.] they have nostrils, but they will not smell.

[Col. 0374B] They have hands, but they will not feel; they have feet, but they will not walk.

They will not cry out with their throat; for there is no spirit in their mouth.

House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord.

You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord; blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.

[Col. 0378A] On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.

If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me.

May my tongue cling to my jaws, if I do not remember you.

If I do not set you, Jerusalem, at the beginning of my joy.

Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem.

Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.

Those who devised to trip up my steps—the proud—hid snares for me.

And they stretched ropes into a trap [Note: [Col. 0382D] Saint Jerome teaches that the words “for my feet” are superfluous here.] for my feet; beside the path they placed a stumbling-block for me. DIAPSALMA.

[Col. 0384A] The head of their circuit [Ms. “of theirs”]; the labor of their lips will cover them.

I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the needy and vengeance for the poor.

Nevertheless, the just will confess your name, and the upright will dwell before your face.

[Col. 0384A] A PSALM OF DAVID [Ms. *TO DAVID*].

Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to the voice of my prayer [Ms. “supplication”] when I cry to you.

Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.

[Col. 0384B] The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice.

With men who practice iniquity; I will not combine with their chosen company.

For my eyes are toward you, Lord, Lord; in you I have hoped. Do not take away my soul.

Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to [Note: [Col. 0385D] The same manuscript has “my supplication”; shortly afterward, “for no living heart will be justified before you.” Then again, in agreement with Augustine: “They placed me in darkness, and my spirit suffered weariness within me; my heart was troubled within me.” “I remembered the days,” and so forth, “I meditated on the works of your hands.” “I stretched out my hands,” [Col. 0386D] and so forth; “I thirsted for you like a waterless land,” instead of “a waterless land is to you.” I know that *thirsted* has also been read and explained appropriately by others instead of *to you*, and I willingly accept it. [Note: [Col. 0397C] Augustine says in his Exposition of Psalm 105: “There are very few manuscripts”—something I have found in none of the Greek copies that I was able to inspect—“that have Halleluia at the end of Psalm 150. See what we noted above from the same source concerning the end of Psalm 147. Since there is both space and permission on the page, I am pleased to append here, as a kind of concluding crown, the testimony of Berno, abbot of Reichenau, from a manuscript letter to Meginfrid preserved by Martène, On the Ancient Rites of the Church, book IV, chapter 3. The author flourished in the middle of the eleventh century. In that letter, speaking of Jerome, he explains more clearly than any other writer of the period the use of what he calls Jerome’s Gallican and Roman Versions. This testimony was not yet known to us when we prefixed the testimonies of other ancient writers to this double Psalter of Jerome. These are his exact words: “Among his other works, Jerome translated the Psalter from Greek into Latin from the corrected translation of the Seventy Interpreters, adding obeli and asterisks; and he gave it to all the churches of Gaul and to some churches of Germany to be sung. For this reason he called it the Gallican Psalter, while the Romans were still singing the Psalter from the corrupt Vulgate edition. From the latter the Romans composed their chant, and they handed down to us the practice of singing it. Hence it happened that the words which they sing in the manner of chant during the Day or Night Offices are mixed together and confusedly inserted into our Psalms, so that the less learned can scarcely discern what belongs to our edition and what to the Roman edition. The devout Father and learned teacher, observing this, combined three editions in one volume: in one column he arranged the Gallican Psalter, which we sing; in another, the Roman; and in the third, the Hebrew.” Compare now Walafrid Strabo, whom we cited among the ancient testimonies. Nor should you understand our Berno, with Martène, as saying that Jerome himself, then physically present, delivered the Psalter to the churches of Gaul and Germany. Rather, as the common saying goes, each person is said to have given what he authored: Jerome gave one translation to the Roman Church and another to the Gallican Church, because one pleased one church and the other the other. Saint Isidore of Seville further reports that Leander, his brother and predecessor in the see of that same church, composed prayers throughout the entire double Psalter, Roman and Gallican. Sigebert of Gembloux also testifies, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 84, concerning Einhard, that he too abbreviated the Gallican Psalter used by us Gauls, selecting from it all the verses containing words of prayer.”]

Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with lyre and harp.

[Col. 0399]

[OTHER PREFACES.]

ADMONITION OF J. MARTIANAEUS ON THE TWO FOLLOWING PREFACES OF SAINT JEROME.

Besides the volumes of Job and David already published by us, the remaining sacred books have perished—books that Jerome had most carefully corrected from the Greek and had given to students of his language, that is, to Latin readers, with obeli and asterisks added. Only two brief prefaces survive, which had been attached to the books of Chronicles and Solomon to explain what Jerome had accomplished in such translations from Greek into Latin. May God grant that those books meet the same fate as the volume of Job, which, except for its preface, had lain unpublished and in darkness down to our own time, but which we now rejoice has come to light complete and uncorrupted. We might hope the same for Chronicles and the works of Solomon, if there were more diligent investigators of Scripture willing to examine with immense labor the ancient monuments of the sacred Bible in the old archives and libraries of the churches. We therefore urge all learned readers again and again: if any manuscript codices of the sacred books are in their possession, let them not hesitate to compare them carefully with the published editions. From such comparison it is readily discovered whether Jerome’s Latin versions according to the Septuagint still survive, especially if the signs of obeli and asterisks occur within the sacred text. O happy would be our age if, after the publication of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, all the translations composed by Jerome from Greek could also be restored in their entirety! Let us therefore, all who are concerned for the public good, seek; perhaps the one who said, “Seek, and you will find,” will open treasures that are still hidden.

In the surviving preface to Chronicles, it should first be noted that Jerome corrected this book not from Greek copies but from the Hebrew. For, having taken as his assistant a renowned teacher of the Law among the Jews, he compared the entire volume of Chronicles with him from the first letter to the last. The book had been so corrupted through the carelessness of scribes in Greek and Latin copies that it contained not so much Hebrew names as certain barbarous and Sarmatian ones inserted into the text. It was therefore necessary to adhere to the Hebrew sources, where these names are found set out at distinct intervals and written with their syllables properly arranged.

It should also be observed that, although Jerome gathered testimonies from his various prefaces in order to blunt Rufinus’s criticism—by which that slanderer accused the holy Doctor of hostility toward the Seventy Interpreters—he nevertheless does not reproduce any part of this prologue in the later book of his Apology, at the end of which all the prefaces to the Old Testament are quoted. We do not yet know precisely why this happened, unless one may conjecture, with Erasmus, that Jerome did not speak from his own judgment when he said that the Seventy Interpreters were full of the Holy Spirit and that they had added much to the sacred books through the authority of the Holy Spirit. Rather, he attributed this opinion to his friends Domnio and Rogatianus, among whom copies of the Septuagint Interpreters perhaps carried such great weight.

Whatever may be thought of Erasmus’s conjecture, it is certain that in six hundred other passages Saint Jerome denies that the Greek version of the Seventy was produced under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. “For,” he says in the prologue to Genesis, “it is one thing to be a prophet, another to be an interpreter. In the one case the Spirit foretells what is to come; in the other, learning and command of language transfer what the interpreter understands.” And again: “In the same books the Holy Spirit arranged testimonies differently through the Seventy Interpreters and differently through the apostles, so that the latter may seem to have falsely claimed that what the former left unmentioned had been written.”

When he brought these arguments against Rufinus in the second book of his Apology, he could not repeat there the words of the subsequent preface to Chronicles in his own defense without immediately being accused of folly in the matter of the Seventy Interpreters, concerning whom he had written such contradictory and mutually conflicting things. He therefore wisely suppressed what he had formerly attributed to the opinion and expression of Domnio, for whom the authority of the Septuagint edition perhaps had the greatest force—while always preserving the honor of the Hebrew style, as did all the other ecclesiastical men of that period, who acknowledged the divine authority of both the Hebrew and the Greek books.

As for the prologue to the books of Solomon, Leander de Saint-Martin has already informed us that this preface was printed in all editions of the Ordinary Gloss, but that Erasmus and the bishop of Reatino omitted it from their collection of the works of Saint Jerome, although it is genuinely the work of that holy Doctor, as we can know from the subject, the opinions, and the manner of writing, which are entirely Jerome’s. Yet the final part of this prologue, manifestly spurious, imposed upon an otherwise highly learned man, who, while illuminating it with his own notes, attempts to attribute it to Saint Jerome. He could certainly have recognized the fraud from the incongruous sense produced by the words of the added section within this prologue. For they are in no way compatible with Jerome as author, as will become clear below in our scholia on this place in the aforementioned preface. We had promised in our notes to publish this brief preface at the end of the first part of the Divine Library; but, changing our plan later, we judged it preferable to place it at the end of this second part of the same Divine Library.

[Col. 0401]

[Note: [Col. 0401B] We said in the preface prefixed to this volume that, apart from the works of Jerome translated from Greek—Job and the Psalter, which we discussed earlier—nothing else remains from the Old Testament except this very preface to the book of Chronicles and the fragment of another preface to the books of Solomon that follows, since the translations of those books themselves were lost long ago amid the great ruin and destruction of his work. See what we discuss there on this subject.]

PREFACE OF JEROME TO THE BOOK OF CHRONICLES ACCORDING TO THE SEPTUAGINT INTERPRETERS.

[Col. 0401]

Eusebius Jerome [Note: [Col. 0401C] Not long afterward he gave the name Ezra to his translation from the Hebrew; yet, surprisingly, he makes no verbal mention of this preface in that letter. There are also several manuscript codices that prefix this prologue not to the Latin translation from the Greek Hexaplaric text, but to the other book of Chronicles translated according to the Hebrew truth. Indeed, in one manuscript praised by Martian, that of Saint Mary of the Gilded, a poorly informed copyist has written: “This prologue, namely, ‘Eusebius,’ etc., ought not to be in this place, but ought to be read and written at the beginning of the second book.” That is wholly false, as is clear from the entire context.] to Domnio and Rogatianus, his friends, greetings in Jesus.

[Col. 0401A] [Note: [Col. 0401C] The manuscript of the Bible belonging to Saint Mary of the Golden House, from which I cited some passages in the preceding prologues, contains this scholion, placed there by the same scribe who, if I remember correctly, copied the exemplar: “This Prologue, namely that of Eusebius, etc., ought not to stand here; rather, it should be read and written at the beginning of the second book.” Yet the writer of this annotation is mistaken, because this prologue [Col. 0401D] belongs to the Latin translation which Jerome published according to the Septuagint, with obeli and asterisks added—not to the second book of Chronicles, translated into Latin from the Hebrew source. Nevertheless, it is written at the beginning of that work in the manuscript Bible belonging to the most eminent Cardinal Bonzi. MART.] Just as those who have seen Athens understand Greek histories more fully, and those who have sailed through Virgil’s third book from the Troad by way of Leucas and the Acroceraunian mountains to Sicily, and from there to the mouths of the Tiber, understand it more clearly, so will he contemplate Sacred Scripture more lucidly who has viewed Judaea with his own eyes and has learned the memories of its ancient cities and the names of its places, whether unchanged or altered [Al. “have learned”]. For this reason I was concerned to undertake this labor with the most learned of the Hebrews, so that we might travel around the province whose name resounds throughout the whole Church of Christ.

For I confess, my dearest Domnion and Rogatian, that I have never trusted my own abilities in the divine books, nor regarded my own opinion as a teacher [Note: [Col. 0401D] All the manuscripts have this reading except the Carcassonne manuscript, which reads “mistress” instead of “master.” MART.] [Al. omits “master”]; rather, even concerning those things which I thought I knew, I was accustomed to ask questions, [Col. 0401B] and all the more concerning those about which I was uncertain. Finally, when you recently demanded by letter that I translate for you the book of Chronicles into the Latin language, I took as my guide a certain teacher of the Law [Note: [Col. 0401D] Several manuscripts read “once the author of the Law,” [Col. 0402B] or “the author.” We have followed the Saint-Germain manuscript no. 4 and the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Mary of the Golden House at Toulouse. One manuscript from our monastery at Narbonne reads, with the printed editions, “a certain learned teacher.” MART. —Martianus omitted the article τὸ before “book”; most printed editions supply it, and in truth it was either added by Jerome himself or at least the work was written as *Paralipomena*. In place of what follows, “once a teacher,” I would prefer to retain, with the earlier editions, “a certain teacher.” [Col. 0402C] Yet I see why Martianus preferred the adverb “once”: evidently, following Morinus, he thought that the Hebrew teacher whom Jerome used as his instructor, and whom he praises in Book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 2, was a Hebrew Christian. We have shown in the Life of the holy Doctor that this opinion, derived from that same testimony, is far removed from every appearance of truth.] who was held in admiration among the Hebrews. I compared the work with him from the beginning to the very last nail, as the saying goes, and thus reassured, I dared to do what you commanded.

I speak frankly to you: in both the Greek and Latin manuscripts this book of names is so corrupt that one might think that not Hebrew names, but a kind of barbarian and Sarmatian collection, has been heaped together [Al. “conjectured”]. This must not be attributed to the Seventy Translators, who, being filled with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0402C] Jerome does not seem to be speaking here from his own judgment, but from the received opinion of those whom he addresses, an opinion widely current at the time. Elsewhere, in almost entire pages of his works, he emphatically denies that the Seventy Translators were θεοπνεύστους (*theopneustous*), “inspired by God”; although here, again, at the end of the Prologue, he implies that they were not without the authority of the Holy Spirit.] translated what was true, but to the errors of the scribes, who, while copying from uncorrected texts, write what is uncorrected. Often, after removing syllables from the middle, they force three names into a single word; or, conversely, because of its length, divide one name into two or three words.

Moreover, the names themselves signify not, as many think [Al. “believe”], human beings, but cities, regions, forests, and provinces; and under their interpretation and figurative form [Note: [Col. 0402C] Here the Author seems unnecessarily to rise to an allegorical sense: because matters not contained in the books of Chronicles are nevertheless said to be praised from them, he introduces them indirectly under interpretation and figure. “If we admit this,” says the distinguished Huet, “everything will indeed be found in everything, and a great opening will be made for human inventions.”] certain histories are related. Concerning these it is said in the Book of Kings: “Are not these things written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?” Yet these matters are not found in our manuscripts.

This must first be known: among the Hebrews, the book of Chronicles is one book; among them it is called [Al. “called”] *Dabre Jamim*, that is, “Words of Days” [Note: [Col. 0402D] In the Memmian Canon these words were corruptly read in the first hand as *Jaomim* and *Jadomim*; some corrector changed this to *Ajomim*. Consult the preceding Galeated Prologue prefixed to the books of Samuel and Kings. MART.]. Because of its length, it has been divided among us, just as some do with Cicero’s dialogue *Brutus*, [Col. 0403A] cutting it into three parts, although it was published as one work by its author [Note: [Col. 0403A] Book II of *On Divination*, chapter 1. Thus there are three books of *On the Orator*, a fourth, *Brutus*, and a fifth, *The Orator*.]

Next, it must also be observed that the names frequently signify not human names or words, but, as I have said, the meanings of things. Finally, all the learning of the Scriptures is contained in this book [Al. omits “in this book”]; and the histories which have either been omitted in their proper places or touched upon only briefly are explained here through certain concise forms of expression. Thus, aided by your prayers, I have sent you a book that will please the well-disposed, though I do not doubt that it will displease the envious. [Note: [Col. 0403A] He repeats the same point in the Prologue to the Book of Psalms according to the Septuagint. There we were able to read “despise and envy,” as we have restored the text here, prompted by one manuscript of Silva Major and another from our monastery at Narbonne. MART.]

For, as Pliny says, most people prefer to despise and envy the best things [Note: [Col. 0403B] We discussed this saying of Pliny above, in the Prologue to the Book of Psalms, and elsewhere. In those places we showed from this very testimony that the true reading should be restored. In most printed editions, however, the word “envy” is lacking.] rather than [Col. 0404A] learn. If anyone wishes to criticize something in this translation, let him question the Hebrews, recall his own conscience, examine the order and texture of the wording, and then, if he can, disparage our labor.

Therefore, wherever you see asterisks—that is, star-shaped signs +—radiating through this volume, know that something has been added from [Note: [Col. 0403B] At the beginning of the Prologue the holy Father himself testified that he compared this book, with a teacher of the Law held in admiration among the Hebrews, from beginning, as they say, to the very last nail. For it was so corrupt not only in the Latin but also in the Greek manuscripts that it seemed to contain not so much Hebrew names as a heap of barbarian and Sarmatian names. This also makes it highly probable that the passages which he here says were added from the Hebrew under asterisks were translated into Latin from the authority and the very words of the original archetype. Such was the holy Translator’s particular diligence in rendering this book. In the other books, both those of this Greek version which survive and those which have been lost, I do not think he applied so much care and study; rather, whatever had originally been supplied under asterisks in the Greek text of the Hexapla which he had before him, he rendered the same into Latin. For at that time he had assigned himself this one task: to translate the Scriptures from Greek, not from Hebrew. See the Preface prefixed to this volume.] the Hebrew which is not found in the Latin manuscripts. But wherever an obelus, namely a transverse stroke ÷, has been placed before a passage, it indicates something which the Seventy Translators added, either for the sake of elegance or by the authority of the Holy Spirit, although it is not read in the Hebrew books.

[Col. 0403]

[Note: [Col. 0403C] This appears in the printed Bibles together with the *Glossa ordinaria*. Martianus, however, fashioned the title in this form. It seems to us rather to be a fragment of a Prologue, and one interpolated in several places with other words, so that it does not consistently display Jerome’s highly refined intellect and taste.] PROLOGUE OF JEROME TO THE BOOKS OF SOLOMON ACCORDING TO THE SEPTUAGINT TRANSLATORS.

[Col. 0403C] I have restored the three books of Solomon—that is, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—to the ancient authority of the Seventy Translators, either marking every superfluous passage with prefixed strokes, ÷, or inserting with stars + [Note: [Col. 0403D] The holy Father may have written “with little stars placed beforehand,” or something similar; from this some scribe may have produced the word “title,” which has no meaning here. Compare the preceding Prologues, in which he gives the same warning about asterisks.] what was lacking, so that more fully, [Note: [Col. 0403D] With notable fraud and audacity, the scribe of the Corbie manuscript no. 14 in the Saint-Germain library removed Paula and Eustochium from this Prologue. He did not want it to read “O Paula and Eustochium,” but “O dearest brothers.” We have said that the same envy of scribes expelled the most holy mother and her virgin daughter from the Prologue to Job above. This illness of mind is certainly very ancient: for in Jerome’s own time many people were displeased that he wrote to women about sacred matters. Thus, in his letter to the virgin Principia, he said: “I know, Principia, daughter in Christ, that many criticize me because I sometimes write to women and prefer the weaker sex to men; and therefore I must first answer my detractors.” A little later he adds: “If it was not shameful for the Apostle to be taught by a woman, why should it be shameful for me, after teaching men, to teach women as well?” and so forth. MART. —In place of the names “Paula and Eustochium,” the old Corbie manuscript, according to Martianus, has “dearest brothers.” Although I regard this as hardly genuine, the very title naming the holy women nevertheless raises a doubt: we know that elsewhere, too, scribes have inserted various names at will in these Prologues. To state my view once and for all, this Prologue often smells to me of scribal hands; nor does the phrase “with the most painstaking accuracy I corrected,” to give one example, seem to have proceeded from Jerome’s pen. The same is true of “I made it understood,” shortly afterward, and other expressions of the kind—things which can be noted by the sons of critics in this very brief composition.] O Paula and Eustochium, you may know what is lacking in our books and what is excessive.

I have also erased and corrected with the most painstaking accuracy those passages which unskilled translators had badly rendered into our language from the Greek. Wherever the light of the sentences had been taken away by a disorderly and perverse arrangement, I restored it to its proper places and made what had been obscure intelligible.

Moreover, in the book which most people title the Wisdom of Solomon, and in Ecclesiasticus, which everyone knows to be the work of Jesus son of Sirach, I restrained my pen, desiring only to correct the Canonical Scriptures for you and to commend my work by things certain rather than doubtful [Note: [Col. 0404D] Here the Prologue ends in the aforementioned Corbie manuscript. [Col. 0405C] In other manuscripts the following is added: “Therefore both Prefaces, from the Greek and from the Hebrew, have been placed at the beginning of this book, because certain passages from the Greek, for clarification of the sense and the edification of the reader, have either been inserted into the Hebrew translation or added from outside. And therefore, reader, whoever you are, always remember the stranger.” These are not Jerome’s words, but those of the person who inserted certain passages from the edition of the Seventy Translators into the holy Doctor’s Hebrew translation. For how could Jerome have placed both of his Prefaces to the books of Solomon at the beginning of his work and inserted certain passages into his Hebrew translation when no Preface or translation from the Hebrew yet existed? No learned person is unaware that the Latin version according to the Seventy Translators, together with Jerome’s Prefaces, was published several years before the holy man issued another translation for us from the Hebrew sources. It is therefore sheer fraud to say in the present Preface, which he placed before his translation according to the Seventy Translators, that both Prefaces had been placed there by him: the latter Preface from the Hebrew did not yet exist, nor did the Hebrew translation. MART.].

[Col. 0405]

APPENDIX TO THE SECOND PART OF THE DIVINE LIBRARY OF SAINT JEROME, CONTAINING THE BOOKS OF WISDOM, ECCLESIASTICUS, AND MACCABEES, ADDED FROM THE VULGATE EDITION TO COMPLETE THE WHOLE OF SCRIPTURE.

HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF WISDOM.

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0405A]

Love righteousness, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.

For he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who have faith in him.

For perverse thoughts separate people from God, but power when tested rebukes the foolish.

For wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sin.

For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, withdraw from thoughts without understanding, and be rebuked by the iniquity that overtakes it.

For the spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and he will not free the blasphemer from his lips. For God is the witness of his inmost parts, a true examiner of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue.

For the spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and this spirit, which contains all things, has knowledge of speech. [Note: [Col. 0406C] The Greek word *pneuma* (πνεῦμα), “spirit,” is neuter, whereas in Latin *spiritus* is masculine. The pronoun τοῦτο, which refers back to *pneuma*, ought therefore to have been rendered consistently in Latin by *hoc*, “this.”]

Therefore whoever speaks unjustly cannot remain hidden, nor will the avenging judgment pass him by.

For inquiry will be made into the thoughts of the ungodly, and the hearing of his words will come before God, for the correction of his iniquities.

For the ear of zeal hears everything, and the tumult of murmuring will not be concealed.

Therefore guard yourselves against murmuring, which is of no benefit, and refrain your tongue from slander, because an obscure utterance will not go in vain; but the mouth that lies kills the soul.

Do not be zealous for death through the error of your life, nor acquire destruction by the works of your hands.

For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction [Note: [Col. 0406C] Some books incorrectly read “of men”; the Greek *zōntōn*, “of the living,” contradicts this.] of the living.

For he created all things that they might exist, and he made the nations of the world capable of healing. There is no destructive poison in them, nor the kingdom of Hades on earth.

For righteousness is perpetual and immortal.

[Col. 0405C] But the ungodly summoned death by their hands and words; [Col. 0406A] considering it their friend, they wasted away and made a covenant with it, because they are worthy to belong to its portion.

CHAPTER TWO.

For they said, thinking wrongly within themselves: “Short and wearisome is the time of our life, and there is no relief at the end of a person, and no one is known to have returned from the underworld.

For we were born from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had never been; for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and reason is a spark that moves our heart.

When this has been extinguished, our body will be ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air. Our life will pass like the trace of a cloud and dissolve like a mist driven away by the rays of the sun and weighed down by its heat.

Our name will be forgotten in time, and no one will remember our works.

[Col. 0406B] For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our end, because it has been sealed and no one returns.

Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us quickly use created things as in youth.

Let us fill ourselves with precious wine and perfumes, and let no flower of the season pass us by.

Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let no meadow remain untouched by our luxury.

Let none of us be excluded from our luxury; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion, and this is our lot.

Let us oppress the poor righteous man and not spare the widow; let us not respect the gray hairs of the aged, long-tested by time.

Let our strength be the law of justice, for what is weak is found to be useless.

Let us therefore lie in wait for the righteous, because he is of no use to us, opposes our works, reproaches us for sins against the Law, and accuses us of sins against our discipline [Col. 0406C].

[Col. 0407A] He claims to possess knowledge of God and calls himself a son of God.

He has become a reproach to our thoughts.

He is burdensome even for us to look upon, because his life is unlike that of others, and his ways are changed.

We are regarded by him as worthless, and he avoids our ways as though they were impurities. He prefers the final destiny of the righteous and boasts that he has God as his father.

Let us see, then, whether his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him; thus we shall know what his end will be.

For if he is truly the son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies.

Let us question him with insult and torment, so that we may know his reverence and test his patience.

Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for, according to his words, he will receive protection.”

They thought these things, and they were deceived, for their wickedness blinded them.

They did not know the mysteries of God, nor hope for the reward of righteousness, nor judge the honor of holy souls.

For God created humanity for incorruption, and made it in the image of his own likeness.

But through the devil’s envy death entered the world.

Those who belong to him imitate him.

CHAPTER THREE.

But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death will not touch them.

In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to die, and their departure was regarded as an affliction.

Their going forth from us was thought to be destruction, but they are in peace.

And although they suffered torments before human beings, their hope is full of immortality.

[Col. 0407C] After being disciplined a little, they will receive great benefits, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself.

He tested them like gold in a furnace and received them as an offering of a burnt sacrifice; in due time they will be regarded with favor.

The righteous will shine, and they will run like sparks through stubble.

They will judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord will reign forever.

Those who trust in him will understand the truth, and the faithful will abide with him in love, because grace and peace are for his elect.

But the ungodly will receive correction according to their thoughts, because they neglected the righteous and withdrew from the Lord.

For unhappy is the one who rejects wisdom and discipline. Their hope is empty, their labors fruitless, and their works useless.

Their women are senseless, and their children are most wicked.

[Col. 0407D] Cursed is their offspring, for blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled and has not known a marriage-bed in sin: she will bear fruit when holy souls are examined.

And the eunuch who has not committed iniquity with his hands or conceived wicked thoughts against God will receive an elect gift of faith and a most acceptable portion in the temple of God.

For glorious is the fruit of good labors, and the root of wisdom does not perish.

[Col. 0408A] But the children of adulterers will come to nothing, and offspring from an unlawful marriage-bed will be destroyed.

Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing, and their old age at the end will be without honor.

And if they die sooner, they will have no hope, nor consolation on the day of judgment.

For the end of an unjust nation is dreadful.

CHAPTER FOUR.

O how beautiful is a chaste generation with glory! Its memory is immortal, because it is known both to God and to human beings.

When it is present, they imitate it; when it has departed, they desire it; and, crowned forever, it triumphs, winning the reward of undefiled contests.

But the multitude of the ungodly, though numerous, will be of no benefit, and illegitimate [Note: [Col. 0407D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II.12.18: “Hence also, because *moschos* (μόσχος; incorrectly *kochos* in the edition) means ‘calf’ in Greek, some people did not understand that *moscheumata* means ‘plantings,’ and translated it as ‘calves.’ This error has taken possession of so many manuscripts that it is scarcely possible to find it written otherwise; yet the meaning is completely clear, since it is made plain by the words that follow: ‘For adulterous plantings will not give roots,’ which is more suitable than ‘calves,’ which walk upon the earth with their feet and do not cling to roots.”] shoots will not send down deep roots nor establish a firm foundation.

Even if they put forth branches for a time, they will be shaken because they are weakly planted, and they will be uprooted by the violence of the winds.

For the branches, still unfinished [Note: [Col. 0408D] Some printed books incorrectly read “completed”; the Greek *atelestatoi* (ἀτελέστατοι) supports the present reading.], will be broken; their fruit will be useless, bitter to eat, and fit for nothing.

For children born of unlawful unions are witnesses against their parents’ wickedness when they are examined.

But the righteous, if death overtakes him, will be at rest.

For honorable old age is not measured by length of time or counted by number of years; a person’s understanding is gray hair.

And an unblemished life is the age of old age.

Having become pleasing to God, he was loved; and while living among sinners, he was taken away.

He was snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit mislead his soul.

For the fascination of frivolity obscures good things, and the instability of desire perverts a guileless mind.

[Col. 0408C] Having been perfected in a short time, he completed many years.

For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to lead him away from the midst of iniquities. But the peoples saw and did not understand, nor did they take such things to heart:

that grace and mercy are upon his holy ones, and that he watches over his elect.

But the dead righteous man condemns the living ungodly, and youth brought swiftly to completion condemns the long life of the unjust.

For they will see the end of the wise man and will not understand what the Lord intended for him or why he protected him.

They will see and despise him, but the Lord will mock them.

After this they will fall without honor and remain in disgrace among the dead forever, because he will shatter them, swollen with pride and voiceless; he will shake them from their foundations, and they will be utterly desolate. They will groan, and their memory will perish.

[Col. 0408D] Trembling, they will come to the remembrance of their sins, and their own iniquities will confront them and convict them.

CHAPTER FIVE.

Then the righteous will stand with great confidence before those who afflicted them and took away their labors.

When they see him, they will be shaken by dreadful fear and astonished at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation.

[Col. 0409A] Saying within themselves, repenting and groaning from anguish of spirit: “These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made an object of reproach.

We foolishly regarded their life as madness and their end as dishonorable.

See how they have been counted among the children of God, and how their lot is among the holy ones.

Therefore we went astray from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine for us, nor did the sun of understanding rise upon us.

We grew weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we traveled difficult paths, but we did not know the way of the Lord.

What did pride profit us? Or what did the boasting of riches contribute to us?

All those things passed like a shadow and like a messenger running by.

And like a ship crossing the surging water: when it has passed, no trace can be found, nor a track of its keel in the waves;

or like a bird flying through the air, of whose journey no sign is found, but only the sound of its wings beating the light wind; cutting the air by the force of its passage, it flew through with beating wings, and afterward no sign of its path is found;

or like an arrow shot at its appointed target: the divided air immediately closes back upon itself, so that its passage is unknown.

So we too, once born, immediately ceased to be; we were unable to show any sign of virtue, but were consumed in our wickedness.

Such things the sinners said in Hades.

For the hope of the ungodly is like down carried away by the wind, and like thin foam scattered by a storm, and like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest who passes by for a single day.

But the righteous live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and their care is with the Most High.

Therefore they will receive a kingdom of glory and a crown of beauty [Col. 0409C] from the hand of the Lord, because he will shelter them with his right hand and defend them with his holy arm.

He will take zeal as armor and arm creation for vengeance against his enemies.

He will put on righteousness as a breastplate and take sure judgment as a helmet.

He will take invincible equity as a shield.

He will sharpen his fierce wrath as a spear, and the whole world will fight with him against the senseless.

Straight bolts of lightning will go forth; like arrows from a well-bent bow, they will be shot from the clouds and strike their appointed place.

Hailstones, full of rock-hard fury, will be hurled; the water of the sea will blaze against them, and the rivers will converge violently.

Against them the spirit of strength will stand, and like a whirlwind it will divide them. Their iniquity will turn the whole earth into a desert, and wickedness will overturn the thrones of the powerful.

CHAPTER SIX.

Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man better than a strong man.

Therefore hear, O kings, and understand; learn, O judges of the ends of the earth.

Give ear, you who rule multitudes and take pride in crowds of nations.

For power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will question your works and examine your thoughts.

For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law [Al. “laws”] of justice, nor walk according to the will of God.

He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because a harsh judgment will be made against those who rule.

For mercy is granted to the lowly, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments.

For God will show partiality to no one, [Col. 0410A] nor will he fear anyone’s greatness, because he himself made small and great, and he cares equally for all.

But a more severe examination awaits the more powerful.

To you, therefore, O kings, are my words, so that you may learn wisdom and not fall away.

For those who keep what is just will be justified justly, and those who learn these things will find what they should answer.

Therefore desire my words, love them, and you will receive discipline.

Wisdom is radiant and never fades, and she is easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her.

She anticipates those who desire her, so that she may show herself to them first.

Whoever rises early for her will not labor, for he will find her sitting at his doors.

To think about her, therefore, is perfect understanding; and whoever keeps watch for her sake will soon be secure.

For she goes about seeking those worthy of her, and she shows herself to them cheerfully on their paths, meeting them in every providence.

For the beginning of her is the most genuine desire for discipline.

Therefore care for discipline is love, and love is the keeping of her laws; keeping the laws is the completion of incorruption.

And incorruption brings one near to God.

Thus the desire for wisdom leads to an everlasting kingdom.

Therefore, if you delight in thrones and scepters, O kings of peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever.

Love the light of wisdom, all you who rule over peoples.

Now I shall explain what wisdom is and how she came to be, and I shall not hide God’s mysteries from you. From the beginning of her birth I shall investigate her, bring her knowledge into the light, and not pass over the truth.

Nor shall I travel with envy wasting away, because such a person will not share in wisdom.

[Col. 0410C] The multitude of the wise is the salvation of the world, and a wise king is the stability of the people.

Therefore receive discipline through my words, and it will benefit you.

CHAPTER SEVEN.
