The nations in Gilead assembled against the Israelites who were within their borders, to destroy them, and they fled to the stronghold of Dathema.

They sent letters to Judas and his brothers, saying: “The nations around us have assembled against us to destroy us.

“They are preparing to come and capture the stronghold to which we have fled, and Timothy is the commander of their army.

“Therefore come now and rescue us from their hands, because many of us have fallen.

[Col. 0478B] “All our brothers who were in the region of Tubin have been killed. Their wives and children have been taken captive, their possessions plundered, and nearly a thousand men have been killed there.”

The letters were still being read when other messengers arrived from Galilee, their tunics torn, reporting the same things.

They said that forces from Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon had combined against them, and that all Galilee was filled with foreigners who intended to consume them.

When Judas and the people heard these reports, a great assembly gathered to consider what they should do for their brothers who were in distress and being attacked by them.

Judas said to his brother Simon: “Choose men for yourself, go, and rescue your brothers in Galilee. I and my brother Jonathan will go into Gilead.”

He left Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, commanders of the people, with the remaining army in Judea to guard it.

He commanded them, saying: “Be in charge of this people, [Col. 0478C] and do not engage in battle against the nations until we return.”

Three thousand men were assigned to Simon to go into Galilee, and eight thousand to Judas for Gilead.

Simon went into Galilee and fought many battles with the nations. The nations were crushed before him, and he pursued them as far as the gate of Ptolemais. Nearly three thousand men of the nations fell, and he took their spoils.

He gathered those who were in Galilee and in Arbata, with their wives, children, and all their possessions, and brought them into Judea with great joy.

Judas Maccabaeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan and traveled three days’ journey through the desert.

The Nabataeans met them, received them peacefully, and told them everything that had happened to their brothers in Gilead,

including that many of them had been captured in Bosor, Bosra, Alima, Casphor, Maked, and Carnaim; all these were fortified and great cities.

Moreover, captives were being held in the other cities of Gilead. They resolved on the following day to move the army against these cities, capture them, and remove their inhabitants all in one day.

Judas and his army suddenly turned by way of the desert toward Bosor and captured the city. He killed every male with the edge of the sword, took all their spoils, and burned it with fire.

They rose from there by night and traveled as far as the stronghold.

At dawn, when they lifted their eyes, behold, there was a great multitude beyond numbering, carrying ladders and machines, to capture the stronghold and assault them.

Judas saw that the battle had begun, and the battle cry rose to heaven like a trumpet, with a great cry from the city.

[Col. 0479A] He said to his army: “Fight today for your brothers.”

He came upon them in three divisions from behind, sounded the trumpets, and cried out in prayer.

The camp of Timothy recognized that he was Maccabaeus and fled before him. They struck them with a great blow, and nearly eight thousand men of them fell that day.

Judas turned aside to Mizpah, assaulted it, and captured it. He killed every male in it, took its spoils, and burned it with fire.

From there he went on and captured Casbon, Maked, Bosor, and the remaining cities of Gilead.

After these events Timothy gathered another army and encamped opposite Raphon, beyond the ravine.

Judas sent men to reconnoiter the army, and they reported to him: “All the nations around us have assembled to join him, a very large army.

“They have hired Arabs as auxiliaries and have encamped beyond the ravine, prepared to come against you for battle.” Judas went out to meet them.

Timothy said to the commanders of his army: “When Judas and his army approach the watercourse, if he crosses to us first, we shall not be able to withstand him, because he will be strong against us.

“But if he fears crossing and encamps beyond the river, we shall cross over to them, and we shall be able to stand against him.”

When Judas approached the watercourse, he stationed the scribes of the people beside the ravine and commanded them, saying: “Do not leave any man behind; let everyone come to battle.”

He crossed over to them first, and all the people followed him. All the nations were crushed before them, threw down their weapons, and fled to the temple that was in Carnaim.

He captured the city itself and burned the temple with fire, together with everyone who was in it. Carnaim was overcome and could not withstand Judas’s attack.

Judas gathered all the Israelites who were in Gilead, from the least to the greatest, together with their wives, children, and a very large army, to come into the land of Judah.

They came as far as Ephron. This was a large city situated at the entrance, very strongly fortified, and there was no way to turn either right or left, since the road passed through its midst.

Those who were in the city shut themselves in and blocked the gates with stones. Judas sent them a peaceful message,

saying: “Let us pass through your land so that we may go to our own land. No one will harm you; we shall pass through only on foot.” But they refused to open to them.

Judas ordered a proclamation to be made in the camp, so that each man should approach the place where he was stationed.

The men of valor advanced. They attacked the city all day and all night, and the city was delivered into his hand.

[Col. 0479D] They killed every male with the edge of the sword, uprooted the city, took its spoils, and passed through the entire city over the slain.

They crossed the Jordan in the great plain opposite Beth-shan.

Judas gathered the stragglers and encouraged the people all along the way until they came into the land of Judah.

They went up to Mount Zion with joy and gladness and offered burnt offerings because none of them had fallen, until they returned in peace.

While Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead and their brother Simon was in Galilee opposite Ptolemais,

Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, commanders [Al. commander] of the army, heard of the successful deeds and the battles that had been fought.

[Col. 0480A] They said: “Let us also make a name for ourselves and go to fight against the nations around us.”

They commanded those who were in their army, and they went toward Jamnia.

Gorgias came out of the city, and his men went out to meet them in battle.

Joseph and Azariah were routed as far as [Al. “to”] the borders of Judea. On that day about two thousand men of the people of Israel fell, and there was a great flight among the people,

because they had not listened to Judas and his brothers, imagining that they would act bravely.

They were not of the seed of those men through whom deliverance had been brought about in Israel.

The men of Judas became exceedingly renowned in the sight of all Israel and of all the nations wherever their name was heard.

They came to them, acclaiming them with good wishes.

Judas and his brothers went out and fought against the children of Esau in the land toward the south. He struck Hebron and its villages, burned its walls and its towers with fire all around,

and moved the camp to go into the land of the foreigners, traversing Samaria.

On that day priests fell in battle while attempting to act bravely, because they went out to battle without counsel.

Judas turned aside to Azotus in the land of the foreigners, demolished their altars, burned the carved images of their gods with fire, took the spoils of the cities, and returned to the land of Judah.

## CHAPTER VI

King Antiochus was traversing the upper regions when he heard that there was in Persia a city called Elymais, very renowned and rich in silver and gold.

It had an exceedingly wealthy temple, with golden hangings, breastplates, and shields left there by Alexander, [Col. 0480C] King Philip’s son, the Macedonian who first reigned in Greece.

He came and sought to capture and plunder the city, but he could not, because the matter became known to those who were in the city.

They rose up for battle, and he fled from there. He departed in great sadness and returned to Babylon.

A messenger came to him in Persia to report that the camps which had been in the land of Judah had been routed,

and that Lysias had gone forth at first with a powerful force but had been routed by the Jews, who had gained strength in weapons, power, and the many spoils they had taken from the camps that had been destroyed.

They had demolished the abomination which he had built upon the altar in Jerusalem, surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and likewise fortified their city Beth-zur.

When the king heard these reports, he was terrified and deeply shaken. He fell onto his bed and became ill from grief, because things had not happened as he had thought.

He remained there many days, for great grief had renewed itself within him, and he supposed that he was dying.

He called all his friends and said to them: “Sleep has departed from my eyes; I am crushed and have collapsed in heart from anxiety.

“And I said in my heart: Into what distress have I come, and into what waves of sorrow am I now plunged? I was cheerful and honored in my power.

“But now I remember the evils that I did in Jerusalem, from which I also took away all the golden and silver spoils that were in it, and I sent orders to remove the inhabitants of Judea without cause.

“Therefore I know that these evils have found me because of this. And behold, I am perishing in great grief in a foreign land.”

He called Philip, one of his friends, and placed him over his entire kingdom.

[Col. 0481A] He gave him his diadem, his robe, and his ring, so that he might bring up his son Antiochus, raise him, and have him reign.

King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year.

Lysias learned that the king had died and appointed his son Antiochus to reign—the youth whom he had raised—and he called him Eupator [Al. Eupator].

Those who were in the citadel had enclosed Israel around the holy places. They were continually seeking evil against them and were a stronghold of the nations.

Judas resolved to destroy them and summoned the entire people to besiege them.

They assembled together, besieged them in the one hundred and fiftieth year, and made ballistae and siege machines.

Some of those who were besieged came out and joined them—certain impious men from Israel.

They went to the king and said: “How long will you refrain from passing judgment and avenging our brothers?

“We resolved to serve your father, walk according to his commands, and obey his edicts.

“Because of this, the children of our people separated themselves from us, and whoever among us was found was killed, and our inheritances were plundered.

“They have not merely stretched out their hand against us, but against all our borders as well.

“And behold, today they have approached the citadel of Jerusalem to seize it, and they have fortified Beth-zur.

“Unless you forestall them quickly, they will do worse things than these, and you will not be able to overcome them.”

When the king heard this, he became angry. He summoned all his friends, the commanders of his army, and those in charge of the cavalry.

Armies of mercenaries also came to him from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.

His army numbered one hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for battle.

[Col. 0481C] They came through Idumea, approached Beth-zur, and fought for many days. They made siege machines, and the defenders came out and burned them with fire, and fought bravely.

Judas withdrew from the citadel and moved the camp to Beth-zechariah, opposite the king’s camp.

The king rose before daylight and drove the armies forward in an assault along the road to Beth-zechariah. The armies drew up for battle, and the trumpets sounded.

They showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries to sharpen them for battle.

They divided the beasts among the legions. Beside each elephant stood one thousand men in linked breastplates, with bronze helmets on their heads, and five hundred chosen cavalrymen were assigned to each beast.

These were stationed beforehand wherever the beast was; wherever it went, they went, and they did not leave it.

There were also strong wooden towers over them, protecting each beast, with siege engines upon them; and over [Col. 0481D] each were thirty-two men of valor who fought from above, together with an Indian elephant-driver.

He stationed the remaining cavalry on either side, so as to stir up the army with the crowds and press upon those packed together in its legions.

When the sun shone upon the golden and bronze shields, the mountains gleamed from them and shone like lamps of fire.

One division of the king’s army was arranged along the high mountains and another in the low places, and they advanced cautiously and in good order.

All the inhabitants of the land were shaken by the sound of the multitude, the movement of the crowd, and the clash of weapons. For the army was exceedingly large and strong.

Judas and his army drew near for battle, and six hundred men of the king’s army fell.

Eleazar son of Saura saw one of the beasts armored with the king’s armor. It towered above the other beasts, and he supposed that the king was upon it.

[Col. 0482A] He offered himself to save his people and acquire an everlasting name.

He ran boldly toward it in the midst of the legion, killing on the right and on the left, and they fell around him on every side.

He went beneath the elephant’s feet, thrust himself under it, killed it, and fell to the ground upon it; and he died there.

When they saw the king’s strength and the attack of his army, they turned away from them.

The king’s camps went up against them toward Jerusalem, and the king’s camps [Al. “approached”] approached Judea and Mount Zion.

He made peace with those who were in Beth-zur, and they came out of the city because they had no provisions while they were shut in, since it was the sabbatical year for the land.

The king captured Beth-zur and stationed a garrison there to guard it.

He turned the camp toward the sanctuary and remained there many days. [Col. 0482B] He stationed ballistae, siege machines, fire-projectors, stone-throwing engines, darts, scorpions for shooting arrows, and slings.

They too made machines against his machines and fought for many days.

There was no food in the city, because it was the seventh year, and those of the foreigners who remained in Judea had consumed the reserves that had been stored.

Only a few men remained in the holy places, because famine had overcome them, and they dispersed, each to his own place.

Lysias heard that Philip, whom King Antiochus had appointed while he was still alive to raise Antiochus his son and reign,

had returned from Persia and Media with the army that had gone with him, and that he was seeking to take over the affairs of the kingdom.

He hastened to go and speak to the king and the commanders of the army: “We are daily growing weak, our food is scant, and the place that we are besieging is fortified; moreover, it is incumbent upon us to make arrangements concerning the kingdom.

“Now therefore let us give these men our right hands, make peace with them and with all their nation,

“and establish for them that they may walk according to their ordinances as before. For they are angry because of their ordinances, which we disregarded, and they have done all these things.”

The proposal pleased the king and the commanders, and he sent to them to make peace; and they accepted it.

The king and the commanders swore an oath to them, and they came out of the fortress.

The king entered Mount Zion and saw the fortification of the place. Then he quickly broke the oath that he had sworn and ordered the surrounding wall to be demolished.

He departed in haste and returned to Antioch. There he found Philip ruling the city, fought against him, and took possession of the city.

## CHAPTER VII

In the one hundred and fifty-first year, Demetrius son of Seleucus went out from the city of Rome and came with a few men to a coastal city, and reigned there.

And when he entered the house of the kingdom of his fathers, the army seized Antiochus and Lysias in order to bring them to him.

When the matter became known to him, he said: “Do not show me their faces.”

And the army killed them. Demetrius then sat upon the throne of his kingdom.

Wicked and impious men from Israel came to him, with Alcimus as their leader, who wished to become a priest.

They accused the people before the king, saying: “Judas and his brothers have destroyed all your friends, and he has driven us from our land.

“Now therefore send a man whom you trust, so that he may go and see all the destruction that he has inflicted upon us and upon the king’s territories, and punish all his friends and their supporters.”

The king chose Bacchides from among his friends. He ruled beyond the great river in the kingdom and was faithful to the king; and he sent him

to see the destruction that Judas had caused. He also appointed the impious Alcimus to the priesthood and ordered him to take vengeance on the children of Israel.

They rose and came with a large army into the land of Judah. They sent messengers and spoke deceitfully to Judas and his brothers with peaceful words.

They paid no attention to their words, for they saw that they had come with a large army.

A gathering of scribes came to Alcimus and Bacchides to seek what was right.

The first among the Hasideans, who were among the children of Israel and were seeking peace from them, also came.

For they said: “A priest descended from Aaron has come; he will not deceive us.”

He spoke peaceful words to them and swore to them, saying: “We will do you no harm, nor your friends.”

They believed him. But he seized sixty of them and killed them in one day, according to the word that is written:

“They poured out the flesh of your holy ones  
and their blood around Jerusalem,  
and there was no one to bury them.”

Fear and trembling fell upon all the people, for they said: “There is no truth or justice in them. They have violated the agreement and the oath that they swore.”

Bacchides moved the camp from Jerusalem and pitched it at Bethzecha. He sent men to seize many of those who had fled from him; he slaughtered some of the people and threw them into a great well.

He entrusted the region to Alcimus and left an auxiliary force with him for his support. Then Bacchides went to the king.

Alcimus was exerting himself vigorously to establish his high-priestly authority.

All those who were disturbing their people gathered around him. They took possession of the land of Judah and inflicted a great slaughter in Israel.

Judas saw all the evils that Alcimus and those who were with him were doing to the children of Israel [variant: “the sons of Israel”]—far more than the nations had done.

He went out into all the surrounding districts of Judea and took vengeance on the deserters, and they ceased from then on to enter the region.

When Alcimus saw that Judas and those who were with him were prevailing, he realized that he could not withstand them. He returned to the king and accused them of many crimes.

The king sent Nicanor, one of his more distinguished commanders, who was hostile to Israel, and ordered him to destroy the people.

Nicanor came to Jerusalem with a large army and sent to Judas and his brothers deceitful, peaceful words, saying:

“Let there be no battle between me and you. I will come with a few men, so that I may see your faces in peace.”

He came to Judas, and they greeted one another peacefully; but the enemies were prepared to seize Judas.

The report reached Judas that they had come to him deceitfully, and he was terrified of him and no longer wished to see his face.

Nicanor realized that his plot had been exposed. He went out to meet Judas in battle near Capharsalama.

Nearly five thousand men of Nicanor’s army fell, and the rest fled into the City of David.

After these events Nicanor went up to Mount Zion. Some of the priests of the people came out to greet him peacefully and to show him the burnt offerings that were being offered for the king.

But he mocked them, rejected them, and profaned them; and he spoke arrogantly.

In anger he swore, saying: “Unless Judas and his army are delivered into my hands, then, when I return in peace, I will burn this house.” And he departed in great anger.

The priests entered and stood before the altar and the Temple, weeping, and said:

“You, Lord, chose this house for the invocation of your name in it, so that it might be a house of prayer and supplication for your people.

“Take vengeance on this man and his army, and let them fall by the sword. Remember their blasphemies, and do not allow them to endure.”

Nicanor departed from Jerusalem and pitched his camp at Beth-horon, and the Syrian army met him.

Judas pitched his camp at Adasa with three thousand men. Judas prayed and said:

“Lord, when those who were sent by King Sennacherib blasphemed you, your angel went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand of them.

“So crush this army before us today, so that the rest may know that he has spoken wickedly against your holy things; and judge him according to his wickedness.”

The armies joined battle on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar. Nicanor’s camp was crushed, and he himself fell first in the battle.

When his army saw that Nicanor had fallen, they threw down their weapons and fled.

They pursued them for a day’s journey, from Adazer until one comes to Gazara, and they sounded the trumpets after them with signals.

Then men came out from all the surrounding strongholds of Judea. They harassed them from the flanks and turned back against them, and all fell by the sword; not one of them was left.

They took their spoils as plunder, cut off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had stretched out arrogantly, brought them, and hung them opposite Jerusalem.

The people rejoiced greatly and celebrated that day with great gladness.

They decreed that this day should be observed every year, on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar.

And the land of Judah was quiet for a few days.

## CHAPTER VIII

Judas heard of the fame of the Romans: that they were powerful in strength and accepted whatever was requested of them; and that whoever approached them, they established friendship with them, for they were powerful in strength.

They heard of their battles and the valorous deeds that they had performed in Galatia, how they had conquered them and brought them under tribute;

and of all that they had done in the region of Spain, and how they had brought under their control the mines of silver and gold that were there, and had gained possession of the whole region through their strategy and perseverance.

They heard how they had crushed and struck with a great blow the places that were very far from them, and the kings who had come against them from the ends of the earth; while the others paid them tribute every year.

They had crushed in war Philip and Perseus, king of the Ceteans, and the others who had taken up arms against them, and had conquered them.

They had also crushed Antiochus, the great king of Asia, who had brought war against them with one hundred and twenty elephants, cavalry, chariots, and a very great army.

They had captured him alive and imposed upon him that he and those who would reign after him should pay a large tribute, give hostages, and comply with the agreed terms.

They had taken from him the region of the Indians, Media, and Lydia, some of his finest regions, and had given them to King Eumenes.

When those who were in Hellas wished to go and destroy them, the matter became known to the Romans.

They sent one of their commanders against them. They fought them, many of them fell, and their wives and children were taken captive. They plundered them, took possession of their land, destroyed their walls, and reduced them to slavery, down to the present day.

They destroyed the remaining kingdoms and islands that had at any time resisted them and brought them under their authority.

With their friends, and with those who found security among them, they preserved [variant: “and preserved”] friendship and conquered kingdoms both near and far. For whoever heard their name was afraid of them.

Those whom they wished to assist in becoming kings did reign; and those whom they wished, they drove from their kingdom. Thus they were exalted.

In all these matters no one wore a diadem, nor did anyone put on purple in order to be glorified by it.

They had established a senate for themselves, and every day three hundred and twenty men deliberated, always taking counsel concerning the multitude, so that they might do what was worthy.

Each year they entrusted their magistracy to one man, who ruled over all their land; all obeyed the one man, and there was among them neither envy nor jealousy.

Judas chose Eupolemus son of John, son of Jacob, and Jason son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to establish friendship and an alliance with the Romans,

and to remove from them the yoke of the Greeks, for they had seen that the kingdom of Israel was being pressed into slavery.

They traveled a very long road to Rome, entered the senate, and said:

“Judas Maccabaeus, his brothers, and the people of the Jews have sent us to establish an alliance and peace with you, and to enroll ourselves as your allies and friends.”

The proposal pleased them.

This is the document that they wrote on bronze tablets and sent to Jerusalem, so that it might remain there among them as a memorial of peace and alliance:

“May it be well with the Romans and the nation of the Jews, at sea and on land, forever; and may sword and enemy be far from them.

“But if war first arises against the Romans or any of their allies throughout all their dominion,

the nation of the Jews shall provide assistance to them wholeheartedly, as circumstances dictate.

“To those who are fighting, they shall neither give nor supply grain, weapons, money, or ships, as was pleasing to the Romans; and they shall observe their commands without receiving anything from them.

“Likewise, if war first arises against the nation of the Jews, the Romans shall assist them wholeheartedly, as circumstances permit.

“To those who assist them, grain, weapons, money, or ships shall not be given, as was pleasing to the Romans; and they shall observe their commands without deceit.

“In accordance with these words the Romans made an agreement with the people of the Jews.

“But if either party should later wish to add or remove anything from these provisions, they shall do so according to their own decision; and whatever they add or remove shall be valid.

“Moreover, concerning the evils that King Demetrius has done to them, we have written to him, saying: ‘Why have you imposed your yoke upon our friends and allies, the Jews?

“‘If therefore they again come to us against you, we shall render them justice and fight with you by sea and land.’”

## CHAPTER IX

Meanwhile, when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, he decided to send Bacchides and Alcimus once more into Judea, together with the right wing.

They traveled by the road that leads to Galgala and pitched their camp at Masaloth, which is in Arbella. They captured it and killed many people.

In the first month of the one hundred and fifty-second year, they brought the army up against Jerusalem.

They rose and went to Berea with twenty thousand men and two thousand cavalry.

Judas had pitched his camp at Laisa, with three thousand chosen men beside him.

When they saw the multitude of the army, because it was large, they were greatly afraid. Many withdrew from the camp, and only eight hundred men remained.

Judas saw that his army had dwindled and that the battle was pressing upon him, and he was brokenhearted, for he had no time to gather them; and he was disheartened.

He said to those who remained: “Let us rise and go against our adversaries, if perhaps we are able to fight them.”

They tried to dissuade him, saying: “We shall not be able to do so. Let us save our lives for now, return to our kinsmen, and then fight against them; but we are few.”

Judas said: “Far be it from us to do this—to flee from them. If our time has come, let us die bravely for our brothers and not bring disgrace upon our glory.”

The army moved out from the camp and stood opposite them. The cavalry was divided into two parts; slingers and archers went before the army, and all the champions of the first engagement were in front.

Bacchides was on the right wing. The legion advanced from both sides, and they sounded the trumpets.

Those who were with Judas also shouted, and the earth shook at the voice of the armies. Battle was joined from morning until evening.

Judas saw that the stronger part of Bacchides’ army was on the right, and all the steadfast men of heart gathered around him.

They crushed the right wing, and he pursued them as far as Mount Azoli.

Those who were on the left wing saw that the right wing had been crushed, and they followed Judas and those who were with him from behind.

The battle grew fierce, and many wounded men fell [variant: “were killed”] from both sides.

Judas fell, and the rest fled.

Jonathan and Simon took up Judas their brother and buried him in the tomb of his ancestors in the city of Modin.

All the people of Israel mourned him with great lamentation and grieved for many days.

They said: “How has the mighty man fallen, who saved the people of Israel?”

The rest of the accounts of Judas’s wars, the valorous deeds that he performed, and his greatness have not been written down, for they were exceedingly numerous.

After Judas’s death, wicked men arose throughout all the territories of Israel, and all who practiced iniquity emerged.

In those days there was a very great famine, and the whole region, together with its inhabitants, surrendered to Bacchides.

Bacchides chose impious men and appointed them as rulers of the region.

They sought out and investigated Judas’s friends, brought them to Bacchides, and he took vengeance on them and mocked them.

Great tribulation arose in Israel, such as had not occurred since the day when no prophet was seen in Israel.

All Judas’s friends gathered together and said to Jonathan:

“Since your brother Judas died, there is no man like him to go out against our enemies—Bacchides and those who are hostile to our nation.

“Now therefore, today, we have chosen you to take his place as our prince and commander, to fight our battle.”

At that time Jonathan assumed the leadership and rose up in the place of his brother Judas.

Bacchides learned of it and sought to kill him.

Jonathan, his brother Simon, and all who were with him learned of it and fled into the wilderness of Tekoa. They settled beside the water of the lake Asphar.

Bacchides learned of it, and on the Sabbath he came with his entire army across the Jordan.

Jonathan sent his brother, the commander of the people, and asked his friends, the Nabateans, to lend them their equipment, which was plentiful.

The sons of Jambri came out from Madaba, seized John and everything that he had, and departed with it.

After these events Jonathan and his brother Simon were informed that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a great wedding and were bringing a bride from Madaba, the daughter of one of the great leaders of Canaan, with great pomp.

They remembered the blood of their brother John. They went up and hid themselves under the shelter of the mountain.

They raised their eyes and saw—and behold, there was a tumult and a great display. The bridegroom came forth, together with his friends and brothers, to meet them [variant: “him”] with tambourines, musicians, and many weapons.

They rose against them from ambush, killed them, and many wounded fell. The rest fled into the mountains, and they took all their spoils.

The wedding was turned into mourning, and the sound of their musicians into lamentation.

They took vengeance for the blood of their brother and returned to the bank of the Jordan.

Bacchides heard of it and came on the Sabbath as far as the bank of the Jordan with a great force.

Jonathan said to his men: “Let us rise and fight against our enemies, for today is not like yesterday or the day before.

“For behold, battle is before us; the water of the Jordan is on this side and that, with banks, marshes, and thickets, and there is no place to turn aside.

“Now therefore cry out to heaven, so that you may be delivered from the hand of your enemies.”

And battle was joined.

Jonathan stretched out his hand to strike Bacchides, but he turned back from him.

Jonathan and those who were with him leapt into the Jordan and swam across the Jordan to them.

One thousand men from Bacchides’ side fell that day. And they returned to Jerusalem.

They built fortified cities in Judea: the stronghold in Jericho, Ammaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Thamnata, Phara, and Thopo, with high walls, gates, and bars.

He placed garrisons in them to wage war against Israel.

He fortified Bethsura, Gazara, and the citadel, and placed auxiliary forces and supplies of food in them.

He took the sons of the leaders of the region as hostages and placed them in the citadel in Jerusalem under guard.

In the one hundred and fifty-third year, in the second month, Alcimus ordered the walls of the inner court of the holy house to be demolished, as well as the works of the prophets; and he began to demolish them.

At that time Alcimus was struck down, his works were obstructed, his mouth was closed, and he was paralyzed. He could no longer speak a word or give orders concerning his household.

Alcimus died at that time in great torment.

When Bacchides saw that Alcimus had died, he returned to the king, and the land was quiet for two years.

All the wicked men deliberated, saying: “Behold, Jonathan and those who are with him dwell securely in silence. Now therefore let us bring Bacchides, and he will seize them all in one night.”

They went and gave him this advice.

He rose in order to come with a large army and secretly sent letters to his associates who were in Judea, so that they might seize Jonathan and those who were with him. But they could not, because their plot became known to them.

He seized fifty men from the region who were military leaders and killed them.

Jonathan, Simon, and those who were with them withdrew to Bethbessen, which is in the wilderness. They rebuilt its ruins and fortified it.

Bacchides learned of it and gathered his entire multitude. He informed those who were from Judea.

He came and pitched his camp above Bethbessen. He besieged it for many days and constructed siege engines.

Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city, went out into the region, and came with a force.

He struck Odaren, his brothers, and the sons of Phaseron in their tents. He began to slaughter them and to increase in valor.

Simon and those who were with him came out of the city and burned the siege engines.

They fought against Bacchides, and he was crushed by them. They afflicted him greatly, because his plan and his engagement had come to nothing.

In anger against the wicked men who had advised him to come into their region, he killed many of them. He himself then considered departing with the rest to his own land.

Jonathan learned of this and sent envoys to him to arrange peace with him and to return his captives.

Bacchides willingly accepted, acted according to his words, and swore that he would do him no harm all the days of his life.

He returned to him the captives whom he had previously taken as plunder from the land of Judah. Then he turned and went to his own land and did not come again into its territories.

The sword ceased from Israel. Jonathan dwelt at Michmash and began there to judge the people; and he exterminated the impious from Israel.

## CHAPTER X

In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander son of Antiochus, who was called the Noble, went up and took Ptolemais; they received him, and he reigned there.

King Demetrius heard of it, gathered a very large army, and went out to meet him in battle.

Demetrius sent Jonathan a letter in peaceful terms, in order to exalt him.

For he said: “Let us anticipate making peace with him before he makes peace with Alexander against us.

“For he will remember all the evils that we did to him, his brother, and his nation.”

He gave him authority to gather an army, manufacture weapons, and be his ally; and he ordered the hostages who were in the citadel to be handed over to him.

Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters in the hearing of all the people and of those who were in the citadel.

They were greatly afraid, because they heard that the king had given him authority to gather an army.

The hostages were handed over to Jonathan, and he returned them to their parents.

Jonathan dwelt in Jerusalem and began to build and renew the city.

He told the workers to build walls and to fortify Mount Zion all around with squared stones; and so they did.

The foreigners who were in the fortresses that Bacchides had built fled.

Each one abandoned his place and went to his own land.

Only in Bethsura did some of those who had abandoned the law and the commandments of God remain, for it was a refuge for them.

King Alexander heard of the promises that Demetrius had made to Jonathan. They told him of the battles and valorous deeds that he and his brothers had performed, and of the hardships that they had endured.

He said: “Can we find any man like this? Now therefore let us make him our friend and ally.”

He wrote a letter and sent it to him in these words:

“King Alexander sends greetings to his brother Jonathan.

“We have heard about you, that you are a man powerful in strength and suited to be our friend.

“Now we appoint you today high priest of your nation, and you shall be called the king’s friend”—and he sent him a purple robe and a golden crown—“and you shall share our concerns with us and maintain friendship with us.”

Jonathan put on the holy vestment in the seventh month, in the one hundred and sixtieth year, on the solemn day of the Feast of Booths. He gathered an army and prepared abundant weapons.

Demetrius heard these words, was exceedingly grieved, and said:

“What have we done, that Alexander has forestalled us in securing the friendship of the Jews for his own protection?

“I too will write them words of entreaty, dignities, and gifts, so that they may be with me as support.”

He wrote to them in these words:

“King Demetrius sends greetings to the nation of the Jews.

“Because you have kept faith with us, remained in our friendship, and have not joined our enemies, we have heard of this and rejoiced.

“Now continue to preserve your faithfulness toward us, and we shall repay you with good things for what you have done with us.

“We shall remit many payments to you and grant you gifts.

“Now I release you and all the Jews from tribute, and I remit the price of salt, the crown taxes, and the third of the seed.

“From this day forward I leave to you half the produce of the trees that belong to my portion, so that it may not be collected from the land of Judah and from the three cities that have been added to it from Samaria and Galilee, from this day and for all time.

“Let Jerusalem be holy and free, together with its territories, and let its tithes and taxes belong to it.

“I also remit authority over the citadel that is in Jerusalem and give it to the high priest, so that he may appoint in it whatever men he chooses to guard it.

“Every Jewish person who is held captive anywhere in my kingdom and is from the land of Judah I leave free without payment, so that all may be released from tribute, including the tribute on their livestock.

“All festival days, Sabbaths, new moons, appointed days, the three days before a festival, and the three days after a festival shall be days of immunity and remission for all Jews who are in my kingdom.

“No one shall have authority to bring any action or raise any matter against any of them for any reason.

“Up to thirty thousand Jewish men shall be enrolled in the king’s army, and provisions shall be given to them as is proper for all the king’s armies. From among them men shall be appointed to serve in the fortresses of the great king.

“From among them officers shall be appointed over the affairs of the kingdom that are conducted in good faith, and leaders shall be appointed from among them. They shall walk according to their laws, as the king commanded in the land of Judah.

“The three cities that have been added to Judea from the region of Samaria shall be reckoned with Judea, so that they may be under one authority and obey no foreign power except that of the high priest.

“Ptolemais and its territory, which I have given as a gift to the holy ones who are in Jerusalem for the necessary expenses of the sanctuary,

“and I grant each year fifteen thousand shekels of silver from the king’s revenues that are assigned to me.

“Whatever remains unpaid by those who were in charge of the affairs in previous years [variant omits “in”] shall from now on be paid toward the work of the Temple.

“In addition to this, the five thousand shekels of silver that they received each year from the sanctuary’s account shall belong to the priests who perform the ministry.

“Anyone who flees for refuge to the Temple that is in Jerusalem or anywhere within its territory shall be released from liability to the king in every matter, and they shall freely possess everything that they have in my kingdom.

“For building or restoring the works of the sanctuary, expenses shall be provided from the king’s account.

“For building the walls in Jerusalem [variant omits “in”] and fortifying them all around, expenses shall be provided from the king’s account, as also for building walls in Judea.”

When Jonathan and the people heard these words, they did not believe them or accept them, for they remembered the great wickedness that he had committed in Israel and how severely he had afflicted them.

They preferred Alexander, because he had been a prince of peaceful words to them, and they had supported him at all times.

King Alexander gathered a large army and brought his camp against Demetrius.

The two kings joined battle. Demetrius’s army fled, and Alexander pursued it and pressed upon them.

The battle became exceedingly fierce until sunset, and Demetrius fell that day.

Alexander sent envoys to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, with this message:

“Since I have returned to my kingdom, sat upon the throne of my fathers, obtained the leadership, crushed Demetrius, and taken possession of our country;

“since I fought against him, he was crushed, his camp by us, and we have sat upon the throne of his kingdom,

“now let us establish friendship with one another. Give me your daughter as a wife, and I shall be your son-in-law; I shall give you gifts, and gifts worthy of you to her.”

King Ptolemy replied, saying: “Blessed is the day on which you returned to the land of your fathers and sat upon the throne of their kingdom.

“Now I will do for you what you have written. But meet me at Ptolemais, so that we may see one another and I may betroth her to you as you have said.”

Ptolemy departed from Egypt, he and his daughter Cleopatra, and came to Ptolemais in the one hundred and sixty-second year.

King Alexander met him, gave him his daughter Cleopatra, and celebrated her wedding at Ptolemais, with royal splendor and great glory.

King Alexander wrote to Jonathan, asking him to come and meet him.

Jonathan went to Ptolemais in glory, met the two kings there, gave them much silver, gold, and gifts, and found favor in their sight.

Wicked men from Israel, evil men who were making accusations against him, gathered before him; but the king paid no attention to them.

He ordered Jonathan to be stripped of his garments and clothed in purple; and so they did. The king seated him beside himself.

He said to his commanders: “Go out with him through the middle of the city and proclaim that no one is to bring any accusation against him concerning any matter, nor trouble him for any reason.”

When those who had accused him saw his glory, which was being proclaimed, and saw him clothed in purple, they all fled.

The king magnified him, enrolled him among his chief friends, appointed him commander, and made him a participant in the leadership.

Jonathan returned to Jerusalem in peace and gladness.

In the one hundred and sixty-fifth year, Demetrius son of Demetrius came from Crete to the land of his fathers.

King Alexander heard of it and was greatly distressed, and returned to Antioch.

King Demetrius appointed Apollonius commander, who governed Coele-Syria. He gathered a large army, approached Jamnia, and sent a message to Jonathan the high priest:

“You alone resist us, while I have become a laughingstock and a reproach because you exercise authority against us in the mountains.

“Now therefore, if you trust in your strength, come down to us onto the plain, and let us confront one another there, for the power of war is with me.

“Ask and learn who I am, and who the others are who support me. They say that your foot cannot stand before us, because your fathers were twice put to flight in their own land.

“Now how will you be able to withstand so much cavalry and such an army on the plain, where there is neither stone nor rock nor any place of escape?”

When Jonathan heard Apollonius’s words, he was stirred in spirit. He chose ten thousand men, departed from Jerusalem, and his brother Simon came to meet him in support.

They pitched their camp at Joppa. The garrison shut Jonathan out from the city—for Apollonius’s garrison was in Joppa—and he besieged it.

Those who were in the city were terrified, opened the gates to him, and Jonathan took possession of Joppa.

Apollonius heard of it and brought up three thousand cavalry and a large army.

He went toward Azotus as though he were merely traveling, then immediately came out onto the plain, because he had a multitude of cavalry and trusted in them. Jonathan pursued him toward Azotus, and they joined battle.

Apollonius secretly left one thousand cavalry behind his camp, to attack them from the rear.

Jonathan learned that there was an ambush behind him. They surrounded his camp and shot darts at the people from morning until evening.

The people stood firm, as Jonathan had commanded; but their horses grew weary.

Simon brought out his army and engaged the legion, for the cavalry were exhausted. He crushed them, and they fled.

Those who were scattered across the plain fled into Azotus and entered Beth-dagon, their idol, to save themselves there.

Jonathan burned Azotus and the cities around it, took their spoils, and burned the temple of Dagon with fire, together with all those who had fled into it.

About eight thousand men fell by the sword or were burned.

From there Jonathan moved the camp and brought it to Ashkelon. The people came out of the city to meet him with great glory.

Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his men, who were carrying much plunder.

When King Alexander heard these reports, he further glorified Jonathan.

He sent him a golden clasp, as was customary to give to the relatives of kings, and granted him Ekron and all its territory as a possession.

## CHAPTER XI

The king of Egypt gathered an army as numerous as the sand along the seashore, together with many ships. He sought by deceit to obtain Alexander’s kingdom and add it to his own.

He went out into Syria with peaceful words. The cities opened themselves to him and came out to meet him, because King Alexander had ordered them to go out to meet him, since he was his father-in-law.

When Ptolemy entered each city, he placed military garrisons in it.

When he approached Azotus, they showed him the temple of Dagon burned with fire, Azotus and its other buildings demolished, the bodies cast out, and the burial mounds that they had made beside the road for those who had been slain in battle.

They told the king that Jonathan had done this, in order to make him hostile to Jonathan; but the king remained silent.

Jonathan met the king at Joppa in glory. They greeted one another, and they spent the night there.

Jonathan went with the king as far as the river called Eleutherus, and then returned to Jerusalem.

King Ptolemy took control of the cities as far as Seleucia on the coast, and he was devising evil plans against Alexander.

He sent envoys to Demetrius, saying: “Come, let us establish an agreement between us. I will give you my daughter, whom Alexander has, and you shall reign in your father’s kingdom.”

For I regret that I gave him my daughter: for he sought to kill me.

And he reproached him because he had coveted his kingdom.

And he took away his daughter and gave her to Demetrius, and [Col. 0492A] separated himself from Alexander; and his hostility became manifest.

And Ptolemy entered Antioch, and placed two diadems upon his head, those of Egypt and Asia.

Now Alexander was king in Cilicia at that time, because the inhabitants of those regions were in revolt.

And Alexander heard this and came against him to battle; and King Ptolemy brought out his army, met him with a strong force, and put him to flight.

And Alexander fled into Arabia, so that he might be protected there; but King Ptolemy was exalted.

And Zabdiel the Arab cut off Alexander’s head and sent it to Ptolemy.

And King Ptolemy died on the third day; and those who were in the fortresses perished at the hands of those who were in the camp.

And Demetrius reigned in the one hundred and sixty-seventh year.

In those days Jonathan gathered those who were in Judea, to attack the citadel that was in Jerusalem; and they made many siege engines against it.

[Col. 0492B] And certain lawless men who hated their own people went to King Demetrius and reported to him that Jonathan was besieging the citadel.

And when he heard this, he became angry; and he immediately came to Ptolemais and wrote to Jonathan not to besiege the citadel, but to come to him quickly for a conference.

When Jonathan heard this, however, he ordered the siege to continue; and he selected men from the elders of Israel and from the priests, and placed himself in danger.

And he took gold, silver, clothing, and many other gifts, and went to the king at Ptolemais, and found favor in his sight.

And certain lawless men of his own people brought accusations against him.

And the king treated him as those before him had treated him; and he exalted him in the sight of all his friends.

And he appointed him to the high-priestly office [Al. of a priest], [Col. 0492C] and to whatever other precious things he had previously possessed, and made him chief among his friends.

And Jonathan asked the king to make Judea, the three districts, Samaria, and its borders exempt from tribute; and he promised him three hundred talents.

And the king agreed, and wrote letters to Jonathan concerning all these matters, containing the following:

“King Demetrius sends greetings to his brother Jonathan and to the Jewish nation.

“Copy of the letter that we wrote concerning you to Lasthenes our kinsman; we have sent it to you so that you might know:

“King Demetrius sends greetings to Lasthenes his kinsman.

“Since the Jewish nation are our friends and keep what is right before us, we have decided to do them good because of their goodwill toward us.

“Therefore we have assigned to them all the territory of Judea, together with the three cities, Lydda and Ramathaim, which were added to Judea from Samaria; and we have decreed that all their borders be exempt, as well as all those who offer sacrifices in Jerusalem, from the things that the king previously received from them each year, from the produce of the land, and from the fruit trees.

“And from this time onward we remit to them the other payments that belonged to us—tithes and taxes—and the salt-pits and the crowns that were brought to us.

“We grant all these things to them; and none of these provisions shall be annulled, either now or at any time.

“Now therefore take care to make a copy of this document and let it be given to Jonathan and placed on the holy mountain, in a prominent place.”

And when King Demetrius saw that the land was quiet before him and that no one resisted him, he dismissed his entire army, each man to his own place, except for the foreign army that he had recruited from the islands of the nations; and all the armies of his ancestors were hostile to him.

Now Tryphon had formerly been one of Alexander’s partisans. When he saw that the whole army was murmuring against Demetrius, he went to Emalchuel the Arab, who was raising Antiochus, the son of Alexander.

And he urged him to hand Antiochus over to him, so that he might reign [Col. 0493A] in place of his father; and he told him how much Demetrius had done and of the hostility of his armies toward him. And he remained there many days.

And Jonathan sent to King Demetrius, asking him to expel those who were in the citadel in Jerusalem and those who were in the garrisons, because they were attacking Israel.

And Demetrius sent to Jonathan, saying: “I will do not only this for you and your nation, but I will also honor you and your nation with glory when the proper time comes.

“Now therefore you will do well if you send me men to help me, for my entire army has withdrawn.”

And Jonathan sent him three thousand valiant men to Antioch. They came to the king, and the king rejoiced at their arrival.

And the inhabitants of the city assembled, one hundred and twenty thousand men, and wished to kill the king.

And the king fled into the palace. The inhabitants of the city seized the city’s roads and began to fight.

And the king summoned the Jews for help, and they all came together to him and dispersed throughout the city.

[Col. 0493B] And on that day they killed one hundred thousand men, set the city on fire, seized much plunder that day, and rescued the king.

And the inhabitants of the city saw that the Jews had gained control of the city as they wished; and they lost heart and cried out to the king with supplications, saying:

“Give us your pledge, and let the Jews cease attacking us and the city.”

And they threw down their arms and made peace. The Jews were honored in the sight of the king and in the sight of all who were in his kingdom, and their name became renowned throughout the kingdom. Then they returned to Jerusalem with much plunder.

And King Demetrius sat upon the throne of his kingdom, and the land was quiet before him.

But he lied in all that he had said, separated himself from Jonathan, did not repay him according to the benefits Jonathan had conferred upon him [Al. granted him], and afflicted him severely.

After this Tryphon returned, with the young Antiochus, and Antiochus reigned and placed a diadem upon himself.

And all the armies that Demetrius had dispersed gathered to Antiochus and fought against Demetrius; and Demetrius fled and turned his back.

And Tryphon took possession of the beasts of war and gained control of Antioch.

And the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan, saying: “I appoint you to the high priesthood, and I appoint you over four cities, so that you may be among the king’s friends.

“And he sent him golden vessels for his service, and granted him the privilege of drinking from gold vessels, wearing purple, and possessing a golden clasp.

“And he appointed his brother Simeon commander from the borders of Tyre to the borders of Egypt.”

And Jonathan went out and traveled through the cities beyond the river; and the entire army of Syria gathered to him for assistance. He came to Ascalon, and the inhabitants came out to meet him with honor.

[Col. 0493D] And from there he went to Gaza. The inhabitants of Gaza shut themselves in, and he besieged it, set fire to the surrounding places, and plundered them.

And the Gazans appealed to Jonathan, and he gave them his pledge. He took their sons as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem, and traveled through the region as far as Damascus.

And Jonathan heard that the officers of Demetrius had revolted at Kadesh, which is in Galilee, with a large army, intending to remove him from the affairs of the kingdom.

And he went out to meet them; but he left his brother Simeon within the province.

And Simeon approached Beth-zur, besieged it for many days, and confined its inhabitants.

[Col. 0494A] And they asked him to accept their pledge, and he gave it to them; and he expelled [Note: [Col. 0493] Other printed books read, “he expelled them from there and then captured,” etc., less accurately.] them from there, captured the city, and stationed a garrison in it.

And Jonathan and his army approached the water of Gennesar, and before dawn they kept watch in the plain of Hazor.

And behold, the foreign army came out against them in the plain and laid an ambush for him in the mountains; but he went out to meet them.

The ambushes rose from their positions and joined battle.

And all those who were on Jonathan’s side fled, and none remained except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Calphi, commanders of the army.

And Jonathan tore his garments, put dust upon his head, and prayed.

Then Jonathan returned against them in battle and put them to flight, and they fought.

And those who had fled from his side saw this, returned to him, and pursued the enemy with him all the way to Kadesh, to their camp; and they reached it.

[Col. 0494B] And three thousand of the foreign army fell that day. Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XII

And Jonathan saw that the time was favorable to him, and he selected men and sent them to Rome to establish and renew friendship with the Romans.

And he sent letters to the Spartans and to other places in the same form.

And they went to Rome, entered the senate-house, and said: “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish nation have sent us to renew the friendship and alliance according to the former agreement.”

And the Romans gave them letters addressed to the authorities in the various places, instructing them to escort the envoys peacefully into the land of Judah.

And this is a copy of the letter that Jonathan wrote to the Spartans:

“Jonathan the high priest, the elders of the nation, the priests, and the rest of the Jewish people send greetings to the Spartans, their brothers.

“Long ago letters were sent to Onias the high priest by Arius, who reigned among you, stating that you are our brothers, as the following written reply makes clear.

“And Onias received the man who had been sent with honor, and accepted the letters in which the alliance and friendship were declared.

“We ourselves had no need of any of this, since we have the holy books that are in our hands for our consolation.

“Nevertheless, we preferred to send to you in order to renew our brotherhood and friendship, lest we should become estranged from you; for many years have passed since you sent to us.

“Therefore, at all times, without ceasing, on feast days and on the other occasions when it is proper, we remember you in the sacrifices that we offer and in the observances, as is lawful and fitting when remembering brothers.

“Accordingly, we rejoice in your glory.

“But we have been surrounded by many troubles and many wars, and the kings around us have attacked us.

“Therefore we did not wish to trouble you, or our other allies and friends, in these wars.

“For we have had help from heaven, and we have been delivered, while our enemies have been humbled.

“Therefore we chose Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason and sent them to the Romans to renew with them our former friendship and alliance.

“We have instructed them also to come to you, greet you, and deliver to you our letters concerning the renewal of our brotherhood.

“And now you will do us a kindness by replying to us concerning these matters.”

And this is the written reply of the letters that Onias had sent:

[Col. 0495A] “Arius, king of the Spartans, sends greetings to Onias the great priest.

“It has been found in the records concerning the Spartans and the Jews that they are brothers and that they are of the race of Abraham.

“And now, since we have learned this, you will do well to write to us concerning your peace.

“We too have written back to you: ‘Our livestock and our possessions are yours, and yours are ours.’ We have therefore commanded that this be reported to you.”

And Jonathan heard that the officers of Demetrius had returned with an army much larger than before to fight against him.

And he went out from Jerusalem and met them in the region of Hamath, for he had not given them time to enter his territory.

And he sent scouts into their camp, and they returned and reported that the enemy intended to fall upon them at night.

When the sun had set, Jonathan ordered his men to keep watch and remain armed and ready for battle throughout the night, and he stationed guards around the camp.

[Col. 0495B] And the enemy heard that Jonathan and his men were ready for battle; and they were afraid and became terrified in their hearts, and they lit fires in their camp.

But Jonathan and those with him did not know this until morning. They saw the fires burning.

And Jonathan pursued them but did not overtake them, for they had crossed the River Eleutherus.

And Jonathan turned aside toward the Arabs called Zabadaeans, struck them, and took their spoils.

And he joined [the surviving text does not state the object], came to Damascus, and traveled throughout that entire region.

Simeon went out and came as far as Ascalon and the nearby garrisons. Then he turned toward Joppa and captured it.

(For he had heard that they intended to surrender the garrison to the party of Demetrius.) And he stationed guards there to protect it.

And Jonathan returned, summoned the elders of the people, and consulted with them about building fortifications in Judea,

[Col. 0495C] and building walls in Jerusalem and raising a great height between the citadel and the city, so as to separate it from the city, that it might stand by itself and they might neither buy nor sell.

And they agreed to build the city. The wall that stood above the ravine toward the east fell, and he repaired it, which is called Caphetetha.

And Simeon built Adiada in the Shephelah, fortified it, and installed gates and bolts.

And when Tryphon planned to reign over Asia, assume the diadem, and [Al. om. and] stretch out his hand against King Antiochus,

fearing that Jonathan might perhaps prevent him and fight against him, he sought to seize and kill Jonathan. So he rose up and went to Beth-shan.

And Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand chosen men for battle and came to Beth-shan.

And Tryphon saw that Jonathan had come with a large army and was about to lay hands upon him, and he was afraid.

And he received him with honor, commended him [Col. 0495D] to all his friends, and gave him gifts. He ordered his armies to obey Jonathan as they obeyed himself.

And he said to Jonathan: “Why have you troubled the entire people, when we are not at war with one another?

“Now therefore send them back to their homes. Choose for yourself a few men to remain with you, and come with me to Ptolemais. I will hand it over to you, together with the remaining garrisons, the army, and all the officials in charge of affairs; then I will turn back and depart. For this is why I have come.”

And Jonathan believed him and did as he said. He dismissed the army, and they went into the land of Judah.

But Jonathan retained three thousand men with him; of these he sent two thousand into Galilee, while one thousand came with him.

When Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the inhabitants of Ptolemais shut the city gates and seized him; and they killed with the sword all who had entered with him.

And Tryphon sent an army and cavalry into Galilee, [Col. 0496A] and into the great plain, to destroy [Al. to destroy, plural] all Jonathan’s companions.

But when they learned that Jonathan had been seized and had perished, they encouraged one another and went out ready for battle.

And when those who had pursued them saw that their lives were at stake, they turned back.

The others all came peacefully into the land of Judah. And they mourned Jonathan and those who had been with him bitterly; and Israel mourned with great mourning.

And all the nations around them sought to crush them, saying:

“They have no leader or helper. Now therefore let us attack them and remove their memory from among mankind.”

## CHAPTER XIII

And Simon heard that Tryphon had gathered a large army to come into the land of Judah and devastate it.

[Col. 0496B] Seeing that the people were in trembling and fear, he went up to Jerusalem and gathered the people.

And he exhorted them, saying: “You know what I and my brothers and my father’s house have done for the laws and for the holy places—what battles and hardships we have endured.

“Because of these things all my brothers have perished for Israel, and I alone remain.

“And now, far be it from me to spare my life in any time of distress, for I am no better than my brothers.

“Therefore I will avenge my nation, the holy places, our sons, and our wives, because all the nations have gathered against us out of hatred.”

And the spirit of the people was kindled as soon as they heard these words.

And they answered with a loud voice, saying: “You are our leader in place of Judas and Jonathan your brother.

“Fight our battle, and whatever you command us, we will do.”

[Col. 0496C] And he gathered all the fighting men and hastened to complete all the walls of Jerusalem, fortifying it on every side.

And he sent Jonathan son of Absalom, together with a new army, to Joppa; and after expelling those who were in it, Jonathan himself remained there.

And Tryphon set out from Ptolemais with a large army to come into the land of Judah, while Jonathan was with him under guard.

But Simon approached Addus, opposite the plain.

And when Tryphon learned that Simon had risen in place of his brother Jonathan and that he would engage him in battle, he sent messengers to him,

saying: “Because of the silver that your brother Jonathan owed in the king’s account, on account of the affairs entrusted to him, we have detained him.

“Now therefore send one hundred talents of silver and his two sons as hostages, so that he may not be released and flee from us; then we will release him.”

And Simon knew that Tryphon was speaking deceitfully to him. [Col. 0496D] Nevertheless, he ordered the silver and the boys to be delivered, lest he incur great hostility from the people of Israel, who might say:

“Because he did not send him the silver and the boys, Jonathan perished.”

And he sent the boys and one hundred talents, but Tryphon broke his word and did not release Jonathan.

After this Tryphon came into the region to devastate it. They traveled around by the road leading to Ador, while Simon and his army went everywhere Tryphon went.

Those who were in the citadel sent messengers to Tryphon, urging him to come quickly through the wilderness and send them provisions.

And Tryphon prepared all his cavalry to come that night. But there was a very heavy snowfall, and he did not come to the Galaadite region.

And when he approached Bascaman [Al. Bescaman], he killed Jonathan and his sons there.

[Col. 0497A] Then Tryphon turned back and went into his own land.

And Simon sent men to take the bones of his brother Jonathan, and he buried them in Modin, the city of his ancestors.

And all Israel mourned him with great mourning, and they lamented him for many days.

And Simon built upon the tomb of his father and his brothers a lofty structure, with polished stone at the back and in front.

And he erected seven pyramids, one opposite another, for his father and mother and his four brothers.

And around these he set great columns; and upon the columns he placed armor, as an eternal memorial. Beside the armor were carved ships, visible to all who sailed the sea.

This is the tomb that he made in Modin, and it remains to this day.

Now Tryphon, while traveling with King Antiochus, who was still young, killed him by treachery.

And he reigned in his place, placed upon himself the diadem of Asia, and caused great devastation in the land.

[Col. 0497B] And Simon built fortifications throughout Judea, strengthening them with high towers, great walls, gates, and bolts; and he stored provisions in the fortresses.

And Simon chose men and sent them to King Demetrius, asking him to remit the tribute of the region, since all Tryphon’s acts had been carried out by plunder.

And King Demetrius answered him concerning these matters and wrote the following letter:

“King Demetrius sends greetings to Simon the high priest, the friend of kings, to the elders, and to the Jewish nation.

“We have received the golden crown and the *bahem* that you sent, and we are prepared to make a great peace with you and to write to the king’s officials that they should remit to you what we have granted.

“For whatever we have established remains valid for you. The fortifications that you have built shall belong to you.

“We also remit the offenses and sins committed up to this day, as well as the crown that you owed. And if anything else in Jerusalem was subject to tribute, it shall no longer be subject to tribute. [Col. 0497C]

“And if any of you are suitable for enrollment among our people, let them be enrolled, and let there be peace between us.”

In the one hundred and seventieth year, the yoke of the nations was removed from Israel.

And the people of Israel began to write in the tablets and public records: “In the first year under Simon the high priest, the great leader and prince of the Jews.”

In those days Simon approached Gaza, surrounded it with camps, made siege engines, approached the city, struck one tower, and captured it.

And those who were inside the siege engine burst into the city, and a great panic arose in the city.

And the people who were in the city went up upon the wall with their wives and children, their garments torn, and cried out with a loud voice, asking Simon to give them his pledge. They said:

“Do not deal with us according to our wickednesses, but according to your mercies.”

[Col. 0497D] And Simon relented and did not destroy them. Nevertheless, he expelled them from the city, cleansed the houses in which idols had been kept, and then entered it with hymns, blessing the Lord.

After removing all impurity from it, he stationed men there who would observe the law. He fortified it and made it his residence.

Those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem were prevented from going out, entering the region, buying, or selling. They suffered severe hunger, and many of them perished from famine.

And they appealed to Simon to accept their pledge, and he did so. He expelled them from there and cleansed the citadel of its contaminations.

And they entered it on the twenty-third day of the second month, in the one hundred and seventy-first year, with praise, palm branches, lyres, cymbals, harps, hymns, and songs, because the great enemy had been crushed out of Israel.

[Col. 0498A] And he decreed that this day should be celebrated every year with rejoicing.

And he fortified the temple mount beside the citadel, and he himself and those with him lived there.

And Simon saw that his son John was a valiant warrior, and he appointed him commander of all the forces; and John lived at Gazara.

## CHAPTER XIV

In the one hundred and seventy-second year, King Demetrius gathered his army and went into Media to obtain reinforcements for himself, so that he might attack Tryphon.

And Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had entered his territories, and he sent one of his officers to capture him alive and bring him to him.

And the officer went and struck Demetrius’s camp, captured him, led him to Arsaces, and placed him in custody.

[Col. 0498B] And all the land of Judah was quiet throughout all the days of Simon, and he sought the welfare of his nation; and his power pleased them, as did his glory, throughout all his days.

And with all his glory he captured Joppa as a harbor and opened access to the islands of the sea.

And he enlarged the borders of his nation and gained possession of the region.

And he gathered many captives and ruled over Gazara, Beth-zur, and the citadel. He removed its impurities, and no one resisted him.

And each man cultivated his land in peace; and the land of Judah yielded its produce, and the trees of the countryside yielded their fruit.

All the elders sat in the streets, discussing the good things of the land, while the young men dressed themselves in glory and garments of war.

And he supplied the cities with provisions and established them as storehouses of fortification, until the fame of his glory was proclaimed to the ends of the earth.

He made peace throughout the land, and Israel rejoiced with great joy.

[Col. 0498C] And each man sat beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there was no one to terrify them.

The one who attacked them disappeared from the land; the kings were crushed in those days.

And he strengthened all the humble among his people, diligently sought the law, and removed every lawless and wicked person.

He glorified the holy places and multiplied the vessels of the sanctuary.

And it was heard in Rome and even among the Spartans that Jonathan had died, and they were greatly distressed.

But when they heard that Simon his brother had become high priest in his place and that he himself possessed the whole region and its cities,

they wrote to him on bronze tablets to renew the friendship and alliance that they had made with Judas and Jonathan, his brothers.

And the letters were read before the assembly in Jerusalem. This is a copy of the letter that the Spartans sent:

“The rulers of the Spartans and the cities send greetings to Simon the great priest, [Col. 0498D] to the elders, the priests, and the rest of the Jewish people, their brothers.

“The envoys who were sent to our people have told us of your glory, honor, and joy, and we rejoiced at their arrival.

“And we recorded what they said in the councils of the people, as follows: ‘Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, envoys of the Jews, came to us to renew our former friendship with them.’

“And it pleased the people to receive the men honorably and to place a record of their words in the separate public archives, so that it might remain as a memorial for the Spartan people. We have written a copy of these matters to Simon the great priest.”

After this Simon sent Numenius to Rome, carrying a great golden shield weighing one thousand minas, to establish an alliance with the Romans. When the Roman people heard

[Col. 0499A] these words, they said: “What thanks shall we render to Simon and his sons?

“For he has restored his brothers, driven Israel’s enemies away from them, and established his freedom for him. They recorded this on bronze tablets and set it up on inscriptions on Mount Zion.”

And this is the text of the inscription:

“On the eighteenth day of the month Elul, in the one hundred and seventy-second year, in the third year under Simon the great priest, at Asaramel.

“In the great assembly of the priests, the people, the leaders of the nation, and the elders of the region, the following matters were made known: Since wars have frequently arisen in our land,

Simon son of Mattathias, of the sons of Jarib, and his brothers exposed themselves to danger and resisted the adversaries of their nation, so that their sanctuary and the law might endure; and they brought great glory to their nation.

And Jonathan gathered his people and became their high priest, and was joined to his people.

[Col. 0499B] And their enemies sought to trample them down, devastate their land, and stretch out their hands against their holy places.

Then Simon stood forth and fought for his nation. He spent much money, armed the valiant men of his nation, and gave them pay.

And he fortified the cities of Judea, and Beth-zur, which was on the borders of Judea, where the enemies’ weapons had formerly been; and he stationed Jewish men there as a garrison.

And he fortified Joppa, which was by the sea, and Gazara, which is on the borders of Azotus, where the enemies had formerly lived; and he settled Jews there. Whatever was suitable for their correction, he placed in those cities.

And the people saw Simon’s deeds and the glory that he intended to bring to his nation, and they appointed him their leader and prince of the priests, because he had done all these things and had preserved justice and faithfulness toward his nation, seeking in every way to exalt his people.

And in his days he prospered in his undertakings, [Col. 0499C] so that the nations were removed from their land, as were those who were in the City of David, in Jerusalem, in the citadel, from which they went out and contaminated everything around the holy places and inflicted great harm upon purity.

And he stationed Jewish men there for the protection of the region and the city, and raised the walls of Jerusalem.

And King Demetrius appointed him high priest.

In accordance with these matters he made him his friend and honored him with great glory.

For he had heard that the Jews had been called by the Romans friends, allies, and brothers, and that they had received Simon’s envoys honorably.

And he had heard that the Jews and their priests had agreed that he should be their leader and high priest forever, until a faithful prophet should arise.

And that he should be their leader, appoint officials over their works, their region, their weapons, and their fortifications.

And that he should have charge of the holy places; that all should listen to him; and that all documents in the region should be written in his name; and that he should be clothed in purple and gold.

And that no one of the people or of the priests should be permitted to annul any of these provisions, contradict anything he said, or convene an assembly in the region without him; and that he should wear purple and use a golden clasp.

Whoever acted outside these provisions or annulled any of them would be liable to punishment.

And it pleased all the people to establish Simon and to act according to these words.

And Simon accepted this, and it pleased him to serve as high priest, to be leader and prince of the Jewish nation and of the priests, and to preside over all.

And they ordered that this document be placed on bronze tablets and set within the enclosure of the holy places, in a prominent location.

A copy of it was to be placed in the treasury, for Simon and his sons.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0500A]
