And King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon the priest and prince of the Jewish nation, and to the entire nation.

They contained the following:

“King Antiochus sends greetings to Simon the great priest and to the Jewish nation.

“Since pestilent men have seized the kingdom of our fathers, I wish to avenge the kingdom and restore it as it formerly was. I have raised a chosen multitude of troops and prepared warships.

“I intend to advance through the region to take vengeance upon those who have corrupted our land and laid waste to many cities in my kingdom.

“Now therefore I confirm to you all the offerings that all the kings before me remitted to you, and whatever other gifts they remitted to you.

“I permit you to strike your own coinage in your territory.

“As for Jerusalem, let it be holy and free; and all [Col. 0500B] the weapons that have been manufactured and the fortifications that you have built and possess shall remain yours [Al. there].

“And every debt owed to the king, and all that will in future be owed to the king, from this time onward and forever, is remitted to you.

“When we have gained our kingdom, we will glorify you, your nation, and the temple with great glory, so that your glory may be made manifest throughout the whole earth.”

In the one hundred and seventy-fourth year Antiochus went out into the land of his fathers, and all the armies gathered to him, so that only a few remained with Tryphon.

And King Antiochus pursued him, and Tryphon came to Dora by the coastal route in flight.

For he knew that disasters had gathered against him, and his army had deserted him.

And Antiochus approached Dora with one hundred and twenty thousand fighting men and eight thousand cavalry.

And he surrounded the city, and ships approached from the sea. [Col. 0500C] They harassed the city by land and sea and allowed no one to enter or leave.

Now Numenius and those who were with him came from the city of Rome, carrying letters written to kings and regions, containing the following:

“Lucius, consul of the Romans, sends greetings to King Ptolemy.

“The envoys of the Jews, our friends, have come to us to renew the former friendship and alliance. They were sent by Simon, prince of the priests, and by the Jewish people.

“They also brought a golden shield weighing one thousand minas.

“Therefore we have decided to write to the kings and regions that they should not harm them, attack them, or attack their cities and territories, and that they should not provide assistance to those who fight against them.

“It has also seemed good to us to accept the shield from them.

“Therefore, if any pestilent men have fled from their territory to you, hand them over to Simon, prince of the priests, so that he may punish them according to his law.”

The same letter was written to King Demetrius, Attalus, Ariarathes, and Arsaces,

[Col. 0500D] and to all the regions: to Lampsacus, the Spartans, Delos, Myndus, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Cos, Side, Aradus, Rhodes, Phaselis, Gortyna, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.

And they wrote a copy of it to Simon, prince of the priests, and to the Jewish people.

King Antiochus again approached Dora with his camp, continually bringing his forces against it and making siege engines; and he confined Tryphon so that he could not come out.

And Simon sent him two thousand chosen men as assistance, together with silver, gold, and abundant vessels.

But Antiochus refused to accept them. He broke all the agreements he had previously made with Simon and separated himself from him.

And he sent Athenobius, one of his friends, to negotiate with him, saying: “You hold Joppa, Gazara, and the citadel that is in [Al. om. in] Jerusalem, cities of my kingdom.

“You have devastated their territories, caused great destruction in the land, and gained control of many places in my kingdom.

“Now therefore surrender the cities that you have occupied, together with the taxes of the places that you control outside the borders of Judea.

“If not, give five hundred talents of silver for them, and another five hundred talents for the devastation that you have caused and for the taxes of the cities. Otherwise we will come and attack you.”

And Athenobius, the king’s friend, came to Jerusalem and saw Simon’s glory, the splendor of the gold and silver, and the abundant display of wealth. He was astonished and reported the king’s words to him.

And Simon answered him and said: “We have taken neither foreign land nor what belongs to others. [Col. 0501B] Rather, we possess the inheritance of our fathers, which our enemies unjustly occupied for a time.

“But when we had the opportunity, we recovered the inheritance of our fathers.

“As for Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, they were themselves inflicting great harm upon our people and our land. For these we give one hundred talents.” Athenobius did not answer him a word.

But when he returned angrily to the king, he reported these words to him, along with Simon’s glory and everything he had seen; and the king became exceedingly angry.

But Tryphon fled by ship to Orthosia.

And the king appointed Cendebaeus as commander of the coastal region and gave him an infantry and cavalry force.

He ordered him to move the camp against Judaea and commanded him to build Gedor, block the gates of the city, and subdue the people. Meanwhile, the king pursued Tryphon.

Cendebaeus reached Jamnia and began to provoke the populace, trample Judaea, take the people captive, kill them, and build Gedor.

[Col. 0501C] He stationed cavalry and an army there, so that they might go out and patrol the road through Judaea, as the king had ordered him.

## CHAPTER XVI

John came up from Gazara and reported to his father Simon what Cendebaeus had done among their people.

Simon summoned his two elder sons, Judas and John, and said to them: “I, my brothers, and my father’s household have fought Israel’s enemies from our youth to this day, and it has prospered in our hands to deliver Israel on several occasions.

“But now I am old. Take my place, then, and that of my brothers; go out and fight for our people. May help from heaven be with you.”

He selected from the region twenty thousand fighting men and cavalry, and they marched against Cendebaeus. They camped at Modin.

They rose in the morning and went out into the plain. And behold, a large army of infantry and cavalry came to meet them, and a rushing river lay between them.

John himself, with his people, brought the camp up opposite them. He saw that the people were hesitant to cross the torrent, so he crossed first; and when the men saw him, they crossed after him.

He divided the people and the cavalry among the infantry. The enemy’s cavalry, however, was exceedingly numerous.

They sounded the sacred trumpets, and Cendebaeus and his camp were put to flight. Many of them fell wounded, while the rest fled into the stronghold.

Then Judas, John’s brother, was wounded. John pursued them until he reached Cedron, which he had built.

They fled as far as the towers that were in the fields of Azotus, and he burned them with fire. Two thousand of them fell, and he returned peacefully to Judaea.

Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed commander in the plain of Jericho, and he possessed much silver and gold,

[Col. 0502B] for he was the son-in-law of the high priest.

His heart was exalted, and he wanted to gain possession of the region. He plotted treachery against Simon and his sons, intending to remove them.

Simon was traveling through the cities in the region of Judaea and caring for them. He himself, together with his son Mattathias and Judas, went down to Jericho in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year, in the eleventh month—that is, the month of Shebat.

The son of Abubus received them by treachery into a small fortress called Dok, which he had built. He prepared a great banquet for them and concealed men there.

When Simon and his sons had become drunk, Ptolemy rose with his men, took up their weapons, entered the banquet, and killed him, his two sons, and some of his servants.

He perpetrated a great deception in Israel and repaid good with evil.

[Col. 0502C] Ptolemy wrote these things and sent them to the king, asking him to send an army to his aid and to hand over to him the region, their cities, and their tribute.

He sent others to Gazara to seize John. He sent letters to the commanders, asking them to come to him, and promising them silver, gold, and gifts.

He sent others to occupy Jerusalem and the Temple Mount.

A certain man ran ahead and informed John in Gazara that his father and brothers had perished, and that Ptolemy had also sent to have him killed.

When he heard this, he was greatly terrified. He seized the men who had come to destroy him and killed them, for he realized that they were seeking his death.

The rest of the deeds of John, his wars and his noble accomplishments, in which he acted courageously, the construction of the walls that he built, and his achievements—

behold, these are written in the book of the records of his priesthood, from the time when he became high priest after his father.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0501]

## CHAPTER I

The brothers who are in Jerusalem, and the Jews and those in the region of Judaea, send greetings to the Jewish brothers throughout Egypt and wish them complete peace.

May God deal kindly with you and remember his covenant, which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.

May he give all of you one heart, so that you may worship him and do his will with a great heart and a willing spirit.

May he open your heart to his law and his commandments and grant peace.

[Col. 0502D] May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and may he not abandon you in a time of distress.

And now we are here praying for you.

In the reign of Demetrius, in the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, we Jews wrote to you amid the tribulation and the calamity that overtook us in those years, after Jason withdrew from the holy land and from the kingdom.

They burned the gate and shed innocent blood. We prayed to the Lord, and he heard us; we offered sacrifice and fine flour, lit lamps, and set out the loaves.

And now celebrate the days of the Festival of Booths in the month of Casleu.

[Col. 0503A] In the one hundred and eighty-eighth year, the people who are in Jerusalem and Judaea, together with the Senate and Judas, send greetings and good health to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the lineage of anointed priests, and to the Jews who are in Egypt.

Having been delivered by God from great dangers, we give him magnificent thanks, since we fought against such a king.

For he caused those who had fought against us and against the holy city to burst forth from Persia.

When he himself was commander in Persia, with an immense army beside him, he fell in the temple of Nanea, deceived by the plan of Nanea’s priests.

For when Antiochus came to the place to live with her, and his friends with him, so that he might receive a large sum as a dowry,

and when the priests of Nanea had set out the money, he entered with a few men within the temple precinct. They closed the temple

[Col. 0503B] after Antiochus had entered; and, opening a concealed entrance in the temple, they threw stones and struck the commander and those who were with him. They dismembered them and, cutting off their heads, cast them outside.

Blessed in every way is God, who delivers the impious to destruction.

Since we are therefore about to celebrate the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, we thought it necessary to inform you, so that you too may celebrate the Festival of Booths and the festival of the fire that was given when Nehemiah, after building the temple and the altar, offered sacrifices.

When our ancestors were being led away to Persia, the priests who were then worshipers of God secretly took fire from the altar and hid it in a valley where there was a deep, dry well. There they concealed it so that the place was unknown to everyone.

After many years had passed, and it pleased God that Nehemiah should be sent by the king of Persia, he sent the descendants of those priests who had hidden the fire to search for it. As they reported to us, they did not find the fire,

[Col. 0503C] but thick water.

He ordered them to draw it up and bring it to him. The priest Nehemiah ordered the sacrifices that had been placed there, as well as the wood and what had been laid upon it, to be sprinkled with that water.

When this had been done and the time came when the sun, which had previously been hidden by clouds, shone out, a great fire was kindled, so that everyone marveled.

All the priests prayed while the sacrifice was being completed: Jonathan began, and the others responded.

Nehemiah’s prayer was as follows:

“Lord God, creator of all things, awesome and strong, just and merciful, who alone are the good king,

alone the giver of all, alone just, almighty, and eternal; you who deliver Israel from every evil, who chose our ancestors and sanctified them:

accept a sacrifice for your whole people Israel, and guard your portion and sanctify it.

Gather our dispersed people; deliver those who are enslaved among the nations, and look upon those who are despised and abhorred, so that [Col. 0503D] the nations may know that you are our God.

Afflict those who oppress us and insult us in their arrogance.

Establish your people in your holy place, as Moses said.”

The priests sang hymns until the sacrifice had been consumed.

When the sacrifice had been consumed, Nehemiah ordered the remaining water to be poured over the larger stones.

When this had been done, a flame was kindled from them; but it was consumed by the light that shone from the altar.

When the matter became known, it was reported to the king of the Persians that, in the place where the priests who had been deported had hidden the fire, water had appeared, and that Nehemiah and those with him had purified the sacrifices with it.

[Col. 0504A] The king considered the matter and investigated it carefully; then he made a temple for it, to establish what had happened.

When he had tested it, he gave the priests many valuable gifts and further offerings, and, taking them in his own hand, distributed them to them.

Nehemiah called the place Nephthar, which means “Purification.” But most people call it Nephi.

## CHAPTER II

It is found in the records of the prophet Jeremiah that he ordered those who were being deported to take the fire, as it had been signified and as he commanded the deportees.

He gave them a law so that they would not forget the commandments of the Lord and would not go astray in their minds when they saw the golden and silver images and their ornaments.

Saying other things of this kind, he urged them not to remove the law from their heart.

[Col. 0504B] The writing also contained an account of how the Prophet, in response to a divine revelation, ordered the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense to accompany him until he reached the mountain on which Moses had ascended and saw God’s inheritance.

When Jeremiah arrived there, he found the site of a cave. [Note: [Col. 0503] Other printed books are silent here and omit the little word, and soon afterward the adverb “there”; yet in the Greek both are clearly present.] He brought the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense inside and blocked the entrance.

Some of those who followed came along with him in order to mark the place for themselves, but they could not find it.

When Jeremiah learned of this, he rebuked them and said: “The place shall remain unknown until God gathers the congregation of the people and shows mercy.

Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the majesty of the Lord will appear, and there will be a cloud, as it also appeared to Moses and as it appeared when Solomon prayed that the place should be sanctified to the great God.”

For he treated wisdom magnificently; and, as one possessing wisdom, he offered the sacrifice of the temple’s dedication and completion.

[Col. 0504C] Just as Moses prayed to the Lord, and fire descended from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, so Solomon also prayed, and fire descended from heaven and consumed the burnt offering.

Moses said that, because what had been offered for sin had not been eaten, it had been consumed.

Likewise, Solomon celebrated the dedication for eight days.

These same things were also included in the records and memoirs of Nehemiah. And, as he founded a library, he gathered from the regions the books of the prophets and of David, the letters of the kings, and records concerning votive offerings.

Likewise Judas also collected all the writings that had been scattered because of the war that had befallen us, and they are in our possession.

Therefore, if you desire these things, send someone to bring them to you.

Since we are about to celebrate the purification, we have written to you. You will do well, then, if you celebrate these days.

But we hope that God, who delivered his people and restored to all the inheritance, kingdom, priesthood, [Col. 0504D] and sanctification,

as he promised in the law, will soon have mercy on us and gather us from under heaven into the holy place.

For he delivered us from great dangers and purified the place.

Concerning Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers, and the purification of the great temple and the dedication of the altar;

and also concerning the battles involving Antiochus called the Noble and his son Eupator;

and concerning the manifestations that came from heaven to those who fought bravely for the Jews, so that, although they were few, they recovered the whole region and put the barbarian multitude to flight;

and recovered the most renowned temple in the whole world, liberated the city, and saw the laws that had been abolished restored, when the Lord had become favorable to them in complete peace—

all this Jason of Cyrene has set down in five books, and we have attempted to abridge it in a single volume.

Considering the multitude of books and the difficulty faced by those who wish to undertake historical narratives because of the abundance of events,

we have taken care, for those who wish to read, that it should be a source of intellectual enjoyment; for those devoted to study, that they might more easily commit it to memory; and for all readers, that benefit might be provided.

We ourselves, who undertook this work of abridgment, have accepted no easy labor—indeed, a task full of sleepless nights and toil.

Just as those who prepare a banquet and seek to satisfy the wishes of others gladly endure labor for the sake of the many,

so we concede the truth of each author’s account while pursuing brevity according to the form given to us.

[Col. 0505B] For just as an architect of a new house must attend to the entire structure, while one who undertakes painting must seek out what is suitable for decoration, so it must be judged in our case as well.

To gather one’s understanding, arrange one’s language, and investigate each individual part with precision belongs to the author of history.

But to pursue concise expression and avoid detailed execution of events should be granted to the abridger.

Accordingly, we shall begin the narrative. It is enough to have said only this about the preface: for it is foolish to pour oneself out before the history and then become brief within the history itself.

## CHAPTER III

When the holy city was living in complete peace, and the laws were still being observed with the greatest care because of the piety of the high priest Onias and the people’s hatred of evil,

it came about that the kings themselves and the rulers considered the place worthy of the highest honor and adorned the temple with the greatest gifts,

so that Seleucus, king of Asia, provided from his revenues all the expenses connected with the ministry of the sacrifices.

But Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, appointed superintendent of the temple, attempted, despite the opposition of the high priest, to devise some unlawful scheme in the city.

When he could not overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thrasaeas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,

and reported to him that the treasury in Jerusalem was filled with countless riches and that the common funds were immense, not belonging to the account of the sacrifices; it was possible, he said, for everything to fall under the king’s control.

When Apollonius reported to the king concerning the money that had been disclosed, the king summoned Heliodorus, who was in charge of his affairs, and sent him with orders to transport the aforementioned money.

Heliodorus immediately undertook the journey, outwardly as though he were traveling through the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,

[Col. 0505D] but in reality to carry out the king’s purpose.

When he came to Jerusalem and was kindly received in the city by the high priest, he spoke of the report that had been given concerning the money and explained why he had come. He asked whether these things were really so.

Then the high priest showed him that the deposits consisted of the provisions of widows and orphans.

Some belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very high standing, among the funds denounced by the wicked Simon. Altogether, there were four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold.

It was utterly impossible, he said, that those who had trusted the place and the temple—honored throughout the world for its reverence and holiness—should be deceived.

But Heliodorus, relying on the instructions he had received from the king, said that the money had to be conveyed to the king in every respect.

When the appointed day arrived, Heliodorus entered to arrange these matters. [Col. 0506A] There was no small amount of alarm throughout the entire city.

The priests threw themselves before the altar in their priestly robes and called upon him from heaven who had established the law concerning deposits, asking him to preserve safely for those who had deposited them the things entrusted to him.

The sight of the high priest’s face wounded the heart of anyone who saw it, for his expression and complexion, altered as they were, revealed the inward grief of his soul.

A certain sadness surrounded the man, and a bodily horror through which the pain of his heart became evident to those looking upon him.

Others also came flocking from their houses, making public supplication because the place was about to be held in contempt.

Women girded with sackcloth around their breasts came through the streets, and young women who had been confined indoors ran out to Onias. Some went to the walls, while others looked out through the windows.

[Col. 0506B] All of them stretched out their hands toward heaven and prayed.

There was a pitiful expectation shared by the gathered multitude and the high priest, who stood in the struggle.

These people called upon almighty God, asking that the things entrusted to them by those who had deposited them should be preserved with complete integrity.

But Heliodorus was carrying out what he had decided, himself present at the treasury with his attendants.

Then the spirit of almighty God made a great manifestation of his presence, so that all who had dared to obey Heliodorus were struck down by God’s power and turned to confusion and terror.

For there appeared to them a horse with a terrifying rider, adorned with splendid trappings. It rushed upon Heliodorus and struck him with its forehooves; the one seated upon it seemed to have golden armor.

Two other young men also appeared, distinguished by their strength, glorious in appearance, and finely dressed. They stood beside him and scourged him without pause, beating him with many blows on both sides.

Suddenly Heliodorus fell to the ground, and they seized him, surrounded by thick darkness, and threw him onto a litter.

The man who had entered the treasury with many runners and attendants was carried away, with no one able to help him, for the manifest power of God had become known.

He lay there, struck by divine power, speechless and deprived of every hope of recovery.

But the people blessed the Lord because he had magnified his place. The temple, which shortly before had been filled with fear and turmoil, was filled with joy and gladness when the almighty Lord appeared.

Then some of Heliodorus’ friends immediately begged Onias to invoke the Most High, so that he might grant life to the man who was at the point of death.

The high priest, however, considered that the king might perhaps suspect that the Jews had plotted some evil against Heliodorus, and he offered a sacrifice for the man’s recovery.

While the high priest was praying, the same young men, dressed in the same garments, stood beside Heliodorus and said: “Give thanks to Onias the priest, for on his account the Lord has granted you life.

“But you have been scourged by God. Proclaim to everyone the greatness and power of God.” After saying this, they disappeared.

After Heliodorus had offered a sacrifice to God and made great vows to the one who had granted him life, and after giving thanks to Onias, he returned to the king with his army.

He testified before everyone concerning the works of the great God that he had seen with his own eyes.

When the king asked Heliodorus who would be suitable to send to Jerusalem another time, he said:

“If you have an enemy or someone plotting against your kingdom, send him there, and you will receive him back scourged—if indeed he survives—because there is truly some power of God in that place.

“For the one whose dwelling is in heaven is the guardian and helper of that place; those who come to do evil he strikes and destroys.”

Thus matters stood concerning Heliodorus and the guarding of the treasury.

## CHAPTER IV

The aforementioned Simon, the informer against the funds and the fatherland, spoke evil of Onias, claiming that Onias himself had incited Heliodorus to do these things and had himself been the instigator of the wrongs.

He dared to call the guardian of the city, the defender of his nation, and the champion of God’s law a conspirator against the kingdom.

But when the enmity progressed so far that murders were even committed through certain associates of Simon,

Onias, considering the danger of the conflict and seeing that Apollonius, as governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was raging to increase Simon’s wickedness, went to the king,

[Col. 0507B] not as an accuser of the citizens, but considering within himself the common welfare of the entire multitude.

For he saw that without royal oversight it was impossible for peace to be restored to affairs and that Simon could not cease from his folly.

After Seleucus’ death, when Antiochus, who was called the Noble, had assumed the kingdom, Jason, Onias’ brother, sought the high priesthood.

He approached the king and promised him three hundred and sixty talents of silver and eighty talents from other revenues.

In addition, he promised another one hundred and fifty if authority were granted him to establish a gymnasium and an ephebeion, and to enroll those in Jerusalem as Antiochenes.

When the king agreed and Jason had obtained the office, [Col. 0507C] he immediately began transferring his fellow citizens to pagan customs.

He removed the privileges that kings had granted the Jews out of consideration for humanity, through John the father of Eupolemus, who had served as a legitimate ambassador to the Romans concerning friendship and alliance, depriving the citizens of their rights and enacting perverse institutions.

Indeed, he dared to establish a gymnasium beneath the citadel itself and to place the finest of the young men in brothels.

This was not a beginning but rather a kind of growth and advance of paganism and foreign customs, because of the impious and unheard-of crime of Jason, who was no priest.

Thus the priests were no longer devoted to the duties of the altar. Instead, despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to participate in the exercises of the gymnasium and in his unjust distributions, and to train in athletic contests.

Having no regard for their ancestral honors, they considered Greek distinctions the finest.

[Col. 0507D] For their sake they were caught up in a dangerous rivalry, imitated Greek institutions, and desired in every respect to resemble those whom they had regarded as enemies and killers.

To act impiously against the divine laws does not go unpunished; the following period will make this clear.

When the five-year contest was being celebrated at Tyre and the king was present,

the criminal Jason sent from Jerusalem sinful men carrying three hundred silver didrachmas as an offering to Hercules. Those who had brought the money asked that it not be spent on sacrifices, since that was not appropriate, but that it be assigned to other expenses.

Yet the money was indeed offered by the sender as a sacrifice to Hercules; because of those present, however, it was used for the construction of triremes.

When Apollonius son of Mnestheus had been sent to Egypt concerning the leading men of King Ptolemy Philometor, Antiochus learned that he had been excluded from the affairs of the kingdom. Concerned with his own interests, he departed from there and came to Joppa, and from there to Jerusalem.

Jason and the city received him magnificently, and he entered amid torchlight and acclamations. From there he turned his army toward Phoenicia.

After three years, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the aforementioned Simon, carrying money to the king and bringing answers concerning necessary affairs.

Menelaus was commended to the king; having magnified the appearance of his authority, he turned the high priesthood toward himself, offering three hundred talents of silver above Jason’s offer.

After receiving the king’s instructions, he came, possessing nothing worthy of the priesthood but carrying the spirit of a cruel tyrant and the fury of a savage beast.

Jason, who had displaced his own brother, was himself deceived and driven out as a fugitive into the Ammonite region.

Menelaus obtained the office, but he did nothing about the money he had promised the king, although Sostratus, who was in charge of the citadel, was collecting it.

For the collection of taxes belonged to him. For this reason both men were summoned before the king.

Menelaus was removed from the priesthood, and his brother Lysimachus succeeded him; Sostratus was appointed over the Cypriots.

While these things were taking place, the people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to start a revolt because they had been given as a gift to Antiochis, the king’s concubine.

The king therefore hurried there to calm them, leaving Andronicus, one of his companions, as his deputy.

Menelaus, thinking that he had found a favorable opportunity, stole certain golden vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus; he sold others in Tyre and in the neighboring cities.

When Onias learned this with complete certainty, he rebuked him, keeping himself in a secure place at Antioch near Daphne.

Menelaus therefore approached Andronicus and asked him [Col. 0508C] to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and, after giving him his right hand with an oath—although Onias was suspicious of him—persuaded him to come out of the asylum. He immediately killed him, without regard for justice.

For this reason not only the Jews but also other nations were indignant and grieved over the unjust murder of such a great man.

When the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, the Jews and the Greeks alike approached him at Antioch, complaining about the unjust murder of Onias.

Antiochus was deeply saddened on account of Onias and moved to pity; he shed tears, remembering the dead man’s sobriety and moderation.

Then, inflamed with anger, he ordered Andronicus to be stripped of his purple robe and led through the whole city. In the very place where he had committed his impiety against Onias, the sacrilegious man was deprived of life, as the Lord repaid him with a punishment worthy of his deed.

After many sacrileges had been committed in the temple by Lysimachus on Menelaus’ advice, and the report had spread, the multitude gathered against Lysimachus, since a great quantity of gold had already been carried away.

As the crowds rose up and their hearts filled with anger, Lysimachus began to employ nearly three thousand men with criminal hands, under the command of a certain tyrant advanced alike in age and madness.

When they understood Lysimachus’ attempt, some seized stones, others strong sticks, and some threw ashes at Lysimachus.

Many were wounded, some were knocked down, and all were put to flight. They killed the sacrilegious man himself beside the treasury.

A trial was therefore begun against Menelaus on account of these things.

When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the elders brought the case before him.

When Menelaus was being defeated, he promised Ptolemy that he would give him a large sum of money to persuade the king.

[Col. 0509A] Ptolemy therefore approached the king, who was seated in a certain courtyard as though to take some refreshment, and diverted him from his judgment.

He released Menelaus, who was guilty of every kind of wickedness, from the charges; but he condemned to death the wretched men who, even if they had pleaded their case before the Scythians, would have been judged innocent.

Thus those who had prosecuted the case on behalf of the city, the people, and the sacred vessels quickly received an unjust punishment.

For this reason the Tyrians too were indignant and showed the greatest generosity toward their burial.

Menelaus, however, because of the greed of those in power, remained in authority, growing in wickedness and plotting against his fellow citizens.

## CHAPTER V

At the same time Antiochus prepared a second expedition into Egypt.

For forty days throughout the city of Jerusalem, horsemen were seen racing through the air, wearing golden robes and armed with spears as though they were military units.

There were also races of horses arranged in ranks, close combat, the movement of shields, crowds of helmeted men with drawn swords, volleys of missiles, the gleam of golden armor, and every kind of breastplate.

Therefore everyone prayed that the portents might turn out favorably.

But when a false report arose that Antiochus had died, Jason, taking no fewer than a thousand men, suddenly attacked the city. As the citizens rushed to the wall, he finally seized the city, while Menelaus fled into the citadel.

Jason did not spare his own citizens in the slaughter, nor did he consider that prosperity against one’s relatives is the greatest evil. He imagined that he was erecting trophies over enemies rather than citizens.

[Col. 0509C] He did not obtain the office; instead, he received confusion as the end of his plots and fled once more into the Ammonite region.

Finally, enclosed for destruction by Aretas, the Arab tyrant, and fleeing from city to city, hated by everyone as a deserter from the laws and accursed as an enemy of his fellow citizens and fatherland, he was driven out into Egypt.

The man who had expelled many from their homeland perished abroad, having gone to Lacedaemon, as though he would find refuge there on account of his kinship.

The man who had cast many away unburied was himself cast away unwept and unburied, obtaining neither a foreign burial nor a share in his ancestral tomb.

After these events, the king suspected that the Jews would abandon their allegiance. For this reason, leaving Egypt in a rage, he seized the city by force of arms.

He ordered the soldiers to kill and spare no one whom they encountered, and to slaughter those they found by going up through the houses.

There were therefore massacres of young men and old men, destruction of women and children, and killings of virgins and infants.

In the course of three days, eighty thousand were killed, forty thousand were bound, and no fewer were sold into slavery.

Nor was this enough for him. He dared also to enter the temple, the holiest place on earth, with Menelaus as his guide, the betrayer of the laws and of his homeland.

With his criminal hands he took the sacred vessels that other kings and cities had deposited to adorn the place and enhance its glory; he handled them disgracefully and defiled them.

Thus Antiochus, deranged in mind, did not consider that God had been angered only briefly because of the sins of those who inhabited the city, and that this was why contempt had befallen the place.

Otherwise, if they had not been entangled in many sins, he too, like Heliodorus, who had been sent by King Seleucus to plunder the treasury, would certainly have been scourged and driven back immediately upon arriving, punished for his audacity.

[Col. 0510A] Yet God did not choose the place because of the nation, but the nation because of the place.

Therefore the place itself became a participant in the people’s misfortunes; afterward it will become a companion of their blessings, and the place that was abandoned in the anger of almighty God will again be exalted with the greatest glory when the great Lord is reconciled with it.

Antiochus, after taking one thousand eight hundred talents from the temple, quickly returned to Antioch, imagining in his arrogance that he would make the land navigable and the sea passable as a road because of the exaltation of his mind.

He also left governors to afflict the people: in Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by birth and more savage in character than the man who had appointed him;

and in Garizim, Andronicus and Menelaus, who oppressed the citizens more harshly than the others.

When he was set against the Jews, he sent the detested commander Apollonius with an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering him to kill all males of full age and to sell the women and young men.

When Apollonius came to Jerusalem, he pretended to be at peace and waited until the holy Sabbath. Then, while the Jews were resting, he ordered his own men to take up their arms.

He slaughtered all who had come out to watch and, moving through the city with armed men, killed an immense multitude.

Judas Maccabaeus, who was the tenth, had withdrawn to a deserted place. There he and his companions lived in the mountains among wild animals, eating grass, so as not to share in the defilement.

## CHAPTER VI

Not long afterward, the king sent an old man from Antioch to compel the Jews to abandon the laws of their ancestors and of God.

He was also to defile the temple in Jerusalem and rename it the temple of Olympian Zeus; and in Garizim, in accordance with those who inhabited the place, the temple of hospitable Zeus.

The onslaught of evils was exceedingly bad and grievous to everyone.

For the temple was filled with the luxury and feasting of the nations, and with men consorting with prostitutes; and women forced their way into the sacred buildings, bringing in things that were not permitted.

The altar too was full of unlawful things prohibited by the laws.

The Sabbaths were not observed, the ancestral feast days were not kept, and no one openly confessed himself to be a Jew.

Under bitter compulsion they were led to sacrifices on the king’s birthday; and when the rites of Liber were celebrated, they were forced to wear ivy crowns and go in procession around in honor of Liber.

A decree was issued to the neighboring Gentile cities, at the urging of the Ptolemies, that they too should act in the same way against the Jews and offer sacrifices.

[Col. 0510D] Those who refused to adopt the customs of the nations were to be killed. It was therefore possible to see misery everywhere.

Two women were brought forward for having circumcised their infants. After the children had been hung at their breasts and the women had been led publicly through the city, they threw them down from the walls.

Others gathered in nearby caves and secretly celebrated the Sabbath. When they were reported to Philip, they were burned in the flames, because, out of reverence for their religion and observance, they were afraid to defend themselves with their hands.

I ask those who are about to read this book not to recoil because of the calamities, but to consider that what happened was not for the destruction but for the correction of our people.

For it is a sign of great beneficence not to allow sinners to act according to their own will for a long time, but to inflict punishment upon them immediately.

[Col. 0511A] For the Lord does not, as with other nations, patiently wait until, when the day of judgment has arrived, he may punish them when their sins have reached their full measure;

so also he has determined that, when our sins have reached their culmination, he will at last take vengeance upon us.

Therefore he never removes his mercy from us; rather, while correcting his people through adversity, he does not abandon them.

But let these things suffice as a brief admonition to us readers. Now, however, we must return to the narrative.

Accordingly, Eleazar, one of the foremost scribes, an advanced man in years and handsome in appearance, was compelled, with his mouth forced open, to eat pork.

But he, embracing a most glorious death rather than a hateful life, willingly went forward to the punishment.

Considering how he ought to approach it and patiently enduring it, he resolved not to admit what was unlawful for the sake of life.

Those standing by, however, moved by a wicked pity and because of their long-standing friendship with the man, took him aside [Col. 0511B] and secretly urged him to have meat brought that he was permitted to eat, so that he might pretend to have eaten, as the king had ordered, meat from the sacrifice:

so that, by doing this, he might be freed from death. Because of their old friendship with the man, they were showing him this kindness.

But he began to reflect upon the dignity appropriate to his age and old age, upon the gray hair of his inborn nobility, and upon the conduct of his life from childhood onward, which had been exemplary. In accordance with the ordinances of the holy law established by God, he answered at once, saying that he wished to be sent ahead into the underworld.

“For it is not worthy of our age,” he said, “to pretend, so that many young people, thinking that Eleazar at ninety years of age had turned to the life of foreigners,

might themselves, because of my pretense and for the sake of a brief period of corruptible life, be led astray, and thereby I might bring disgrace and condemnation upon my old age.

[Col. 0511C] For even if I escape the punishments of human beings in the present time, I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, whether alive or dead.

Therefore, by departing bravely from life, I shall appear worthy of my old age;

and I shall leave the young a noble example, if with a ready spirit and courage I undergo an honorable death for the sake of the most grave and holy laws.”

After saying these things, he was immediately dragged away to the punishment.

Those who were leading him, though shortly before they had been more lenient, were turned to anger because of the words he had spoken, which they considered to have been uttered through arrogance.

But as he was being killed by blows, he groaned and said: “Lord, who possesses holy knowledge, you clearly know that, although I could have been freed from death, I endure severe bodily pains; but in my soul, because of fear of you, I gladly suffer these things.”

And in this manner he departed from life, leaving behind not only for the young but also for the whole nation the memory of his death [Col. 0511D] as an example of virtue and courage.

## CHAPTER VII

It also happened that seven brothers, together with their mother, were arrested and compelled by the king to eat pork contrary to the law, being tortured with whips and ox-hide thongs.

One of them, who was the eldest, said: “What are you seeking, and what do you wish to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the ancestral laws of God.”

The king, therefore, became angry and ordered frying pans and bronze cauldrons to be heated. When they had immediately been heated,

he ordered the tongue of the one who had spoken first to be cut out; and, after the skin of his head had been stripped away, the ends of his hands and feet were also cut off while his other brothers and his mother looked on.

And when he had already been rendered wholly useless, he ordered fire to be brought near and the man, still breathing, to be roasted in the frying pan. While he was being tortured there for a long time, the others, together with their mother, encouraged one another to die bravely,

[Col. 0512A] saying: “The Lord God will look upon the truth and will comfort us, just as Moses declared in the proclamation of his song: ‘And he will be comforted in his servants.’”

After the first one had died, they led the next in the same manner to mock him. After the skin of his head, together with his hair, had been stripped away, they asked whether he would eat before being punished throughout his whole body, limb by limb.

But he answered in the ancestral language: “I will not.” Therefore this man also, in the next place, suffered the tortures of the first.

And when he was at his final breath, he said: “You, most wicked man, destroy us in the present life; but the King of the world will raise us who have died for his laws to the resurrection of eternal life.”

After him the third was mocked. When ordered to do so, he quickly put out his tongue and steadfastly extended his hands.

And he said with confidence: “I possess these limbs from heaven, but for the sake of God’s laws I now despise them, because I hope to receive them back from him.”

[Col. 0512B] Thus the king and those who were with him marveled at the young man’s spirit, because he regarded the tortures as nothing.

After he too had died in this manner, they tortured the fourth in the same way.

And when he was already near death, he said: “It is better to await hope from God, having been put to death by human beings, trusting that we shall be raised again by him; but for you there will be no resurrection to life.”

When they brought forward the fifth, they tortured him. But he looked at him

and said: “Although you possess power among human beings and, being corruptible, do whatever you wish, do not think that our race has been abandoned by God.

But wait patiently, and you will see his great power, how he will torture you and your offspring.”

After him they led away the sixth. As he began to die, he said: “Do not err without cause. We suffer these things because of our own sins against our God, and things worthy of wonder have taken place among us.

But do not suppose that you will escape punishment for having attempted to fight against God.”

The mother, however, was extraordinarily admirable and worthy of honorable remembrance. As she watched her seven sons perish within the space of a single day, she bore it with good courage because of the hope she had in God.

She encouraged each of them in the ancestral language, filled with wisdom, and, implanting masculine courage in her womanly reasoning,

she said to them: “I do not know how you appeared in my womb; for I did not give you spirit and soul, nor did I myself put together the life and limbs of each of you.

But the Creator of the world, who formed the birth of humankind and discovered the origin of all things, will in his mercy restore spirit and life to you again, just as now you despise yourselves for the sake of his laws.”

Antiochus, believing that he was being despised, and at the same time provoked by the contemptuous voice of the one reproaching him, while the youngest son still remained, encouraged him not only with words but also solemnly affirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and happy, that he would regard him as a friend if he abandoned the laws of his ancestors, and that he would provide him with whatever he needed.

But when the young man was in no way inclined toward these promises, the king summoned the mother and urged her to advise the young man for his salvation.

After he had urged her at length, she promised that she would persuade her son.

Accordingly, having apparently yielded to this, she mocked the cruel tyrant and said in the ancestral language: “My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, nursed you for three years, nourished you, and brought you to this age.

I beg you, my child, look toward heaven and earth and all that is in them, and understand that God made these things and the human race from nothing.

Thus it will happen that you will not fear this executioner, but, having become worthy of your brothers, receive death, so that in [Col. 0513A] that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers [Al. ‘he may receive you’].”

While she was still saying these things, the young man said: “Whom are you waiting for? I do not obey the king’s command, but the command of the law that was given to us through Moses.

But you, who have become the inventor of every evil against the Hebrews, will not escape the hand of God.

For we suffer these things because of our sins.

And if the Lord our God has been angry with us for a little while because of admonition and correction, he will again be reconciled with his servants.

But you, wicked man and most disgraceful of all human beings, do not foolishly exalt yourself through empty hopes while inflamed against his servants.

For you have not yet escaped the judgment of the omnipotent God, who sees all things.

My brothers, having endured a little pain for a short time, have been established under the covenant of eternal life; but you will pay the just penalties for your arrogance at God’s judgment.

I, like my brothers, surrender my soul and body [Col. 0513B] for the ancestral laws, calling upon God to become merciful more quickly to our nation, and that, amid torments and blows, you may confess that he alone is God.

But in me and in my brothers the wrath of the Almighty will cease, which has justly come upon our whole race [Al. ‘our whole people’].”

Then the king, inflamed with anger, raged against him more cruelly than against all the others, unable to bear that he had been mocked.

And this one also died pure, trusting entirely in the Lord.

Finally, after her sons, the mother too was put to death.

Thus enough has been said about the sacrifices and the excessive cruelties.

## CHAPTER VIII

Judas Maccabeus and those who were with him secretly entered the fortified places. Calling together their relatives and friends, and taking with them those who had remained in Judaism, [Col. 0513C] they brought together six thousand men.

They called upon the Lord to look upon the people who were being trampled by everyone and to have mercy on the temple, which was being polluted by the impious.

They also prayed that he would have mercy on the destruction of the city, which was about to be leveled at once, and hear the voice of the blood crying out to him.

They asked him also to remember the most wicked deaths of innocent children, the blasphemies uttered against his name, and to become indignant over these things.

But when Maccabeus had gathered a multitude, he became unbearable to the nations, for the Lord’s anger had been turned into mercy.

Coming suddenly upon fortresses and cities, he set them on fire; and, occupying strategic positions, he inflicted no small slaughter upon the enemy.

He was especially inclined to such raids by night, and the fame of his courage spread everywhere.

When Philip saw the man gradually advancing to success and observed that matters were more frequently turning out well for him, he wrote to Ptolemy, commander of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, asking him to bring assistance to the king’s affairs.

The latter quickly sent Nicanor, son of Patroclus, one of his foremost friends, [Note: [Col. 0513] Some books prefer *datis*; in the Greek, however, it is *ὑποτάξας* (“having subjected” or “having placed under his command”).] giving him no fewer than twenty thousand armed men drawn from the various nations, so that he might destroy the entire Jewish race. Gorgias, a military man and highly experienced in warfare, was also assigned to him.

Nicanor determined to raise from the captivity of the Jews the two thousand talents of tribute that was owed to the Romans by the king.

Immediately he sent to the coastal cities, calling them to purchase Jewish slaves, promising to sell ninety slaves for a talent, without considering the vengeance that would overtake him from the Almighty.

[Col. 0514A] When Judas learned of this, he informed the Jews who were with him of Nicanor’s arrival.

Some of them, being afraid and not trusting in God’s justice, turned to flight.

Others sold whatever they had left to him [Al. ‘to them’], while at the same time entreating the Lord to rescue them from the wicked Nicanor, who had sold them before he came face to face with them.

And if not for their sake, then at least for the sake of the covenant made with their fathers, and for the invocation of his holy and glorious name over them.

Maccabeus gathered seven thousand of those who were with him and urged them not to make peace with the enemies or fear the multitude of the enemies who were coming unjustly against them, but to contend bravely.

They were to keep before their eyes the insult unjustly inflicted by these men upon the holy place, as well as the injury done to the city that had been treated as a laughingstock, and the further overturning of the ancient institutions.

“They,” he said, “trust in weapons and also in boldness; [Col. 0514B] but we trust in the omnipotent Lord, who by a single nod can destroy both those who come against us and the whole world.

He also reminded them of the assistance God had given their ancestors, and that in the time of Sennacherib one hundred and eighty-five thousand had perished.

He reminded them also of the battle they had fought against the Galatians in Babylonia: when the matter came to the point and their Macedonian allies hesitated, they themselves, only six thousand in number, destroyed one hundred and twenty thousand, because assistance had been given them from heaven, and afterward received many benefits in return.

Strengthened by these words, they became ready to die for the laws and the fatherland.

He appointed his brothers commanders over the two divisions: Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan, assigning fifteen hundred men to each.

After the sacred book had also been read to them by Ezra and the sign of God’s assistance had been given, he himself, as commander of the first line, engaged Nicanor.

[Col. 0514C] With the Almighty as their ally, they killed more than nine thousand men. They compelled the greater part of Nicanor’s army, weakened by wounds, to flee.

After taking the money of those who had come to purchase them, they pursued them everywhere.

But they returned when the hour was late, for it was before the Sabbath. For this reason they did not continue the pursuit.

They gathered their weapons and spoils and kept the Sabbath, blessing the Lord who had delivered them on that day and allowed the beginning of mercy to fall upon them.

After the Sabbath, they distributed the spoils among the wounded, orphans, and widows; the remainder they and their men kept.

After these events, and after all had joined in supplication, they asked the merciful Lord to be reconciled with his servants to the end.

Of those who were with Timothy and Bacchides and had fought against them, they killed more than twenty thousand [Col. 0514D] and captured high fortifications. They divided many spoils in equal portions among the weak, orphans, and widows, and also made provision for the elderly.

After carefully collecting their weapons, they stored everything in suitable places; the remaining spoils they carried to Jerusalem.

They also killed Philarchus, who had been with Timothy, a wicked man who had afflicted the Jews in many ways.

When they celebrated their victory in Jerusalem, they burned Callisthenes—the man who had set fire to the sacred gates—after he had taken refuge in a certain house, repaying him with a fitting reward for his impieties.

The most criminal Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants to purchase the Jews,

having been humbled by the Lord’s assistance at the hands of those whom he had considered worthless, [Col. 0515A] laid aside his splendid garment and, fleeing through the interior, came alone to Antioch, having incurred the greatest misery through the destruction of his army.

And the man who had promised the Romans that he would pay their tribute from the captives of Jerusalem now proclaimed that the Jews had God as their protector and that, because of him, they were invulnerable, since they followed the laws established by him.

## CHAPTER IX

At the same time Antiochus was returning dishonorably from Persia.

For he had entered what is called Persepolis and attempted to plunder the temple and oppress the city. But when the multitude rushed to arms, they were put to flight, and thus it happened that Antiochus returned shamefully after his flight.

When he came near Ecbatana, he learned what had happened to Nicanor and Timothy.

Inflamed with anger, he thought that he could turn against the Jews the injury inflicted by those who had driven him to flight. [Col. 0515B] Therefore he ordered his chariot to be driven and pressed on without interruption, being driven forward by heavenly judgment, because he had spoken so arrogantly, saying that he would come to Jerusalem and make it a mass grave for the Jews.

But the Lord God of Israel, who sees all things, struck him with an incurable and invisible disease. As soon as he had finished these very words, a dreadful pain seized his bowels and bitter torments of his inner organs.

And this was entirely just, since he had tortured the bowels of many others with new and varied tortures, although he in no way ceased from his own wickedness.

Moreover, filled with arrogance and breathing fire in his spirit against the Jews, and ordering the business to be hastened, it happened that, as he was rushing along, he fell from his chariot, and his limbs were tormented by the violent impact upon his body.

He who had imagined that he could command even the waves of the sea, filled with arrogance beyond human measure, and who had weighed the heights of mountains in a balance, was now humbled to the ground and carried in a litter, bearing clear witness in his own person to the power of God.

[Col. 0515C] Thus worms poured forth from the body of the impious man, and his flesh, while he was still alive and in pain, fell away; his army was also oppressed by his stench and foul odor.

And no one could carry him because of the intolerable stench—him who shortly before had imagined that he touched the stars of heaven.

From this point, brought down from his great arrogance, he began to come to knowledge of himself, instructed by the divine scourge, as his pains increased from moment to moment.

When he could no longer endure even his own stench, he said: “It is right to be subject to God, and that a mortal should not think himself equal to God.”

This wicked man prayed to the Lord, from whom he was not going to obtain mercy.

And the city to which he had been hurrying in order to reduce it to the ground and make it a mass grave, he now desired to set free.

And the Jews whom he had said he would not even consider worthy of burial, but would hand over to birds and wild beasts to be devoured, and would destroy together with their children, he now promised to make equal to the Athenians [Col. 0515D].

He also promised to adorn the holy temple, which he had previously plundered, with the finest gifts, to multiply the sacred vessels, and to provide from his own revenues the expenses pertaining to the sacrifices.

In addition to these things, he promised that he would become a Jew, travel through every inhabited region of the earth, and proclaim the power of God.

But since the pains did not cease—for the just judgment of God had come upon him—he wrote in despair to the Jews, in the form of a supplication, a letter containing the following:

“King and ruler Antiochus sends abundant greetings to the excellent citizens, the Jews, and wishes them health and happiness.

[Col. 0516A] If you are well, and your children, and everything is proceeding according to your wishes, we give the greatest thanks.

And I, being in sickness, but remembering you kindly, having returned from the regions of Persia and been seized by a serious illness, have considered it necessary to take thought for the common welfare.

Not despairing of myself, but having great hope of escaping this illness,

I have considered that my father also, whenever he led the army in the upper regions, indicated who would succeed him in the rule,

so that, if anything contrary happened or difficult news were announced, those in the provinces, knowing to whom supreme authority had been left, would not be thrown into confusion.

Furthermore, considering the powerful men nearby, and those neighboring rulers who were lying in wait and awaiting the outcome, I have designated my son Antiochus as king. I often commended him to many of you when I was returning to the upper kingdoms, and I have written to him what follows.

I therefore ask and entreat you, remembering the benefits bestowed publicly [Col. 0516B] and privately, that each of you preserve loyalty toward me and toward my son.

For I trust that he will act with moderation and humanity, follow my purpose, and be well disposed toward you all.”

Thus the murderer and blasphemer, struck down most grievously and treated as he had treated others, died a miserable death in a foreign land among the mountains.

His foster-brother Philip was transporting his body. Fearing Antiochus’s son, he went to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.

## CHAPTER X

Maccabeus and those who were with him, while the Lord protected them, recovered the temple and the city.

He demolished the altars that foreigners had erected in the streets, as well as the shrines.

After purifying the temple, they made another altar. From stones that had been burned, they kindled fire and offered sacrifices after two years; they also placed incense, lamps, and the bread of the Presence [Col. 0516C].

After these things had been done, they prostrated themselves on the ground and prayed to the Lord that they might not again fall into such evils, but that, if they should ever sin, they might be corrected more gently by him and not handed over to barbarous and blasphemous men.

On the day on which the temple had been polluted by foreigners, its purification took place on that same day, the twenty-fifth day of the month of Casleu.

They celebrated with joy for eight days, in the manner of the Feast of Booths, remembering that shortly before they had spent the solemn feast of Booths in the mountains and caves like wild animals.

Therefore they carried thyrsi, green boughs, and palms before the one who had prospered the cleansing of his place.

By common command and decree they resolved that the entire Jewish nation should celebrate these days every year.

Such, then, was the end of the life of Antiochus, who was called the Noble.

Now we shall relate what happened concerning Eupator, the impious Antiochus’s son, briefly passing over the evils that occurred in the wars.

For when he had received the kingdom, he appointed a certain Lysias over the affairs of the kingdom, as commander of the forces of Phoenicia and Syria.

Ptolemy, who was called Macer, was steadfast in justice and determined to be well disposed toward the Jews, especially because of the injustice that had been done to them, and to deal peacefully with them.

But when he was accused before Eupator by his friends [Note: [Col. 0515] The Greek likewise reads *ὑπὸ τῶν φίλων*, “by friends”; other standard books have “by enemies.”], and frequently heard himself called a traitor because he had abandoned Cyprus, which had been entrusted to him by Philometor, and, after transferring to Antiochus the Noble, had also withdrawn from him, he ended his life by poison.

Gorgias, however, who was commander of the region, took foreign troops and repeatedly fought against the Jews.

[Col. 0517A] The Jews who held strategic fortifications received those who had been driven from Jerusalem and attempted to wage war.

Those who were with Maccabeus, entreating the Lord in prayer to be their helper, attacked the fortifications of the Idumeans.

They pressed forward with great force, captured the positions, killed those who came against them, and slaughtered altogether no fewer than twenty thousand.

Some, however, had fled into two very strongly fortified towers, possessing every provision for resistance.

Maccabeus, leaving Simon, Joseph, and Zacchaeus, together with a considerable number of those who were with them, to attack them, turned himself to the battles that were pressing more urgently elsewhere.

Those who were with Simon, led by greed, were persuaded by certain men in the towers and, after receiving seventy thousand didrachmas, allowed some of them to escape.

When Maccabeus was informed of what had happened, [Col. 0517B] he assembled the leaders of the people and accused them of having sold their brothers for money by releasing their adversaries.

He therefore killed these men, who had become traitors, and immediately captured the two towers.

By arms and by hand, he prospered in everything and killed more than twenty thousand in the two fortifications.

Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, gathered an army of foreign peoples and assembled Asian cavalry. He arrived as though he intended to capture Judea by force of arms.

When Maccabeus and those who were with him saw him approaching, they entreated the Lord, sprinkling dust upon their heads and girding their loins with sackcloth.

They threw themselves down at the base of the altar, asking that he be merciful to them, hostile to their enemies, and opposed to their adversaries, as the law says.

After the prayer, they took up arms, advanced some distance from the city, and, having come near the enemy, halted.

At sunrise the two sides engaged. [Col. 0517C] The Jews had the mighty Lord as the guarantor of victory and success; the others possessed a warlike spirit as their commander.

But while the battle was fierce, five men appeared to the adversaries from heaven, riding horses adorned with golden bridles and giving leadership to the Jews.

Two of them, taking Maccabeus between them and surrounding him with their weapons, kept him safe; against the enemy they hurled weapons and thunderbolts. As a result, the enemy were both blinded and thrown into confusion, and they fell.

Twenty thousand five hundred men and six hundred cavalrymen were killed.

Timothy, however, fled to Gazara, a fortified stronghold commanded by Chereas.

Maccabeus and those who were with him besieged the stronghold joyfully for four days.

Those inside, trusting in the strength of the place, cursed excessively and hurled wicked words and blasphemies.

But when the fifth day dawned, twenty young men from [Col. 0517D] among those who were with Maccabeus, inflamed in spirit because of the blasphemy, bravely approached the wall and climbed it with fierce courage.

Others also climbed in the same way and began to set fire to the towers and gates, and to burn alive those blasphemers themselves.

After the stronghold had been devastated over the course of two days, they killed Timothy, who was hiding in a certain place they had discovered, as well as his brother Chereas and Apollophanes.

After these events, they blessed the Lord in hymns and confessions, because he had done great things in Israel and given them victory.

## CHAPTER XI

But shortly afterward Lysias, the king’s administrator and kinsman, and governor of affairs, was deeply angered by what had happened.

[Col. 0518A] Gathering eighty thousand men and all the cavalry, he came against the Jews, supposing that he would make the captured city a dwelling place for the nations,

and that he would turn the temple into a source of profit, as with the other shrines of the nations, and sell the priesthood year by year.

He gave no thought at all to the power of God, but, with his mind unrestrained, trusted in the multitude of infantry, the thousands of cavalry, and eighty elephants.

After entering Judea and approaching Bethsura, which lay in a narrow place five stadia from Jerusalem, he attacked that stronghold.

When Maccabeus and those who were with him learned that the strongholds were being attacked, they prayed to the Lord with weeping and tears, and the whole multitude prayed together that he would send a good angel for the salvation of Israel.

Maccabeus himself first took up arms and urged the others to share the danger with him and bring aid to their brothers.

As they advanced together with ready courage, [Col. 0518B] a horseman appeared from Jerusalem, going before them, dressed in white and, in golden armor, brandishing a spear.

Then they all together blessed the merciful Lord and took courage, ready not only to penetrate the fiercest beasts but even iron walls.

Thus they went forth eagerly, having an assistant from heaven and the Lord showing mercy to them.

Rushing upon the enemy like lions, they struck down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred cavalrymen.

They put them all to flight; many of them, wounded and naked, escaped. Lysias himself also escaped by fleeing shamefully.

Because he was not senseless, he reflected within himself upon the defeat that had befallen him and understood that the Hebrews were invincible because they relied upon the help of the omnipotent God. He therefore sent to them

and promised that he would agree to everything that was just [Col. 0518C] and compel the king to become their friend.

Maccabeus accepted Lysias’s requests, having regard in every respect for their welfare. Whatever Maccabeus wrote to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king granted.

For Lysias had written a letter to the Jews containing the following:

“Lysias sends greetings to the people of the Jews.

Joannes and Abesalom, who were sent by you, delivered documents and requested that I carry out what was conveyed through them.

Whatever, therefore, could be brought before the king, I have presented; and whatever the circumstances allowed, he granted [Al. ‘I granted’].

If, therefore, you preserve your loyalty in these matters, I shall henceforth try to be a cause of good things for you.

Concerning the rest, I have given instructions individually, both to these men and to those sent by me, to confer with you. [Note: [Col. 0517] Other standard books omit the words “both to these men,” which are nevertheless in the Greek: *τούτοις τε καὶ τοῖς παρ’ ἐμοῦ*, etc.]

Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the twenty-fourth day of the month Dioscorus.”

The king’s letter contained the following:

“King Antiochus sends greetings to his brother Lysias.

After our father was transferred among the gods, and we desire those who are in our kingdom to live without disturbance and to attend diligently to their own affairs,

we have learned that the Jews did not agree with my father that they should be transferred to Greek rites, but wished to retain their own institution and therefore asked us to grant them their lawful customs.

Therefore, desiring that this nation also should be at peace, we have decided and decreed that the temple be restored to them, so that they may live according to the custom of their ancestors.

You will therefore do well if you send to them and give them your right hand, so that, having learned our will, they may be of good courage and attend to their own interests.”

The king’s letter to the Jews was as follows:

“King Antiochus sends greetings to the senate of the Jews and to the other Jews.

[Col. 0519A] If you are well, that is as we wish; we too are well.

Menelaus came to us and said that you wished to go down to your people who are with us.

Accordingly, to those who travel until the thirtieth day of the month Xanthicus, we give guarantees of security.

The Jews may use their own foods and laws, as previously, and none of them shall in any way suffer harassment because of what was done through ignorance.

We have also sent Menelaus to confer with you.

Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus.”

The Romans also sent a letter, which read as follows:

“Quintus Memmius and Titus Manilius, envoys of the Romans, send greetings to the people of the Jews.

What Lysias, the king’s kinsman, has granted you, we too have granted.

Concerning whatever he judged should be referred to the king, send someone immediately, after conferring carefully among yourselves, [Col. 0519B] so that we may decide as is appropriate for you. For we are going to Antioch.

Therefore hasten to write back, so that we too may know what your wishes are.

Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus.”

## CHAPTER XII

After these agreements had been made, Lysias went on to the king, while the Jews devoted themselves to agriculture.

But those who had remained—Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, and also Hieronymus and Demophon, as well as Nicanor the Cypriarch—did not allow them to live in quiet and peace.

The people of Joppa committed a crime of this kind: they asked the Jews who lived among them to board boats that they had prepared, together with their wives and children, as though no hostility existed between them.

In accordance, therefore, with the common decree of the city, and while the Jews themselves consented and suspected nothing because of the supposed peace, [Col. 0519C] when they had gone out into the open sea, the Joppaeans drowned no fewer than two hundred of them.

When Judas learned of this cruelty perpetrated against men of his own nation, he commanded the men who were with him; and, after invoking God as the just judge,

he came against the murderers of his brothers. He set fire to the harbor at night and burned the boats; those who had escaped the fire he killed with the sword.

After doing this, he departed as though he would return again and uproot all the people of Joppa.

But when he learned that those in Jamnia also intended to act in the same way toward the Jews living among them,

he likewise came upon the people of Jamnia by night and set fire to the harbor and the ships, so that the light of the fire could be seen from Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.

From there, after they had gone nine stadia and were proceeding toward Timothy, five thousand Arab men and five hundred cavalry engaged them.

When the battle became fierce and, through God’s assistance, turned out favorably, [Col. 0519D] the remaining Arabs, having been defeated, asked Judas to give them his right hand, promising to provide pasture and to be useful in other matters.

Judas, judging that they would truly be useful in many respects, promised peace; and after the right hands had been exchanged, they departed to their tents.

He also attacked a certain strongly fortified city, surrounded by bridges and walls, inhabited by a mixed multitude of nations, whose name was Casphin.

Those inside, trusting in the stability of the walls and the store of provisions, acted carelessly, provoking Judas with curses, blaspheming, and saying things that were unlawful.

Maccabeus, however, invoked the great Ruler of the world, who in the time of Joshua caused Jericho to fall without battering rams or siege engines, and furiously attacked the walls.

By the will of the Lord he captured the city and caused innumerable slaughter, so that the adjoining pond, two stadia [Col. 0520A] in width, seemed to flow with the blood of those who had been killed.

From there they departed seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Characa, to the Jews who are called Tubianites.

They did not capture Timothy in those regions; and, having accomplished nothing, he returned, leaving a very strong garrison in a certain place.

Dositheus and Sosipater, commanders who were with Maccabeus, killed the ten thousand men whom Timothy had left in the garrison.

Maccabeus, having arranged six thousand men around him and organized them by cohorts, advanced against Timothy, who had with him one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

When Timothy learned of Judas’s arrival, he sent the women, the children, and the remaining baggage ahead to the stronghold called Carnion, for it was impregnable and difficult to approach because of the narrowness of the surrounding places.

When Judas’s first cohort appeared, fear fell upon the enemy through the presence of God, who sees all things. [Col. 0520B] They turned to flight, each one away from the other, so that they were struck down more by their own men and weakened by the blows of their own swords.

But Judas pressed on vigorously, punishing the profane, and struck down thirty thousand of them.

Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, and with many entreaties begged to be released alive, since he had many relatives and brothers among the Jews, who would be deceived by his death.

When he had given his assurance that he would restore them according to the agreement, they released him unharmed for the sake of his brothers’ safety.

Judas then marched out against Carnion, having killed twenty-five thousand men.

After their flight and slaughter, he moved his army against the fortified city of Ephron, in which a multitude of people of various nations lived. Sturdy young men stood upon the walls and fought bravely; and the city contained many siege machines and a supply of missiles.

[Col. 0520C] But when they had invoked the Almighty, who by his power shatters the strength of enemies, they captured the city; and of those who were inside they struck down twenty-five thousand.

From there they went to the city of Scythopolis, which was six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.

The Jews who were in the territory of the Scythopolitans testified that the people there had treated them kindly, even in times of misfortune, and had dealt moderately with them.

Giving them thanks, and exhorting them also henceforth to show kindness toward their people, they came to Jerusalem as the solemn day of Weeks was approaching.

After Pentecost they went out against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.

He came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.

When they engaged them, it happened that a few of the Jews fell.

But a certain Dositheus, a horseman of the Bacenorites and a brave man, seized Gorgias. When he wished to capture him alive, a certain Thracian horseman rushed upon him and severed his shoulder; thus Gorgias escaped to Maresa.

While those who were with Esdrin were fighting for a longer time and had become exhausted, Judas invoked the Lord to be their helper and commander in battle.
