He began in his native language, and, raising a cry with hymns, threw Gorgias’s soldiers into flight. Judas then gathered his army and came to the city of Odollam. When the seventh day arrived, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the Sabbath in that place.

On the following day Judas came with his men to take up the bodies of those who had fallen and place them with their relatives in their ancestral tombs.

They found beneath the tunics of the slain votive offerings of idols that were at Jamnia, from which the Law forbids Jews. Thus it became clear to everyone that this was the reason they had fallen.

Accordingly, they all blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest.

[Col. 0521A] Then they turned to prayer and begged that what had happened might be blotted out as a sin. But the very valiant Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves free from sin, since they saw before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who had fallen.

After taking up a collection, he sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to have a sacrifice offered for the sins of the dead, thinking well and devoutly about the resurrection.

(For if he had not hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead.)

And because he considered that those who had fallen asleep in godliness had a splendid reward laid up for them:

Therefore it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins.

## CHAPTER XIII

In the one hundred and forty-ninth year Judas learned that Antiochus Eupator was coming with a great multitude against [Col. 0521B] Judea,

and with him Lysias, the governor and administrator of affairs, who had with him one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand cavalry, [Alternative: *et* omitted] twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots fitted with scythes.

Menelaus also joined them. With great deceitfulness he pleaded with Antiochus, not hoping for the safety of his country but hoping to be appointed to a position of authority.

But the King of kings stirred up Antiochus’s anger against the sinner. When Lysias suggested that this man was the cause of all their troubles, he ordered him—as was their custom—to be seized and killed on the spot.

There was in that place a tower fifty cubits high, with a mound of ashes all around it; it overlooked a precipice.

From there he ordered the sacrilegious man to be thrown into the ashes, with everyone pushing him toward destruction.

Thus the transgressor of the Law was made to die by such a law, and Menelaus was not given burial in the earth.

[Col. 0521C] And quite justly so: since he had committed many offenses against the altar of God, whose fire and ashes were holy, he himself was condemned to death among the ashes.

But the king, unrestrained in mind, was coming, intending to show himself to the Jews more wicked than his father.

When Judas learned this, he ordered the people to invoke the Lord day and night, asking him—as always, and now also—to help them,

since they feared being deprived of the Law, the homeland, and the holy Temple, and feared that he would not allow the people, who had only recently breathed a little, to be subjected again to blasphemous nations.

While all were doing this together and asking the Lord for mercy with weeping and fasting, prostrated continuously for three days, Judas encouraged them to prepare themselves.

He himself, together with the elders, considered that before the king brought his army against Judea and captured the city, they should go out and entrust the outcome of the matter to the judgment of the Lord.

Thus giving all power to God, the Creator of the world, and exhorting his men to fight bravely and stand unto death for the laws, the Temple, the city, the homeland, and the citizens, he stationed the army near Modin.

After giving his men the sign of God’s victory and choosing the bravest young men, he attacked the royal camp by night and killed four thousand men there, along with the largest of the elephants and those who were upon it.

Filling the enemy camp with the greatest fear and confusion, and having succeeded, they withdrew.

This happened at daybreak, with the Lord’s protection assisting him.

But the king, having had a taste of the Jews’ courage, attempted by strategy to overcome the difficulty of the terrain.

He brought his camp against Bethsura, which was a fortified stronghold of the Jews; but he was driven back, stumbled, and was weakened.

Judas sent provisions to those who were inside.

A certain Rhodocus [Col. 0522A] from the Jewish army disclosed the secrets to the enemy; when investigated, he was seized and imprisoned.

Again the king addressed those who were in Bethsura: he gave his right hand; he received it; he departed.

He engaged Judas and was defeated. But when he learned that Philip, who had been left in charge of affairs, had rebelled at Antioch, he was thrown into confusion. He begged the Jews for peace, submitted to them, swore to everything that seemed just, was reconciled with them, offered sacrifice, honored the Temple, and presented gifts.

He embraced Maccabeus and appointed him commander and governor from Ptolemais to the Gerrenians.

When he came to Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais took the agreement of friendship very badly, indignantly fearing that the treaty might be broken.

Then Lysias ascended the tribunal, explained the situation, and calmed the people. He returned to Antioch, and in this way the king’s departure and return proceeded.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0522B] After a period of three years Judas and those with him learned that Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, had come with a strong army and ships, entering through the harbor of Tripolis and proceeding to suitable places.

He had occupied the regions against Antiochus and his commander Lysias.

Now a certain Alcimus, who had been high priest but had voluntarily defiled himself during the period of compromise, realizing that there was no means of salvation for him and no access to the altar,

came to King Demetrius in the one hundred and fiftieth year, offering him a golden crown, a palm branch, and, in addition, branches that seemed to belong to the Temple. On that very day he held his tongue.

When he found an opportune moment for his madness, he was summoned by Demetrius to the council and asked what means and policies the Jews relied upon.

He replied: “Those called the Hasideans of the Jews, led by Judas Maccabeus, are fomenting wars and stirring up rebellions; they do not allow the kingdom to remain at peace.

“For I too, deprived of the glory of my ancestors—that is, of the high priesthood—have come here.

“First, I remain faithful to the king’s interests; second, I also look after the citizens. For through the perversity of those men our entire people is suffering no little distress.

“But I beg you, O king, once you have learned these things, to take care, in accordance with your humanity known to all, both of the country and of our people.

“For as long as Judas survives, it is impossible for affairs to be at peace.”

After Alcimus had spoken in this way, the other friends, behaving with hostility toward Judas, inflamed Demetrius.

He immediately sent Nicanor, commander of the elephants, as leader into Judea,

ordering him to seize Judas himself, disperse those who were with him, and appoint Alcimus high priest of the greatest Temple.

[Col. 0522D] Then the nations that had fled Judas from Judea joined Nicanor in groups, considering the Jews’ miseries and disasters to be the prosperity of their own affairs.

When the Jews heard of Nicanor’s arrival and of the gathering of the nations, they covered themselves with dust and prayed to him who had established his people, that he would guard them forever, and who protects his own portion by evident signs.

At the commander’s order they immediately set out from there and assembled at the fortress of Dessau.

Simon, Judas’s brother, had engaged Nicanor, but was terrified by the sudden arrival of the adversaries.

Nevertheless, when Nicanor heard of the courage of Judas’s companions and the greatness of spirit that they possessed in the struggles for their homeland, he feared passing judgment by bloodshed.

Therefore he sent Posidonius, Theodosius [Alternative: Theodotius], and Mattathias ahead to exchange pledges and receive them.

After the matter had been discussed for a long time, and the commander himself had referred it to the multitude, everyone was of one opinion: to agree to friendship.

Accordingly, they appointed a day on which they would confer privately with one another; seats were brought out and set in place for each.

Judas ordered armed men to occupy suitable positions, lest something harmful should suddenly arise from the enemy; and they held an appropriate conference.

Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and did nothing unjust. He dismissed the crowds of people who had gathered.

He always held Judas dear in his heart and was favorably disposed toward the man.

He asked him to marry and beget children. Judas married, lived in peace, and they lived together as friends.

But when Alcimus saw their mutual affection and agreements, he came to Demetrius and said that Nicanor was consenting to another’s interests and that Judas, who was plotting against the kingdom, had appointed him as his successor.

Therefore the king, angered and provoked by these most wicked accusations, wrote to Nicanor, saying that he was indeed greatly displeased by the agreement of friendship, but nevertheless ordered him to send Maccabeus bound to Antioch as quickly as possible.

When Nicanor learned this, he was thrown into confusion and was deeply troubled that he should annul the agreements, since Judas had done him no harm.

But because he could not resist the king, he watched for an opportunity to carry out the order.

Maccabeus, seeing Nicanor behaving more harshly toward him and presenting his customary greeting more fiercely, understood that this harshness was not well intentioned. He gathered a few of his men and hid himself from Nicanor.

When Nicanor learned that the man had cleverly forestalled him, he came to the greatest and most holy Temple. While the priests were offering the customary sacrifices, he ordered them to hand over the man.

When they declared under oath that they did not know where the man being sought was, he stretched out his hand toward the Temple,

he swore, saying: “Unless you hand Judas over to me bound, I will level this sanctuary of God to the ground, tear up the altar, [Col. 0523C] and consecrate this Temple to Liber Pater.”

After saying this, he departed. But the priests, stretching out their hands toward heaven, invoked him who was always the defender of their nation, saying:

“You, Lord of all, who need nothing, have willed that the Temple of your dwelling should be among us.

“And now, holy Lord of all holiness, preserve forever undefiled this house which has recently been cleansed.”

Now a certain Razias, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was reported to Nicanor. He was a man who loved the city and was highly respected; because of his affection he was called the father of the Jews.

For many years he had maintained a life of self-restraint in Judaism, and was content to surrender body and soul for perseverance.

Wishing to display the hatred he bore toward the Jews, Nicanor sent five hundred soldiers to seize him.

For he thought that if he captured him, he would inflict the greatest disaster upon the Jews.

When the troops wished to rush into his house, break down the door, and set it on fire, and he was already about to be captured, he struck himself with a sword,

choosing conspicuously to die rather than become subject to sinners and suffer disgraceful insults contrary to his birth.

But since, in his haste, he had not dealt the blow accurately, and the troops were breaking in through the doors, he boldly ran to the wall and manfully threw himself down into the crowd.

When they quickly gave way to his fall, he landed upon the middle of his neck.

While he was still breathing, inflamed in spirit, he rose; and while his blood was pouring out in a great stream and he was covered with grievous wounds, he ran through the crowd.

Then, standing upon a certain steep rock and already drained of blood, he embraced his entrails with both hands and threw them upon the crowd, calling upon the Lord of life and spirit to restore them to him again. Thus he died.

## CHAPTER XV

When Nicanor learned that Judas was in the region of Samaria, he planned to engage in battle with all his force on the Sabbath day.

But the Jews who were compelled to follow him said: “Do not act so fiercely and barbarously; instead, honor the day of sanctification and honor him who sees all things.”

That wretched man asked whether there was someone powerful in heaven who had commanded the Sabbath day to be observed.

When they answered him, “There is the living Lord himself, powerful in heaven, who commanded the seventh day to be observed,”

he said: “And I am powerful upon earth; I command arms to be taken up and the king’s affairs to be carried out.” Nevertheless, he did not succeed in carrying out his plan.

Nicanor, lifted up in the height of his arrogance, had planned to erect a common trophy over Judas.

[Col. 0524B] But Maccabeus always trusted, with complete hope, that help would come to him from God.

He exhorted his men not to fear the arrival of the nations, but to remember the assistance given them from heaven and now to hope that victory would come to them from the Almighty.

He addressed them concerning the Law and the Prophets, and, reminding them also of the battles they had previously fought, made them more ready.

Thus, while raising their spirits, he also showed them the deceitfulness of the nations and their violation of oaths.

He armed each of them not with the protection of shield and spear, but with excellent words and exhortations, setting forth a dream worthy of belief, by which he gladdened them all.

The vision was as follows: Onias, who had been high priest, a good and kindly man, modest in appearance, temperate in conduct, and eloquent in speech, trained from childhood in the virtues, stretched out his hands and prayed for the whole Jewish people.

After this another man appeared, remarkable for his age and glory and of great dignity in appearance, standing near him.

Onias answered and said: “This is the lover of his brothers and of the people of Israel; this is the one who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city—Jeremiah, the prophet of God.”

Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and gave Judas a golden sword, saying:

“Take this holy sword as a gift from God; with it you will strike down the adversaries of my people Israel.”

Thus, after Judas had encouraged them greatly with good words, by which their courage could be raised and the spirits of the young men strengthened, they resolved to fight and engage bravely, so that valor might decide the outcome, since the holy city and the Temple were in danger.

Their concern for their wives and children, as well as for their brothers and relatives, was indeed less; but greatest and first was their fear for the sanctity of the Temple.

Nor were those who were in the city without great concern for those who were about to engage the enemy.

When all were already expecting the judgment to come, the enemies were present, and the army had been arranged, with the beasts and horsemen placed in a suitable position,

Maccabeus, considering the arrival of the multitude, the varied array of weapons, and the ferocity of the beasts, stretched out his hands toward heaven and invoked the Lord who performs wonders. He gives victory to the worthy not according to the power of weapons but as it pleases him.

While invoking him, he spoke as follows [Alternative: *in hoc*]:

“You, Lord, who sent your angel under King Hezekiah and struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib,

“now, ruler of the heavens, send your good angel before us in fear and trembling at the greatness of your arm,

“so that those who come with blasphemy against your holy people may fear you.”

And with these words he concluded his prayer.

[Col. 0525A] Nicanor and those who were with him advanced with trumpets and songs.

But Judas and those with him, having invoked God, entered the battle with prayers.

Fighting with their hands but praying to the Lord in their hearts, they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand, rejoicing greatly in the presence of God.

When they had ceased fighting and were returning with joy, they learned that Nicanor had fallen with all his weapons.

Then a shout arose and confusion was stirred up, and in their native language they blessed the almighty Lord.

Judas, who in every respect was prepared to die in body and spirit for his fellow citizens, ordered that Nicanor’s head and the hand with the shoulder cut from it be carried to Jerusalem.

When he arrived there, he summoned his fellow citizens and the priests to the altar, and called for those who were in the citadel.

He displayed Nicanor’s head and the impious hand with which Nicanor, stretching it out against the holy house of almighty God, had boasted magnificently.

[Col. 0525B] He ordered the tongue of the impious Nicanor to be cut into pieces and given to the birds, [Col. 0526A] while the madman’s hand was hung up opposite the Temple.

Therefore everyone blessed the Lord of heaven, saying: “Blessed is he who has kept his place undefiled.”

He hung Nicanor’s head at the top of the citadel, so that it might be a clear and visible sign of God’s help.

Accordingly, by common agreement they all decreed that this day should in no way pass without celebration.

They decreed that it should be celebrated on the thirteenth day of the month Adar, which in the Syriac language is called the day before Mordecai’s day.

Thus, after the events concerning Nicanor and after the Jews had possessed the city from that time onward, I too will bring my account to an end here.

Although I would indeed like this to have been well done and worthy of history, if it is less worthy, I must be granted indulgence.

For just as it is harmful always to drink wine or always to drink water, whereas using them alternately is pleasurable, so also, for readers, if the style is always exact and elaborate, it will not be pleasing. Here, then, it will be concluded.

[Col. 0525] The Books of the Maccabees end here.

## The Third Part of the Divine Library of Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, Presbyter of Stridon, Containing the New Testament

### The Evangelical Order

In it are the books: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John.

[Col. 0525]

## Jerome’s Preface to the Four Gospels

Jerome to the most blessed Pope Damasus.

You compel me to make a new work from an old one, so that, after the copies of the Scriptures have been scattered throughout the whole world, I may sit as a kind of arbiter; and because they differ among themselves, I may decide which are those that agree with the Greek truth. [Col. 0525C]

[Note: [Col. 0525C] From this passage, and much more clearly from the whole context that follows, it is evident that Jerome did not prepare a wholly new Latin translation of the Gospels from the Greek. Rather, he compared the old Latin text commonly in use with the Greek original and corrected it—as he says below—by collating Greek manuscripts, but ancient ones. He moderated his pen so that it would not differ greatly from the customary Latin reading; after correcting only those matters that seemed to alter the sense, he allowed the rest to remain as it had been.]

This is greater labor, but a dangerous presumption: to judge others while being judged by everyone; to change the language of an old man and bring an already aging world back to the beginnings of infancy. For who, learned or unlearned alike, when he has taken a volume into his hands and sees that what he reads differs from the wording he once absorbed, will not immediately burst into protest, calling me a falsifier and sacrilegious, because I dare to add, change, or correct anything in the ancient books?

Two reasons console me against this hostility: first, that you, who are the highest priest, command it to be done; and second, that what varies is not true is confirmed even by the testimony of those who revile us. If confidence is to be placed in Latin copies, let them say in which ones; for there are almost as many copies as there are manuscripts.

[Note: [Col. 0526C] A copy of this kind, written with the utmost care on extremely thin parchment dyed purple and in letters of gold and silver, of such great antiquity that it easily surpasses, insofar as is known—or at least has hitherto become known—the age of manuscripts, is still preserved in the library of the Church of Verona. Nearly ten years ago we read through it and carefully compared certain excerpts that seemed more important with another extremely ancient manuscript of the Church of Vercelli, to which we had gone for this very reason. Although both books are mutilated and badly damaged by the ravages of time, especially the Veronese, in which even the letters of most of what remains have been eaten away and worn out, often escaping the sharpness of the eyes, we nevertheless learned from definite indications—which we will reproduce when the matter requires it—that what this holy Father testifies here is true: formerly there were almost as many copies of the Latin Version as there were manuscripts. Although they certainly predate Jerome’s revision and indeed preserve an older Version, they nevertheless differ in quite a few places so greatly that they cannot at all seem to have been taken from the same Latin copy that was in use among everyone. We learned the same thing from the edition of the Gospel according to Matthew which Martianaeus entitled the Old Latin and Italic Version and was the first to publish in a separate volume from ancient manuscripts. We have repeatedly observed that it differs not only from other ancient books cited by him, but also from this Veronese manuscript of ours and from the Vercelli manuscript itself. The most ancient manuscript of Beza is also cited, as is another Royal Parisian manuscript, or Claromontanus, from which it is believed that the older Version can be restored. We also know that similar manuscripts remain in the libraries of Italy, though we have not had the opportunity to inspect them ourselves. I have no doubt that these manuscripts precede Jerome’s revision; but I scarcely believe—or rather, scarcely at all—that the Version called Italic by Augustine, or the Old Vulgate, which alone was available to all the Latin churches, can be accurately and certainly reconstructed from any one of them—not even from the Veronese. So true is Jerome’s statement, which we ourselves have learned through experience in comparing manuscripts.]

But if the truth is to be sought from many copies, why, returning to the Greek original, should we not correct what has been badly rendered by faulty translators, perversely amended by ignorant presumptuous men, or added or altered by inattentive copyists?

Nor am I arguing here about the Old Testament, which was translated into Greek by the seventy elders and reached us by a third stage.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] From Hebrew into Greek, and from Greek into Latin.]

I do not ask what Aquila or Symmachus understood, or why Theodotion proceeds midway between the new and the old. Let that be considered the true translation which the Apostles approved.

I am now speaking of the New Testament, which is unquestionably Greek, except for the Apostle Matthew, who first published the Gospel of Christ in Judea in Hebrew letters.

[Note: [Col. 0527D] We have stated elsewhere, especially in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, that we more closely follow the opinion of those who maintain that Matthew’s Gospel too was written in Greek by Matthew himself, not in Hebrew or Syriac. To pass over here the arguments we have assembled elsewhere on this matter, this is especially advantageous for that position: just as the Gospels of the other evangelists and the writings of the New Testament, Matthew’s Gospel itself is believed to survive in an authentic form in the language and letters in which it was written. Conversely, those who defend the opposing view must settle, by another and more obscure traditional inquiry, to whom the Greek translation should be attributed, since the original Hebrew text was lost long ago. For Papias, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.39, testifies that “each one translated it into Greek as he was able” (*ὡς ἠδύνατο ἕκαστος*), according to his learning and use. Those who assign the work to a particular translator differ astonishingly among themselves. Some attribute the translation to James, the first bishop of Jerusalem; others to the Apostle John; others to Barnabas; others to Paul or Luke; and finally some report that Matthew himself became the Greek translator of his own Gospel. In such a variety of opinions, you have nothing certain to follow.]

This certainly disagrees with our language and leads it along different channels from the same stream; one source must be sought.

[Note: [Col. 0528C] Thus read all the older and better manuscripts. Several more recent manuscripts, along with the printed editions, read “into different channels of streams,” or “toward different channels,” and so forth. MART.]

I pass over the copies that a perverse dispute among a few people claims were named after Lucian and Hesychius.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] These are the works marked as apocryphal and rejected in the Gelasian Decree: “The Gospels falsified by Lucian. The Gospels falsified by Hesychius.” See Husserius, *Syntagma on the Seventy Interpreters*, chapter 7.]

They were no more permitted to correct anything in the Old Testament after the Seventy Interpreters than their correction was useful in the New, since Scripture, having already been translated into the languages of many nations, demonstrates that what was added is false.

Accordingly, this present little preface promises only four Gospels, whose order is: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, established by a corrected collation of Greek manuscripts, but ancient ones.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] “We ordered numerous manuscripts.” MART.]

So that they would not differ too greatly from the customary Latin reading, we moderated our pen in such a way that, after correcting only those things that seemed to alter the sense, we allowed the rest to remain as they had been.

We have also set out the Canons that Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, following Ammonius of Alexandria, arranged in ten numbers, just as they are found in Greek. If anyone inquisitive wishes to know which passages in the Gospels are identical, similar, or unique, let him learn this from their arrangement.

For a great error has grown up in our copies: when one evangelist said more about the same matter than another, they thought that the one who had said less needed to be supplemented and added the material.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] Consult what we stated in our Prologues concerning the Latin Gospel of Matthew received in the Church before Jerome, where we presented examples of such additions. MART.]

Or, when one expressed the same sense in a different way, the person who had first read one of the four judged that the others too should be corrected according to its model. Hence it happened that everything is mixed together among us: in Mark there are many passages from Luke and Matthew; again, in Matthew there are many from John and Mark; and in the others passages proper to the others are found.

When, therefore, you read the Canons that follow, once the error of confusion has been removed, you will know both the similarities of all the books and restore to each its own proper passages.

In the First Canon the four agree: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

In the Second, three agree: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

In the Third, three agree: Matthew, Luke, and John.

In the Fourth, three agree: Matthew, Mark, and John.

In the Fifth, two agree: Matthew and Luke.

In the Sixth, two agree: Matthew and Mark.

In the Seventh, two agree: Matthew and John.

In the Eighth, two agree: Luke and Mark.

In the Ninth, two agree: Luke and John.

In the Tenth, each has published his own material, which is not found in the others.

[Note: [Col. 0529B] Thus read all manuscript copies; the printed editions, however, read: “the particular things which each has,” and so forth. MART.]

In each Gospel, beginning with one and continuing to the end of the books, a different number increases [Alternative: *accrescit*, “grows”].

This number, written in black, has beneath it another number in a different color, proceeding up to ten; it indicates the Canon in which the first number is to be sought.

[Note: [Col. 0529B] Because of the difference in colors, it seemed more convenient to distinguish the numbers themselves: the numbers which the holy Father had written in red we have represented with what he calls Arabic numerals, and those written in black with Roman numerals.]

Therefore, when you have opened the book and wish to know, for example, to which Canon a certain chapter belongs, you will immediately be informed by the number written beneath it. Returning to the beginnings, where the distinct collection of the Canons is found, and finding that same Canon at once from the heading at its front, you will find the number you were seeking for that evangelist, which is also marked by its inscription. Then, by examining nearby the paths of the other books, you will note what numbers they have opposite it.

When you know this, you will return to the volumes of the individual evangelists and, without delay, upon finding the numbers you had previously marked, [Note: [Col. 0529B] Because of the difference in colors, it seemed more convenient to distinguish the numbers themselves: the numbers which the holy Father had written in red we have represented with what he calls Arabic numerals, and those written in black with Roman numerals.] you will find [Alternative: “may find”] the places in which they said either the same things or similar things.

[Note: [Col. 0529B] Before the conclusion and greeting of this letter or preface, the following material is found in the printed editions and in some manuscript books:

“It should also be understood, lest anyone unfamiliar with the matter be caught by an error arising from the similarity of the numbers, that if, in the notation of distinct Canons, three evangelists in any Canon have the same number marked twice, three times, four times, or even more in succession, while the fourth has different numbers, this means that the three said the matter once in that place, whereas the fourth places it in the body of his volume as many times as different numbers have been set against the continuous series of the others’ numbers.

“Likewise, if in any one of them, or even in two of them, the same Canon number is found placed twice, three times, four times, or more in succession, while different numbers are found in the others, there will be no doubt that the number of that Canon, or of those Canons, repeated twice or three times, shows that what they said once in the volume is expressed by the other one or ones as many times, with one and the same meaning, as they have presented a difference in the notation of the numbers. This rule will be observed in the comparison of all nine Canons. In the Tenth, however, since it contains only the material proper to each individual evangelist, no comparison can be made with what exists in only one.”

“I pray that you may prosper in Christ and remember me, most blessed Pope.”

Two manuscript copies retain this entire addition. One is in our monastery of Saint Andrew; the other is in the monastery of the Carthusian Fathers near Avignon. Several other very ancient manuscripts—including the Vatican manuscripts, the Saint-Germain manuscripts, one of Saint William’s in the desert, our Crassense manuscript, and others—contain nothing beyond what we have published.

The addition, therefore, has been sewn onto Jerome’s letter by some more recent writer. This is shown most clearly by our Saint-Germain manuscript, no. 6, where this section is set apart as a separate preface or distinct argument from the preceding letter to Damasus. At the end it does not have the conclusion or greeting, “I pray that you may prosper…” but immediately after the words “what exists in only one” it adds: “THE ARGUMENT ENDS.” MART.]

I pray that you may prosper in Christ and remember me, most blessed Pope.

[Col. 0529]

## [THE CANONS OF THE GOSPELS]

# EUSEBIUS OF CAESAREA

> **[Note: Col. 0529D]** Since Jerome testifies that he transcribed the Canons arranged by Eusebius as they are found in Greek and prefixed them to his version of the New Testament—and since the Canons themselves are properly displayed in the editions of Jerome, including the edition prepared by Martianay—it would also have been worthwhile to place before them, for the benefit of the diligent reader, Eusebius’s own letter to his brother Carpianus, in which he explains the rationale of those Canons and his own work, so that the matters indicated there only by numerical signs might more conveniently be understood from this letter. In fact, the letter is found not only in Greek editions of the New Testament, following the examples of Erasmus and Robert Estienne, but was once widely circulated in Latin in the *Orthodoxographs*; it also frequently occurs in ancient biblical manuscripts cited by the Venerable Cardinal Thomasius, who reprinted it from the old Latin version. Martianay omitted it, a fact that learned men wonder at and deeply regret. We present it here in both Greek and Latin, transcribed from the recent edition of Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book V, chapter 4, although we think what he maintains in book IV, chapter 5—that the Latin version is Jerome’s—is indeed highly probable, but we do not dare assert it with certainty.]

## LETTER ON THE FOLLOWING CANONS OF THE GOSPELS

> **[Note: Col. 0529]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

### [Col. 0529C] Eusebius to his brother Carpianus: greetings in the Lord.

A certain Ammonius of Alexandria,

> **[Note: Col. 0530D]** Some ancient authorities attribute this work of Harmony anonymously to the heretic Tatian. Others think that the Harmony which belonged, or was believed to belong, to Tatian was later attributed to Ammonius of Alexandria, and conversely that the work genuinely regarded as Ammonius’s was ascribed to Tatian. Father Nourry attempted to settle this dispute in a special dissertation, but remained hesitating between the two possibilities and came close to declaring the entire work spurious and corrupt. As for the Evangelical Canons associated with this Harmony, our Jerome and others assert that they were devised by Ammonius, although this letter of Eusebius to Carpianus says otherwise: Eusebius states in it that, on the occasion of Ammonius’s Harmony, he devised these Canons according to a definite arrangement.]

with great zeal and industry has left us one Gospel made out of four. For he took the contents of three Gospels and, gathering together all the passages similar to those in Matthew’s Gospel as though into a single whole, appended them there. As a result, so far as the sequence of the reading is concerned, the continuous style of the other three appears to have been interrupted.

But so that, while the body—that is, the text—of the other Gospels remains intact, you might be able to know the particular and familiar places in which they said the same or similar things, and to discuss them accurately, I took the opportunity provided by that man’s work and, by another method, marked out for you ten numerical titles.

The first contains the numbers in which similar things were said by all four: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

The second contains those in which three speak: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

The third contains those in which three speak: Matthew, Luke, and John.

The fourth contains those in which three speak: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

The fifth contains those in which two speak: Matthew and Luke.

The sixth contains those in which two speak: Matthew and Mark.

The seventh contains those in which two speak: Matthew and John.

The eighth contains those in which two speak: Mark and Luke.

The ninth contains those in which two speak: Luke and John.

The tenth contains the passages about which each of them wrote individually.

This, then, is the subject of the titles set out below; their clear explanation is as follows. For in each of the Gospel passages a number appears, beginning gradually with the first, then the second, and finally the third, and proceeding in order through the books all the way to the end. With each number, a notation inserted by a line distinction indicates to which of the ten titles the number belongs.

Thus, if it is the first, it is clearly in the first; if it is the second, in the second; and so on up to the tenth. Therefore, if, after opening any one of the four Gospels, you wish to examine a particular chapter and learn who has said similar things, and to recognize the particular places of each in which they have spoken about the same matters with the same meaning as the passage you are reading, you have only to note the displayed number and seek it in the title indicated by the title’s marginal notation. You can immediately learn from the headings written at the front how many and which of them have said the similar things you are seeking.

Then, going to the remaining Gospels by means of the same number that they contain, you will see the numbers placed beside one another, and you will find that they said similar things in their own particular places.

### [Col. 0530C] Εὐσέβιος Καρπιανῷ ἀγαπητῷ ἀδελφῷ ἐν Κυρίῳ χαίρειν.

**Eusebius to Carpianus, his beloved brother: greetings in the Lord.**

Ammonius of Alexandria, having undertaken, as one might expect, much labor and zeal, has left us the Gospel “according to the four,” placing beside Matthew the concordant passages of the other evangelists. As a necessary consequence, the continuous sequence of the other three was disrupted, so far as the form of the reading is concerned.

But so that, while the entire body and sequence of the others are preserved, you might know the proper places of each evangelist in which they dealt with the same matters and speak truthfully about them, taking my starting point from the labor of the man mentioned above, I have marked out for you by another method the following ten Canons.

The first contains the numbers in which all four said similar things: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

The second contains those in which the three speak: Matthew, Mark, and Luke.

The third contains those in which the three speak: Matthew, Luke, and John.

The fourth contains those in which the three speak: Matthew, Mark, and John.

The fifth contains those in which the two speak: Matthew and Luke.

The sixth contains those in which the two speak: Matthew and Mark.

The seventh contains those in which the two speak: Matthew and John.

The eighth contains those in which the two speak: Mark and Luke.

The ninth contains those in which the two speak: Luke and John.

The tenth contains the passages about which each of them wrote individually.

This, then, is the arrangement of the Canons set out below; their clear explanation is as follows. In each of the four Gospels a number is set out separately, beginning with the first, then the second and the third, and proceeding in order throughout the entire book to its end. Beside each number there is a notation in red ink indicating in which of the ten Canons the number occurs.

For example, if it is αʹ, it is clearly in the first; if βʹ, in the second; and so on up to the tenth.

Therefore, if, after opening any one of the four Gospels, you wish to examine any chapter you choose, learn who has said similar things, and find the proper places in each Gospel in which they dealt with the same matters, take up the displayed number of the passage you are reading and seek it within the Canon to which the notation in red ink directs you. You will immediately learn from the headings written at the front of the Canon how many and which evangelists have said similar things.

And when you also examine the numbers of the remaining Gospels that are placed beside the number you are examining in the Canon, and seek them in the proper places of each Gospel, you will find them saying similar things.

> **[Note: Col. 0541D]** We collated and examined the complete text of the four Gospels against three manuscripts which we were able to find in the Vatican Library and which are, among all the manuscripts of Jerome’s version, the most ancient. Two of them, superior to all the others, once belonged to the Queen of Sweden and are now designated by the numbers 10 and 14. A note at the end indicates that the former was made for the use of Wenceslaus. The third belongs to the old Vatican collection; it is written throughout in what are called uncial letters, gilded with gold, and is also covered with an ancient carved ivory binding, which they display on account of the book’s elegance. It is nevertheless of good substance, although not of the antiquity commonly attributed to it. In some places we also consulted a very large codex from the same library, the Palatine manuscript numbered 5. It is indeed of good correction and quality, but much more recent, barely reaching the twelfth century. It is also said that at the Abbey of St. Epternacus there is a text of the Gospels written in ancient Saxon letters and corrected from St. Jerome’s own autograph, as is noted at the end of the book: “I corrected it, as I have set it down, according to the manuscript from the library of the presbyter Eugippius [thus], which they say belonged to St. Jerome. In the sixth indiction, after the consulship of Basil, a man of consular rank, in the seventeenth year.”]

## [Col. 0541B] Chapter I

### [I, 3]

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.

Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac, however, begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah and his brothers. Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez begot Hezron. Hezron begot Aram. Aram begot Amminadab. Amminadab begot Nahshon. Nahshon begot Salmon. Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab. Boaz begot Obed by Ruth. Obed begot Jesse. Jesse begot David the king. David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife. Solomon begot Rehoboam. Rehoboam begot Abijah. Abijah begot Asa. Asa begot Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat begot Joram. Joram begot Uzziah. Uzziah begot Jotham. Jotham begot Ahaz. Ahaz begot Hezekiah. Hezekiah begot Manasseh. Manasseh begot Amon. Amon begot Josiah. Josiah begot Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the Babylonian exile.

After the Babylonian exile, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel. Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel begot Abiud. Abiud begot Eliakim. Eliakim begot Azor. Azor begot Zadok. Zadok begot Achim. Achim begot Eliud. Eliud begot Eleazar. Eleazar begot Matthan. Matthan begot Jacob. Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.

### [Col. 0542B] [II, 10]

Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian exile, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian exile to Christ, fourteen generations.

### [III, 5]

Now the birth of Christ took place in this way. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together she was found to have conceived in the womb by the Holy Spirit.

### [IV, 10]

Joseph her husband, being righteous and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly. But while he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying:

“Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife, for that which has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.

“All this took place so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the Prophet might be fulfilled:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son,  
> and they shall call his name Emmanuel,

which is interpreted, ‘God with us.’”

When Joseph awoke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord commanded him and took his wife.

> **[Note: Col. 0542D]** Some manuscripts read, “and he did not know her,” and so forth. The same reading occurs in the text of the *Commentaries on Matthew*. —Martianay.

And he did not know [another reading: “knew”] her until she had borne her firstborn son; and he called his name Jesus.

## Chapter II

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea,

> **[Note: Col. 0542D]** The other manuscript of the Queen of Sweden reads “of Judah”; formerly it read “of Judea,” as in the Greek, τῆς Ἰουδαίας. On this reading, see the holy Doctor in his *Commentaries*.

in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying:

“Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.”

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born.

### [V, 7]

They said to him, “In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it is written through the Prophet:

> And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah,  
> are by no means least among the rulers of Judah;  
> for from you shall come a ruler  
> who will shepherd my people Israel.”

### [VI, 10]

Then Herod secretly summoned the Magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. Sending them to Bethlehem, he said:

“Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and worship him.”

When they had heard the king, they departed; and behold, the star which they had seen in the East went before them until it came and stood above the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own country by another way.

When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying:

“Rise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you. For Herod is about to seek the child in order to destroy him.”

He rose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt. He remained there until the death of Herod, so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the Prophet might be fulfilled:

> Out of Egypt I called my son.

Then Herod, seeing that he had been deceived by the Magi, became exceedingly angry. He sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and throughout all its districts, from two years old and under, according to the time that he had carefully learned from the Magi.

Then was fulfilled what had been spoken through Jeremiah the Prophet:

> A voice was heard in Ramah,  
> weeping and loud lamentation:

> Rachel weeping for her children,  
> and she refused to be comforted,  
> because they are no more.

> **[Note: Col. 0543D]** The Greek text has more: θρῆνος καὶ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὀδυρμὸς πολύς, “lamentation, weeping, and much wailing,” which you may render, “groaning, weeping, and much wailing,” and so forth.

When Herod had died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying:

“Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the child’s life are dead.”

He rose, took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there; and, having been warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee. And coming there, he settled in a city called Nazareth, so that what had been spoken through the Prophets might be fulfilled:

> He shall be called a Nazarene.

But the herdsmen fled, and, going into the city, reported everything, including what had happened to those who had been possessed by demons. And look, the whole city came out to meet Jesus; and when they saw him, they begged him to depart from their boundaries.

## [Chapter IX. LXX, 1.]

And getting into the boat, he crossed over and came to his own city. And look, they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed. When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.”

And look, some of the scribes said within themselves: “This man blasphemes.” And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts? For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“Rise, take up your bed, and [Col. 0551D] go to your house.” And he rose and went to his house.

When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings.

## [LXXI, 2.]

And as Jesus was passing from there, he saw a man sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew. And he said to him: “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. [Col. 0552A]

## [LXXII, 2.]

And it happened that, while he was reclining at table in the house, look, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

## [LXXIII, 2.]

But Jesus, hearing this, said: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill. Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

Then the disciples of John approached him, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?”

And Jesus said to them: “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.

“No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment; for it tears away its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear is made. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, and the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. Rather, they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

## [LXXIV, 2.]

While he was saying these things to them, look, a certain ruler approached and worshiped him, saying: [Note: [Col. 0552D] In place of the word Domine, “Lord,” the Greek text here has ὅτι, “because”; the Regina manuscripts entirely lack it.]

“Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.”

And Jesus rose and followed him, along with his disciples. And look, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years approached from behind and touched the fringe of his garment. For she was saying within herself: “If I only touch his garment, I will be saved.”

But Jesus turned and, seeing her, said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith [Col. 0552C] has saved you.” And the woman was saved from that hour.

And when Jesus came into the ruler’s house and saw the flute players and the tumultuous crowd, he said: “Go away; for the girl is not dead, but sleeping.” And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he entered and took her hand. And the girl arose. And this report went out throughout that whole region.

## [LXXV, 10.]

As Jesus was passing from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.”

When he had come into the house, the blind men approached him. And Jesus said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” [Note: [Col. 0552D] Neither the Greek exemplar nor the older Latin books add vobis, “for you.”]

They said to him: “Certainly, Lord.”

Then he touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith, let it be done for you.” And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, saying: “See that no one knows.” [Col. 0552D] But they went out and spread his fame throughout that whole region.

As they were going out, look, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. When the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled, saying: “This has never appeared in Israel.”

But the Pharisees said: “He casts out demons by the ruler of demons.” [Col. 0553A]

## [LXXVI, 2.]

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness.

## [LXXVII, 6.]

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were troubled and lying about like sheep without a shepherd.

## [LXXVIII, 5.]

Then he said to his disciples: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” [Note: [Col. 0553D] Two Regina manuscripts have ut ejiciat, “that he may send out,” closer to the Greek verb ἐκβάλῃ.]

## [Chapter X. LXXIX, 2.]

And calling his twelve disciples together, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, so that they might cast them out and heal every disease and every sickness.

## [LXXX, 2.]

Now these are the names of the twelve Apostles: First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean; and Judas Iscariot [Alternative: “Schariotes,”] who also betrayed him.

## [LXXXI, 10.]

Jesus sent these twelve, commanding them and saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel.” [Note: [Col. 0554D] One of our manuscripts also prefers the singular civitatem, “city,” as it is in the Greek text.]

## [LXXXII, 2.]

As you go, proclaim, saying: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received without payment; give without payment. Do not acquire gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, [Col. 0553C] nor sandals, nor a staff; for the laborer is worthy of his food.

## [LXXXIII, 2.]

Whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy; and remain there until you depart.

## [LXXXIV, 5.]

When you enter a house, greet it, saying: “Peace to this house.” And if that house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you.

## [LXXXV, 2.]

And whoever does not receive you, nor hear your words, when you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Amen I say to you: It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city.

## [LXXXVI, 5.]

Look, I am sending you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. [Col. 0553D]

## [LXXXVII, 1.]

Beware of people. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you. And you will be brought before governors and kings on my account, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.

## [LXXXVIII, 2.]

When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you should speak; for what you should speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.

Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his son; and children will rise up against their parents and put them to death. [Col. 0554A] And you will be hated by everyone on account of my name; but whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.

## [LXXXIX, 10.]

When they persecute you in this city, flee into another. Amen I say to you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

## [XC, 3.]

A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master. It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his master.

## [XCI, 10.]

If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more the members of his household? Therefore do not fear them.

## [XCII, 2.]

For nothing is covered that will not be revealed, nor hidden that will not be known.

## [XCIII, 5.]

What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops. And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Therefore do not fear: you are worth more than many sparrows.

Everyone, therefore, who acknowledges me before people, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven.

## [XCIV, 2.]

But whoever denies me before people, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.

## [XCV, 5.]

Do not suppose that I came to bring peace upon the earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be members of his household. [Col. 0554C]

## [XCVI, 5.]

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.

## [XCVII, 3.]

Whoever finds his life will lose it; and whoever loses his life on my account will find it.

## [XCVIII, 1.]

Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.

## [XCIX, 10.]

Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.

## [C, 6.]

And whoever gives one of these least ones only a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—amen I say to you, he will certainly not lose his reward.

[Col. 0554D] ## [Chapter XI. CI, 10.]

And it happened that, when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he departed from there to teach and proclaim in their cities.

## [CII, 5.]

When John heard in prison about the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

And Jesus answered and said to them: “Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized; and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.”

As they were departing, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: [Col. 0555A] “What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who dress in soft clothing are in kings’ houses. But what did you go out to see—a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

## [CIII, 2.]

For this is the one about whom it is written: “Look, I am sending my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.”

## [CIV, 5.]

Amen I say to you, among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist; but the one who is lesser in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.

## [CV, 5.]

From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men seize it.

## [CVI, 10.]

For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to receive it, he is Elijah who is to come. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. [Col. 0555B]

## [CVII, 5.]

To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call out to their companions and say: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not mourn.”

For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say: “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: “Look, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” And wisdom is justified by her children.

## [CVIII, 5.]

Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented.

“Woe to you, Chorazin” [Alternative: “Corazain”]; “woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. [Col. 0555C] Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

“And you, Capernaum, will you perhaps be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell.”

## [CIX, 10.]

For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Sodom, it might have remained until this day. Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.

## [CX, 5.]

At that time Jesus answered and said: [Note: [Col. 0555D] I confess, in the sense of the Greek ἐξομολογοῦμαι. The Regina manuscripts also have this reading.]

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you.

## [CXI, 3.]

“All things have been handed over to me by my Father.

## [CXII, 3.]

“And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.

## [CXIII, 10.]

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.

## [Chapter XII. CXIV, 2.]

At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat. But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to him: “Look, your disciples are doing what is not permitted [Note: [Col. 0556D] These same manuscripts add eis, “for them,” which some Greek exemplars also have.] to do on the Sabbaths.”

But he said to them: [Col. 0556A] “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not permitted for him or those with him to eat, but only for the priests?

## [CXV, 10.]

“Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without blame? But I tell you that something greater than the temple is here. If you had understood what this means—‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’—you would never have condemned the innocent.

## [CXVI, 2.]

“For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

And when he had departed from there, he came into their synagogue. And look, there was a man who had a withered hand; and they questioned him, saying: “Is it permitted to heal on the Sabbaths?”—so that they might accuse him.

But he said to them: “Which person among you will there be who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! Therefore it is permitted to do good on the Sabbaths.”

Then he said to the man: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out, and it was restored to health like the other.

## [CXVII, 4.]

But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him about how they might destroy him.

## [CXVIII, 10.]

Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all. And he ordered them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

“Look, my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul has been well pleased. I will place my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim judgment to the Gentiles. He will not contend or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed, nor extinguish a smoking wick, until he brings judgment to victory; and in his name the Gentiles will hope.”

## [CXIX, 5.]

Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw.

## [CXX, 7.]

And all the crowds were astonished and said: “Can this be the Son of David?”

## [CXXI, 2.]

But when the Pharisees heard this, they said: “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons.”

## [CXXII, 2.]

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be devastated, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?

“And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

“Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house.

“Whoever is not with me is against me; and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

## [CXXIII, 2.]

“Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

## [CXXIV, 10.]

“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.

## [CXXV, 5.]

“A good man brings good things out of a good treasury, and an evil man brings evil things out of an evil treasury.

## [CXXVI, 10.]

“But I say to you that people will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word that they speak. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.

## [CXXVII, 5.]

Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying: “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” [Col. 0557B]

## [CXXVIII, 5.]

But he answered and said to them: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

“The men of Nineveh will rise up in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and look, something greater than Jonah is here.

“The Queen of the South will rise up in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and look, something greater than Solomon is here.

## [CXXIX, 5.]

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’

“And when it comes, it finds it unoccupied, swept clean, and adorned. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the final state of that person becomes worse than the first. So will it also be for this most evil generation.”

## [CXXX, 2.]

While he was still speaking to the crowds, look, his mother and brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak with him. But someone said to him: “Look, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you.”

But he answered the one who told him and said: “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hands toward his disciples, he said: “Look, my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, and sister, and mother.”

## [Chapter XIII. CXXXI, 2.]

On that day Jesus went out from the house [Col. 0557D] and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered to him, so that, when he had gone up into [Alternative: omits in] a boat, he sat, while the whole crowd stood on the shore. And he spoke many things to them in parables, saying:

“Look, the sower went out to sow. And while he was sowing, some seeds fell beside the road, and the birds [Note: [Col. 0557] The word coeli, “of heaven,” which most Greek exemplars also omit, is absent from the two Regina manuscripts.] of heaven came and ate them. But others fell upon rocky ground, where they did not have much soil; and they sprang up immediately because they had no depth of soil. When the sun rose, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered.

“Others fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. But others fell upon good soil and produced fruit: one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

And the disciples approached and said to him: “Why do you speak to them in parables?”

He answered and said to them: “Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.

## [CXXXII, 5.]

“For whoever has, it will be given to him, and he will abound; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.

## [CXXXIII, 1.]

“Therefore I speak to them in parables, because, though seeing, they do not see; and though hearing, they do not hear, nor understand. And in them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says:

“‘With hearing you will hear and will not understand; and seeing you will see and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn back, and I heal them.’” [Col. 0558B]

## [CXXXIV, 5.]

“But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. For amen I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.

## [CXXXV, 2.]

“You, therefore, hear the parable of the sower. Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it: the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. This is the one sown beside the road.

“But the one sown upon rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is temporary. When tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately scandalized.

“But the one sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.

“But the one sown upon good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it, and bears fruit and produces, one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold.

## [CXXXVI, 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0557] The word coeli, “of heaven,” which most Greek exemplars also omit, is absent from the two Regina manuscripts.]

“He presented another parable to them, saying: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while the people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds over the middle of the wheat, and went away.

“But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared. The household servants approached the master and said to him: ‘Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, does it have weeds?’

“And he said to them: ‘An enemy has done this.’

“The servants said to him: ‘Do you want us to go and gather them?’

“And he said: ‘No, lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them. Let both grow until the harvest, and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles for burning; but gather the wheat into my barn.’”

[CXXXVII, 2.] He put before them another parable, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field. It is indeed the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is larger than all garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and dwell in its branches.”

[CXXXVIII, 5.] He spoke another parable to them: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.”

[CXXXIX, 6.] Jesus said all these things to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them, so that what had been spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world.”

[CXL, 10.] Then, having dismissed the crowds, he went into the house. His disciples came to him, saying: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” He answered [Note: The Regina manuscripts, along with Greek manuscripts of better quality, also omit the pronoun “to them” (illis).] them: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.” The field is the world. The good seed—these are the children of the kingdom. The weeds are the children of the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the consummation of the age. The reapers are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and those who commit iniquity, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear.

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and, rejoicing over it, goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls. When he has found one precious pearl, he goes away and sells everything he had and buys it.

“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it ashore, sat down, and collected the good fish into containers, but threw the bad away. So will it be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

[Note: Most Greek manuscripts place before this the words: “Jesus says to them” (Λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς), that is, “Jesus says to them.”]

“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him: “Yes.” He said to them: “Therefore every scribe who has been instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old.”

And it happened that, when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there.

[CXLI, 1.] Coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogues, so that they were astonished and said: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is this not the craftsman’s son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph [alternative: Joses], and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us? Where, then, did this man get all these things?” And they took offense at him.

[CXLII, 1.] But Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house.” And he did not perform many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.

## Chapter XIV

[CXLIII, 2.] At that time Herod the Tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his attendants: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works are performed through him.”

[CXLIV, 2.] For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother. John had said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have her.” Although he wanted to kill him, he feared the people, because they regarded him as a prophet.

[CXLV, 6.] On Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced in their midst and pleased Herod. Therefore he promised her under oath to give her whatever she might ask of him. But she, prompted by her mother, said: “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.” The king was grieved; yet, because of the oath and those reclining at table with him, he ordered it to be given. He sent and beheaded John in prison. His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. His disciples came, took his body, buried it, and went and reported to Jesus.

[CXLVI, 3.] When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place by himself. When the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. As he went ashore, he saw a great crowd, had compassion on them, and healed their sick.

[CXLVII, 1.] When evening came, his disciples approached him, saying: “The place is deserted, and the hour has already passed. Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go to the villages and buy food for themselves.” But Jesus said to them: “They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat.” They answered him: “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.” He said to them: “Bring them here to me.”

After ordering the crowd to recline on the grass, he took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up toward heaven, blessed them, broke them, and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. They all ate and were satisfied. They took up what remained of the fragments—twelve baskets full. The number of those who ate was five thousand men, besides women and children.

[CXLVIII, 6.] Immediately [Note: Two Regina manuscripts read “immediately ordered the disciples,” omitting the name Jesus; the Greek text differs.] Jesus compelled the disciples to get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, until he had dismissed the crowds.

[CXLIX, 2.] After dismissing the crowd, he went up the mountain by himself to pray.

[CL, 4.] When evening came, he was there alone. The boat was being tossed by the waves in the middle of the sea, for the wind was contrary. During the fourth watch of the night, he came to them, walking on the sea. When they saw him [alternative addition: the disciples] walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying: “It is a phantom.” And they cried out in fear. Immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
