But the Jews who were disobedient stirred up and embittered the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers. Therefore they remained for a considerable time, acting boldly in the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting that signs and wonders be done through their hands. [Col. 0706D]

The population of the city was divided: some were with the Jews, but others with the apostles. When an assault was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, to insult and stone them, they understood this and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the surrounding region; and there they were preaching the gospel.

And a certain man in Lystra, infirm in his feet, sat there, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked. He heard Paul speaking. Paul looked at him, and seeing that he had faith to be saved, [Col. 0707A] said in a loud voice: “Stand upright on your feet.” And he leaped up and walked.

When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices, saying in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have become like men and have come down to us.” And they called Barnabas Jupiter, but Paul Mercury, because he was the leader in speaking.

The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was before the city, brought bulls and garlands before the gates and, together with the crowds, wanted to offer sacrifice. When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their garments and rushed out among the crowd, crying out and saying: “Men, why are you doing these things? We also are mortal human beings, like you, and we proclaim to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them; [Col. 0707B] who in past generations allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without witness, doing good from heaven, giving rains and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.”

Even with these words, they scarcely restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them.

But some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium; and after persuading the crowds and stoning Paul, they dragged him outside the city, supposing that he was dead. When the disciples surrounded him, he rose and entered the city; and on the following day he departed with Barnabas for Derbe.

After preaching the gospel to that city and teaching many, they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples and exhorting them to remain in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. [Col. 0707C] Having appointed presbyters for them in each church, and prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

Then, passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia. After speaking the word of the Lord in Perga, they went down to Attalia; and from there they sailed to Antioch, from which they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had completed.

When they had arrived and gathered the church together, they reported how much God had done with them, and that he had opened to the Gentiles a door of faith. They remained there for no short time with the disciples.

## Chapter XV

And certain men who had come down from Judea were teaching the brothers: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” So, when no small dispute had arisen between Paul and Barnabas and them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, together with certain others from among them, should go up to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem concerning this question. [Col. 0707D]

They, therefore, sent on their way by the church, passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles; and they brought great joy to all the brothers. When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were received by the church, the apostles and the elders, and they announced how great a work God had done with them.

But some who belonged to the sect of the Pharisees and had believed rose up, saying: “It is necessary to circumcise them and to command them also to keep the Law of Moses.” [Col. 0708A] The apostles and the elders gathered to consider this matter.

When there had been much debate, Peter rose and said to them: “Men and brothers, you know that from ancient days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. And God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us; and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.

“Now, therefore, why are you testing God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”

Then the whole multitude fell silent; and they listened to Barnabas and Paul recounting how many signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them. [Col. 0708B]

After they had fallen silent, James replied, saying: “Men and brothers, listen to me. Simon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name. And the words of the Prophets agree with this, as it is written:

“‘After these things I will return and rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen; and I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up, so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name has been invoked, says the Lord, who does these things.’

“Known from eternity to the Lord is his work. Therefore I judge that we should not trouble those who turn to God from the Gentiles, but should write to them that they abstain from the pollutions of idols, from fornication, [Note: [Col. 0707D] Our Jerome bears witness to the presence of the word *and*—that is, “and from strangled animals”—in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter V, verse 2, in only certain Latin copies; [Col. 0708D] there are also some Greek copies of excellent quality that do not have it.] and from strangled animals, [Col. 0708C] and from blood.

“For Moses has had, from ancient times, in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath.”

Then it pleased the apostles and the elders, together with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, who was called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers; and they wrote through their hands:

**THE APOSTLES and the elder brothers, to the brothers who are among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings.**

“Since we have heard that certain men who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, although we gave them no such command, it has seemed good to us, assembled together, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, [Col. 0708D] men who have surrendered their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Therefore we have sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will also report the same things to you in words. For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from sacrifices offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled animals, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”

So, having been dismissed, they went down to Antioch; and gathering the multitude, they delivered the letter. When they had read it, they rejoiced over the consolation. Judas and Silas, who themselves were also prophets, [Col. 0709A] consoled the brothers at length in their speech and strengthened them. After spending some time there, they were dismissed in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

But it seemed good to Silas to remain there; Judas, however, went alone to Jerusalem. Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of the Lord with many others.

After some days Paul said to Barnabas: “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are.” Barnabas wanted to take John with him as well, the one who was called Mark. But Paul insisted that the one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work ought not to be received. A disagreement arose between them, so that they parted company. [Col. 0709B]

Barnabas, taking Mark with him, sailed to Cyprus. But Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of God. He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches and instructing them to observe the commands of the apostles and the elders.

## Chapter XVI

He came to Derbe and Lystra. And behold, there was a certain disciple there named Timothy, the son of a faithful Jewish woman, with a Gentile father. [Note: [Col. 0709D] In the Greek, *widow* (χήρας) appears in place of *Jewish woman* (Ἰουδαίας); likewise, in the ancient Latin translations, the old books [Col. 0710D] read *widow* rather than *Jewish woman*. Jerome himself preferred that reading in his *Letter to Augustine*.]

The brothers who were in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him. Paul wanted him to set out with him; and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Gentile.

As they passed through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decrees [Col. 0709C] established by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. And the churches were strengthened in faith and increased in number daily.

After passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia. When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. After passing through Mysia, they went down to Troas.

And a vision appeared to Paul during the night: a certain Macedonian man was standing and pleading with him, saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.” When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to depart for Macedonia, being convinced that God had called us to evangelize them.

Sailing from Troas, we came by a straight course to Samothrace, and on the following day to Neapolis; [Col. 0709D] and from there to Philippi, which is the first city of that part of Macedonia, a colony. We remained in that city for several days, conferring together.

On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate beside the river, where there seemed to be a place of prayer; and sitting down, we spoke with the women who had gathered. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, also heard us. The Lord opened her heart to attend to what was spoken by Paul.

When she had been baptized, and her household also, she pleaded with us, saying: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, enter my house and remain there.” And she prevailed upon us.

Now it happened, as we were going to prayer, that [Col. 0710A] a certain slave girl who had a spirit of Python came to meet us; she brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling. Following Paul and us, she cried out, saying: “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” She did this for many days.

But Paul, being distressed, turned and said to the spirit: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out at that very hour.

When her masters saw that their hope of profit had gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. Presenting them to the magistrates, they said: “These men are disturbing our city, although they are Jews, and they are proclaiming a custom which it is not lawful for us to accept or practice, since we are Romans.”

And the crowd rose up against [Col. 0710B] them. The magistrates, tearing their garments, ordered them to be beaten with rods. After inflicting many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, instructing the jailer to guard them carefully. Having received such an order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

At midnight Paul and Silas were praying and praising God, and those who were in custody were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s chains were loosened.

When the jailer awoke and saw the doors of the prison open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.” [Col. 0710C]

Having asked for a light, he entered; and trembling, he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he led them outside and said: “Lords, what must I do to be saved?”

They said: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.

Taking them at that hour of the night, he washed their wounds; and he himself and his entire household were baptized immediately. Then he brought them into his house, set a table before them, and rejoiced with his whole household, having believed in God.

When day came, the magistrates sent lictors, saying: “Release those men.” The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders that you be released. Now, therefore, go out and depart in peace.”

[Col. 0710D] But Paul said to them: “They have publicly beaten us, uncondemned, although we are Romans, and have thrown us into prison; and now they are sending us out secretly? No indeed! Let them come themselves and lead us out.”

The lictors reported these words to the magistrates. They were afraid when they heard that the men were Romans. So they came and pleaded with them; and leading them out, they asked them to leave the city.

After coming out of the prison, they entered Lydia’s house; and when they had seen the brothers, they consoled them and departed.

## Chapter XVII

After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. [Col. 0711A] According to his custom, Paul entered among them and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures, opening and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that “this Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ.”

Some of them believed and joined Paul and Silas, along with a great multitude of the devout Gentiles and not a few noble women. But the Jews, becoming jealous and taking certain wicked men from the common crowd, gathered a mob and stirred up the city. They attacked Jason’s house and sought to bring them out before the people.

When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the city authorities, crying out: “These are the men who have stirred up the city; they have come here also, and Jason has received them. And they all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” [Col. 0711B]

They stirred up the crowd and the city authorities, who heard these things. After receiving security from Jason and the others, they released them.

The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they entered the synagogue of the Jews. These were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. Many of them believed, including not a few honorable Gentile women and men.

But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Beroea also, they came there, agitating and disturbing the crowds. At once the brothers sent Paul away to go as far as the sea. But Silas and Timothy remained there. [Col. 0711C]

Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. After receiving instructions from him for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.

While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him when he saw that the city was given over to idolatry. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the worshipers, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be present.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him. Some said: “What does this babbler want to say?” Others: “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign demons,” because he was proclaiming Jesus and the resurrection to them. [Col. 0711D]

They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying: “May we know what this new teaching is that is spoken by you? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. Therefore we wish to know what these things mean.” (Now all the Athenians and the resident foreigners spent their time in nothing else but either saying or hearing something new.)

Standing in the middle of the Areopagus, Paul said: “Men of Athens, I see that in every respect you are, as it were, rather more religious. For as I passed through and observed your objects of worship, I also found an altar on which was written: ‘To an unknown god.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.

“The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands, nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and everything. [Col. 0712A] He made from one the whole human race to inhabit the entire face of the earth, determining appointed times and the boundaries of their habitation, so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel after him and find him, although he is not far from each one of us.

“For in him we live and move and exist, as some of your own poets have also said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ Therefore, since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to suppose that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image fashioned by human art and thought.

“Having overlooked the times of this ignorance, God now announces to human beings that everyone everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom he has appointed, giving assurance to all by raising him from the dead.”

[Col. 0712B] When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said: “We will hear you about this again.” Thus Paul went out from among them.

But certain men joined him and believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

## Chapter XVIII

After these things, leaving Athens, he came to Corinth. Finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy, together with his wife Priscilla—for Claudius had ordered all the Jews to depart from Rome—he approached them.

Because he practiced the same trade, he stayed with them and worked; they were of the tentmaking trade. And every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, introducing the name of the Lord Jesus and persuading both Jews and Greeks.

[Col. 0712C] When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself wholly to the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. But when they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said to them: “Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”

Leaving there, he entered the house of a certain man named Titus Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was adjoining the synagogue. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his entire household; and many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed and were baptized.

The Lord said to Paul by night in a vision: “Do not fear [the text reads *Nli*; evidently, ‘Do not fear’], but speak and do not be silent, because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”

He remained there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

[Col. 0712D] When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up with one accord against Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying: “This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law.”

As Paul was beginning to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews: “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or some serious crime, O Jews, I would rightly bear with you. But if they are questions about a word, names, and your own law, you yourselves must see to it. I do not wish to be judge of these matters.” And he drove them away from the tribunal.

Then they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him before the tribunal; but Gallio paid no attention to any of these things.

After Paul had remained many more days, he said farewell to the brothers and sailed for Syria, [Col. 0713A] accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. He had his head shaved at Cenchreae, for he had a vow. He arrived at Ephesus and left them there. He himself entered the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.

When they asked him to remain for a longer time, he did not consent, but said farewell, saying: “I will return to you again, God willing.” And he departed from Ephesus. Going down to Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, then went down to Antioch.

After spending some time there, he departed, traveling successively through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, arrived at Ephesus, mighty in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught [Col. 0713B] accurately the things concerning Jesus, knowing only the baptism of John.

He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of the Lord to him more accurately.

When he wanted to go to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he arrived, he contributed greatly to those who had believed. For he vigorously refuted the Jews publicly, demonstrating from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

## Chapter XIX

Now it happened, while Apollos was in Corinth, that Paul, after passing through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”

[Col. 0713C] They said to him: “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” He said: “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They replied: “Into John’s baptism.”

Paul said: “John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him—that is, in Jesus.”

When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. There were about twelve men in all.

Entering the synagogue, he spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading them concerning the kingdom of God. But when some became hardened and did not believe, speaking evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus.

[Col. 0713D] This continued for two years, so that all who dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Gentiles. God performed extraordinary miracles through Paul’s hands, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out.

But some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying: “I adjure you by [Col. 0714A] Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” There were seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who were doing this.

But the evil spirit answered them: “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize; but who are you?” And the man in whom the most evil demon was, leaping upon them and overpowering both, prevailed against them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.

This became known to all the Jews and Gentiles who dwelt in Ephesus; and fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. Many of those who believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Closer to the Greek, the holy interpreter reads in the preface to his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*: “Many also of those who had practiced curious arts brought their books together, burned them before everyone, calculated their value, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver.” Thus powerfully the word of the Lord grew and was strengthened, and so forth. [Col. 0714D]]

Many also of those who had practiced curious arts brought their books together and burned them publicly. After calculating their value, [Col. 0714B] they found it to be fifty thousand denarii. Thus the word of God grew mightily and was confirmed.

After these things had been completed, Paul resolved in the Spirit, after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying: “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” Sending two of those who ministered to him, Timothy and Erastus, into Macedonia, he himself remained for a time in Asia.

At that time no small disturbance arose concerning the way of the Lord. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Diana, brought no small profit to the craftsmen. Summoning them and the workers of that kind, he said:

“Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this trade. And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus, but in almost the whole of Asia, this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great multitude, saying that those are not gods which are made by hands. [Col. 0714C]

“And not only is this part of our business in danger of coming into disrepute, but [Note: [Col. 0714D] Here again, the holy interpreter reads more closely according to the Greek: “And the temple of the great goddess Diana will be regarded as nothing, and her majesty will also begin to be destroyed, whom all Asia and the whole world worship,” and so forth.] the temple of the great Diana will be regarded as nothing; and her majesty, whom all Asia and the world worship, will also begin to be destroyed.”

When they heard this, they were filled with anger and cried out, saying: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater, having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians and companions of Paul.

When Paul wanted to enter among the people, the disciples did not permit him. Some of the leading men of Asia, who were his friends, also sent to him, begging him not to give himself up to the theater. Others were shouting different things.

[Col. 0714D] For the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had gathered. From the crowd they brought out Alexander, the Jews pushing him forward. Alexander, having requested silence with his hand, wanted to give an account before the people.

But when they recognized that he was a Jew, one cry arose from everyone, as they shouted for about two hours: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!”

When the town clerk had quieted the crowds, he said: “Men of Ephesus, who among human beings does not know that the city of the Ephesians is a worshiper of the great Diana, [Col. 0715A] and of the offspring of Jupiter? Since these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to remain calm and do nothing rash.

“For you have brought these men here, though they are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of your goddess. If, therefore, Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a case against anyone, court sessions are held and there are proconsuls; let them accuse one another.

“But if you are seeking anything concerning some other matter, it can be settled in a lawful assembly. For we are also in danger of being accused of today’s riot, since there is no charge concerning this gathering for which we can give an account.” And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly., who among human beings does not know that the city of the Ephesians is a worshiper of the great Diana and of the offspring of Jupiter? Since these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to remain calm and do nothing rash.

“For you have brought these men here, though they are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of your goddess. If, therefore, Demetrius and the craftsmen who are with him have a case against anyone, court sessions are held and there are proconsuls; let them accuse one another.

“But if you are seeking anything concerning some other matter, it can be settled in a lawful assembly. For we are also in danger of being accused of today’s riot, since there is no one responsible for this gathering whose conduct we could explain.” And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

## Chapter XX

*[Source cols. 0715B–0716D]*

After the uproar had ceased, Paul summoned the disciples and, having encouraged them, bade them farewell and set out to go to Macedonia. When he had passed through those regions and had encouraged them at length, he came to Greece. After he had spent three months there, a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to sail for Syria; so he decided to return through Macedonia.

He was accompanied by Sopater, son of Pyrrhus, of Beroea; by Aristarchus and Secundus, of the Thessalonians; by Gaius of Derbe and Timothy; and by Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. These men went on ahead and waited for us at Troas. We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them at Troas within five days, where we stayed seven days.

On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul was speaking with them. Since he intended to depart the next day, he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. A young man named Eutychus was sitting on the window ledge. As he was sinking into a deep sleep while Paul continued speaking for a long time, overcome by sleep he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead.

Paul went down, bent over him, and, embracing him, said, “Do not be troubled, for his life is in him.” Then he went upstairs, broke the bread, and ate; after speaking with them at length until dawn, he departed. They brought the boy back alive and were greatly comforted.

We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there; for he had arranged this, since he himself intended to make the journey by land. When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene. Sailing from there, we reached Chios on the following day; the next day we put in at Samos, and on the day after that we came to Miletus.

Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not be delayed in Asia. For he was hurrying, if it were possible for him, to celebrate the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem.

From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the church. When they had come to him and were assembled together, he said to them:

“You know how I lived among you throughout the whole time, from the first day on which I entered Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and tears, and amid the trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews; how I withheld nothing useful, so as not to announce and teach it to you publicly and from house to house.

> **[Note: [Col. 0715D] Alternatively, the Father himself, in the Preface praised above, has: ‘I withheld nothing of what was useful to you, so as to announce and teach it publicly and privately,’ apparently from the Old Latin edition.]**

testifying both to Jews and to Gentiles repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

“And now, behold, bound in spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions await me in Jerusalem. But I fear none of these things, nor do I count my life as more precious than myself, provided that I complete my course and the ministry of the word that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of the grace of God.

“And now, behold, I know that you will all see my face no more—you among whom I passed, preaching the kingdom of God.

> **[Note: [Col. 0715D] The same author, in the same place: ‘Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all. [Col. 0716D] For I did not withhold from announcing to you the whole will of God,’ and so forth.]**

“Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all. For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood.

“I know that after my departure savage wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock. And from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples away after them.

> **[Note: [Col. 0716D] The same author also has: ‘Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease to admonish each one with tears,’ and then: ‘to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance.’]**

“Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease to admonish each one of you with tears. And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified.

“I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing, as you yourselves know. For you know that these hands provided for my needs and for those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by laboring in this way we ought to support the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

After he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. Great weeping arose among them all; and falling upon Paul’s neck, they kissed him, grieving especially over the word he had spoken, that they would see his face no more. Then they escorted him to the ship.

## Chapter XXI

*[Source cols. 0717A–0718C]*

When it happened that we had sailed away from them, we came by a straight course to Cos, and on the following day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. Having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and sailed. When Cyprus came into view, leaving it on our left, we sailed toward Syria and arrived at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.

Having found the disciples, we stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When the days were over, we departed and continued on our way, all of them escorting us with their wives and children as far as outside the city. Kneeling on the shore, we prayed. After we had said farewell to one another, we went aboard the ship, while they returned to their homes.

When we had completed the voyage from Tyre, we came down to Ptolemais. After greeting the brothers, we stayed with them for one day. On the following day we departed and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him. He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

After we had stayed there several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. When he came to us, he took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said:

“Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man to whom this belt belongs in this way and will hand him over to the hands of the Gentiles.”

When we heard this, both we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” Since we could not persuade him, we fell silent, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”

After those days, having made our preparations, we went up to Jerusalem. Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing Mnason, a Cypriot, an old disciple, with whom we were to lodge.

When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. After greeting them, he related one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. When they heard it, they glorified God and said to him:

“You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. They have heard about you, that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom. What, then, is to be done? The multitude will certainly assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived.

“Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow. Take these men with you, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the reports they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the law.

“As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have written our judgment: that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, having purified himself with them, entered the temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification until the offering should be presented for each one of them.

When the seven days were nearly completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out:

“Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this place. Moreover, he has even brought Gentiles into the temple and defiled this holy place.”

For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him and supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. The whole city was thrown into confusion, and the people rushed together. They seized Paul and dragged him outside the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.

While they were seeking to kill him, word reached the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

Then the tribune approached, seized him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He began asking who he was and what he had done. But some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another. Since he could not learn the truth because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.

When Paul reached the steps, it happened that he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd. For the multitude of people followed, shouting, “Away with him!”

As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “Is it lawful for me to say something to you?” He replied, “Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian who recently stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?”

Paul said to him, “I am indeed a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. But I ask you to permit me to speak to the people.” When he had given permission, Paul, standing on the steps, signaled with his hand to the people. When there was a profound silence, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

## Chapter XXII

*[Source cols. 0718C–0719C]*

“Men, brothers and fathers, hear now the defense that I make before you.”

When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they kept still more silent. And he said:

“I am a Jewish man, born in Tarsus of Cilicia but brought up in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the truth of the ancestral law, being zealous for the law, as all of you are today. I persecuted this Way even to the point of death, binding and handing over to prison both men and women, as the high priest and all the elders can testify concerning me. From them I also received letters to the brothers, and I was traveling to Damascus to bring those who were there bound to Jerusalem, so that they might be punished.

“As I was traveling and approaching Damascus at midday, suddenly a great light from heaven shone around me. Falling to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’

“Those who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking with me. I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Rise and go to Damascus; there you will be told about everything that you must do.’

“Since I could not see because of the brilliance of that light, I was led by the hand by my companions and came to Damascus. A certain Ananias, a man devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, came to me. Standing beside me, he said, ‘Saul, brother, regain your sight.’ And at that very moment I looked up at him.

“He said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from his mouth, because you will be his witness to all people of the things you have seen and heard. And now, why do you delay? Rise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’

“It happened that when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance and saw him saying to me, ‘Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’

“I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I was imprisoning and beating in the synagogues those who believed in you. And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by, consenting and guarding the clothing of those who were killing him.’

“And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”

They listened to him up to this word, and then raised their voices, saying, “Away with such a man from the earth! For it is not right that he should live.”

While they were shouting, throwing off their clothes, and tossing dust into the air, the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, flogged, and tortured, so that he might learn the reason for which they were shouting against him.

When they had bound him with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen, and one who has not been condemned?”

When he heard this, the centurion approached the tribune and reported it, saying, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.”

The tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” He replied, “Yes.” The tribune answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I was born to it.”

Immediately, therefore, those who were about to torture him withdrew from him. The tribune also became afraid after learning that he was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him.

On the following day, wishing to know more precisely why he was being accused by the Jews, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. Then he brought Paul down and set him before them.

## Chapter XXIII

*[Source cols. 0719D–0721A]*

Looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Men, brothers, I have lived before God with a completely good conscience up to this day.”

The high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth. Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit judging me according to the law, and contrary to the law you order me to be struck?”

Those standing nearby said, “Do you revile God’s high priest?”

Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people.’”

But Paul, knowing that one part of the council was Sadducees and the other Pharisees, cried out in the council:

“Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is because of the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged.”

When he had said this, dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, while the Pharisees confess both.

A great clamor arose. Some of the Pharisees stood up and argued, saying, “We find nothing evil in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?”

When great dissension arose, the tribune, fearing that Paul might be torn apart by them, ordered the soldiers to go down, seize him from their midst, and bring him into the barracks.

On the following night the Lord stood beside him and said, “Take courage. For just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”

When day came, some of the Jews formed a conspiracy and bound themselves by an oath, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. There were more than forty men who had made this conspiracy.

They approached the chief priests and elders and said, “With an oath we have bound ourselves to taste nothing until we kill Paul. Therefore you, together with the council, now inform the tribune that he should bring him down to you, as though you intended to inquire more accurately into his case. We, before he comes near, are ready to kill him.”

When Paul’s sister’s son heard of the plot, he came, entered the barracks, and reported it to Paul. Paul summoned one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.”

The centurion took him and led him to the tribune, saying, “Paul the prisoner asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to say to you.”

The tribune took him by the hand, withdrew with him privately, and asked him, “What is it that you have to report to me?”

He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down tomorrow to the council, as though they intended to inquire more accurately about him. But do not believe them, for more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him. They have bound themselves by oath not to eat or drink until they kill him, and now they are ready, waiting for your promise.”

The tribune then dismissed the young man, ordering him not to tell anyone that he had made this known to him.

He summoned two centurions and said to them, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, together with seventy cavalrymen and two hundred spearmen, beginning at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts, so that they may put Paul on them and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

For he was afraid that the Jews might seize and kill him, and that afterward he himself might be accused of having accepted money. He wrote a letter containing the following:

**CLAUDIUS LYPSIAS to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings.**

“When this man had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, I came upon them with troops and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. Wishing to know the charge they were bringing against him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused concerning questions of their law, but that he had committed no offense deserving death or imprisonment.

“When I was informed of the plot they had prepared against him, I sent him to you, also instructing his accusers to state their case before you. Farewell.”

So the soldiers, according to the orders they had received, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. On the following day, leaving the cavalry to continue with him, they returned to the barracks.

When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul before him. After reading it and asking from which province he was, and learning that he was from Cilicia, he said, “I will hear you when your accusers arrive.” And he ordered that he be kept in Herod’s praetorium.

## Chapter XXIV

*[Source cols. 0721B–0722A]*

After five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a certain orator named Tertullus. They brought charges against Paul before the governor.

When Paul had been summoned, Tertullus began his accusation, saying:

“Since through you we enjoy great peace and many reforms are being made through your foresight, excellent Felix, we accept this everywhere and in every way with complete gratitude. But, so that I may not detain you any longer, I ask you in your clemency to hear us briefly.

“We have found this man to be a plague, stirring up disturbances among all the Jews throughout the world and an instigator of the Nazarene sect. He even attempted to profane the temple, and we seized him, wishing to judge him according to our law. But the tribune Lysias came upon us with great force and took him from our hands, ordering his accusers to come before you. By examining him yourself, you can learn from him about all the matters of which we accuse him.”

The Jews also joined in, asserting that these things were so.

Paul answered, after the governor had signaled to him to speak:

“Knowing that for many years you have been judge over this nation, I can defend my case with confidence. You can ascertain that it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship. They did not find me disputing with anyone in the temple, nor stirring up a crowd in the synagogues or throughout the city; nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.

“But this I admit to you: according to the Way—which they call a sect—I serve the Father and my God, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets. I have hope in God, a hope that these men themselves also expect: that there will be a resurrection of the just and the unjust. In this respect I also strive always to keep my conscience without offense toward God and toward men.

“After many years I came to bring alms to my nation and offerings and vows. In connection with these they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd or in an uproar. But there were certain Jews from Asia who ought to have been present before you and to bring charges if they had anything against me. Or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before the council, except for this one statement that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged by you today.’”

Felix postponed their case, knowing very accurately about the Way, and said, “When the tribune Lysias comes down, I will hear your case.” He ordered the centurion to guard him, but to allow him some freedom and not to prevent any of his people from ministering to him.

After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and heard him concerning faith in Christ Jesus. As Paul discussed righteousness, chastity, and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened and answered, “For the present, go away; when I have an opportunity, I will summon you.”

At the same time he was hoping that money would be given to him by Paul. Therefore he sent for him frequently and conversed with him.

When two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Wishing to grant the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul imprisoned.

## Chapter XXV

*[Source cols. 0722B–0723B]*

When Festus arrived in the province, after three days he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. The chief priests and the leading Jews brought charges against Paul before him. They asked him as a favor against Paul to order him brought to Jerusalem, while they were preparing an ambush to kill him on the way.

Festus answered that Paul was to be kept in Caesarea and that he himself would soon depart. “Therefore,” he said, “let those among you who have authority go down with me; if there is any crime in the man, let them accuse him.”

After spending no more than eight or ten days among them, he went down to Caesarea. On the following day he sat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought in. When he had been brought in, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem surrounded him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove, while Paul defended himself:

“I have committed no offense either against the law of the Jews, or against the temple, or against Caesar.”

Festus, wishing to grant the Jews a favor, answered Paul, saying, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me concerning these matters?”

Paul said, “I stand before Caesar’s tribunal; there I must be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you know very well. If I have done wrong or committed anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing in the charges they bring against me, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar.”

Then Festus, after conferring with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go.”

After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus. Since they spent several days there, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying:

“There is a man here who was left imprisoned by Felix. When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews brought charges against him and requested a sentence against him. I answered them that it is not the Roman custom to condemn any person before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself against the charges.

“So when they had assembled here without any delay, on the following day I sat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought in. When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge concerning the matters I had suspected. Instead, they had certain questions concerning their own superstition against him, and concerning a certain dead Jesus whom Paul asserted to be alive.

“Since I was uncertain how to investigate such questions, I asked whether he wished to go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning these matters. But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of Augustus, I ordered him kept until I could send him to Caesar.”

Agrippa said to Festus, “I myself would like to hear the man.” He replied, “Tomorrow you shall hear him.”

On the following day, Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the audience hall together with the tribunes and the leading men of the city. At Festus’s command, Paul was brought in.

Festus said:

“King Agrippa, and all you men who are present with us, you see this man concerning whom the whole Jewish multitude appealed to me in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer. But I discovered that he had done nothing deserving death. Since he himself appealed to Augustus, I decided to send him.

“But I have nothing certain to write about him to my lord. Therefore I have brought him before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination I may have something to write. For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without indicating the charges against him.”

## Chapter XXVI

*[Source cols. 0723B–0724C]*

Agrippa said to Paul, “You are permitted to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:

“Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to be able to defend myself before you today, especially because you are acquainted with all the customs and controversies among the Jews. Therefore I ask you to hear me patiently.

“All the Jews know my manner of life from my youth, which from the beginning was spent among my nation in Jerusalem. They have known me from the outset—if they are willing to testify—that I lived as a Pharisee according to the strictest sect of our religion.

“And now I stand subject to judgment because of the hope in the promise made by God to our fathers. Our twelve tribes, serving night and day, hope to attain this promise. It is concerning this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews. Why is it judged incredible among you that God raises the dead?

“I myself once thought that I ought to act in many ways against the name of Jesus the Nazarene. And I did so in Jerusalem. Having received authority from the chief priests, I shut up many of the saints in prison; and when they were put to death, I cast my vote against them. Frequently punishing them in all the synagogues, I tried to force them to blaspheme. In my extreme fury against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.

“When I was traveling to Damascus with authority and permission from the chief priests, at midday on the road I saw, O king, a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and around those traveling with me. When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language:

> “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.”

“I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as a servant and witness both of the things you have seen and of those in which I shall appear to you, rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles—to whom I now send you—to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a share among the sanctified through faith in me.’

“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. Rather, I first announced to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, and throughout all the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing works worthy of repentance.

“For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and attempted to kill me. But, having been helped by God, I stand to this day, testifying to both small and great, saying nothing beyond what the Prophets and Moses said would happen: whether the Christ is passible (capable of suffering), and whether, as the first from the resurrection of the dead, he is to proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.”

While he was making this defense, Festus cried out loudly, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is driving you mad.”

But Paul said, “I am not mad, excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sound judgment. For the king knows about these matters, to whom I also speak boldly. I am convinced that none of these things has escaped his notice, since this was not done in a corner. Do you believe the Prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe.”

Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time you would persuade me to become a Christian.”

Paul replied, “I would pray to God that, whether in a short time or in a long time, not only you but also all who hear me today might become such as I am—except for these chains.”

Then the king rose, and the governor, and Bernice, and those sitting with them. After they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”

Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

## [Chapter XXVII]

When it had been decided that he should sail for Italy, Paul and the other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort. They boarded a ship from Adramyttium and began sailing along the coast of Asia, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, remaining with us. The next day we reached Sidon. Julius treated Paul humanely and allowed him to go to his friends and receive their care. From there, after putting out to sea, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary. Having sailed across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Lystram, which is in Lycia; and there the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and transferred us to it.

After we had sailed slowly for many days and had scarcely reached the vicinity of Cnidus, since the wind prevented us from proceeding, we sailed under the lee of Crete, near Salmone. With difficulty sailing along its coast, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Thalassa. Since considerable time had passed and sailing was already unsafe—because the fast had also already gone by—Paul advised them, saying:

“Men, I see that the voyage is beginning to involve injury and great loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”

But the centurion trusted the helmsman and the shipmaster more than what Paul was saying. Since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, most of them decided that they should sail from there, if somehow they could reach Phoenix and winter there—a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.

When a south wind began to blow, and they thought that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor from Asson and sailed along Crete. But not long afterward a storm-wind called Euroaquilo came down against it. When the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to the wind and were driven along.

Running under the lee of a certain island called Cauda, we were scarcely able to secure the ship’s boat. After it had been hoisted aboard, they used supports, binding the ship around with cables, and, fearing that they might run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and were carried along in this manner. When we had been violently tossed by the storm, on the following day they jettisoned the cargo; and on the third day they threw the ship’s equipment overboard with their own hands.

For many days neither sun nor stars appeared, and a considerable storm continued to threaten us; all hope of our safety had now been taken away. After there had been much fasting, Paul then stood among them and said:

“Men, you ought indeed to have listened to me and not have put out from Crete, thereby avoiding this injury and loss. And now I urge you to be of good courage. For there will be no loss of life among you, except of the ship. For this night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me, saying, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar; and behold, God has granted you all those who are sailing with you.’ Therefore, men, be of good courage; for I believe God that it will be exactly as it was told me. But we must run aground on a certain island.”

When the fourteenth night came, as we were sailing about in the Adriatic around midnight, the sailors suspected that some land was appearing to them. They cast a sounding line and found twenty fathoms; and, having moved a little farther, they found fifteen fathoms. Fearing that we might run aground in rough places, they dropped four anchors from the stern and wished for day to come.

But when the sailors were seeking to flee from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under the pretext that they intended to extend anchors from the bow, Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers:

“Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.”

Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and allowed it to fall away.

As daylight began to appear, Paul urged everyone to take food, saying:

“Today is the fourteenth day that you have been waiting and have remained fasting, taking nothing. Therefore I urge you to take food for your survival, because not one of you will lose a hair from his head.”

After saying this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the presence of all, broke it, and began to eat. When they had all become more confident, they too took food. We were 276 persons in all on the ship. When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.

When it became day, they did not recognize the land; but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, toward which they planned, if possible, to run the ship ashore. After raising the anchors, they committed themselves to the sea, at the same time loosening the fastenings of the rudders. Then, having raised the foresail according to the direction of the wind, they made for the beach.

When we came to a place between two seas, they ran the ship aground. The bow remained fixed and immovable, but the stern was being broken apart by the force of the waves. The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest anyone swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, prevented this and ordered those who could swim to cast themselves overboard first, make their way to safety, and reach the land; and the rest were to follow, some on planks and others on pieces of the ship. And so it happened that all the persons escaped safely to land.

## [Chapter XXVIII]

After we had escaped, we learned that the island was called Malta. The natives showed us no ordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and refreshed us all, because rain was threatening and it was cold.

When Paul had gathered a considerable bundle of sticks and placed it on the fire, a viper, emerging because of the heat, fastened upon his hand. When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another:

“Surely this man is a murderer, and though he has escaped from the sea, vengeance does not allow him to live.”

But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm. They expected that he would swell up or suddenly fall down and die. After waiting a long time and seeing that no harm came to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

In that region there were estates belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius. He welcomed us and entertained us courteously for three days. It happened that the father of Publius was lying sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him and, after praying and laying his hands upon him, healed him.

After this had happened, all the others on the island who had illnesses came to him and were healed. They also honored us with many honors and, when we sailed, supplied us with what was necessary.

After three months we sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island and bore the emblem of the Castors. When we reached Syracuse, we stayed there three days. From there, sailing around the coast, we came to Rhegium. After one day, when a south wind had arisen, we reached Puteoli on the second day. There we found brothers and were asked to remain with them for seven days; and so we came to Rome.

From there, when the brothers heard about us, they came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage.

When we arrived in Rome, Paul was allowed to remain by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. After three days he summoned the leading Jews. When they had assembled, he said to them:

“Men, brothers, although I had done nothing against the people or against the ancestral customs, I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans. After they had examined me, they wanted to release me, because there was no cause of death in me. But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar—not as though I had anything to accuse my nation of. For this reason, therefore, I asked to see you and speak with you. For it is on account of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.”

But they said to him:

“We have neither received letters from Judea concerning you, nor has any of the brothers who arrived reported or spoken anything evil about you. But we ask to hear from you what you think, for we know that this sect is everywhere opposed.”

After they had appointed a day, many came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening he explained matters to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and persuading them concerning Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets. Some were convinced by what was said, but others did not believe.

Since they were not in agreement with one another, they departed after Paul had spoken one word:

“Rightly did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying:

‘Go to this people and say:
You will hear with your ears and will not understand;
you will indeed see and will not perceive.
For the heart of this people has become dull,
and they have heard with their ears heavily,
and they have closed their eyes,
lest they should perhaps see with their eyes
and hear with their ears
and understand with their heart
and turn, and I should heal them.’

“Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.”

After he had said these things, the Jews departed, having much discussion among themselves.

He remained for a full two years in his rented lodging and welcomed all who came to him, preaching the kingdom of God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with complete confidence and without hindrance.

[Col. 0727] The book of the Acts of the Apostles ends.

## [THE EPISTLES OF PAUL]

## THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS BEGINS

**[Note: We have read through these Epistles of Paul and the other Apostles according to the Vatican exemplar edited by Martianay, against the testimony of the Palatine manuscript, which is preserved in the same Vatican Library under number 57. We found it to be the oldest of all, and of better quality and reliability than the others.]**

## [Chapter I]

Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had previously promised through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was designated the Son of God in power according to the spirit of holiness by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Through him we have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles for his name’s sake, among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ—to all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always remember you in my prayers, asking that somehow at last I may have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you.

For I long to see you, so that I may impart some spiritual gift to you for your strengthening—that is, that we may be mutually encouraged among you by one another’s faith, both yours and mine.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you—and have been prevented until now—so that I might have some fruit among you, as also among the other Gentiles. I am a debtor both to Greeks and to Barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish; thus, as far as lies with me, I am ready to preach the Gospel to you also who are in Rome.

For I am not ashamed of the Gospel. For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: “But the righteous shall live by faith.”

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest among them. For God has manifested it to them.

For his invisible attributes, understood and seen from the creation of the world through the things that have been made—both his eternal power and divinity—are perceived, so that they are without excuse.

For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and reptiles.

Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions. Their females exchanged natural use for that use which is against nature. Likewise, the males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense that was due for their error.

And just as they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper: filled with every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, greed, and evil; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, boastful, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without fidelity, without mercy.

Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them.

## [Chapter II]

Therefore you are without excuse, every person who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge.

We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. Do you suppose, then, O man, who judges those who do such things and yet does them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know—[the manuscript reads: “being ignorant”]—that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?

But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each one according to his works: eternal life to those who, through perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, but believe iniquity.

Tribulation and anguish upon every human soul that works evil, the Jew first and the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, the Jew first and the Greek. For there is no partiality with God.

For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and all who have sinned in the law will be judged through the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.

For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, although they do not have the law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness with them, and their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending them, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ.

**[Note: In the Palatine manuscript, more closely following the Greek text: “the thoughts mutually accusing or even defending one another, on the day,” etc.]**

But if you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve what is excellent, instructed by the law; if you are confident that you are a guide of the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing the form of knowledge and truth in the law—then you who teach another do not teach yourself. You who preach against stealing, steal. You who say that one must not commit adultery, commit adultery. You who abhor idols, commit sacrilege. You who glory in the law dishonor God through transgressing the law—for “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,” as it is written.

Circumcision indeed profits if you observe the law. But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

Therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the ordinances of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will not the uncircumcision that is by nature, fulfilling the law, judge you who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law?

**[Note: More correctly, at least in accordance with the Greek text, κρινεῖ ἡ φύσεως ἀκροβυστία—“the uncircumcision by nature will judge”; in the Palatine manuscript the word *id* (“that”) is omitted.]**

**[Note: The Palatine manuscript has *custodias*—“keep”—instead of *observes*; in several Greek books, φυλάσσῃς (*phylassēs*, “keep/guard”) is read instead of πράσσῃς (*prassēs*, “do/practice”).]**

For it is not the one who is so outwardly a Jew, nor is circumcision outwardly, in the flesh; but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter. His praise is not from human beings but from God.

## [Chapter III]

What advantage, then, does the Jew have? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.

What, then, if some of them did not believe? Surely their unbelief will not abolish the faithfulness of God? Certainly not. But God is truthful, and every human being a liar, as it is written:

**[Manuscript reading: *enim* (“for”).]**

“So that you may be justified in your words,
and prevail when you are judged.”

But if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous when he brings wrath?—I speak according to human reasoning. Certainly not. Otherwise, how will God judge the world?

For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? And why should we not—as we are slanderously accused, and as some claim that we say—“Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is just.

What, then? Are we superior to them? Not at all. For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin, as it is written:

“There is no righteous person, not even one;
there is no one who understands;
there is no one who seeks God.
All have turned aside;
together they have become useless.
There is no one who does good,
not even one.
Their throat is an open tomb;
with their tongues they practiced deceit.
The venom of asps is under their lips.
Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.
Their feet are swift to shed blood;
destruction and misery are in their ways,
and they have not known the way of peace.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God. For no flesh will be justified before him by works of the law, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.
