Nevertheless, neither is man without woman nor woman without man in the Lord. For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman; but all things are from God.

Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman grows her hair long, it is her glory? For her hair has been given to her as a covering.

But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the church of God.

Now in giving this instruction I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse. For first of all, when you gather together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you [Col. 0754D] [Ms. omits “among you”], and I partly believe it. For there must also be factions, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.

Therefore, when you gather together in one place, it is not to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat. One is hungry, and another is drunk.

Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was handed over, took bread [Col. 0755A], and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat; this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

Likewise also the cup, after he had eaten, saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.” For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and thus let him eat from that bread and drink from the cup. For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

For this reason many among you are weak and sick [Col. 0755B], and many are sleeping. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. Yet when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world.

Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment. I will arrange the remaining matters when I come.

## [Chapter XII]

Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were gentiles, you were led away, going after mute images, wherever you were led.

Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus.” And no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit.

There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities [Col. 0755C], but it is the same God who works all things in all.

But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the benefit of all. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of speech.

But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wishes.

For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or gentiles, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one [Col. 0755D] Spirit [Note: [Col. 0755D] More closely following the Greek text, the Palatine manuscript has the active form: “we drank one Spirit,” ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν, and so forth.].

For the body is not one member but many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body? And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body?

If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If it were entirely hearing, where would smelling be? But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he wished. If they were all one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body.

The eye cannot say to the hand [Col. 0756A], “I have no need of you”; nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.” Rather, the members of the body that seem to be weaker are more necessary; and those members of the body that we think less honorable, we surround with greater honor. And our less presentable members have greater dignity, while our presentable members have no need of this.

But God has composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may care for one another equally. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.

Now you are Christ’s body, and individually members.

And God has placed some in the church: first [Col. 0756B] apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers; afterward gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues [Note: [Col. 0756D] The Palatine manuscript does not know the words “interpretations of speech,” which are also found only in a few Greek manuscripts.], interpretations of speech.

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?

But earnestly desire the greater gifts [Ms. “gifts”]. And I will show you a still more excellent way [Ms. “I will demonstrate”].

## [Chapter XIII]

If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge [Col. 0756C], and if I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.

And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn [Ms. “so that it may burn”], but do not have love, it benefits me nothing.

Love is patient; it is kind. Love does not envy; it does not act improperly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it does not reckon evil; it does not rejoice over injustice but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

Love never fails. But prophecies will be abolished, tongues will cease, and knowledge will be abolished. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when what is perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished [Col. 0756D].

When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I abolished the things belonging to childhood.

Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know just as I also have been known.

But now these three remain: faith, hope, and love. And the greatest of these is love.

### Chapter XIV

Pursue love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts—especially that you may prophesy. For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God, for no one understands him; yet in the Spirit he speaks mysteries. But the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation. The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but the one who prophesies edifies the Church [Note: The name “of God,” which the Greek text likewise omits, is absent from the Palatine manuscript.].

Now I wish that you all spoke in tongues, but especially that you prophesied. For the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps [Ms. adds *ut*, “that”] he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification. But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching?

Even lifeless things that produce sound—whether flute or lyre—if they do not give distinct notes, how will what is being played on the flute or lyre be recognized? Indeed, if the trumpet gives an indistinct sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also with you: unless through the tongue you give a clear utterance, how will what is being said be understood? For you will be speaking into the air.

There are, for example, so many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without sound. Therefore, if I do not know the force of the sound, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to abound in them for the edification of the Church. Therefore, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit.

What then is to be done? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind; I will sing praise with the spirit, and I will sing praise also with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninitiated say “Amen” to your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying? For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified.

I give thanks to my God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Yet in the Church I prefer to speak five words with my mind, so that I may instruct others as well, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue.

Brothers, do not become children in your understanding; but in malice be infants, while in understanding be mature. In the Law it is written:

> “By people of other tongues  
> and by other lips  
> I shall speak to this people;  
> yet even then they will not listen to me,”

says the Lord.

Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers; whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. If, then, the whole Church gathers together in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninitiated people or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are insane? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an uninitiated person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all; the secrets of his heart become manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.

What then is to be done, brothers? Whenever you gather, each of you has a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let everything be done for edification. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and in turn; and let one interpret. But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the Church, and speak to himself and to God.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge. [Col. 0758A] But if something is revealed to another who is sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be encouraged. And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of disorder but of peace, as I teach in all the churches of the saints.

Let women keep silent in the churches, for they are not permitted to speak but are to be subject, as the Law also says. If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church.

Did the word of God originate with you? Or did it reach only you? If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are the Lord’s commandments. But if anyone does not recognize this, he will not be recognized.

Therefore, brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But let everything be done decently and in proper order.

### Chapter XV

Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you stand, and through which you are being saved—if you hold fast to the manner in which I preached it to you, unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures; that he appeared to Cephas, and afterward to the eleven. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles. Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.

For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me. Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed [Ms. *praedicavimus*, “we preached”].

But if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty as well. Moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ—whom he did not raise, if indeed the dead are not raised [Note: This whole section, “if the dead do not rise, neither …,” is found neither in the Palatine manuscript nor in most Greek books]. For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.

If we have hoped in Christ in this life only, we are more pitiable than all human beings. But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For since death came through a human being, through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead. And just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ, who have believed in his coming. Then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power [Note: The Palatine manuscript adds “and dominion,” which is not found in the Greek archetype.]. For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when it says, “All things have been subjected to him,” clearly this excludes the one who subjected all things to him. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.

Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead are not raised at all? Why, then, are they baptized for them? And why are we in danger every hour? Every day I die, by the glory that I have in you, brothers, in Christ Jesus our Lord. If, speaking in human terms, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what benefit is it to me if the dead are not raised? “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

Do not be deceived: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals.” Awake to righteousness and do not sin. For some have no knowledge of God; I say this to your shame.

But someone will say, “How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body will they come?” Foolish person, what you sow does not come to life unless it first dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain—perhaps of wheat or of one of the other kinds. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.

Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one kind of flesh of human beings, another of animals, another of birds, and another of fish [Note: In the Palatine manuscript: “another of animals, another flesh of birds,” and so forth; the Greek text also varies here.]. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of heavenly bodies and another of earthly bodies. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body. If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one, as it is written: “The first human being, Adam, became a living soul”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.

But the spiritual was not first, but the animal; afterward the spiritual. The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.

Now this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption. Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality. And when this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass:

> “Death has been swallowed up in victory.  
> Where is your victory, O death?  
> Where is your sting, O death?”

The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the Law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.

### Chapter XVI

Concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also must do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside for himself, storing up whatever he has prospered in, so that collections will not take place when I come.

And when I arrive, I will send those whom you approve by letters to carry your gift to Jerusalem. And if it is worthwhile for me to go as well, they will go with me.

I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia—for I shall pass through Macedonia. Perhaps I shall remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not wish to see you now merely in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.

I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and evident door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

If Timothy comes, see to it that he is without fear among you; for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am. Therefore let no one despise him. Send him on in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

Concerning our brother Apollos, I inform you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers; yet it was certainly not his will to come at this time. He will come when he has an opportunity [Note: In the Palatine manuscript the wording is much more harmonious and closer to the Greek verb *eukairēsē* (εὐκαιρήσῃ): “when it is opportune for him.”].

Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act courageously, and be strengthened. Let everything among you be done in love.

Now I urge you, brothers—you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus: they are the firstfruits of Achaia, and they devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Be subject also to such people, and to everyone who cooperates and labors [Note: The Palatine manuscript adds “among you”; these two words are not found in the Greek text.].

I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking on your part. For they refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore recognize such people.

The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church in their house; with them I am lodging. All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. If anyone does not love the Lord our Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Maranatha.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript adds “Amen,” a word omitted by the Greek text.]. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

*Here ends the First Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians.*

---

## THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS BEGINS

### Chapter I

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the Church of God that is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are throughout Achaia.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may be able to console those who are in every kind of distress through the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.

For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us [Ms. *vobis*, “in you,”], so also through Christ our consolation abounds [Note: The Palatine manuscript entirely omits this whole section—“whether we are consoled for your consolation,” etc. A little later it reads more closely to the Greek text, “which works in endurance” (*en hypomonē*, ἐν ὑπομονῇ).]. Whether we are afflicted for your consolation and salvation, or whether we are consoled for your consolation, or whether we are encouraged for your encouragement and salvation, which produces endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer, our hope for you is firm, knowing that just as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will be partners in the consolation.

For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation that occurred in Asia: we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living. Indeed, we ourselves had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not place our confidence in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead. He delivered us from such great dangers, and he is delivering us; in him we have hoped that he will also continue to deliver us, while you assist on our behalf through prayer, so that thanks may be given on our behalf by many persons for the gift bestowed upon us through many [Note: In place of *ex multis personis*, the Palatine manuscript reads, more closely following the Greek *en pollōn prosōpōn* (ἐν πολλῶν προσώπων), “from many faces.”].

For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and the sincerity of God—and not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God—we have conducted ourselves in this world, and especially toward you.

For we write nothing else to you [Ms. omits *vobis*, “to you”] than what you read and understand [Ms. *cognoscitis*, “understand”]. I hope that you will understand fully, just as you have understood us in part, namely, that [Ms. adds *nos*, “we”] we are your glory, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

With this confidence I wanted first to come to you, so that you might have a second benefit, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come to you from Macedonia, and to be sent on by you to Judaea.

When I intended this, did I perhaps act with fickleness? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there is “Yes and No”? But God is faithful: our word [Ms. *fit*, “is”] to you was not “Yes and No” [Note: Someone, perhaps from an older Latin translation, has added here, “but it is Yes in him.” Thus also shortly afterward: “it was not Yes and No in him, but …”].

For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not “Yes and No,” but “Yes” has been realized in him. For however many promises of God there are, in him is the “Yes”; therefore, through him also comes the “Amen” to God, for our glory.

Now the one who establishes us with you in Christ [Ms. *Christus Dominus*, “Christ the Lord”] and who anointed us is God. He also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts [Ms. *Spiritum*, “the Spirit,”].

But I call God as witness against my life that, to spare you, I did not come again to Corinth—not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers for your joy, for you stand firm in faith.

### Chapter II

I decided this within myself: not to come to you again in sorrow. For if I cause you sorrow, who is there to make me glad except the one who is made sorrowful by me? And I wrote this very thing to you so that, when I came, I would not have sorrow upon sorrow from those over whom I ought to rejoice, having confidence in all of you that my joy belongs to all of you.

For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears—not so that you might be made sorrowful, but so that you might know the love that I have for you in such abundance.

But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not caused sorrow to me, except in part, lest I burden all of you. For such a person, this punishment inflicted by the majority is sufficient, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest perhaps someone of this kind be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

Therefore I urge you to confirm your love toward him. For this is also why I wrote: to learn by experience whether you are obedient in everything.

But to whomever you have granted forgiveness for anything, I grant it as well. For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I did for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads, “for we are not ignorant of his cunning thoughts”; in Greek there is only *ta noēmata* (τὰ νοήματα), “his designs.”].

When I came to Troas for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit because I did not find Titus my brother. So, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia.

But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us reveals the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, the fragrance of death leading to death; to others, the fragrance of life leading to life. And who is sufficient for these things?

For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God; rather, from sincerity, as from God, in the presence of God, we speak in Christ.

### Chapter III

Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we perhaps need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people. You are manifestly a letter of Christ, prepared by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.

Now we have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God. He also made us competent ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Now if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which is being abolished, how will the ministry of the Spirit not be even more in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory [Ms. *abundavit*, “abounded”]. Indeed, what was glorious in this respect was not glorified, because of the surpassing glory. For if what is being abolished came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory.

Therefore, since we have such hope, we act with great confidence, and not as Moses placed a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not look intently at what was being abolished; rather, their minds were hardened. For to this very day the same veil remains unlifted at the reading of the old covenant, because it is abolished in Christ. But to this very day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.

But whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Lord’s Spirit.

### Chapter IV

Therefore, since we have this ministry [Note: Following the Greek text, the Palatine manuscript adds the pronoun *hanc*, “this”], in accordance with the mercy we have received, we do not lose heart. Rather, we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning and not adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of truth commending ourselves to every human conscience in the presence of God.

But if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing. Among them the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine upon them [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript omits the pronoun “upon them,” which is found in most Greek books.].

For we do not preach ourselves but Jesus Christ as Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus. For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” himself has shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may belong to God and not come from us. In every respect we are afflicted, but not crushed; perplexed, but not despairing; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.

For we who live are always being handed over to death because of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. Thus death is at work in us, but life in you.

But having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, “I believed because I spoke,” we also believe, and therefore we speak, knowing that the one who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and place us with you.

For everything is for your sake, so that grace, having abounded through many, may increase thanksgiving to the glory of God. Therefore we do not lose heart. Though our outer person is being corrupted, our inner person is being renewed day by day.

For this momentary and light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

### Chapter V

For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, an everlasting house in the heavens, not made by human hands. For in this we groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven [Ms. *in coelo*, “in heaven”]. If indeed, once clothed, we are not found naked.

For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now the one who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.

Therefore, being always confident and knowing that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight—we are confident, and we prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

And therefore we make it our aim, whether away or at home, to please him. For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but to God we are manifest, and I hope that we are manifest also in your consciences. We do not commend ourselves again to you, but give you an opportunity to boast on our behalf, so that you may have something to say to those who boast in appearance and not in heart.

Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are of sound mind, it is for you. For the love of Christ compels us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all—Christ [Note: The name “Christ,” which is also absent from the Greek archetype, is not added in the Palatine manuscript]—so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them.

Therefore, from now on we know no one according to the flesh. Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away. Behold, they have become [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript omits the word “all things,” although it is found in most Greek copies] new.

But everything is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and he placed in us the word of reconciliation.

Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

### Chapter VI

As fellow workers, we also urge you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says:

> “At an acceptable time I heard you,  
> and on the day of salvation I helped you.”

Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed, but in everything presenting ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in sincere love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as disciplined and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own inward parts. In return for this—I speak as to children—be enlarged yourselves.

Do not become unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership is there between righteousness and lawlessness? Or what fellowship between light and darkness? What agreement between Christ and Belial? Or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever? And what agreement does the temple of God have with idols?

For you are the temple of the living God, as God says:

> “I will dwell among them  
> and walk among them,  
> and I will be their God,  
> and they will be my people.”

Therefore:

> “Come out from their midst  
> and be separate,”

says the Lord,

> “and do not touch what is unclean;  
> and I will receive you.  
> I will be a father to you,  
> and you will be sons and daughters to me,”

says the Lord Almighty.

### Chapter VII

Therefore, since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, completing holiness in the fear of God.

Receive us. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. I do not say this to condemn you. For we have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

I have great confidence in you; I have much reason to boast about you. I am filled with consolation; I abound in joy in all our tribulation.

For even when we came to Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every kind of tribulation: outwardly conflicts, inwardly fears. But God, who consoles the humble, consoled us by the arrival of Titus—not only by his arrival, but also by the consolation with which he was consoled among you, as he reported to us your mourning and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced even more [Note: The Palatine manuscript likewise reads “in the consolation with which,” instead of “the consolation by which.”].

For although I caused you sorrow by the letter, I do not regret it. And if I did regret it, seeing that the letter caused you sorrow, though only for a time, now I rejoice—not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance. For you were made sorrowful according to God, so that you might suffer no loss through us.

For sorrow according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, but worldly sorrow produces death. For behold, this very thing—that you were made sorrowful according to God—how great earnestness it produced in you; but also defense, but also indignation, but also fear, but also longing, but also zeal, but also punishment. In everything you showed yourselves to be pure in the matter.

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but to make our earnest concern for you manifest—the concern that we have for you before God [Note: According to the Greek exemplar, the Palatine manuscript reads: “our earnest concern, which we have for you, toward you, before God” (*tēn spoudēn hēmōn tēn hyper hymōn pros hymas enōpion tou Theou*, τὴν σπουδὴν ἡμῶν τὴν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ)].

For this reason we were consoled. In our consolation we rejoiced even more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. And if I have boasted to him about you, I have not been put to shame. Rather, just as we spoke everything to you in truth, so also our boasting before Titus proved to be true. His inward affections toward you are all the stronger, as he remembers the obedience of you all and how you received him with fear and trembling.

I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you.

### Chapter VIII

We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid much testing through tribulation, the abundance of their joy existed [Note: The Palatine manuscript omits *fuit*, “existed,” as does the Greek text], and their deepest poverty overflowed into the riches of their generosity. For I testify to them [Ms. adds *Dei*, “of God”] according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing, with much entreaty, begging us for the grace and participation in the ministry that is performed for the saints.

And not as we hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us through the will of God. Thus we urged Titus that, just as he began, so he should also complete this grace among you.

But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, all earnestness, and your love for us—so also abound in this grace. I do not say this as a command, but by the earnestness of others I am testing the genuineness of your love.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that although he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.

And I give my opinion in this matter, for this is beneficial to you. You began not only to do but also to desire this from the previous year; now complete it in deed, so that just as the willingness to desire was ready, so also may the completion be according to what you have.

For if the willingness is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. For this is not so that there may be relief for others and distress for you, but according to equality. At the present time, let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, and there may be equality, as it is written:

> “The one who gathered much did not have too much,  
> and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”

But thanks be to God, who gave [Ms. adds *nobis*, “to us”] the same earnest concern for you in the heart of Titus, because he accepted the exhortation; but, being more earnest, he went to you of his own accord.

We also sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. Not only that, but he has also been appointed by the churches as our traveling companion in this grace that is administered by us for the glory of the Lord and to carry out our willing purpose, while avoiding this: that anyone should blame us in this abundance that is administered by us [Note: The Palatine manuscript adds here the words “for the glory of God,” of which there is neither trace nor indication in the Greek text.].

For we take care to do what is good not only in the presence of God but also in the presence of human beings.

And we sent with them our brother, whom we have often tested as being earnest in many things. But now he is much more earnest, with great confidence in you—whether concerning Titus, who is my partner and your helper, or concerning our brothers, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.

Therefore, demonstrate before them, and before the churches, the proof of your love and of our boasting about you.

## Chapter IX

Now concerning the ministry for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you to the Macedonians: that Achaia has been ready since last year, and your zeal has stirred up very many.

But I have sent the brothers, so that our boasting about you in this matter may not prove empty, and so that, as I said, you may be ready; lest, if Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to say you—should be put to shame in this undertaking. Therefore I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go ahead to you and prepare this promised blessing, so that it may be ready—as a blessing, not as an act of greed.

I say this: Whoever [Ms. reads: “Because”] sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each person give as he has determined in his heart [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads *destinavit cordi* (“has determined in [his] heart”), closer to the Greek προαιρεῖται τῇ καρδίᾳ; it nevertheless does not add *suo* (“his”)], not out of sorrow or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.

God is able to make every grace abound toward you, so that, always having complete sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work, as it is written:

> He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor;  
> his righteousness remains forever and ever.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript prefers absolutely *in aeternum* (“forever”) instead of *in saeculum saeculi* (“forever and ever”); in Greek, there is only εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.]

Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed, and will increase the harvest of your righteousness, so that, enriched in every respect, you may abound in complete generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God.

For the ministry of this service not only supplies what the saints lack, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord. Through the testing of this ministry, they glorify God for your obedience in confessing the Gospel of Christ and for the generosity of your fellowship with them and with everyone, while they pray for you and long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you.

Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift.

## Chapter X

Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ—I who am humble in appearance when among you, but, when absent, am confident toward you. I ask that, when present, I may not have to act boldly with the confidence by which I am thought to be bold against certain people who suppose that we walk according to the flesh.

For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds: we destroy arguments and every height that raises itself against the knowledge of God, and we take every understanding captive into obedience to Christ. We are ready to punish every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled.

Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we. For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us [Ms. omits: “us”] for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be put to shame.

Let no one think that I am trying to terrify you through my letters. For, they say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Let such a person consider this: that what we are in word through letters when absent, that we shall also be in deed when present.

For we do not dare to insert ourselves among, or compare ourselves with, certain people who commend themselves. But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, show no understanding.

We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule by which God assigned us a measure reaching even to you. For we do not stretch ourselves beyond our limits, as though we had not reached you; indeed, we have reached you in the Gospel of Christ.

We do not boast beyond measure in the labors of others, but we have the hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be magnified among you according to our rule in abundance, so as to preach the Gospel even in regions beyond you, without boasting in another’s sphere about what has already been prepared.

“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.

## Chapter XI

Would that you would bear with a little of my foolishness! Indeed, bear with me. For I am jealous over you with God’s own jealousy. I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may somehow be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ. For if someone comes and preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or if you receive another spirit that you did not receive, or another Gospel that you did not accept, you rightly put up with it.

For I consider that I was in no way inferior to the chiefest apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every respect we have made this manifest to you.

Or did I commit sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I freely preached the Gospel of God to you? I stripped other churches, receiving support for serving you. When I was with you and in need, I was a burden to no one; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. In every respect I kept myself, and will keep myself, from being a burden to you.

The truth of Christ is in me: this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows that I do.

And what I am doing I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us. For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.

[Note: In agreement with the Greek text, the Palatine manuscript omits the adverb *sicut* (“as”) here.]

And no wonder: for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their works.

Again I say: Let no one think that I am foolish; otherwise, receive me as foolish, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness, in this matter of boasting.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. For you gladly put up with fools, since you yourselves are wise. You put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face.

I say this by way of dishonor, as though we had been weak in this respect. But in whatever anyone dares—I speak in foolishness—I too dare.

They are Hebrews? I am too. They are Israelites? I am too. They are Abraham’s seed? I am too. They are ministers of Christ?—I speak as one less wise—I am more so [Note: The Palatine manuscript adds the balanced phrase *et ego* (“I too”), which is not found in the Greek text]: in far more labors, in prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure, in frequent danger of death.

Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck. I spent a night and a day in the deep sea; often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labor and hardship, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.

Apart from these external matters, there is my daily pressure upon me: concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?

If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of what belongs to my weakness. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.

In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; but I was lowered through a window in a basket along the wall, and so I escaped his hands.

## Chapter XII

If it is necessary to boast—it is not expedient, to be sure—I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up as far as the third heaven.

And I know that such a person—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up into paradise and heard secret words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak.

On behalf of such a person I will boast; but on my own behalf I will boast of nothing except my weaknesses. For even if I wished to boast, I would not be foolish, since I would be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one may think more of me than what he sees in me or hears from me.

And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to strike me with blows.

[Note: Closer to the Greek particle ἵνα, the Palatine manuscript reads *ut* (“that”) instead of *qui* (“who”).]

Because of this I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me. And he said to me: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”

Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. For this reason I take pleasure in my weaknesses [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript, in accordance with the Greek text, omits the pronoun *meis* (“my”)], insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ. For whenever I am weak, then I am powerful.

I have become foolish—you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you, since I was in no way inferior to the chiefest apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of my apostleship were nevertheless accomplished among you [Note: Again adhering more closely to the Greek archetype, the Palatine manuscript reads: “The signs indeed of an apostle were accomplished,” corresponding to Τὰ μὲν σημεῖα τοῦ ἀποστόλου κατειργάσθη] in all endurance, in signs, wonders, and mighty works.

For what is it in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this injustice.

Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I shall not burden you. For I do not seek what belongs to you, but you. For children ought not to store up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children.

I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, even if, while loving you more, I am loved less.

But let it be so: I did not burden you, yet, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps?

[Note: Where the Greek has Πάλιν (“again”), the Palatine manuscript has *Iterum* (“again”).]

Have you been thinking all along that we are defending ourselves to you? We speak before God in Christ; and everything, beloved, is for your edification.

For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and that I may be found by you as you do not wish; that there may perhaps be quarrels, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, slander, whispering, arrogance, and disorder among you; and that, when I come again, God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many who sinned previously and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and licentiousness they practiced.

## Chapter XIII

Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you. “On the testimony of two or three witnesses every matter shall stand.”

I have already said [Ms. adds: “for”], and I now say in advance—as when present [Ms. adds: “to you”], so also now absent—to those who sinned previously and to all the others: If I come again, I will not spare you.

Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ, who is not weak toward you but powerful among you? For although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God. And we too are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God among you.

Test yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. Or do you not recognize yourselves—that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless, perhaps, you are disqualified.

But I hope that you will recognize that we are not disqualified. We pray to God that you do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good, even if we should appear disqualified.

For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. We rejoice when [Ms. reads: “whenever”] we are weak and you are powerful. This also we pray for: your restoration.

Therefore I write these things while absent, so that, when present, I may not act harshly according to the authority that the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction.

Finally, brothers, rejoice. Be made complete; be encouraged; be of one mind; live in peace. And the God of peace and love will be with you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you. Amen.

The Second Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Corinthians ends.

---

# The Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Galatians Begins

## Chapter I

Paul, an apostle not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers who are with me—to the churches of Galatia:

Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in the grace of Christ to another Gospel—which is not another Gospel, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ.

But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a Gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone preaches to you a Gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.

For now am I persuading human beings, or God? [Note: The Palatine manuscript reads *Aut* (“or”); the Greek likewise has ἤ.] Or am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.

For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel preached by me is not according to human beings. For I neither received it from a human being nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

For you heard about my former way of life in Judaism: that I persecuted the church of God beyond measure and ravaged it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my nation, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.

But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult flesh and blood.

Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; rather, I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus. Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. In what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying.

Afterward I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they had only heard: “The one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once ravaged.” And they glorified God in me.

## Chapter II

Then, after fourteen years, I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along also. I went up according to a revelation, and I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles—but privately before those who seemed to be something—lest I should be running, or should have run, in vain.

Yet not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised. This was because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might reduce us to slavery.

We did not yield to them in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you. But from those who seemed to be something—whatever they once were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality—I received nothing from those who seemed to be something.

On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcised—for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised worked also through me among the Gentiles—and when they recognized the grace given to me [Note: In a different order, together with certain Greek books, the Palatine manuscript also has: “the grace given to me, Peter, James, and John, who,” etc. Further, wherever the name Cephas occurs below, that manuscript, with the Greek text, has *Peter*. This is especially noteworthy for the familiar controversy concerning Peter rebuked by Paul: following Chrysostom and several other ancients, more recent critics maintain that this was Cephas, not the apostle Peter. Finally, below, for *credimus* (“we believe”), the Palatine manuscript, with the same Greek books, has *credidimus* (“we have believed”).], James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.

They asked only that we remember the poor, which very thing I was eager to do.

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was at fault. For before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision.

And the other Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before everyone:

“If you, although a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews? We are Jews by nature and not sinners from among the Gentiles.

“Knowing that a human being is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; for by works of the law no flesh will be justified.

“But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? Certainly not. For if I rebuild the things I destroyed, I prove myself to be a transgressor.

“For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

“I do not reject the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.”

## Chapter III

O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, so that you should not obey the truth—before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified among you?

I wish to learn only this from you: Did you receive the Spirit through works of the law, or through hearing with faith? Are you so foolish? Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being brought to completion by the flesh? Have you suffered so many things in vain—if indeed it is in vain?

Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works mighty deeds among you do so through works of the law, or through hearing with faith?

As it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

Know [Ms. reads: “You know”], therefore, that those who are from faith are sons of Abraham. And Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham: “In you all the nations shall be blessed.”

Therefore those who are from faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. For all who are from works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.”

Now that no one is justified before God by the law is evident, because “the righteous one shall live by faith.” But the law is not from faith; rather: “The one who does these things shall live by them.”

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.

Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a humanly confirmed covenant no one rejects or adds conditions to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “And to your seed,” who is Christ.

This is what I mean: a covenant previously confirmed by God is not annulled by the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, so as to abolish the promise. For if the inheritance is from the law, it is no longer from the promise [Ms. reads: *repromissione*, “the promise”]. But God granted it to Abraham through a promise.

Why, then, the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made. It was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.

Now a mediator is not for one party alone, but God is one.

Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could [Ms. reads: “can”] give life, righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ.

Before faith came, we were kept under the law, confined until the faith that was to be revealed. Therefore the law was our custodian toward Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But once faith has come, we are no longer under a custodian.

For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus.

And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise.

## Chapter IV

Now I say: For as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of everything; rather, he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father.

So we too, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

[Ms. adds: “of God.”]

And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts [Ms. reads: “our hearts”], crying: “Abba, Father.”

Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then also an heir through God.

But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. Now, having come to know [Ms. reads: “having known”] God—or rather, having been known by God—how are you turning back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew?

You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest I have labored over you in vain.

Become as I am, because I too became as you are, brothers, I beseech you. You have done me no wrong. You know that it was because of an infirmity of the flesh that I preached the Gospel to you previously; and you did not despise or reject your temptation in my flesh. Rather, you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

Where, then, is your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if possible [Ms. reads: “had been possible”], you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.

So then [Ms. adds: “I”], have I become your enemy by telling you the truth? They zealously court you, but not rightly; they want to exclude you so that you may court them.

But it is good to be zealous for what is good always, and not only when I am present with you.

My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you, I would like to be present with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.

Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through the promise.

These things are said allegorically. For these are two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar.

[Note: Closer to the Greek text, the Palatine manuscript reads “from Mount Sinai” (*a monte Sina*) instead of “on Mount Sinai” (*in monte Sina*). Immediately afterward it reads: “Now Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which is joined to the one that is now Jerusalem and serves with her children.”]

For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, corresponding to the Jerusalem that now is, and she is enslaved with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free; she is our mother.

For it is written:

> Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear;  
> break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor;  
> for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous  
> than those of her who has a husband.

But we, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. Yet just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now.

But what does Scripture say?

> Cast out the slave woman and her son,  
> for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir  
> with the son of the free woman.

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman—the freedom with which Christ set us free.

## Chapter V

Stand firm, and do not again submit yourselves to a yoke of slavery.

Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing. I testify again to every person who receives circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

You are severed from Christ, you who seek to be justified in the law; you have fallen away from grace.

For through the Spirit, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but faith working through love.

You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?

[Note: The Palatine manuscript adds the words *nemini consenseritis* (“do not agree with anyone”), which are not found here in the Greek text.]

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise; but whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.

As for me, brothers, if I still [Ms. omits: “still”] preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Then the stumbling block of the cross has been abolished.

Would that those who trouble you would even mutilate themselves!

For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.

[Note: The name *Spiritus* (“Spirit”), which is absent from most Greek manuscripts, is lacking in the Palatine manuscript.]

For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.

I say, then: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these oppose one another, so that you may not do whatever you wish.

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

Now the works of the flesh are evident: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions,

[Note: For the same word, αἱρέσεις, which alone occurs in the Greek text, the Palatine manuscript supplies the twofold rendering *sectae, haereses* (“factions, heresies”).]

envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who practice such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering,

[Note: Here the Palatine manuscript, along with several Greek manuscripts, omits the noun *mansuetudo* (“gentleness”); shortly afterward it likewise omits *castitas* (“chastity”).]

gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law.

Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.

Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another.

## Chapter VI

Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, each considering himself, lest he too be tempted.

Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

Let each person examine his own work, and then he will have his boast in himself alone and not in another. For each person will bear his own burden.

Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.

Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap without growing weary. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.

All who wish to make a good showing in the flesh [Ms. omits: “they”] compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not keep the law; rather, they wish you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And upon all who follow this rule be peace and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body.

[Ms. omits: “Jesus.”]

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

The Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Galatians ends.

---

# The Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Ephesians Begins

## Chapter I

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, to all the saints who are in Ephesus and the faithful in Christ Jesus:

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love.

He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he favored us in his beloved Son.

In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the administration of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him.

In him we too [Note: The words *et nos* (“we too”), which are not present in the Greek archetype, are omitted by the Palatine manuscript.] have perhaps been called, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory—we [Ms. omits: “we”] who first hoped in Christ.

[Ms. omits: “we.”]

In him you also, when you heard the word of truth—the Gospel of your salvation—in him also, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the acquired possession, to the praise of his glory.

Therefore I also, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him.

May the eyes of your heart be enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling [Ms. omits: “his”], what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe [Ms. reads: “have believed”], according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.

And he placed everything under his feet and gave him as head above every church,

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads *super omnia Ecclesiae* (“above all things for the Church”), a reading that we prefer to the others, together with manuscripts of better quality and the ancient Corbie Bibles, in accordance with the Greek, ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ. Saint Jerome himself bears witness to this reading in his Commentaries on this passage, where he repeats it two or three times and explains it literally.]

which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things.

## [Chapter II]

And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the children of unbelief [Note: Here the Palatine manuscript, closer to the Greek, reads “in the sons.”]: among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts [Note: Jerome himself prefers to read “of minds,” and seems to reject the reading found in the Latin codices. Compare his Commentaries on this passage.], and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.

But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—for by grace you have been saved—and raised us up together with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves: it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.
