All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know [Col. 0807B] God, but deny him by their works, being abominable, unbelieving, and disqualified for every good work.

## [Chapter II]

But speak what befits sound teaching: that older men be sober, dignified, prudent, sound in faith, love, and patience. Likewise, older women in holy bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, that they may teach good sense to younger women: to love their husbands and children, to be prudent, chaste, sober, attentive to their households, kind, subject to their husbands, so that God’s word may not be blasphemed. Likewise exhort younger men to be sober. In all things present yourself as an example of good works: in teaching, integrity, and seriousness; sound and irreproachable speech, so that an opponent may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say [Col. 0807C] about us.

Teach slaves to be subject to their masters, pleasing them in all things, not contradicting, not defrauding, but displaying all good faith, that they may adorn in all things the teaching of God our Savior. For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and godly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and appearing of the glory [Col. 0808A] of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works. Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

## [Chapter III]

Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey a command, to be ready for every good work; to blaspheme no one, not to be quarrelsome, but gentle, showing all meekness toward all people. For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, led astray, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared, [Col. 0808B] he saved us, not from works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out abundantly upon us through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope [Note: [Col. 0808C] In accordance with the Greek ζωῆς, “of life” appears to be required in place of “of the way”; the manuscripts, however, do not support it.] of eternal life. The saying is faithful, and I want you to insist on these matters, so that those who believe God may take care to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful for people.

But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, disputes, and quarrels about the law, for they are useless and vain. Avoid a heretical person after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned. When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make haste to come to me [Col. 0808C] at Nicopolis, for I have decided to winter there. Diligently send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos ahead, so that they lack nothing. Let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for necessary needs, that they may not be unfruitful. All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. The grace of God be with you all. Amen.

[Col. 0807] Here ends the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to Titus.

[Col. 0807]

# THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO PHILEMON BEGINS

[Col. 0807D] ## [Chapter I]

Paul, prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved fellow worker, and to Apphia our sister [Note: [Col. 0807D] With certain Greek books, the Palatine manuscript does not add “most beloved.”] most beloved, and Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0808D] I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, that the fellowship of your faith may become evident in recognition of every [Note: [Col. 0807D] The same manuscript reads, “in recognition of every good [Col. 0808D] work which is in you,” etc., omitting *work*, a word which is not in the Greek text either.] good work which is in you in Christ [Col. 0809A] Jesus. For I had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.

Therefore, though I have much boldness in Christ Jesus to command you what is fitting, yet because of love I rather entreat you, being such a one as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I entreat you for my son Onesimus, whom I begot in chains, who was formerly useless to you but now is useful both to you and to me, and whom I have sent back [Note: [Col. 0809B] Here the Palatine manuscript omits the pronoun “to you,” which is absent from the Greek archetype as well.] to you. Receive him as my own heart. I wished to keep him with me, that he might minister to me on your behalf in the chains of the Gospel; but without your consent I wished to do nothing, lest your good deed be as if compelled but voluntary. For perhaps he departed from you for a while for this reason: that you might receive him forever, no longer [Col. 0810A] as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord!

If, therefore, you hold me as a partner, receive him as you would me. And if he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge this to me. I, Paul, have written it with my own hand: I will repay it—not to say to you that you owe me even yourself. Yes indeed, brother; let me have joy of you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in [Note: [Col. 0809B] The same manuscript reads, “Refresh my heart in Christ. Having written [Col. 0810B] to you confident of your obedience,” etc., more contentious in relation to the Greek wording.] the Lord. Confident of your obedience, I wrote to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare lodging for me also, for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you; so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0809] Here ends the Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to Philemon.

[Col. 0809]

# THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS BEGINS

[Col. 0809B] ## [Chapter I]

In many portions and in many ways, God, who formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last [Ms. “last of all”] days spoken to us through the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. Since he is the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and sustains all things by the word of his power, having accomplished purification of sins, [Col. 0809C] he sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high [Note: [Col. 0809D] In Martianay’s edition it is wrongly written as two words, *sed et*, for *sedit* (“sat down”), or *sedet* (“sits”).], having become so much greater than the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.

For to which of the angels did he ever say: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”? And again: “I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me”? And when he again brings the firstborn into the world, he says: “Let all God’s angels worship him.” Of the angels he says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son: “Your throne, O God, is for age upon age; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with oil of exultation above your companions.” And: “You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of [Col. 0809D] your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them [Note: [Col. 0809D] The Palatine manuscript reads “you will wrap them up,” and the Greek ἑλίξεις, in place of [Col. 0810D] ἀλλάξεις, “you will change them.”], and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail.” But to which of the angels did he ever say: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies [Col. 0810B] a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on account of those who will inherit salvation?

## [Chapter II]

Therefore we must give more abundant attention to what we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense, [Col. 0810C] how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? After it began to be proclaimed through the Lord, it was confirmed to us [Ms. “in us”] by those who heard, God bearing witness by signs, wonders, various powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.

For God did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak. But someone testified somewhere, saying [Note: [Col. 0810D] The same manuscript reads “someone saying”; Greek: τίς λέγων.]: “What is a human being, that you remember him, or a son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things under his feet.” For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him. Yet we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by God’s grace he might taste death for everyone.

For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to perfect through sufferings [Col. 0811A] the author of their salvation. For both the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one; for this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: [Note: [Col. 0811D] The same manuscript has “I shall declare,” and likewise omits the pronoun “my” in “my children,” in accordance with the Greek exemplar.] “I shall declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I shall praise you.” And again: “I shall put my trust in him.” And again: “Behold, I and my children whom God gave me.” Therefore, since the children share in flesh and blood, he likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life. For he certainly does not take hold of angels, but takes hold of Abraham’s seed. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, that he might become a merciful [Col. 0811B] and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the people’s sins. For because he himself suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

## [Chapter III]

Therefore, holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to the one who made him, as Moses also was in all his house. For this one was counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, by as much as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house. For every house is built by someone, but God is the one who created all things. Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a son over his own house. We are that house if we hold firm to the end the confidence and boast of hope [Col. 0811C].

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me; they tried me and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with this generation and said: ‘They always go astray in heart; they have not known my ways.’” [Note: [Col. 0811D] In accordance with certain Greek books, the Palatine manuscript reads “in which” rather than “as.”] “As I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter my rest.’” Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. Rather, exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “Today,” lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become sharers in Christ, if indeed we hold firm to the end the beginning of his substance.

[Col. 0811D] While it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in that provocation.” For some who heard provoked him, though not all who came out of Egypt through Moses. But with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, except those who were unbelieving [Col. 0812A]? Thus we see that they could not enter [Note: [Col. 0812D] The Palatine manuscript adds from the following context, “into his rest”; these words are nevertheless absent from the Greek exemplar.] because of unbelief.

## [Chapter IV]

Let us therefore fear lest, while the promise of entering his rest remains, any of you should be thought to have fallen short. For good news was proclaimed to us as also to them, but the word heard did not benefit them, not being united [Ms. “union”] with faith in those who heard. For we who have believed enter into rest, as he has said: “As I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter my rest,’” although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For somewhere he spoke concerning the seventh day in this manner: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage: “They shall not enter my rest.”

Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news did not enter because of unbelief, he again appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying in David after so long a time, as was said above: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another day. Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God. For the one who entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his own. Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief. For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

[Col. 0812C] No creature is invisible before him; rather, all things are naked and laid open to his eyes, to whom we must give account. Therefore, having a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every way according to our likeness, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with confidence, that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.

## [Chapter V]

For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters concerning God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can have compassion on those who [Note: [Col. 0812D] The Palatine manuscript reads, “who were ignorant,” etc.] are ignorant and stray, since he too is surrounded with weakness. Therefore [Col. 0812D] he must offer for sins, both for himself and for the people. No one takes this honor for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was. So too Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” As he says also in another place: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being called by God high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. About him we have much to say and it is difficult to explain, because you have become dull in hearing. For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the rudiments of the beginning of God’s words; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word [Ms. adds “and”] of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the mature [Col. 0813B], who through practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil.

## [Chapter VI]

Therefore, leaving behind the elementary teaching of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection [Ms. “to maturity”], not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works [Note: [Col. 0813D] The same manuscript reads “but of faith,” closer to the Greek καὶ πίστεως, “and of faith.”] and faith toward God; of instruction concerning baptisms, the laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if indeed God permits.

For it is impossible for those once enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, become sharers in the Holy Spirit, likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they again crucify for themselves the Son of God and hold him up to public contempt. For land that drinks the rain often falling upon it [Col. 0813C] and produces [Ms. “sprouts”] useful vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives blessing from God; but land producing thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is for burning.

But we are persuaded concerning you, beloved, of better things, things nearer to salvation, though we speak in this way. For God is not unjust to forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, in having ministered to the saints and continuing to minister. But we desire each one of you to display the same diligence for the full assurance of hope until the end, that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.

For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: “Unless I bless you with blessing and multiply you with multiplication.” Thus, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise. For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and for confirmation an oath is the end of every dispute among them. In this way, God, desiring more abundantly to show the heirs of the promise the immovability of his purpose, interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us might have the strongest consolation. We have this hope as a secure and firm anchor of the soul [Col. 0814A], entering even within the veil, where Jesus entered for us as a forerunner, having become high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

### [Chapter VII]

For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him—and to whom Abraham also apportioned a tenth of everything—is, first, interpreted as “king of righteousness”; then also “king of Salem,” that is, “king of peace”; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life [Ms. omits *vitae*], but likened to the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.

Consider how great this man was, to whom even the patriarch Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest things. Indeed, those among the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment, according to the law, to take tithes from the people—that is, from their brothers—although they themselves also came forth from the loins of Abraham. But he whose genealogy is not reckoned among them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who possessed the promises. Beyond all contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater.

Here mortal men receive tithes, but there it is testified that he lives. And, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who received tithes, was himself tithed, for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.

Therefore, if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is changed, there must also be a change of the law. For the one about whom these things are said belonged to another tribe, from which no one attended the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe concerning which Moses said nothing about priests.

And it is still more evident if another priest arises according to the likeness of Melchizedek, one who was made not according to the law of a fleshly commandment but according to the power of an indestructible life. For he testifies: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

On the one hand, there is an annulment of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness—for the law brought nothing to perfection—while on the other hand there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God. And insofar as this did not happen without an oath—for the others became priests without an oath, but this one with an oath, through him who said to him, “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever”—to that same extent Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant.

The others became priests in greater number because death prevented them from continuing; but he, because he remains forever, possesses a permanent priesthood. Hence he is also able to save forever those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for us.

[Note: [Col. 0813] The Palatine manuscript also prefers *pro eis* (“for them”), along with the Greek ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν.]

For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like the priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all when he offered himself [Ms. *se*, “himself,” instead of *seipsum*]. For the law appoints as priests men who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, perfected forever.

### [Chapter VIII]

Now the main point of what is being said is this: “We have such a high priest, who has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens” [Ms. *excelsis*, “in the highest places”], “a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord established, not man.”

For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; therefore it is necessary that this one too should have something to offer. If, then, he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law, serving a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. This is what Moses was told when he was completing the tabernacle: “See that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”

But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, just as he is also mediator of a better covenant, which has been enacted upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second. But, finding fault with them, he says:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—for they did not remain in my covenant [Note: [Col. 0815D] In the same manuscript, *non permanserunt* (“they did not remain”) occurs, corresponding to the Greek οὐκ ἐνέμειναν], and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds and write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach each one his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

By saying “new,” he has made the first obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near disappearance.

### [Chapter IX]

The first covenant indeed had ordinances of worship and a worldly sanctuary. For a tabernacle was prepared, the first one, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place [Ms. *quod*, “which,” instead of *quae*].

Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold. In it was a golden jar containing manna, and Aaron’s staff that had sprouted, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. About these things it is not now necessary to speak in detail.

When these things had been arranged in this way, the priests continually entered the first tabernacle, performing the services of worship; but into the second the high priest entered alone, once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people.

By this the Holy Spirit signified that the way into the holy places had not yet been disclosed, while the first tabernacle still had its standing; this is a figure for the present time. Accordingly, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot, according to conscience, perfect the worshiper, consisting only in foods, drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation.

But Christ, having appeared as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, entered once for all into the Holy Place, having secured eternal redemption.

For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of a heifer’s ashes, sanctify the defiled for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

And therefore he is mediator of a new covenant, so that, death having taken place for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a covenant, the death of the one who made the covenant must necessarily take place. For a covenant becomes valid over the dead; otherwise it has no force while the one who made it is alive.

Hence even the first covenant was not inaugurated without blood. For when every commandment of the law had been spoken by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood.

And almost everything, according to the law, is cleansed with blood; and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Therefore it was necessary that the copies of the heavenly things should be cleansed by these means, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these.

For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, copies of the true ones [Ms. *manufactis sanctis*, “holy places made with hands”], but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the Holy Place every year with another’s blood; otherwise he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. But now, once for all, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the abolition of sin through his sacrifice.

And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so also Christ, having been offered once to take away the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin, for the salvation of those who await him.

### [Chapter X]

For, since the law possesses only a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things themselves, it can never, by the same sacrifices that they offer continually year after year, perfect those who draw near. Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, once cleansed, would have had no further consciousness of sin. But in those sacrifices there is a yearly remembrance of sins.

For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Therefore, when he comes into the world, he says:

“Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me. Burnt offerings [and sacrifices] for sin did not please you” [Note: [Col. 0817D] The Palatine manuscript more correctly adds the conjunction *et* (“and”): in Greek, καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας, which the same manuscript again preserves shortly afterward in agreement with the Greek; [Col. 0818D] the note continues there].

“Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come—in the heading of the book it is written concerning me—to do your will, O God’” [Ms. *facerem*, “I was doing,” instead of *faciam*, “I will do”].

After saying above, “You neither desired nor took pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings for sin, which are offered according to the law,” he then said, “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God.” He takes away the first in order to establish the second. By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all [Ms. *in semel*, “in once,” instead of *semel*].

And every priest stands daily ministering and repeatedly offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this one, having offered one sacrifice for sins, has taken his seat forever at the right hand of God, from then on waiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool for his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.

The Holy Spirit also testifies to us. For after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them upon their minds,” he also says, “I will remember their sins and their iniquities no more.” And where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.

Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence for entering the holy places by the blood of Jesus, a new and living way that he inaugurated for us through the veil—that is, through his flesh—and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful. And let us consider one another for the provocation of love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.

For if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a terrifying expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.

Anyone who set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by one who trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified a profane thing, and insulted the Spirit of grace?

For we know him who said: “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay.” And again: “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

But remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings, sometimes being made a public spectacle through reproaches and tribulations, and sometimes becoming companions of those who were treated in such a way. For you also sympathized with those in bonds and joyfully accepted the seizure of your possessions, knowing that you possessed a better and abiding substance.

Therefore do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need endurance, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.

“For yet a very little while, and the one who is coming will come, and will not delay. But my righteous one shall live by faith; and if he draws back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”

But we are not of those who draw back to destruction, but of faith for the acquiring of the soul.

### [Chapter XI]

Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. For by it the elders received testimony.

By faith we understand that the ages were fitted together by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things.

By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.

By faith Enoch was taken up so that he would not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. For before his removal he received testimony that he had pleased God. Without faith it is impossible to please him. For the one who approaches God must believe that he exists and that he becomes the rewarder of those who seek him.

By faith Noah, having received a divine response concerning things not yet seen, feared and prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. Through it he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes through faith.

By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed by going out to the place he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise. For he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for conceiving offspring, even beyond the proper time of her age, because she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man—and one as good as dead—there arose descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as countless as the sand on the shore of the sea.

All these died in faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. And if they had remembered the one from which they departed, they would have had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he prepared a city for them.

By faith Abraham, when tested, offered Isaac; he was offering his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said, “In Isaac your offspring shall be called.” He reckoned that God was able even to raise him from the dead; hence, figuratively speaking, he also received him back.

By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave instructions concerning his bones.

By faith Moses, when born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful; and they did not fear the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasure of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking toward the reward.

By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger; for he endured as seeing the invisible one. By faith he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch them.

By faith they crossed the Red Sea as through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after being encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the disobedient, because she had received the spies in peace.

And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets. Through faith they conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, and put foreign armies to flight. Women received their dead back through resurrection.

Others were tortured, refusing release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and in addition bonds and imprisonment. They were stoned, sawn in two, tested, killed by the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins, destitute, oppressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, and in caves and hollows of the earth.

And all these, though approved through their testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they would not be perfected apart from us.

### [Chapter XII]

Therefore, since we too are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. For the joy set before him he endured the cross, disregarding its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.

Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary and lose heart. You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin, and you have forgotten the exhortation that speaks to you as sons:

“My son, do not disregard the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” [Ms. *recepit*, “received”].

Endure discipline. God is dealing with you as sons. For what son is there whom a father does not discipline? But if you are without discipline, in which all have shared, then you are illegitimate and not sons.

Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we respected them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a few days according to their own will, but he does so for our benefit, so that we may share in his holiness.

All discipline at the time seems not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful [Ms. *potissimum*, “especially great,” instead of *pacatissimum*, “most peaceful”] fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

Therefore lift up your drooping hands and strengthen your weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no lame person may go astray but rather be healed. Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, that no root of bitterness springing up may cause trouble, and that through it many may be defiled.

Let there be no fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.

For you have not approached a tangible mountain and burning fire, and darkness, gloom, storm, the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words—those who heard it begged that no further word be spoken to them. For they could not endure what was commanded: “Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” And so terrifying was the sight that Moses said: “I am terrified and trembling.”

But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and a multitude of myriads of angels, and the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous who have been perfected, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.

See that you do not refuse the one who is speaking. For if those did not escape when they refused him who spoke on earth, much less shall we, if we turn away from him who speaks from heaven. His voice then shook the earth; but now he has promised, saying: “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.”

The phrase “Yet once more” indicates the removal of the things that can be shaken, as things made, so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.

Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, through which we may serve God in a pleasing manner, with reverence and awe. For indeed our God is a consuming fire.

### [Chapter XIII]

Let brotherly love remain among you [Note: [Col. 0819] The Palatine manuscript omits the words *in vobis* (“among you”), in accordance with the Greek text].

And do not forget hospitality, for through it some, without knowing it, received angels as guests [Ms. *placuerunt*, “were pleasing,” instead of *latuerunt*, “were hidden”]. Remember those in bonds as though bound with them, and those who suffer ill-treatment as though you yourselves were in the body.

Let marriage be honorable among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

Let your conduct be free from avarice, content with what you have. For he himself has said: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” Thus we may confidently say: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear. What can man do to me?”

Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you. Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Do not be led away by various and strange teachings. For it is good to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which did not benefit those who walked in them.

We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the Holy Place by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.

Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have a lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come.

Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. And do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for God is pleased with such sacrifices.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for that would not benefit you.

Pray for us, for we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to conduct ourselves honorably in all things. I urge you all the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.

Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with every good thing so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

But I ask you, brothers, to bear with this word of exhortation, for I have written to you in very few words [Ms. *praepaucis*, “in exceedingly few words,” instead of *perpaucis*]. Know that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes soon, I shall see you with him.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. The brothers from Italy greet you [Note: [Col. 0821] The word *fratres* (“brothers”), which is also absent from the Greek text, is likewise omitted by the Palatine manuscript].

Grace be with you all. Amen.

[Col. 0821] The Epistle of the Blessed Apostle Paul to the Hebrews ends.

### [CANONICAL EPISTLES]

[Col. 0821]

## Prologue to the Seven Canonical Epistles
[Note: [Col. 0821C] That this prologue is not Jerome’s, but belongs to a man both of a much later age and of almost the lowest bench, is established by such certain arguments that recent critics—and Martianaeus himself—would seem to be laboring the obvious if we wished to demonstrate it. For the whole texture of the discourse cries out that it has been badly pieced together here and there from scraps of Jerome: the style itself is inelegant where the Author adds passages of his own; the sentences are loose and smell of later centuries, as does that first statement about the order of the Epistles among the Greeks, “who are sound in doctrine and follow the right faith”; there are also new expressions, such as his calling these Epistles “Canonical,” whereas Jerome consistently called them “Catholic”; and other matters of the same kind, which it would take too long to pursue and which you will find refuted at the end of the book by the Benedictine Editor. They had already been refuted by Richard Simon in *Critical History of the New Testament*, vol. I, chap. 18, and in P. Martene’s *Itinerary*, part II, p. 79.

There will therefore be someone who might prefer that this writing be rejected altogether and consigned among the spurious works [Col. 0821D]. But since manuscripts commonly contain it—including those which we shall soon cite—and since most of the older editions of the Bible also contain it, such as the Nuremberg edition of 1475, the Venetian edition of 1498, the Basel edition of 1506, the Paris edition of 1563, the two Lyons editions of 1520 and 1589, and the Antwerp edition of 1617, it has seemed preferable to print it, as you see here, in a different type, to indicate that it is the offspring of another Author.

As for our manuscripts, none of the three better-quality copies that we consulted bears Jerome’s name in its inscription. The first is older than all the others we have seen; it formerly belonged to the library of Nonantola and now to that of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in Rome. The second is Veronese, in the library of the Friars Observant of Saint Bernardino; although this book contains the whole New Testament, it does not contain the Apocalypse. The third is in our possession, having been obtained from some Milanese collection. One also frequently encounters a great many others of this kind in the libraries of Italy, especially in Florence, at San Marco and in the Laurentian Library; conversely, there are others, though rarer, which, with a bolder falsehood, prescribe the name “Jerome.”

We shall speak below, in its proper place, of others who either omit the verse of the Epistle of Saint John concerning the heavenly witnesses—the reason for which this preface was composed—or quote it in a form somewhat different from the Vulgate reading. For the present, these observations suffice to remove the most disgraceful of all the slanders by which Faustus Socinus, the head of his impious sect bearing his name, attacked Jerome, as though he were the true Author of this prologue. He says:

“When he happened to obtain a copy, or even several copies, in which that clause had been added—namely, the testimony of the three witnesses in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit—he began, against the reading of the other copies, both Latin and Greek, to defend and advance that clause as genuine, publicly complaining that it had been erased from the common copies through the guilt and fraud of heretics.”

Saint Jerome certainly did not write this; nor had that clause disappeared from the Latin or Greek copies in his time; nor, finally, had that monster of a man emerged from the pit of hell who would so often turn the carelessness of scribes into a slander against the sacred text. See Martianaeus.

“Here this prologue to the seven Canonical Epistles has already felt the censor’s pen of the recent writer, who also indicated that he expected our observations upon it when he undertook his discussion, especially concerning the Cambridge manuscript of the Gospels. Having thus been challenged by him, we fear that one who has said whatever he wished may hear from us what he by no means wishes to hear. For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. If he once joins us in pursuing it, then whatever we demonstrate that he wrote carelessly and without sufficient fidelity, he will be obliged simply to acknowledge and correct.

And because the pure light of truth could not shine upon the reader unless the darkness of falsehoods and errors were first removed, it will be part of our undertaking first to note whatever is found in the recent *Critical History of the New Testament* that is discordant with the truth of the facts [Col. 0823B]. Once these matters have been examined and discussed, we shall set forth, with the utmost fidelity and equal diligence, how the facts stand in the ancient books.

“What he first observes about this preface, in chapter eighteen of the first volume of his *Critical History of the New Testament*, is not sufficiently accurate and does not approach the truth. For when he asserts that this prologue is found in Latin copies transcribed only within the last six hundred years, but is not found with equal consistency in other, older manuscripts, he either lacks confidence in his own evidence or has not applied enough diligence. It is certain, in fact, that the very oldest biblical codices lacking the prologue are rarer than those in which it is written.

And lest anyone think that by this statement I am merely putting off the critical writer, I shall cite books that are most substantial witnesses to my assertion. Two very ancient manuscript codices of the sacred Scriptures exist in the Royal Library, and two likewise of the same age and standing in the Colbertine Library. The Royal copies are numbered [Col. 0823C] 3561 and 3564; the Colbertine copies are numbered 1 and 158. All these exemplars are recognized as having been copied before the time of Charles the Bald, or during his time, without anyone disputing the point. Yet of these four most excellent and high-quality manuscripts, three of the more notable ones contain the aforementioned prologue written before the seven Canonical Epistles.

Here, then, is an evident argument against the opinion of the recent critic, especially if the same confirmation is added from four more manuscripts of our own library at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where copies belonging both to us and to the monastery of Corbie survive, written on parchment eight hundred years ago. What occurs in the Royal and Colbertine codices occurs also in ours: among them there is no copy, except the one numbered 15, that does not contain the prologue to the seven Apostolic Epistles. Anyone wishing to consult them may identify them by these numbers: 2, 4, and 23.

Thus, of eight manuscript codices older than the others, six consistently retain the preface, commonly ascribed to Jerome [Col. 0823D]. In more recent copies, however, it is not found in every case or in every place: it is absent from the Colbertine codices numbered 6155 and 6180. Certainly, if I remember correctly, it is missing more frequently in those than in the older copies just mentioned.

For when I was formerly seeking this prologue in many codices copied four hundred years ago and located in Occitania and Aquitaine, it seemed to me, as I recall, that it was often absent from them. Even if this were not so, however, the absence of the prologue from several older books contributes nothing to proving that it is spurious. For some genuine prefaces of Jerome are likewise absent from certain very ancient manuscripts. For example, in the Royal manuscript numbered 3564 the preface to the book of Ezra is absent [Col. 0824A]; and, stranger still, in three copies of the Canon of Hebrew Truth, Jerome’s preface to the Psalter translated from Hebrew is absent.

It would be utterly absurd, on account of such carelessness among ancient scribes, to deny Jerome the authorship of the aforesaid little prefaces, which are written under his name in so many other manuscript codices. Nothing, therefore, in the argument for the spuriousness of the prologue is compelling—an argument which the recent author attempts to establish from its absence in certain ancient copies.

“He observes, secondly, that neither Jerome’s name nor that of any other writer was placed at the head of the prologue in certain older manuscripts; from this he concludes that it is reasonable to believe that Jerome was not the author of the little preface. But, with due respect to this diligent man, I would say that those who support their opinion by such slight conjectures are not well practiced in reading ancient codices.

For it is most clearly established that no name is more frequently omitted from the title of Jerome’s prefaces when they are found copied by drowsy scribes. Manuscript biblical codices of this kind include the following: the codex of our monastery of Montmajour near Arles; the codex of the eminent Cardinal de Bonzi, preserved in his library at Narbonne; the Canon of Hebrew Truth belonging to the Church of Carcassonne; and finally the codex of our monastery of Saint Mary the Gilded near Toulouse. In all these copies every author’s name is omitted from the inscription of the prefaces, and the text reads in this manner: ‘The Preface to the Book of Joshua begins’; ‘The Prologue to the Books of Kings begins’; ‘The Preface to Job begins’; ‘The Prologue to the Books of Ezra’; and so forth.

Nor is Jerome’s name omitted only in these manuscripts; it is also commonly omitted in the Royal, Colbertine, and Saint-Germain codices. Royal manuscript 1564 gives Daniel’s prologue this title: ‘The Prologue to Daniel the Prophet begins.’ The ancient Colbertine manuscript numbered 61 reads: ‘The Preface to Joshua and Judges begins.’ And for the book of Jeremiah: ‘The Prologue of Jeremiah the Prophet begins.’ Our Saint-Germain manuscript no. 15 reads at the beginning of Chronicles: ‘The Book of the Words of the Days begins . . . The Prologue begins. If the Septuagint . . .’

And not to linger too long in listing such examples, the Saint-Germain biblical codex no. 164 preserves the copied prefaces of Saint Jerome without any heading or inscription whatsoever. Let our critic now consider how far his conjectures are removed from actual experience, from the ordinary practice of reading, and therefore from tested truth itself.

“Thirdly, what he says is in agreement with the truth, namely, that this prologue is not found in Royal manuscript no. 3564. But he is entirely mistaken when he says that there are two manuscripts of the same age in our library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in which the prologue to the seven Canonical Epistles is not read. For in all the manuscripts of our library that we have carefully examined—except the one numbered 15—that prologue is found complete, entire, and finished in every respect [Col. 0824D].

“A fourth error follows—if indeed it is one error rather than several—where he attempts to show that the compiler of the biblical collection, who first brought together all the books of the Latin Vulgate, that is, of the Old and New Testaments, in a single volume, published the prologue placed at the head of the Canonical Epistles.

He says that the little preface attached to the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles in the copy of Charles the Bald was not written by Jerome for this purpose, but was taken from his longer prologue, which we call the *Galeatus*. It is said to read in these words: ‘The Acts of the Apostles seem indeed to sound forth a bare history and to weave the history of the nascent Church; but if we know . . .’

It is manifest that this thoughtlessness slipped from him [Col. 0825A]. For who does not know that in Jerome’s *Galeatus* prologue there is complete silence concerning the books of the New Testament? Nor would the critical author have forgiven this hallucination even in one of his associates, had he found one of them, in a decisive style, reciting the *Galeatus* prologue as Jerome’s Epistle to Paulinus.

On this occasion the memory of a ridiculous question comes to mind. A man otherwise learned once asked us how, in the Canon of Hebrew Truth, there could be a testimony from the First Epistle of Blessed John, where there is mention of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We were certainly ashamed to find so learned a man so ignorant in the study of the divine Scriptures that he was looking for the fifth chapter of the Epistle of the Apostle John in the Pentateuch of Moses, or among the Prophets, or among the Hagiographa.

But let us return to the matter at hand. The preface placed at the head of the Acts of the Apostles in the Royal manuscript of Charles the Bald is excerpted from the Epistle of Saint Jerome to Paulinus. There, after a summary and mystical exposition of the Old Testament, he also briefly touches upon the New Testament, indicating in passing what each book contains [Col. 0825B]. We know that those portions which are copied in manuscript codices in the form of prefaces at the head of the individual volumes of both the Old and New Testaments were taken from this Epistle.

Thus the compiler of the Latin Vulgate by no means lacked a little preface by Jerome, so that he would have had to compose a new one, as the recent critic claims. For in the same Epistle to Paulinus Jerome says beautifully concerning the seven Canonical Epistles:

‘James, Peter, John, and Jude issued seven Epistles, both mystical and concise, at once short and long—short in words, long in meaning—so that scarcely anyone fails to stumble in reading them.’

These words are read at the head of the seven Epistles in Colbertine manuscript no. 158, although some unknown and imprudent corrector attempted to erase them. They are written in the same place in three other manuscripts of the Colbertine Library, whose numerical designations are 2767, 3214, and 6449 [Col. 0825C].

The person who first assembled the books of the Latin Vulgate could therefore use this little preface before the seven Canonical Epistles, just as he placed at the head of the Acts and the Apocalypse certain passages taken from Jerome’s writing to Paulinus. The whole mass of our critic’s arguments therefore collapses, since it rests entirely upon conjectures in which we have shown him to have gone astray more than sufficiently.

We, taking another path, shall attempt to make evident the spuriousness of the prologue now under discussion by several stronger arguments.

“First, the case is established from the name ‘Canonical Epistles,’ which was unknown to Jerome, as is readily proved from his own words, which are read in more than one place in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. Thus, in the section on Peter, or the first chapter of that work, he writes as follows:

‘Simon Peter . . . wrote two Epistles, which are called Catholic; of these, the second is denied by most to be his, because its style differs from the first.’

In the section on James he insists on the same point, saying:

‘James, who is called the brother of the Lord . . . appointed bishop of Jerusalem, wrote only one Epistle, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles; it too is asserted by some to have been published under his name, although, little by little, as time passed, it gained authority.’

Finally, in the section on Jude, adding the same statement about the seven Epistles, he composed the whole chapter in this way:

‘Jude, the brother of James, left a short Epistle, which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles. Since it takes testimony from the book of Enoch, which is apocryphal, it is rejected by most. Nevertheless, through its antiquity and use it has already earned authority and is counted among the Holy Scriptures.’

You see, therefore, reader, that Jerome nowhere used the name ‘Canonical Epistles’; rather, whenever he wrote anything about them, he always said ‘which are called Catholic,’ [Col. 0826A] or ‘which is one of the seven Catholic Epistles.’

The fabricator of the spurious prologue, by contrast, calls them nothing other than ‘Canonical’: ‘The order is not the same,’ he says, ‘of the seven Epistles which are called Canonical,’ and so forth. From this designation there arises no slight conjecture that the author of the prologue wrote after the time of Cassiodorus, who calls these same seven Epistles ‘Canonical’ in book 8 of *On the Institution of Divine Letters*:

‘The eighth codex,’ he says, ‘contains the Canonical Epistles of the apostles.’

And again:

‘But when great anxiety concerning the remaining Canonical Epistles was troubling us, suddenly, by the Lord’s generosity, a codex written in the Greek style by Didymus was granted to us for the exposition of the seven Canonical Epistles.’

By this differing usage in naming the seven Apostolic Epistles, we easily detect that the author of the prologue attached to them was different from Jerome and later than he. Jerome, together with Athanasius in his festal Epistle and with the author of the *Synopsis* attributed to him, calls them ‘Catholic’; that false Jerome, the writer of the suspect prologue, calls them ‘Canonical,’ together with Cassiodorus [Col. 0826B].

The Council of Laodicea, however, called the same Epistles ‘Canonical’ when it presented a list and catalogue of the divine Scriptures. But, as far as I know, Jerome nowhere lists them under this name; he was always accustomed to call the Epistles ‘Catholic.’ From this we prove with considerable clarity that the writer of the controversial prologue was someone other than Jerome, and entirely different from him—whoever he may finally have been, whether Victor of Vita or some anonymous person who first undertook to join all the books of the Latin Vulgate into a single corpus.

“We may investigate the spuriousness of the same prologue once more from the fact that its author boasts as though he had achieved something great and had procured a considerable benefit for the Church of God by restoring the seven Canonical Epistles to their proper order. He also says that their sequence is different among the Greeks, who are sound in doctrine and follow the right faith, and in the Latin copies.

The latter statement is altogether false, as is clear from canon 59 or 60 of the Council of Laodicea [Col. 0826C], where the seven Epistles are listed in this order: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. Athanasius observes the same sequence in his festal Epistle, as does the author of the *Synopsis of Scripture* attributed to Athanasius; likewise Gregory of Nazianzus in his poem on the genuine Scriptures, John of Damascus in book IV, chapter 18, of *On the Catholic Faith*, and Nicephorus the Patriarch of Constantinople at the end of his *Chronology*. From the latter Anastasius the Librarian rendered the following into Latin:

‘The Catholic Epistles: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude—seven in all; the verses, 1,300.’

Where, then, did that false Jerome get the claim that among the Greeks, who are sound in doctrine and follow the right faith, the order of the seven Epistles called Canonical is not the same as that found in the Latin copies, and that Peter’s two Epistles come first among the others? Who followed the right faith more faithfully among the Greeks than Athanasius, Gregory the Theologian, and John of Damascus? Yet among them the order of the seven Catholic, or Canonical, Epistles is the same as that found in the Latin copies [Col. 0826D].

What great benefit can there be in that sequence of the Epistles in which the Epistle of James is placed first, so that the author of the prologue equates the restoration of this order with the purity and integrity of the Evangelists? ‘Just as,’ he says, ‘we formerly corrected the Evangelists according to the rule of truth, so, with God’s help, we have restored these to their proper order.’

It contributes nothing to sound doctrine or right faith whether the Epistle of James is placed first or last, provided that we ascribe to it, together with the Catholic Church, the authority of Canonical Scripture. Let Peter’s Epistles come first; let John’s come last; let James’s stand in the middle, and Jude’s another place: those who follow the right faith gain nothing from it, nor do those lose anything who have more reverence for the word of God than curiosity about preserving a particular order of reading.

We also know that this order of the Canonical Epistles, which the false Jerome valued so highly, was neglected by the true Jerome in his edition, if Cassiodorus is to be believed. For although Cassiodorus, a man most devoted to study, reviewed the various divisions of divine Scripture, he never mentions among them the order of the Epistles which the author of the suspect prologue calls their proper order.

Indeed, in chapter twelve of *On the Institution of Divine Letters* he gives a different sequence. The heading of that chapter is: ‘The Division of Divine Scripture According to Jerome.’ In this division, therefore—Jerome’s division, or catalogue of the books of sacred Scripture—we read the following in Cassiodorus after the Evangelists have been listed:

‘After these follow the Epistles of the apostles: two of Peter, fourteen of Paul, three of John, one of James, and one of Jude; one book of the Acts of the Apostles by Luke; and one book of the Apocalypse of John.’

If we believe this sequence of books to be genuine and proper to Jerome, and if we do not deny our confidence to Cassiodorus as he discusses it, then we may rightly pronounce the writer of the prologue an impostor [Col. 0827B].

Add to this the canon of Scripture given by Augustine in book II, chapter 8, of *On Christian Doctrine*, where the following order of the Canonical Epistles appears:

‘With these forty-four books the authority of the Old Testament is concluded. The New Testament, however, consists of the four books of the Gospel . . . the fourteen Epistles of the Apostle Paul . . . two of Peter, three of John, one of Jude, and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one book of the Apocalypse of John.’

Who does not know that Augustine followed Jerome’s edition in the New Testament and preferred it to all other Latin versions? How, then, did the constant praiser of Jerome’s edition care so little about the order of the Canonical Epistles, and regard it as of no importance that the Catholic interpreter had restored it with God’s help? The composer of the prologue therefore attributed greater significance to the restored sequence of these Epistles than Augustine and Jerome are found to have attributed to it in the passages cited.

For this reason, whoever he was who attempted to defend and support his own composition by the authority of Jerome’s glorious name must be judged to be someone other than Jerome [Col. 0827C].

We do know that Jerome, in his Epistle to Paulinus, discussed James, Peter, John, and the Apostle Jude in the same order in which the Epistles are now found in the Latin Bibles. But it is one thing to follow the customary sequence, established by usage, or at least one that differs among different authors; it is another to hope to perform a work of the greatest value by restoring the supposed proper order of the Canonical Epistles.

There are still Latin manuscript codices in which these Epistles are copied according to the sequence of the Greeks, who give the first place to Peter’s Epistles. For the biblical manuscript of the Colbertine Library numbered 245 observes this order among the Canonical Epistles: two of Peter, one of James, three of John, and one of Jude. Yet in that book we read the testimony of the First Epistle of Blessed John, where the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit are said to be one.

From these considerations it is clear—unless our judgment deceives us—that the arranger, or restorer, of the order of the seven Canonical Epistles, and likewise the author of the prologue, was later in age than Jerome.

“If we also judge the author of the preface by its style, the fraud immediately becomes apparent in his words. He could not reproduce Jerome’s style and manner of expression; rather, amid the very deception and the assumed persona with which he fraudulently clothed himself, he shows himself to be far removed from Jerome.

There is a similar argument in Jerome’s preface to the twelve minor prophets and in the spurious prologue to the seven Canonical Epistles; but the phrases and periods found in the two are dissimilar and uneven. At the beginning of the genuine preface Jerome writes:

‘The order of the twelve prophets is not the same among the Hebrews as it is among us. Therefore, according to what is read there, they have also been arranged here.’

But at the beginning of the false prologue the same ideas are expressed differently:

‘The order among the Greeks, who are sound in doctrine and follow the right faith, of the seven Epistles called Canonical, is not the same as that found in the Latin copies. Since Peter is first in the number of the apostles, his Epistles should also be first in the order of the others.’

I confidently assert that in the whole compass of those words there is nothing that bears the mark of Jerome’s phraseology or style. And where will you find in Jerome that barbarous expression *quodquia*? Such gross Latinity is utterly abhorrent to Jerome’s eloquence; and equally abhorrent are the many grammatical defects of expression that repeatedly occur throughout the text of that prologue.

It must therefore rightly be regarded as false and spurious, even though the name of the virgin Eustochium is heard in it. ‘Deceivers,’ says the false Ambrose in his Epistle to the Thessalonians, ‘are accustomed to forge an Epistle under the name of some distinguished man, so that the authority of the name may commend what cannot be accepted on its own merits’ [Col. 0828B].

Thus many things are found, as time passed, to have been fabricated under Jerome’s name that are utterly unworthy of so great a man and could not belong to his age. In two manuscript codices of our monastery of Saint Andrew near Avignon, I found a certain sermon on the Assumption of Blessed Mary the Virgin inscribed in this manner:

‘The sermon of Blessed Jerome the priest to Paula and Eustochium, and to the virgins living under their direction, on the Assumption of Holy Mary, begins.’

The name of Jerome therefore contributes nothing to a false work, nor does the address to Paula and Eustochium add any authority, since many other arguments demonstrate that the composition is fabricated and spurious.

“Furthermore, many manuscript codices, including ancient ones, inscribe this spurious prologue under Jerome’s name. The Corbie codex no. 23 in our Saint-Germain Library retains, written in red ink, this title: ‘The Prologue of Saint Jerome the Priest begins.’ The very ancient biblical codex now preserved in the Colbertine Library under no. 158 reads in the same way; Jerome’s name, however, appears to have been added to it by a second hand.

In two manuscripts of Saint Andrew near Avignon it is headed in these words: ‘The Prologue of Blessed Jerome the Priest to the Seven Canonical Epistles begins.’ Several other older and more recent copies have the same form. The remaining copies, without the name of any author, read: ‘The Prologue to the Seven Canonical Epistles begins.’

“So much for the prologue and its inscription.

“Let us now proceed to the Testimony of John, on account of which this spurious prologue appears to have been written under Jerome’s name. Avoiding the tedium of an extended dispute and compressing our words, we warn the reader that verse 7 of chapter 5 of the First Epistle of Blessed John is missing in many very ancient manuscript exemplars, while in several of the same age it has been supplied in the margins of the books. In more recent copies it is always present, though not always in the same order, because in them verse 8—namely, what is read as verse 8 in the Latin Vulgate—very often precedes verse 7, according to the consecutive arrangement of the sacred text:

‘For there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.’

In the same form, many older manuscript codices supply the testimony of the incomprehensible Trinity, though we have said that it was omitted by the first hand of the scribes. The situation is therefore the same in all manuscript codices, both old and recent. But if we remember that such omissions easily arise through a slip and an unintended accident among ancient copyists, the great disagreement among so many old codices will trouble no one. Nothing is easier than omitting words that are repeated immediately afterward in the same form.

Nor will you find any class of books in which similar faults of omission have not become established. Jerome teaches in book VI of his *Commentary on Jeremiah*, on chapter 30, that many things were omitted in the Septuagint translators because they were said a second time. The passage is noteworthy and fully settles our case; it will therefore be useful to present it in full together with its sacred context.

In Jeremiah, chapter 30, verses 14 and 15, we read as follows:

‘All your lovers have forgotten you and will not seek you, for I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with a cruel chastisement; because of the multitude of your iniquity your sins have become hard. Why do you cry out over your brokenness? Your pain is incurable; because of the multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins I have done these things to you.’

Explaining this passage in his *Commentaries*, Jerome appropriately observed, among many other points:

‘What follows—“Why do you cry out over your brokenness? Your pain is incurable because of the multitude of your iniquity”—is not found in the Septuagint, evidently because “because of the multitude of your iniquity and your grievous sins” is said a second time; and those who were writing from the beginning thought that it had been added.’

Thus four clauses were omitted in the Greek copies of the Septuagint translators because the same words had been said a second time and repeated in the prophet Jeremiah.

But we have found an even more convenient passage, or a more effective example, for proving our omission in the book of Joshua, chapter 21, verse 36, according to the Vulgate’s division and numbering of the verses. For the threefold repetition of the words ‘four cities with their suburbs,’ which are read in verses 35, 36, and 37, gave scribes an opportunity for error; deceived by the similarity, or by the same closing phrase, they omitted the middle verse, verse 36. Such similarity confuses the eyes not only of careless copyists but sometimes even of diligent ones when they are transcribing books.

For this reason, many older Hebrew manuscript codices existed in which the words of verse 36 were entirely absent, just as they are absent from the more reliable Latin copies of Jerome’s version. We wish this passage of Joshua to be consulted in column 275 and following of our edition.

If this frequently happened among Hebrew and Greek copyists of books, why should a prudent reader deny that similar omissions occurred among the Latins? A slip was entirely likely in the First Epistle of Blessed John, chapter 5, verses 7 and 8, because of the same words, which are said twice: ‘there are three who bear witness,’ and again, ‘and these three are one.’

For those who were writing Greek copies of the New Testament from the beginning, after they had written on the parchment *hoti treis eisin hoi martyrountes* (ὅτι τρεῖς εἴσιν οἱ μαρτυροῦντες), that is, ‘because there are three who bear witness,’ could easily, when turning back to the exemplar before their eyes, join the earlier words to the later ones, leaving out everything in between. Thus, through the error of scribes, the two verses coalesced into one in very many books.

And when they ought to have followed with the words, ‘in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one,’ they placed, immediately after the words *hoti treis eisin*, ‘because there are three,’ the words belonging to the other verse:

*en tē gē: to Pneuma, kai to hydōr, kai to haima; kai hoi treis eis to hen eisin* (ἐν τῇ γῇ· τὸ Πνεῦμα, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ τὸ αἷμα· καὶ οἱ τρεῖς εἰς τὸ ἕν εἰσιν),

that is, ‘on earth: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood; and these three are one.’

The Latins who translated John’s Epistle from such imperfect copies omitted the complete verse in which the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit are said to be one. Nor does the defect of a mutilated exemplar impede Jerome’s emendation, even if we grant that his own edition did not contain verse 7 of chapter 5 of Saint John’s First Epistle—just as it does not matter that in the genuine edition of the holy Doctor, the book of Joshua mentioned above lacked the same passage, which was not found in the copies of Hillel.

On the contrary, the deficiency of the translation proves the fidelity of the translator when it resembles the original exemplar. Nor does a faithful interpreter alter any testimony concerning the Hebrew or Greek truth. Therefore, whether you say that Jerome omitted the verse or that it was not omitted in John’s Epistle, you will gain nothing from the matter except the carelessness or error of ancient writers, who in many copies forced two verses into one.

“If that were not the case, why did the holy martyr Cyprian write in book *On the Unity of the Church*: ‘Of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit it is written: And these three are one’?
