In the printed edition there follows the Third Book of Ezra. But in the Gothic exemplar, since it follows the translation of Saint Jerome, who regards the Third and Fourth Books of Ezra as apocryphal in his prologue to Ezra, the aforesaid books are not present. In the printed edition they occupy pages 148 through 159. In the codex the Book of Esther follows.

In the printed edition there follows the Prologue of Blessed Jerome to the Psalter, which he corrected according to the Septuagint edition. This little preface is not found in the Gothic exemplar, but rather the one he wrote to Sophronius, beginning, “I know that certain people think …,” which is found in volume VII of the works of Blessed Jerome, before the version of the Psalms according to the Hebrew truth. The Gothic exemplar contains this Psalter; and therefore, since it is a different version from the one printed here, we did not compare it with this one. In the printed edition, the aforesaid Psalter continues through page 203.

# THE BOOK OF WISDOM

[Col. 0979]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0979D]

### Chapter I

Verse 5. “From what comes upon it”: “from what comes upon it” (*superveniente*).

Verse 8. “Cannot be hidden, nor”: “will not be able to be hidden, but not even” (*non poterit latere, sed nec*).

Verse 9. “For”: absent from the manuscript.

Ibid. “Of words”: “of a word.”

Ibid. “To God”: “to the Lord.”

Ibid. “Of iniquities”: “of iniquity.”

Verse 11. “An obscure saying”: “a hidden answer.”

Ibid. “Kills”: “will kill.”

Verse 14. “On earth”: “in the land of the living.”

Verse 15. “For righteousness is everlasting and immortal”: “For righteousness is immortal.”

Verse 16. “But the ungodly, etc.”: “For injustice is the acquisition of death; but the ungodly, etc.”

### Chapter II

[Col. 0980D]

Verse 1. “There is a time”: the manuscript adds “there is.”

Verse 2. “As though not”: “as those who were not born.”

Ibid. “Breath”: “breathing.”

Ibid. “To be moved”: “to be burned.”

Verse 3. “Extinguished”: “extinguished” (feminine).

Ibid. “Our”: absent from the manuscript.

Ibid. “Soft air”: “slippery air.”

Ibid. “And our life will pass like a trace of a cloud”: absent from the manuscript.

Ibid. “Mist”: absent from the manuscript.

Ibid. “Will be dissolved”: “will be dispersed.”

Verse 4. “And the name, etc.”: at this place an entire line was erased, and the following words were written above it in more recent Gothic letters: “And our life is like the traces of a cloud, and like a mist it will be dissolved, which has been driven away by the rays of the sun and made heavy by its heat. And the name, etc.”

Verse 5. “For the time of our shadow is a passing thing, and not”: these words too are written in more recent Gothic letters; at their beginning some older writing has been erased.

Ibid. “Returns”: “will return.”

Ibid. “In youth”: “youth.”

Verse 7. “Meadow”: “prepared.”

Verse 9. “Let none of you be excluded from our luxury”: “everywhere.” These words too are written more recently, with some older writing erased; *nostrum* (“our”) is written in place of *vestrum* (“your”).

Verse 10. “Neither let us reverence the veteran”: “let us reverence the veteran.”

Verse 11. “Is found”: “will be found.”

Verse 12. “Is contrary to the works”: “is contrary to the works.”

Verse 13. “To have knowledge of God”: “that he has knowledge of God.”

# THE FOURTEEN LETTERS OF THE APOSTLE PAUL

[Col. 1069]

## THE LETTER OF THE APOSTLE PAUL TO THE ROMANS

[Col. 1069C] Jerome, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “The Apostle Paul,” etc. [not found in the manuscript].

*Anathema* means “destruction.” *Maranatha*, however, is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because of the proximity of the two languages, it sounds partly Hebrew. It means: “Our Lord has come,” so that the sense is: destruction at the coming of the Lord for those who do not love him and do not believe that he has come or will come. The end.

This is how it stands in the manuscript immediately after the end of the preceding letter; it was written by the same scribe who wrote the rest.

## The First Epistle of Paul to the Thessalonians

[Col. 1079]

[Col. 1079C] (This Epistle is not found here in the Gothic codex, but the one that follows is found.)

## The Epistle to the Laodiceans

Paul, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ, to the brothers who are in Laodicea: grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

I give thanks to Christ through all my prayer, because you remain in him and persevere, looking toward the promise on the day of judgment. Nor has the empty talk of certain people who insinuate themselves deprived you of this, but they seek to overturn you from the truth of the Gospel which is preached by me. And now God will bring it about that those who are from me may reach the advancement of the truth of the Gospel, serving and showing kindness, and carrying out the work of salvation unto eternal life.

And now my bonds, which I suffer in Christ, are openly displayed; in them I rejoice and am glad. And this is for me unto perpetual salvation: that this very weeping, through your prayers, is unto the ministering of the Holy Spirit, whether through life or through death. For it is life for me to live in Christ, and joy to die [Col. 1079D]; and he himself, in you, will by his mercy bring it about that you have the same love and are of one mind.

Therefore, beloved, just as you heard of my presence, so retain it and act with fear of God; and it will be life for you forever. For God is the one who works in you. Do without delay whatever you do; and whatever it is, beloved, rejoice in Christ, and beware of filthy men devoted to profit.

Let your requests be openly known before God, and be steadfast in the mind of Christ. Do whatever things are sound, true, chaste, just, and lovely. Retain in your heart the things you heard and received, and there will be peace for you.

The saints greet you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. And have the Epistle to the Colossians read to you. The end.

## The Apocalypse of the Apostle John

[Column 1091]

[Column 1091B] (This argument is prefixed to the Apocalypse in the Gothic manuscript, though without an author.)

[Column 1091C] Blessed John the apostle, after the passion and ascension of our Lord and Savior, established by his own instruction a church in one of the cities of Asia called Ephesus, over which he presided until the day of his death. For there, having most happily completed the course of the present life, he died and was buried at an advanced age, as ecclesiastical history reports. While he was most earnestly preaching the faith of Christ throughout all Asia to Jews and Gentiles, before he wrote his Gospel, he was banished for that same faith which he preached by Domitian, son of Vespasian, who had succeeded his brother Titus in the empire, in the fifteenth year of his reign, to the island of Patmos; and there he wrote this Apocalypse. Thus, just as through Moses—who was the meekest of all men—the opening of the Book of Genesis took its beginning from the incorruptible beginning, so through John, more beloved than the other disciples, an incorruptible ending might be supplied in the conclusion of the New Testament. He himself says that the one who spoke both through Moses and through John is: “I am Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω), the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” For God is love, who is both beginning without beginning and end without end. Hence the Godhead (perhaps “love” should be read) is the end of the commandment. Therefore, throughout almost all the volumes of divine Scripture, nothing else is conveyed than love of God and of one’s neighbor. As love is therefore the fullness of the law, so this Apocalypse is the perfect fullness of the Law of both the Old and the New Testaments. Accordingly, he wrote, in accordance with the mystical sacraments of the sevenfold Spirit, to seven churches, whose leaders—and, through them, all the churches throughout the world—he praises for their virtues under the designation of angelic dignity, or reproves for their indulgences. The end.
